translations.an10.13:1: “Mendicants, there are these ten fetters. What ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, sensual desire, and ill will. These are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: “Mendicants, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is declared the best of all sentient beings—be they footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; with perception or without perception; or with neither perception nor non-perception. In the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is declared to be the best of them.
translations.an10.15:2: Just as the footprints of all creatures that walk can fit inside an elephant’s footprint, and the elephant’s footprint is declared the best of them because of its size; in the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is declared to be the best of them.
translations.an10.15:3: Just as the rafters of a peaked house all lean to the peak, slope to the peak, and meet at the peak, and the peak is declared the best of them; in the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is declared to be the best of them.
translations.an10.15:7: Just as all lesser kings are vassals of a wheel-turning monarch, and the wheel-turning monarch is declared the best of them; in the same way …
translations.an10.15:8: Just as the radiance of all the stars is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance, and the moon’s radiance is declared the best of them; in the same way …
translations.an10.15:9: Just as in the autumn, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun, rising into the expanse, dispels all darkness from space as it shines and glows and radiates; in the same way …
translations.an10.17:1: “Mendicants, live with a protector, not without one. Living without a protector is suffering. There are these ten qualities that create a protector. What ten? It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the code of conduct, with proper conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest fault, keeping the rules of training they’ve undertaken. Since a mendicant is ethical … this is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.17:2: Furthermore, a mendicant is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that is entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reciting them, mentally scrutinizing them, and comprehending them theoretically. Since a mendicant is very learned … this is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.17:3: Furthermore, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates. Since a mendicant has good friends … this is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:10: Furthermore, a mendicant is mindful. They have utmost mindfulness and alertness, and can remember and recall what was said and done long ago. Thinking: ‘This mendicant is mindful …’ the senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think it is worth speaking to and advising them. Being compassionately treated by the seniors, the middles, and the juniors, they can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:11: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering. Thinking: ‘This mendicant is wise …’ the senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think it is worth speaking to and advising them. Being compassionately treated … they can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:2: “Mendicants, live with a protector, not without one. Living without a protector is suffering. There are these ten qualities that create a protector. What ten? It’s when a mendicant is ethical … and keeps the rules of training they’ve undertaken. Thinking: ‘This mendicant is ethical …’ the senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think it is worth speaking to and advising them. Being compassionately treated by the seniors, the middles, and the juniors, they can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:4: Furthermore, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates. Thinking: ‘This mendicant has good friends …’ the senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think it is worth speaking to and advising them. Being compassionately treated by the seniors, the middles, and the juniors, they can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:5: Furthermore, a mendicant is easy to admonish, having qualities that make them easy to admonish. They are patient and take instruction respectfully. Thinking: ‘This mendicant is easy to admonish …’ the senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think it is worth speaking to and advising them. Being compassionately treated by the seniors, the middles, and the juniors, they can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant is skilled and tireless in the diverse duties of their spiritual companions, understanding how to do them, capable of doing and organizing them. Thinking ‘This mendicant is skilled and tireless…’ the senior mendicants think it worth speaking to and instructing them, the middle mendicants… and the junior mendicants think it worth speaking to and instructing them. For one compassionated by seniors, middles, and juniors, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant loves the teaching and is delightful to converse with, filled with great joy in the teaching and training. Thinking ‘This mendicant loves the teaching…’ the senior mendicants… the middle mendicants… the junior mendicants think it worth speaking to and instructing them. For one compassionated by seniors, middles, and juniors, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant lives with energy aroused for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off in skillful qualities. Thinking ‘This mendicant lives with energy aroused…’ the senior mendicants… the middle mendicants… the junior mendicants think it worth speaking to and instructing them. For one compassionated by seniors, middles, and juniors, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, mendicants, a mendicant is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and supplies for the sick. Thinking ‘This mendicant is content…’ the senior mendicants… the middle mendicants… the junior mendicants think it worth speaking to and instructing them. For one compassionated by seniors, middles, and juniors, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that creates a protector.
translations.an10.20:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants…
translations.an10.20:10: And how has a mendicant calmed bodily activity? It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the ending of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pain or pleasure, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. That is how a mendicant has calmed bodily activity.
translations.an10.20:11: And how is a mendicant well freed in mind? It’s when a mendicant’s mind is freed from greed, freed from hate, and freed from delusion. That is how a mendicant is well freed in mind.
translations.an10.20:2: “Mendicants, there are these ten abodes of the noble ones in which the noble ones have stayed, are staying, or will stay. What ten? It’s when a mendicant has given up five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has eliminated individual truths, has totally given up the search, has unclouded thoughts, has calmed bodily activity, is well freed in mind, and is well freed by wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how has a mendicant given up five factors? It’s when a mendicant has given up sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. That is how a mendicant has given up five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how does a mendicant possess six factors? It’s when a mendicant, seeing a sight with the eye, is neither happy nor sad, but remains equanimous, mindful and aware. Hearing a sound with the ear … Smelling an odor with the nose … Tasting a flavor with the tongue … Touching a touch with the body … Knowing a thought with the mind, they are neither happy nor sad, but remain equanimous, mindful and aware. That is how a mendicant possesses six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how has a mendicant a single guard? It’s when a mendicant possesses a mind guarded by mindfulness. That is how a mendicant has a single guard.
translations.an10.20:6: And how has a mendicant four supports? It’s when a mendicant, after reflection, uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and removes some things. That is how a mendicant has four supports.
translations.an10.20:7: And how has a mendicant eliminated individual truths? It’s when a mendicant has dispelled, eliminated, thrown out, rejected, let go of, given up, and relinquished all the various individual truths of ordinary ascetics and brahmins, such as: ‘The world is eternal’, or ‘The world is not eternal’, or ‘The world is finite’, or ‘The world is infinite’, or ‘The soul and the body are the same thing’, or ‘The soul and the body are different things’, or ‘A Realized One exists after death’, or ‘A Realized One does not exist after death’, or ‘A Realized One both exists and does not exist after death’, or ‘A Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death’. That is how a mendicant has eliminated individual truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how has a mendicant totally given up the search? It’s when a mendicant has given up the search for sensual pleasures, given up the search for continued existence, and settled the search for the spiritual life. That is how a mendicant has totally given up the search.
translations.an10.20:9: And how has a mendicant unclouded thoughts? It’s when a mendicant has given up thoughts of sensuality, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty. That is how a mendicant has unclouded thoughts.
translations.an10.24:1: At one time Venerable Mahācunda was staying in the land of the Cetis at Sahajāti. There Venerable Mahācunda addressed the mendicants: “Reverends, mendicants!” “Reverend,” those mendicants replied. Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Suppose, friends, a person who is rich claims to be rich, one who is wealthy claims to be wealthy, one with property claims to have property. And when an occasion requiring wealth arises, he is able to produce money, grain, silver, or gold. Then people would know about him: ‘This venerable one is indeed rich and claims to be rich, is wealthy and claims to be wealthy, has property and claims to have property. Why is that? Because when an occasion requiring wealth arises, this venerable one is able to produce money, grain, silver, or gold.’
translations.an10.24:2: Friends, a mendicant might claim knowledge: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching.’ But if they are overcome by greed, hate … delusion … anger … hostility … offensiveness … contempt … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire, they should be understood like this: ‘This venerable does not understand in such a way that greed is absent. That is why they are overcome by greed. This venerable does not understand in such a way that hate … delusion … anger … hostility … offensiveness … contempt … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire is absent. That is why they are overcome by wicked desire.’
translations.an10.24:3: Friends, a mendicant might claim development: ‘I am developed in body, developed in ethical conduct, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.’ But if they are overcome by greed, hate … delusion … anger … hostility … offensiveness … contempt … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire, they should be understood like this: ‘This venerable does not understand in such a way that greed is absent. That is why they are overcome by greed. This venerable does not understand in such a way that hate … delusion … anger … hostility … offensiveness … contempt … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire is absent. That is why they are overcome by wicked desire.’
translations.an10.24:5: Suppose, friends, a person who is poor claims to be rich, one who is penniless claims to be wealthy, one with no property claims to have property. And when an occasion requiring wealth arises, he is unable to produce money, grain, silver, or gold. Then people would know about him: ‘This venerable one is indeed poor yet claims to be rich, is penniless yet claims to be wealthy, has no property yet claims to have property. Why is that? Because when an occasion requiring wealth arises, this venerable one is unable to produce money, grain, silver, or gold.’
translations.an10.24:9: Friends, a mendicant might claim knowledge and development: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching; I am developed in body, developed in ethical conduct, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.’ If they are not overcome by greed, hate … delusion … anger … hostility … offensiveness … contempt … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire, they should be understood like this: ‘This venerable understands in such a way that greed is absent. That is why they are not overcome by greed. This venerable understands in such a way that hate … delusion … anger … hostility … offensiveness … contempt … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire is absent. That is why they are not overcome by wicked desire.’
translations.an10.29:1: Mendicants, as far as Kāsi and Kosala extend, and as far as the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, King Pasenadi is reckoned the foremost. But even King Pasenadi is liable to alteration and change. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with the best, they lose desire for what is worse, let alone what is low.
translations.an10.29:10: Not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are blue, with blue color, blue hue, and blue tint. They’re like a flax flower that’s blue, with blue color, blue hue, and blue tint. Or like a cloth from Vārāṇasī that’s smoothed on both sides, blue, with blue color, blue hue, and blue tint. In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are blue, with blue color, blue hue, and blue tint. Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’ This is the fifth dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: Not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are yellow, with yellow color, yellow hue, and yellow tint. They’re like a kaṇikāra flower that’s yellow, with yellow color, yellow hue, and yellow tint. Or like a cloth from Vārāṇasī that’s smoothed on both sides, yellow, with yellow color, yellow hue, and yellow tint. In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are yellow, with yellow color, yellow hue, and yellow tint. Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’ This is the sixth dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: Not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, with a red glow. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, with a red glow; or just as a cloth from Vārāṇasī, smoothed on both sides, is red, red in color, red in appearance, with a red glow; in the same way, not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, with a red glow. Thinking, ‘Mastering them, I know and see’, they are percipient in this way. This is the seventh dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:13: Not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, with a white glow. Just as the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, with a white glow; or just as a cloth from Vārāṇasī, smoothed on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, with a white glow; in the same way, not perceiving forms internally, someone sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, with a white glow. Thinking, ‘Mastering them, I know and see’, they are percipient in this way. This is the eighth dimension of mastery. These are the eight dimensions of mastery.
translations.an10.29:14: The best of these eight dimensions of mastery is when, not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, with a white glow; and thinks, ‘Mastering them, I know and see.’ There are sentient beings who are percipient in this way. But even for sentient beings who are percipient in this way, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they become dispassionate towards the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: There are these four modes of practice. What four? Painful practice with slow insight, painful practice with swift insight, pleasant practice with slow insight, and pleasant practice with swift insight. These are the four modes of practice.
translations.an10.29:16: The best of these four modes of practice is the pleasant practice with swift insight. There are sentient beings who practice in this way. But even for sentient beings who practice in this way, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they become dispassionate towards the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: There are these four perceptions. What four? One perceives the limited. One perceives the expansive. One perceives the measureless. One perceives the dimension of nothingness, thinking, ‘There is nothing.’ These are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The best of these four perceptions is when one perceives the dimension of nothingness, thinking, ‘There is nothing.’ There are sentient beings who are percipient in this way. But even for sentient beings who are percipient in this way, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they become dispassionate towards the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: As far as the moon and sun revolve and shine, lighting up the quarters, so far does the thousand-fold world system extend. In that thousand-fold world system there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sinerus the king of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Western Koyānas, a thousand Northern Kurus, a thousand Eastern Videhas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand Great Kings, a thousand realms of the Gods of the Four Great Kings, a thousand realms of the Gods of the Thirty-Three, a thousand realms of the Yāma Gods, a thousand realms of the Tusita Gods, a thousand realms of the Gods Who Delight in Creation, a thousand realms of the Gods Who Control What is Created by Others, and a thousand Brahmā realms. As far as the thousand-fold world system extends, the Great Brahmā is reckoned the best there. But even for the Great Brahmā there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they become dispassionate towards the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, mendicants, some ascetics and brahmins who declare supreme purification. The best of those who declare supreme purification is when, having completely transcended the dimension of nothingness, one enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. They teach the Dhamma for the direct knowledge and realization of that. There are sentient beings who speak in this way. But even for sentient beings who speak in this way, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they become dispassionate towards the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, mendicants, when this world contracts. As the world contracts, sentient beings are mostly reborn in the realm of streaming radiance. There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the sky, steadily glorious, and they remain for a very long time. As the world contracts, the gods of streaming radiance are reckoned the best. But even for the gods of streaming radiance there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they become dispassionate towards the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: There are these ten universal dimensions of meditation. What ten? One perceives the earth universal above, below, across, undivided and measureless. One perceives the water universal … the fire universal … the air universal … the blue universal … the yellow universal … the red universal … the white universal … the space universal … One perceives the consciousness universal above, below, across, undivided and measureless. These are the ten universal dimensions of meditation.
translations.an10.29:5: This is the best, mendicants, of these ten dimensions of universal meditation: when someone perceives the consciousness universal above, below, across, undivided, and infinite. There are sentient beings who perceive in this way. But even for sentient beings who perceive in this way, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned, they lose desire for the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:6: Mendicants, there are these eight dimensions of mastery. What eight? Perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’ This is the first dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:7: Perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’ This is the second dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:8: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’ This is the third dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:9: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’ This is the fourth dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.51:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how is a mendicant skilled in the ways of their own mind? Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornment. If they were to check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water, and saw a blemish or spot there, they would try to remove it. But if they didn’t see a blemish or spot there, they would be happy and full of joy, thinking: ‘It’s my good fortune, I am clean!’ In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities: ‘Do I usually live full of covetousness or not? Do I usually live with a mind full of ill will or not? Do I usually live overcome by dullness and drowsiness or free of them? Do I usually live restless or peaceful? Do I usually live full of doubt or having gone beyond doubt? Do I usually live irritable or loving? Do I usually live with a corrupted mind or an uncorrupted mind? Do I usually live with a stressed body or a relaxed body? Do I usually live lazy or energetic? Do I usually live unimmersed or immersed?’
translations.an10.51:4: If, while checking, a mendicant knows: ‘I usually live full of covetousness, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness, doubt, irritability, with a corrupted mind, a stressed body, lazy, and unimmersed,’ then they should apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, mindfulness, and situational awareness to give up those bad, unskillful qualities. Suppose a person’s clothes or head were on fire. To extinguish it, they would apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, mindfulness, and situational awareness. In the same way, that mendicant should apply extraordinary desire … to give up those bad, unskillful qualities.
translations.an10.54:2: And how is a mendicant skilled in the ways of their own mind? Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornment. If they were to check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water, and saw a blemish or spot there, they would try to remove it. But if they didn’t see a blemish or spot there, they would be happy and full of joy, thinking: ‘It’s my good fortune, I am clean!’ In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities: ‘Do I have internal serenity of heart? Do I not have internal serenity of heart? Do I have the higher wisdom of discernment of principles? Do I not have the higher wisdom of discernment of principles?’
translations.an10.54:5: If, while checking, a mendicant knows: ‘I don’t have internal serenity of heart, nor do I have the higher wisdom of discernment of principles,’ then they should apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, mindfulness, and situational awareness to get those skillful qualities. Suppose a person’s clothes or head were on fire. To extinguish it, they would apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, mindfulness, and situational awareness. In the same way, that mendicant should apply extraordinary desire … to get those skillful qualities. After some time they have both internal serenity of heart and the higher wisdom of discernment of principles.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, while checking, a mendicant knows: ‘I have internal serenity of heart and the higher wisdom of discernment of principles,’ then they should become established in those skillful qualities and make a further effort to end the defilements.
translations.an10.58:1: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you: ‘Reverends, in what are all things rooted? What is their source? What is their origin? Where do they meet? What is their chief? What is their ruler? What is their superior? What is their core? Where do they resolve? What is their culmination?’ If asked this, how would you answer them?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha, sir, guided by the Buddha, and take refuge in the Buddha. It would be good if the Buddha himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Buddha, the mendicants will remember it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Well then, mendicants, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an10.59:1: “So you should train like this: ‘Our minds will be familiar with the life of renunciation, and arisen bad, unskillful qualities will not occupy our minds. Our minds will be familiar with the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of ugliness, and the perception of danger. Knowing the even and uneven nature of the world, our minds will be familiar with that perception. Knowing the arising and cessation of the world, our minds will be familiar with that perception. Knowing the origin and ending of the world, our minds will be familiar with that perception. Our minds will be familiar with the perception of giving up, the perception of fading away, and the perception of cessation.’ That is how you should train.
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? It’s when a mendicant has gone to a forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and reflects like this: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, cessation, extinguishment.’ This is called the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world? It’s when a mendicant meditates giving up any attachments, mental fixations, and underlying tendencies regarding the world, not grasping them. This is called the perception of non-delight in the whole world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of dissatisfaction with all conditions? It’s when a mendicant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted by all conditions. This is called the perception of dissatisfaction with all conditions.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? It’s when a mendicant has gone to a forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of them. Just mindful, they breathe in. Just mindful, they breathe out. Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’ Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling physical processes.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling physical processes.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing mental processes.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing mental processes.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling mental processes.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling mental processes.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in gladdening the mind.’ … ‘I’ll breathe in immersing the mind in samādhi.’ … ‘I’ll breathe in freeing the mind.’ … ‘I’ll breathe in observing impermanence.’ … ‘I’ll breathe in observing fading away.’ … ‘I’ll breathe in observing cessation.’ … They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’ This is called mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If, Ānanda, you speak these ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it’s possible that upon hearing them his illness will subside right away.”
translations.an10.60:2: “Sir, Venerable Girimānanda is sick, suffering, gravely ill. Sir, please go to the mendicant Girimānanda out of compassion.” “If, Ānanda, you speak ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it’s possible that upon hearing them his illness will subside right away.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of ugliness, the perception of danger, the perception of giving up, the perception of fading away, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of dissatisfaction with all conditions, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? It’s when a mendicant has gone to a forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and reflects like this: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, choices are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus they meditate observing impermanence in these five grasping aggregates. This is called the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘The eye is non-self, forms are non-self, the ear is non-self, sounds are non-self, the nose is non-self, odors are non-self, the tongue is non-self, tastes are non-self, the body is non-self, tactile sensations are non-self, the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self.’ Thus he dwells contemplating non-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of non-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of foulness? Here, Ānanda, a monk reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the tips of the hair, enclosed by skin and full of various kinds of impurities: ‘There are in this body hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidney, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, gorge, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, oil of the joints, and urine.’ Thus he dwells contemplating foulness in this body. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of foulness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘This body has much suffering, many drawbacks. Thus, in this body various afflictions arise, such as: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, headache, ear-disease, mouth-disease, toothache, lip-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach-ache, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera, leprosy, boils, plague, tuberculosis, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scab, chickenpox, scabies, hemorrhage, diabetes, piles, pustules, fistula; illnesses originating from bile, phlegm, wind, or their combination; illnesses born of seasonal changes, born of uneven care, born of assault, born of the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.’ Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, wipes it out, and makes it non-existent. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will... He does not tolerate an arisen thought of cruelty... He does not tolerate arisen evil, unskillful qualities; he abandons them, dispels them, wipes them out, and makes them non-existent. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: “Mendicants, a first point of ignorance is not discerned such that it can be said: ‘Before this, there was no ignorance, then later it came into being.’ Thus is this said, mendicants, yet it is discerned: ‘Ignorance has a specific condition.’
translations.an10.61:2: I say, mendicants, that ignorance has a nutriment, it is not without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: ‘The five hindrances.’ I say, mendicants, that the five hindrances have a nutriment, they are not without a nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: ‘The three kinds of misconduct.’ ... ‘Lack of sense restraint.’ ... ‘Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension.’ ... ‘Improper attention.’ ... ‘Lack of faith.’ ... ‘Listening to incorrect teaching.’ ... ‘Association with bad persons.’
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, mendicants, when association with bad persons is fulfilled, it fulfills listening to incorrect teaching; when listening to incorrect teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills lack of faith; when lack of faith is fulfilled, it fulfills improper attention; when improper attention is fulfilled, it fulfills lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension; when lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills lack of sense restraint; when lack of sense restraint is fulfilled, it fulfills the three kinds of misconduct; when the three kinds of misconduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the five hindrances; when the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance. Thus is the nutriment for this ignorance, and thus is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:4: Suppose, mendicants, when it rains heavily on a mountain top, the water flowing down the slope fills the mountain clefts, chasms, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, chasms, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. The small pools, being full, fill the large pools; the large pools, being full, fill the small rivers; the small rivers, being full, fill the large rivers; the large rivers, being full, fill the great ocean. Thus is the nutriment for this great ocean, and thus is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, mendicants, when association with good persons is fulfilled, it fulfills listening to the true teaching; when listening to the true teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills faith; when faith is fulfilled, it fulfills proper attention; when proper attention is fulfilled, it fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension; when mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills sense restraint; when sense restraint is fulfilled, it fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; when the three kinds of good conduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness; when the four establishments of mindfulness are fulfilled, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; when the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. Thus is the nutriment for this true knowledge and liberation, and thus is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. After finishing some polite and friendly talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Could it be, Reverend Sāriputta, that a mendicant might attain such a state of immersion that they would not perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, air in air, the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, this world in this world, or the other world in the other world; yet they would still be perceiving?”
translations.an10.7:4: “But how, Reverend Sāriputta, could a mendicant attain such a state of immersion …?” “One time, Reverend Ānanda, I was staying right here in Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove. There I attained such a state of immersion that I did not perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, air in air, the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, this world in this world, or the other world in the other world; yet I was still perceiving.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Mendicants, someone with three qualities who has not given up three stains is cast down to hell just as if placed there. What three? They are unethical, and they haven’t given up the stain of unethical conduct. They are jealous, and they haven’t given up the stain of jealousy. They are stingy, and they haven’t given up the stain of stinginess. Someone with these three qualities who has not given up these three stains is cast down to hell just as if placed there.
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, mendicants, in whatever region a mendicant truly understands: ‘This is suffering’; truly understands: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; truly understands: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; truly understands: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. This is the second thing that a mendicant should remember for the rest of their life.
translations.an3.15:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Benares, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an3.15:2: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a king named Sacetana. Then King Sacetana addressed his chariot-maker: ‘My good chariot-maker, in six months a battle will take place. Can you make me a new pair of wheels?’ ‘I can, Your Majesty,’ the chariot-maker replied to King Sacetana. Then, six months less six nights later, the chariot-maker finished one wheel. Then King Sacetana addressed the chariot-maker: ‘My good chariot-maker, in six days the battle will take place. Is the new pair of wheels finished?’ ‘In these six months less six nights, Your Majesty, one wheel has been finished.’ ‘But can you, my good chariot-maker, finish the second wheel in these six days?’ ‘I can, Your Majesty,’ the chariot-maker replied. He finished the second wheel in six days, took the new pair of wheels, and went to King Sacetana. He said to King Sacetana: ‘Here is your new pair of wheels finished, Your Majesty.’ ‘What is the difference between the wheel finished in six months less six nights and the wheel finished in six days? I don’t see any difference between them.’ ‘There is a difference, Your Majesty. See the difference, Your Majesty.’
translations.an3.15:3: Then the chariot-maker rolled the wheel that was finished in six days. It rolled as far as the impulse allowed, then it wobbled and fell to the ground. But when he rolled the wheel finished in six months less six nights, it rolled as far as the impulse allowed, then stood still as if fixed to an axle.
translations.an3.15:5: Now, mendicants, you might think: ‘Surely the chariot-maker at that time was someone else?’ But you should not see it like that. I was the chariot-maker at that time. Back then I was skilled in the crookedness, faults, and flaws of wood. Now I am the Worthy One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, skilled in the crookedness, faults, and flaws of body, speech, and mind. Any monk or nun who has not given up the crookedness, faults, and flaws of body, speech, and mind has fallen from this teaching and training, just like the wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: Any monk or nun who has given up the crookedness, faults, and flaws of body, speech, and mind is established in this teaching and training, just like the wheel finished in six months less six nights.
translations.an3.1:3: So, mendicants, a fool is perilous, while a wise person is safe. A fool is dangerous, while a wise person is free of danger. A fool is threatened, while a wise person is free of threats. There is no peril, danger, or threat from a wise person.
translations.an3.20:1: “Mendicants, a shopkeeper who possesses three factors soon achieves greatness and abundance in wealth. What three? It’s when a shopkeeper is shrewd, capable, and inspires confidence. And how is a shopkeeper shrewd? It’s when a shopkeeper knows their product: ‘This product, bought for this much and sold for this much, will bring this much capital and this much profit.’ That is how a shopkeeper is shrewd.
translations.an3.20:2: And how is a shopkeeper capable? It’s when a shopkeeper is skilled at buying and selling products. That is how a shopkeeper is capable.
translations.an3.20:3: And how does a shopkeeper inspire confidence? It’s when wealthy householders or their sons—rich, with great wealth and property—know this about a shopkeeper: ‘This shopkeeper is shrewd and capable; they are able to support their wife and children and pay us back from time to time.’ They deposit wealth with him, saying: ‘Here, good shopkeeper, take this money, support your wife and children, and pay us back from time to time.’ That is how a shopkeeper inspires confidence. A shopkeeper who possesses these three factors soon achieves greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: In the same way, a mendicant who possesses three qualities soon achieves greatness and abundance in skillful qualities. What three? It’s when a mendicant is shrewd, capable, and inspires confidence. And how is a mendicant shrewd? It’s when a mendicant truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. That is how a mendicant is shrewd.
translations.an3.20:5: And how is a mendicant capable? It’s when a mendicant lives with energy roused for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to skillful qualities. That is how a mendicant is capable.
translations.an3.22:1: “Mendicants, these three patients are found in the world. What three? Here, there is a patient who does not recover from that illness, regardless of whether they get suitable food or not, suitable medicine or not, and a capable carer or not.
translations.an3.22:3: But here, there is a patient who recovers from that illness only if they get suitable food, not if they don’t; only if they get suitable medicine, not if they don’t; only if they get a capable carer, not if they don’t.
translations.an3.22:4: In this case, it is for the sake of the patient who recovers only if they get suitable food … that food for the sick, medicine for the sick, and a carer for the sick have been allowed. And it is for the sake of this patient that other patients should also be cared for. These are the three patients found in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: In the same way, these three people similar to patients are found in the world. What three? Here, there is a person who does not enter the sure path of rightness regarding skillful qualities, regardless of whether they get to see the Realized One or not, and regardless of whether they get to hear the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One or not.
translations.an3.22:6: Here, there is a person who enters the sure path of rightness regarding skillful qualities, regardless of whether they get to see the Realized One or not, and regardless of whether they get to hear the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One or not.
translations.an3.24:1: “Mendicants, these three people are very helpful to another person. What three? The person through whom one goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Teaching, and the Sangha. This person is very helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, the person through whom one truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. This person is very helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, the person through whom one realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and lives having realized it with their own insight due to the ending of defilements. This person is very helpful to that person. These are the three people who are very helpful to another person.
translations.an3.2:1: “A fool is characterized by their deeds, mendicants, a wise person is characterized by their deeds. Wisdom shines in behavior. A fool is known by three things. What three? Bad conduct of body, speech, and mind. A fool is known by these three things.
translations.an3.2:2: A wise person is known by three things. What three? Good conduct of body, speech, and mind. A wise person is known by these three things.
translations.an3.30:4: A person with upside-down wisdom, / stupid and incompetent. / Even if they often go / into the presence of mendicants,
translations.an3.30:5: they are unable to learn / the beginning, middle, or end of the talk, / for they have no wisdom.
translations.an3.30:6: A person with wisdom like a lap / is said to be better than that. / Even if they often go / into the presence of mendicants,
translations.an3.30:8: A person with wide wisdom / is said to be better than those. / Even if they often go / into the presence of mendicants,
translations.an3.32:4: “Here, Ānanda, a mendicant thinks: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.’ In this way, Ānanda, a mendicant might attain a state of immersion such that regarding this body with its consciousness, there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’; and regarding all external signs, there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’; and they would enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through which there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’.”
translations.an3.33:1: Then Venerable Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him: “Sāriputta, I could teach the Dhamma in brief; I could teach the Dhamma in detail; I could teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail. But those who understand are rare.” “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One! Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma in brief, in detail, and both in brief and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
translations.an3.33:2: “So, Sāriputta, you should train like this: ‘Regarding this body with its consciousness, there shall be no underlying tendencies to conceit, “I-making” and “mine-making”; and regarding all external signs, there shall be no underlying tendencies to conceit, “I-making” and “mine-making”; and we will enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through which there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, “I-making” and “mine-making”.’ That is how you should train, Sāriputta.
translations.an3.33:3: When a mendicant has no underlying tendencies to conceit, ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’ regarding this body with its consciousness; and no underlying tendencies to conceit, ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’ regarding all external signs; and enters and dwells in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through which there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’—this is called a mendicant who has cut off craving, untied the fetters, and by rightly understanding conceit has made an end of suffering. And it was in connection with this, Sāriputta, that it was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Udaya:
translations.an3.33:4: ‘The abandoning of sensual perceptions, and of unhappiness too; the dispelling of dullness, and the warding off of remorse.
translations.an3.34:1: “Mendicants, there are these three sources for the origin of deeds. What three? Greed is a source for the origin of deeds; hate is a source for the origin of deeds; delusion is a source for the origin of deeds.
translations.an3.34:10: Any deed done without delusion—born of non-delusion, sourced in non-delusion, originated by non-delusion—when delusion has vanished, that deed is given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is not liable to arise in the future.
translations.an3.34:11: Suppose there were seeds that were intact, unspoiled, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, and well-embedded. A person would burn them with fire, reduce them to ash, and sweep the ash away in a strong wind or float it away down a swift stream. Then those seeds would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and not liable to arise in the future. In the same way, any deed done without greed—born of non-greed, sourced in non-greed, originated by non-greed—when greed has vanished, that deed is given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is not liable to arise in the future.
translations.an3.34:13: Born of greed, born of hate, and born of delusion, O ignorant one; whatever deed is done by him, whether little or much, it must be experienced right here; no other site exists.
translations.an3.34:2: Any deed done in greed—born of greed, sourced in greed, originated by greed—ripens wherever his individual existence is generated. Wherever that deed ripens, there he experiences the result of that deed, either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or on some subsequent occasion.
translations.an3.34:5: Suppose there were seeds that were intact, unspoiled, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, and well-embedded in a good field, in soil that was well-prepared, and the sky were to provide a steady stream of rain. Then those seeds would come to growth, increase, and expansion. In the same way, any deed done in greed—born of greed, sourced in greed, originated by greed—ripens wherever his individual existence is generated. Wherever that deed ripens, there he experiences the result of that deed, either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or on some subsequent occasion.
translations.an3.34:6: Any deed done in hate... Any deed done in delusion—born of delusion, sourced in delusion, originated by delusion—ripens wherever his individual existence is generated. Wherever that deed ripens, there he experiences the result of that deed, either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or on some subsequent occasion. These, mendicants, are the three sources for the origin of deeds.
translations.an3.34:9: Any deed done without hate—born of non-hate, sourced in non-hate, originated by non-hate—when hate has vanished, that deed is given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is not liable to arise in the future.
translations.an3.35:3: “Well then, prince, I will ask you a question in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, prince? Suppose a householder or householder's son had a bungalow, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows closed. And in it was a couch spread with a long-fleeced woolen rug, a white woolen bedspread, a wool coverlet embroidered with flowers, a spread of antelope hide, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends. And a lamp was burning there, and four wives were attending to him in all agreeable ways. What do you think, prince? Would he sleep happily or not? Or how do you see this?” “He would sleep happily, sir. He is one of those in the world who sleep happily.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, prince? Might not feverish passions arise in that householder or householder’s son, born of lust, either physical or mental, burning with which he would sleep in misery?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.an3.35:8: The brahmin who is extinguished always sleeps happily; He does not cling to sensual pleasures, cool, without attachments.
translations.an3.39:10: Living in this way, knowing the Dhamma without attachment; The intoxications with health, youth, and life [were destroyed].
translations.an3.39:2: I had three palaces, monks: one for winter, one for summer, and one for the rainy season. In the rainy-season palace, monks, during the four months of the rains, entertained by female musicians, I did not come down to the lower palace. While in other people’s homes servants and workers are given broken rice with sour gruel, in my father’s house servants and workers were given wheat, rice, and meat.
translations.an3.39:3: Possessed of such prosperity and such refinement, it occurred to me: ‘An uninstructed worldling, though himself subject to old age, not exempt from old age, feels horrified, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is old, overlooking himself. I too am subject to old age, not exempt from old age. If I, being subject to old age, not exempt from old age, were to feel horrified, humiliated, and disgusted on seeing another who is old, that would not be proper for me.’ While I reflected thus, monks, all intoxication with youth vanished.
translations.an3.39:4: An uninstructed worldling, though himself subject to sickness, not exempt from sickness, feels horrified, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is sick, overlooking himself: ‘I too am subject to sickness, not exempt from sickness. If I, being subject to sickness, not exempt from sickness, were to feel horrified, humiliated, and disgusted on seeing another who is sick, that would not be proper for me.’ While I reflected thus, monks, all intoxication with health vanished.
translations.an3.39:5: An uninstructed worldling, though himself subject to death, not exempt from death, feels horrified, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is dead, overlooking himself: ‘I too am subject to death, not exempt from death. If I, being subject to death, not exempt from death, were to feel horrified, humiliated, and disgusted on seeing another who is dead, that would not be proper for me.’ While I reflected thus, monks, all intoxication with life vanished.
translations.an3.39:7: Intoxicated with youth, monks, a monk gives up the training and returns to the lower life. Intoxicated with health, monks, a monk... Intoxicated with life, monks, a monk gives up the training and returns to the lower life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to disease, subject to old age, and also subject to death; Being such themselves, ordinary people are disgusted [by others].
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted with beings of such nature; That would not be proper for me, living in this way.
translations.an3.40:1: “There are these three authorities, monks. What three? The authority of oneself, the authority of the world, the authority of the Dhamma. What is the authority of oneself? Here, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, nor for almsfood, nor for lodging, nor for the sake of future existence. But I am immersed in birth, aging, and death, in sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering can be discerned. If I were to seek the same sort of sensual pleasures that I abandoned when I went forth from the home life into homelessness, or even worse ones, that would not be proper for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and unperturbed, my mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Making himself the authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, he maintains himself in purity. This is called the authority of oneself.
translations.an3.40:3: And what is the authority of the Dhamma? Here, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth... for the sake of robes... But I am immersed in birth... Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering can be discerned. The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced by the wise for themselves. My fellow monks live knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline, were to live lazy and negligent, that would not be proper for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be aroused... my mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Making the Dhamma the authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, he maintains himself in purity. This is called the authority of the Dhamma. These, monks, are the three authorities.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secrecy in the world for one doing evil deeds; Your self knows, man, whether it is true or false.
translations.an3.40:5: Indeed, my friend, you despise the witness—your self; You who hide the evil existing within yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: Devas and Tathagatas see the fool walking unevenly in the world; Therefore, one governed by self, governed by the world, prudent and meditative; Governed by Dhamma, acting according to Dhamma, the sage striving for truth does not fall away.
translations.an3.48:1: “Mendicants, relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, the great sal trees grow in three ways. What three? They grow in branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow in bark and shoots; they grow in softwood. Relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, the great sal trees grow in these three ways.
translations.an3.48:2: In the same way, mendicants, relying on a faithful head of the family, the people within grow in three ways. What three? They grow in faith, they grow in ethical conduct, they grow in wisdom. Relying on a faithful head of the family, the people within grow in these three ways.
translations.an3.48:3: Just as a rocky mountain in a great forest grove; relying on it, the trees, the lords of the forest, grow.
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins—old, elderly, advanced in years, reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years old—approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After finishing the greetings and polite talk, they sat to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: 'Master Gotama, we are brahmins—old, elderly, advanced in years, reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years old. But we have done no good deeds, done no skillful deeds, done nothing to secure us from fear. Let Master Gotama advise us, let Master Gotama instruct us, for our long-lasting welfare and happiness.'
translations.an3.51:2: “Indeed, brahmins, you are old, elderly, advanced in years, reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years old. And you have done no good deeds, done no skillful deeds, done nothing to secure you from fear. This world, brahmins, is being swept away by old age, sickness, and death. When the world is being swept away by old age, sickness, and death, restraint of body, speech, and mind is the shelter, the cave, the island, the refuge, and the support for one who has passed away.
translations.an3.51:3: Life is swept away, the span is short; there are no shelters for one swept away by old age. Seeing this danger in death, one should do meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
translations.an3.52:4: So the world is burning with old age and death; one should salvage [wealth] by giving; what is given is well salvaged.
translations.an3.57:2: “Vaccha, those who say: ‘The ascetic Gotama says this: “Gifts should be given only to me... gifts given to others’ disciples are not very fruitful”’ do not repeat what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue. Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstruction for three people, is a bandit for three people. Which three? They obstruct the merit of the giver, they obstruct the gain of the recipients, and their own self is already broken and damaged. Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstruction for these three people, is a bandit for three people.
translations.an3.5:1: “Mendicants, a fool is known by three qualities. What three? They ask a question irrationally, they answer a question irrationally, and when another answers a question rationally with rounded, coherent, and relevant words and phrases, they do not rejoice. A fool is known by these three qualities.
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After finishing the greetings and polite talk, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: 'Master Gotama, we are brahmins. We perform sacrifices and get others to perform sacrifices. In that case, Master Gotama, whoever performs a sacrifice and whoever gets others to perform a sacrifice, all of them practice a path of merit extending to many people, namely, that based on sacrifice. But, Master Gotama, regarding one who goes forth from the home life into homelessness from this or that family, he tames only himself, calms only himself, extinguishes only himself. In that case, he practices a path of merit extending to only one person, namely, that based on going forth.'
translations.an3.60:10: Here, brahmin, someone does not declare [the state of mind] by means of a sign, but having heard the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, they declare: ‘Such is your mind, such is your mind, such is your thought.’ Even if they declare much, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: Here, brahmin, someone does not declare [the state of mind] by means of a sign, nor by hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, but having heard the sound of the vibration of thoughts while one is thinking and pondering, they declare: ‘Such is your mind, such is your mind, such is your thought.’ Even if they declare much, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: Here, brahmin, someone does not declare [the state of mind] by means of a sign, nor by hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, nor by hearing the sound of the vibration of thoughts while one is thinking and pondering, but by encompassing with their own mind the mind of one who has entered a concentration free from thought and examination, they understand: ‘According to how the mental formations of this good person are directed, immediately after this thought, they will think this thought.’ Even if they declare much, it is exactly so, not otherwise. This, brahmin, is called the miracle of reading minds.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, someone instructs thus: ‘Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to this, do not attend to that; abandon this, enter and dwell in that.’ This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, which miracle appeals to you as the most excellent and sublime?
translations.an3.60:14: “In that case, Master Gotama, regarding the miracle where someone wields the various kinds of psychic power... wielding bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma world—this miracle, Master Gotama, is experienced only by the one who performs it; it belongs only to the one who performs it. This miracle, Master Gotama, seems to me like the nature of a magic trick.
translations.an3.60:16: And as for the miracle where someone instructs: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that! Focus your mind like this, don’t focus it like that! Give this up, and live having achieved that!’ This miracle appears to me to be the finest and most sublime of the three.
translations.an3.60:17: It’s incredible, Master Gotama, it’s amazing! How well this was said by Master Gotama. And we consider Master Gotama to possess all three of these miracles. For Master Gotama wields the various kinds of psychic power … controlling the body as far as the Brahmā realm. And Master Gotama understands the mind of another who has entered the immersion without placing the mind and keeping it connected: ‘Given how this person’s mental intentions are directed, immediately after this mind state they will think this thought.’ And Master Gotama instructs: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that! Focus your mind like this, don’t focus it like that! Give this up, and live having achieved that!’
translations.an3.60:18: “Brahmin, your words are certainly intrusive and personal, but I will answer you. For I do wield the various kinds of psychic power … controlling the body as far as the Brahmā realm. And I do understand the mind of another who has entered the immersion without placing the mind and keeping it connected: ‘Given how this person’s mental intentions are directed, immediately after this mind state they will think this thought.’ And I do instruct: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that! Focus your mind like this, don’t focus it like that! Give this up, and live having achieved that!’”
translations.an3.60:19: “But is there even one other mendicant who possesses these three miracles, apart from Master Gotama?” “There are not just one hundred, brahmin, or two, three, four, or five hundred, but many more mendicants who possess these three miracles.” “But where are those mendicants dwelling now, Master Gotama?” “Right here, brahmin, in this Saṅgha of mendicants.”
translations.an3.60:2: “Well then, brahmin, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like. What do you think? Take the case where a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed. He says: ‘Come! This is the path, this is the practice. Practicing like this, I realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual life with my own insight, and I declare it. Come, you too practice like this! Practicing like this, you too will realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual life with your own insight, and live having achieved it.’ So the Teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly. And there are many hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands of them.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? This being so, is this a practice of merit for one person or for many people, that is, on account of going forth?” “This being so, Master Gotama, it is a practice of merit for many people, that is, on account of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:4: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava, “Of these two practices, brahmin, which appeals to you as being simpler and less troublesome, yet of greater fruit and benefit?” When he said this, Saṅgārava said to Ānanda, “Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are those I honor and praise.”
translations.an3.60:5: For a second time Venerable Ānanda said to him, “I’m not asking you who you honor and praise. I’m asking which of these two practices appeals to you as being simpler and less troublesome, yet of greater fruit and benefit?” For a second time Saṅgārava said to Ānanda, “Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are those I honor and praise.”
translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Buddha, “Even when asked a legitimate question by Ānanda for a third time, the brahmin Saṅgārava falters and doesn’t answer. Why don’t I get him off the hook?” So the Buddha said to Saṅgārava, “Brahmin, what was the conversation among the royal officials sitting together at the royal compound today?” “This was the conversation, Master Gotama: ‘Formerly, there were fewer mendicants, but more who displayed superhuman miracles of psychic power. But these days there are more mendicants, but fewer who display superhuman miracles of psychic power.’ That was the conversation.”
translations.an3.60:8: “Brahmin, there are these three miracles. What three? The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of telepathy, and the miracle of instruction. And what is the miracle of psychic power? It’s when someone wields the various kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; appearing and disappearing; going unimpeded through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; and controlling the body as far as the Brahmā realm. This is called the miracle of psychic power.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of psychic reading? Here, brahmin, someone reveals by means of a sign: ‘Thus is your mind, such is your mind, so is your thought.’ Even if he reveals much, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: ‘These four noble truths,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not reproached by wise ascetics and brahmins. Thus was it said. And in reference to what was this said? Based on the six elements, monks, there is the descent into the womb. When there is descent, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling. For one who feels, monks, I declare: ‘This is suffering,’ I declare: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ I declare: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ I declare: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, (…) death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wishes for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, grasping; with grasping as condition, continued existence; with continued existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, the cessation of continued existence; with the cessation of continued existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: But for those who fall back on past deeds as the essential truth, monks, there is no desire or effort [with the thought]: ‘This should be done’ or ‘This should not be done.’ Thus, since what should be done and what should not be done is not found as true and reliable, the term ‘ascetic’ does not legitimately apply to them, as they live without mindfulness and without guard. This, monks, is my first legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view.
translations.an3.61:8: These, monks, are the three sectarian bases which, when questioned, pressed, and cross-examined by the wise, even if followed to their conclusion, end in non-action.
translations.an3.61:9: But this Dhamma, monks, taught by me, is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not reproached by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what is the Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not reproached by wise ascetics and brahmins? ‘These six elements,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me... ‘These six bases of contact,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me... ‘These eighteen mental preoccupations,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me... ‘These four noble truths,’ monks, is the Dhamma taught by me, unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not reproached by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of these three terrors that part mother and son. What three? There comes a time, monks, when a great fire breaks out. When the great fire breaks out, villages are burnt, towns are burnt, and cities are burnt. When villages, towns, and cities are burning, there the mother does not get [to help] the son, nor does the son get [to help] the mother. This, monks, is the first terror that parts mother and son, of which the uninstructed worldling speaks.
translations.an3.62:2: Again, monks, there comes a time when a great cloud rises up. When the great cloud rises up, a great flood occurs. When the great flood occurs, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, and cities are swept away. When villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there the mother does not get [to help] the son, nor does the son get [to help] the mother. This, monks, is the second terror that parts mother and son, of which the uninstructed worldling speaks.
translations.an3.62:3: Again, monks, there comes a time when there is danger and an uprising of wild tribes, and the people mount their vehicles and flee in all directions. When there is danger and an uprising of wild tribes, and the people are mounting their vehicles and fleeing, there the mother does not get [to help] the son, nor does the son get [to help] the mother. This, monks, is the third terror that parts mother and son, of which the uninstructed worldling speaks. These, monks, are the three terrors that part mother and son, of which the uninstructed worldling speaks.
translations.an3.62:4: Mendicants, an uneducated ordinary person speaks of these three perils where a mother and child are together as perils where a mother and child are separated. What three?
