There comes a time when a great fire breaks out. When the great fire breaks out, villages, towns, and cities burn. When they are burning, there comes a time when sometimes a mother sees her child, and a child sees their mother. An uneducated ordinary person speaks of this first peril where a mother and child are together as a peril where a mother and child are separated.
translations.an3.62:5: Furthermore, there comes a time when a great cloud bursts. When the great cloud bursts, a great flood arises. When the great flood arises, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. When they are being swept away, there comes a time when sometimes a mother sees her child, and a child sees their mother. An uneducated ordinary person speaks of this second peril where a mother and child are together as a peril where a mother and child are separated.
translations.an3.62:6: Furthermore, there comes a time when there is a peril of wild savages, and the country people mount their carts and flee. When there is a peril of wild savages and the country people mount their carts and flee, there comes a time when sometimes a mother sees her child, and a child sees their mother. An uneducated ordinary person speaks of this third peril where a mother and child are together as a peril where a mother and child are separated. These are the three perils where a mother and child are together that an uneducated ordinary person speaks of as perils where a mother and child are separated.
translations.an3.62:7: There are, mendicants, these three perils where a mother and child are separated. What three? The peril of old age, the peril of sickness, and the peril of death. A mother cannot ensure this regarding her aging child: ‘I am aging, let not my child age.’ Nor can a child ensure this regarding their aging mother: ‘I am aging, let not my mother age.’
translations.an3.62:8: A mother cannot ensure this regarding her sick child: ‘I am sick, let not my child be sick.’ Nor can a child ensure this regarding their sick mother: ‘I am sick, let not my mother be sick.’
translations.an3.62:9: A mother cannot ensure this regarding her dying child: ‘I am dying, let not my child die.’ Nor can a child ensure this regarding their dying mother: ‘I am dying, let not my mother die.’ These are the three perils where a mother and child are separated.
translations.an3.63:1: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans with a large Sangha of mendicants when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Veṇāgapura. The brahmin householders of Veṇāgapura heard: “It is said that the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Veṇāgapura. This good report about Master Gotama has circulated: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ He realizes with his own insight this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, and makes it known to others. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. He reveals the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. It is good to see such perfected ones.”
translations.an3.63:11: “It’s incredible, Master Gotama, it’s amazing! Who else but Master Gotama could obtain such high and luxurious beds whenever he wants, without trouble or difficulty, other than Master Gotama?
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmin householders of Veṇāgapura went up to the Buddha. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their joined palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. Seated to one side, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Veṇāgapura said to the Buddha:
translations.an3.63:5: “Brahmin, there are these three high and luxurious beds that I get whenever I want, without trouble or difficulty. What three? The divine high and luxurious bed, the high and luxurious bed of Brahmā, and the noble high and luxurious bed. These are the three high and luxurious beds that I get whenever I want, without trouble or difficulty.”
translations.an4.10:10: Beings undergo transmigration, journeying to birth and death. Having understood sensual pleasures and the yoke of being in every way;
translations.an4.10:9: Yoked with the yoke of sensuality and the yoke of being, both; yoked with the yoke of views, surrounded by ignorance.
translations.an4.18:1: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of not going off course. What four? One does not go off course due to desire, ill will, delusion, or fear. These are the four ways of not going off course.”
translations.an4.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Vajjis at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an4.1:4: “Ethics, immersion, and wisdom, and supreme freedom: these things have been understood by the illustrious Gotama.
translations.an4.24:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāketa in the Kāḷaka Monastery. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this—
translations.an4.24:2: “Mendicants, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind, that I know.
translations.an4.24:5: Mendicants, if I were to say, ‘I know it and I don’t know it,’ that would be just the same.
translations.an4.24:7: So, mendicants, having seen what is to be seen, the Realized One doesn’t conceive of what is seen, doesn’t conceive of what is unseen, doesn’t conceive of what is to be seen, and doesn’t conceive of a seer. Having heard … Having sensed … Having known what is to be known, he doesn’t conceive of what is known, doesn’t conceive of what is unknown, doesn’t conceive of what is to be known, and doesn’t conceive of a knower. So, mendicants, the Realized One is the Such One regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and known. And I say that there is no Such One who is better or finer than that Such One.
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed, / or clung to as truth by others, / the Such One is not caught in the midst of those who are self-limited, / nor would he imagine it as true or false.
translations.an4.28:1: Mendicants, these four noble traditions are primal, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated; they are not being adulterated, and they will not be adulterated; they are not despised by sensible ascetics and brahmins. What four? Take a mendicant who is content with any kind of robe, and praises such contentment. They don’t try to get robes in an improper, unacceptable way. If they don’t get a robe, they’re not upset. If they do get one, they use it without being tied to it, infatuated with it, or blindly attached to it, seeing the drawback and understanding the escape. And they don’t praise themselves or put down others because of their contentment with any kind of robe. A mendicant who is skillful, tireless, aware, and mindful in this is said to stand in the ancient, primal noble tradition.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, a mendicant enjoys meditation and loves to meditate, and enjoys giving up and loves to give up. And they don’t praise themselves or put down others because of this. A mendicant who is skillful, tireless, aware, and mindful in this is said to stand in the ancient, primal noble tradition. These are the four noble traditions …
translations.an4.28:5: When a mendicant has these four noble traditions, if they live in the east, they conquer discontent; discontent doesn’t conquer them. If they live in the west … north … south, they conquer discontent; discontent doesn’t conquer them. Why is that? Because a sage conquers both discontent and delight.
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent doesn’t conquer the sage, / the sage conquers discontent. / The sage conquers discontent, / for the sage is a conqueror of discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: Mendicants, there are these four wheels. When gods and humans possess them, the four-wheeled chariot rolls on, and they soon achieve greatness and abundance of wealth. What four? Living in a suitable region, relying on good people, proper self-determination, and past merit. These are the four wheels, possessing which gods and humans keep the four-wheeled chariot rolling, and soon achieve greatness and abundance of wealth.
translations.an4.32:1: Mendicants, there are these four ways of being inclusive. What four? Giving, kindly speech, taking care, and equality. These are the four ways of being inclusive.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kindly speech, / taking care here, / and equality in things / as fit for each case; / these ways of being inclusive in the world / are like a linchpin for a rolling chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If there were no such ways of being inclusive, / neither mother nor father / would be respected and honored / by their children.
translations.an4.33:1: Mendicants, towards evening the lion, king of beasts, comes out from his lair, yawns, looks all around the four directions, and roars his lion’s roar three times. Then he sets out on the hunt. Hearing the roar of the lion, king of beasts, most animals are filled with fear, awe, and terror. Those who live in holes hide in holes; those who live in water hide in water; those who live in forests hide in forests; and birds take to the sky. Even those royal elephants bound by strong leather bonds in villages, towns, and capital cities burst and break those bonds, void their bowels and urine in terror, and flee here and there. So powerful is the lion, king of beasts, among the animals, so majestic and mighty.
translations.an4.33:2: In the same way, when the Realized One arises in the world, perfected and fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed, he teaches the Dhamma: ‘Such is personality, such is the origin of personality, such is the cessation of personality, such is the practice that leads to the cessation of personality.’ Hearing the Realized One’s teaching, most of the gods—even those who are long-lived, beautiful, and happy, lasting long in their high palaces—are filled with fear, awe, and terror. ‘Oh no! It seems we are impermanent, though we thought we were permanent! It seems we are unstable, though we thought we were stable! It seems we are not eternal, though we thought we were eternal! It seems that we are impermanent, unstable, not eternal, and included within personality.’ So powerful is the Realized One in the world with its gods, so majestic and mighty.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, with direct knowledge, / rolls the Wheel of Dhamma— / the Teacher without peer / in the world with its gods—
translations.an4.33:4: he teaches personality and its cessation, / the origin of personality, / and the noble eightfold path / that leads to the stilling of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “Mendicants, there are these four supreme kinds of confidence. What four? Whatever beings there are—footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; with form or formless; percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One is declared the foremost among them. Those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost. And for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:2: Whatever conditioned phenomena there are, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost among them. Those who have confidence in the Noble Eightfold Path have confidence in the foremost. And for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:3: Whatever phenomena there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost among them, that is, the crushing of pride, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those who have confidence in the Dhamma of dispassion have confidence in the foremost. And for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:4: Whatever communities or groups there are, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the foremost. And for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost. These, mendicants, are the four supreme kinds of confidence.
translations.an4.34:5: For those with confidence in the foremost, knowing the foremost Dhamma; with confidence in the foremost Buddha, the unsurpassed recipient of offerings;
translations.an4.34:6: with confidence in the foremost Dhamma, the happiness of the stilling of passion; with confidence in the foremost Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit;
translations.an4.34:7: giving gifts to the foremost, foremost merit increases; foremost lifespan, beauty, fame, reputation, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.35:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “Master Gotama, we describe a great man of great wisdom as possessing four qualities. What four? Here, Master Gotama, he is learned in various fields of learning. He understands the meaning of whatever is said: ‘This is the meaning of that statement; this is the meaning of that statement.’ He is mindful, able to remember and recall what was done and said long ago. He is skilled and diligent in the duties to be done by householders; he possesses sound judgment about them in order to carry them out and arrange them. We describe a great man of great wisdom as possessing these four qualities. If I am to be approved, let Master Gotama approve me; if I am to be criticized, let Master Gotama criticize me.”
translations.an4.35:6: He who knew the release from the snare of death for all beings; who declared the rightful Dhamma for the welfare of gods and humans; seeing and hearing whom, many people gain confidence.
translations.an4.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabya. The brahmin Doṇa was also traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabya. The brahmin Doṇa saw the wheels on the soles of the Blessed One’s feet, with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in every detail. Seeing this, it occurred to him: “It is wonderful! It is amazing! These surely cannot be the footprints of a human being.” Then the Blessed One left the road and sat down at the foot of a tree, crossing his legs, holding his body erect, and setting up mindfulness before him. Then the brahmin Doṇa, following the Blessed One’s footprints, saw him sitting at the foot of the tree—graceful, inspiring confidence, with peaceful faculties and peaceful mind, having attained the highest taming and serenity, like a tamed and guarded elephant with controlled faculties. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One and said to him:
translations.an4.36:2: “Will the master be a god?” “No, brahmin, I will not be a god.” “Will the master be a gandhabba?” “No, brahmin, I will not be a gandhabba.” “Will the master be a yakkha?” “No, brahmin, I will not be a yakkha.” “Will the master be a human being?” “No, brahmin, I will not be a human being.”
translations.an4.36:4: “Brahmin, those taints by the non-abandoning of which I might be a god have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. Those taints by the non-abandoning of which I might be a gandhabba … a yakkha … a human being have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. Just as a blue, red, or white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises above the water and stands unsoiled by the water, even so, brahmin, though born in the world and grown in the world, I have overcome the world and dwell unsoiled by the world. Remember me, brahmin, as a Buddha.
translations.an4.37:1: “Mendicants, a monk possessing four qualities is incapable of declining and is right in the presence of Nibbāna. What four? Here, a monk is accomplished in virtue, guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how is a monk accomplished in virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good behavior and lawful resort, seeing fear in the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. It is in this way that a monk is accomplished in virtue.
translations.an4.37:3: And how does a mendicant guard the sense doors? Here, having seen a sight with the eye, a mendicant does not grasp at the signs or details. Since, if the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of desire and aversion would overwhelm them, they practice for its restraint, they protect the faculty of sight, they achieve restraint over the faculty of sight. Having heard a sound with the ear … Having smelled an odor with the nose … Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … Having touched a touch with the body … Having known a thought with the mind, they do not grasp at the signs or details. Since, if the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of desire and aversion would overwhelm them, they practice for its restraint, they protect the faculty of mind, they achieve restraint over the faculty of mind. That is how a mendicant guards the sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how is a mendicant moderate in eating? Here, a mendicant eats food after reflecting properly: ‘Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for fattening, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the spiritual life. In this way, I will end old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and I will have a blameless life and live in comfort.’ That is how a mendicant is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how is a mendicant dedicated to wakefulness? Here, a mendicant purifies their mind from obstructive qualities by walking back and forth and sitting during the day. In the first watch of the night, they purify their mind by walking and sitting. In the middle watch of the night, they lie down on their right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot on top of the other, mindful and aware, focusing on the time of rising. In the last watch of the night, they rise and purify their mind by walking and sitting. That is how a mendicant is dedicated to wakefulness. A mendicant who possesses these four qualities is incapable of declining and is close to Nibbāna.
translations.an4.37:6: A mendicant established in ethics, restrained in the sense faculties, moderate in eating, and dedicated to wakefulness;
translations.an4.37:7: living like this, ardent, tireless day and night, developing skillful qualities to attain the sanctuary from the yoke.
translations.an4.38:1: “Mendicants, a mendicant who has dispelled personal truths is called ‘one who has totally given up searching, whose bodily formation has been tranquilized, and who is withdrawn’. And how has a mendicant dispelled personal truths? Here, whatever the various personal truths of ordinary ascetics and brahmins—such as ‘the world is eternal’, ‘the world is not eternal’, ‘the world is finite’, ‘the world is infinite’, ‘the soul and the body are the same’, ‘the soul and the body are different’, ‘a Realized One exists after death’, ‘a Realized One does not exist after death’, ‘a Realized One both exists and does not exist after death’, ‘a Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all these have been dispelled, eliminated, thrown out, vomited up, released, abandoned, and relinquished. That is how a mendicant has dispelled personal truths.
translations.an4.38:4: And how is a mendicant withdrawn? Here, a mendicant has abandoned the conceit ‘I am’, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it is unable to arise in the future. That is how a mendicant is withdrawn. A mendicant who has dispelled personal truths is called ‘one who has totally given up searching, whose bodily formation has been tranquilized, and who is withdrawn’.
translations.an4.38:5: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for continued existence, and the search for a holy life; the grasping at views as truth, and the accumulation of standpoints regarding views:
translations.an4.38:6: for one who is detached from all passion, who is liberated by the destruction of craving, searches have been relinquished, and standpoints regarding views have been eradicated.
translations.an4.52:1: “Mendicants, there are these four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, foods of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. What four? Here, a noble disciple possesses experiential confidence in the Buddha: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ This is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, food of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, a noble disciple possesses experiential confidence in the Teaching: ‘The Teaching is well explained by the Buddha, visible in this very life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.’ This is the second stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, food of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, a noble disciple possesses experiential confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals. This Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the supreme field of merit for the world.’ This is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, food of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, a noble disciple possesses the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones, which is unbroken, impeccable, spotless, unblemished, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, and leading to immersion. This is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, food of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. These are the four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, foods of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:5: Whoever has faith in the Realized One, unwavering and well established; and whose ethical conduct is good, loved by the noble ones and praised;
translations.an4.52:6: Whoever has confidence in the Saṅgha, and whose view is straightened out; they say that person is not poor, their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: At one time the Buddha was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. A number of householders and housewives were also traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Buddha left the road and sat at the foot of a certain tree. The householders and housewives saw the Buddha seated at the foot of the tree. Seeing him, they approached the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to those householders and housewives as they sat to one side:
translations.an4.53:10: If both are faithful and generous, self-controlled, living by the Dhamma, they come together as husband and wife, speaking lovingly to one another.
translations.an4.53:11: Many benefits come to them, and they dwell at ease. Their enemies are downhearted, when both are equal in virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: “Householders, there are these four ways of living together. What four? A corpse lives with a corpse; a corpse lives with a god; a god lives with a corpse; a god lives with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a corpse live with a corpse? It’s when the husband kills living creatures, steals, commits sexual misconduct, lies, and uses alcoholic drinks that cause negligence. He is unethical, of bad character, living at home with a heart overcome by the stain of stinginess, abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. And the wife is also one who kills living creatures, steals, commits sexual misconduct, lies, and uses alcoholic drinks that cause negligence. She is unethical, of bad character, living at home with a heart overcome by the stain of stinginess, abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. That is how a corpse lives with a corpse.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is unethical, miserly, and abusive. But the wife is virtuous, generous, and free of stinginess. She is a goddess living with a corpse of a husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, generous, and free of stinginess. But the wife is unethical, miserly, and abusive. She is a corpse living with a god of a husband.
translations.an4.5:1: “Mendicants, these four people are found in the world. What four? The person who goes with the stream; the person who goes against the stream; the person who stands fast; and the brahmin who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land. And who is the person who goes with the stream? It’s someone who indulges in sensual pleasures and does bad deeds. This is called the person who goes with the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And who is the person who goes against the stream? It’s someone who doesn’t indulge in sensual pleasures or do bad deeds. They live the spiritual life in its entirety and purity, even with pain and sadness, weeping with a tearful face. This is called the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And who is the person who stands fast? It’s someone who, with the ending of the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously and will become extinguished there, not liable to return from that world. This is called the person who stands fast.
translations.an4.5:4: And who is the person who is a brahmin who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land? It’s someone who, with the ending of defilements, realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and lives having achieved it. This is called the person who is a brahmin who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land. These are the four people found in the world.
translations.an4.5:5: People who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free of greed, enjoying sensual pleasures here: they go to birth and old age again and again. Overcome by craving, they go with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore the wise one here, with established mindfulness, not engaging in sensual pleasures and bad deeds, should give up sensual pleasures, even if it’s painful. They call that person one who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: Someone who has given up the five defilements is a trainee who is complete, not liable to decline. Having mastered their mind, with faculties settled, that person is called one who stands fast.
translations.an4.62:2: “Householder, there are these four kinds of happiness that a layperson who enjoys sensual pleasures may achieve from time to time and occasion to occasion. What four? The happiness of ownership, the happiness of using wealth, the happiness of debtlessness, and the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what is the happiness of ownership? It’s when a gentleman has wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and righteously got. He thinks: ‘I have wealth acquired by energetic striving … righteous and righteously got.’ He achieves happiness and joy. This is called the happiness of ownership.
translations.an4.62:5: And what is the happiness of debtlessness? It’s when a gentleman owes no debt, great or small, to anyone. He thinks: ‘I owe no debt, great or small, to anyone.’ He achieves happiness and joy. This is called the happiness of debtlessness.
translations.an4.62:6: And what is the happiness of blamelessness? It’s when a noble disciple has blameless bodily, verbal, and mental conduct. He thinks: ‘I have blameless bodily, verbal, and mental conduct.’ He achieves happiness and joy. This is called the happiness of blamelessness. These are the four kinds of happiness that a layperson who enjoys sensual pleasures may achieve from time to time and occasion to occasion.
translations.an4.62:7: Knowing the happiness of debtlessness, and the happiness of ownership next, a mortal enjoys the happiness of using wealth. Then, with wisdom, they see clearly.
translations.an5.23:1: “Mendicants, there are these five corruptions of gold, corrupted by which gold is not pliable, not workable, not radiant, but brittle and not capable of being properly worked. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver. These are the five corruptions of gold... But when gold is freed from these five corruptions, it becomes pliable, workable, radiant, not brittle, and capable of being properly worked. Whatever kind of ornament one wishes to make—whether a ring, earrings, a necklace, or a gold chain—it serves that purpose.
translations.an5.23:2: In the same way, mendicants, there are these five corruptions of the mind, corrupted by which the mind is not pliable, not workable, not radiant, but brittle and not rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. These are the five corruptions of the mind... But when the mind is freed from these five corruptions, it becomes pliable, workable, radiant, not brittle, and rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. Whatever state realizable by direct knowledge one inclines the mind toward realizing by direct knowledge, one becomes capable of realizing it, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.23:3: If one wishes: ‘May I wield the various kinds of psychic power—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; may I fly through the air cross-legged like a bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; may I exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma world’—one becomes capable of realizing it, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.23:4: If one wishes: ‘May I hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those far and near, with the divine ear element that is purified and surpasses the human’—one becomes capable of realizing it, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.23:5: If one wishes: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate; a mind without hate as a mind without hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as contracted; a scattered mind as scattered; an expansive mind as expansive; an unexpansive mind as unexpansive; a surpassable mind as surpassable; an unsurpassable mind as unsurpassable; a concentrated mind as concentrated; an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; a liberated mind as liberated; an unliberated mind as unliberated’—one becomes capable of realizing it, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.25:1: “Mendicants, when right view is supported by five factors, it has liberation of heart as its fruit and reward, and liberation by wisdom as its fruit and reward.
translations.an5.26:1: “Mendicants, there are these five bases of liberation, in which—for a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute—the unliberated mind is liberated, the unexhausted taints are exhausted, and the unreached supreme sanctuary from the yoke is reached.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, it is not that the Teacher or a respected spiritual companion teaches the Dhamma to a mendicant, but rather the mendicant teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as they have heard and learned it. As the mendicant teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as they have heard and learned it, they experience the meaning and the text of the Dhamma. Experiencing the meaning and the text, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss. For one who is blissful, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the second basis of liberation in which—for a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute—the unliberated mind is liberated, the unexhausted taints are exhausted, and the unreached supreme sanctuary from the yoke is reached.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, it is not that the Teacher teaches the Dhamma... nor does the mendicant teach the Dhamma in detail to others, but rather the mendicant recites the Dhamma in detail as they have heard and learned it. As the mendicant recites the Dhamma in detail as they have heard and learned it, they experience the meaning and the text of the Dhamma. Experiencing the meaning and the text, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss. For one who is blissful, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the third basis of liberation in which—for a mendicant who dwells diligent... the unreached supreme sanctuary from the yoke is reached.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, mendicants, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a mendicant, nor does a respected companion in the holy life, nor do they recite the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it, nor do they think about and explore the Dhamma in their mind as they learned and memorized it. But rather, a certain basis of concentration is well grasped, well attended to, well considered, and well penetrated by wisdom. In whatever way a basis of concentration is well grasped, well attended to, well considered, and well penetrated by wisdom, they understand the meaning and the text of that teaching. When they understand the meaning and the text, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, they feel bliss. Being blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi. This is the fifth basis of liberation, in which—for a mendicant who is diligent, keen, and resolute—the unreleased mind is released, the unexhausted defilements come to an end, and the unattained supreme sanctuary from the yoke is attained.
translations.an5.27:1: “Mendicants, develop immeasurable concentration, alert and mindful. When you develop immeasurable concentration, alert and mindful, five knowledges arise personally within you. What five? The knowledge arises personally that: ‘This concentration is blissful in the present and results in bliss in the future.’ The knowledge arises personally that: ‘This concentration is noble and spiritual.’ The knowledge arises personally that: ‘This concentration is not practiced by unworthy people.’ The knowledge arises personally that: ‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained by calming, attained through unification, not held in place by forceful suppression.’ The knowledge arises personally that: ‘I enter this mindfully and emerge from it mindfully.’
translations.an5.28:1: “Mendicants, I will teach the development of noble right concentration with five factors. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an5.28:10: Suppose there was a chariot harnessed to thoroughbreds standing at a crossroads on level ground, with a goad lying ready. A deft trainer, a driver of tamable horses, might mount it, take the reins in his left hand and the goad in his right, and drive out and back wherever he wishes. In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated noble right concentration with five factors in this way, they become capable of realizing any state that can be realized by direct knowledge to which they extend their mind, whenever there is an opening.
translations.an5.28:15: If they wish: ‘With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human … may I understand how sentient beings are reborn according to their deeds,’ they become capable of realizing it, whenever there is an opening.
translations.an5.28:7: When noble right concentration with five factors has been developed and cultivated in this way, a mendicant becomes capable of realizing any state that can be realized by direct knowledge to which they extend their mind, whenever there is an opening.
translations.an5.28:8: Suppose a water jar was placed on a stand, full of water to the brim so a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to tip it in any direction, would water pour out?” “Yes, sir.” “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated noble right concentration with five factors in this way, they become capable of realizing any state that can be realized by direct knowledge to which they extend their mind, whenever there is an opening.
translations.an5.28:9: Suppose there was a square pond on level ground, surrounded by an embankment, full of water to the brim so a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to loosen the embankment anywhere, would water pour out?” “Yes, sir.” “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated noble right concentration with five factors in this way … whenever there is an opening.
translations.an5.2:1: “Mendicants, there are these five powers of a trainee. What five? The power of faith, the power of conscience, the power of prudence, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what is the power of faith? It’s when a noble disciple has faith. They believe in the awakening of the Realized One: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ This is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what is the power of conscience? It’s when a noble disciple has a conscience. They are conscientious about bad conduct of body, speech, and mind; they are conscientious about entering into bad, unskillful qualities. This is called the power of conscience.
translations.an5.2:4: And what is the power of prudence? It’s when a noble disciple is prudent. They are prudent regarding bad conduct of body, speech, and mind; they are prudent regarding entering into bad, unskillful qualities. This is called the power of prudence.
translations.an5.2:5: And what is the power of energy? It’s when a noble disciple lives with energy roused for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to skillful qualities. This is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what is the power of wisdom? It’s when a noble disciple is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering. This is called the power of wisdom. These are the five powers of a trainee.
translations.an5.30:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans with a large Sangha of mendicants when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala. There the Buddha stayed in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. He has this good reputation: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ He realizes with his own insight this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, and makes it known to others. He teaches Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. He reveals a spiritual practice that is entirely full and pure. It is good to see such perfected ones.” Then, when the night had passed, the brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala took plenty of hard and soft food and went to the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. When they arrived, they stood outside the gate making a loud noise and clamor.
translations.an5.30:3: “Please, sir, let the Blessed One accept it now! Let the Holy One accept it! Now is the time for the Blessed One to accept. Wherever the Blessed One goes now, the brahmin householders, the people of the town and the country, will incline that way. Just as when it rains heavily, the water flows down the slope, in the same way, wherever the Blessed One goes now, the brahmin householders, the people of the town and the country, will incline that way. Why is that? Because of the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.”
translations.an5.31:1: At one time … in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. Then Princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, went up to the Buddha, bowed to him, sat down to one side, and said to him:
translations.an5.31:10: In the same way, a faithful person accomplished in virtue outshines all stingy people in the world with their generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a thundering cloud, wreathed in lightning, with a hundred peaks, pours down on the earth, filling the high and low places;
translations.an5.31:12: so too a disciple of the fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in vision, wise, surpasses the stingy person in five respects.
translations.an5.31:2: “Sir, suppose there were two disciples of the Buddha with equal faith, equal virtue, and equal wisdom. One is a giver, the other is not. When their bodies break up, after death, they would be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm. But when they are gods, would there be any difference or distinction between them?”
translations.an5.31:3: “There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha. “The one who is a giver, when born as a god, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine sovereignty. The giver surpasses the non-giver in these five respects when they are gods.”
translations.an5.31:4: “But sir, if they pass away from there and come back to this state of existence, when they are humans, would there be any difference or distinction between them?” “There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha. “The one who is a giver, when born as a human, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: human lifespan, human beauty, human happiness, human fame, and human sovereignty. The giver surpasses the non-giver in these five respects when they are humans.”
translations.an5.31:5: “But sir, if they both go forth from the home life into homelessness, when they have gone forth, would there be any difference or distinction between them?” “There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha. “The one who is a giver, when gone forth, surpasses the non-giver in five respects. They usually use robes that have been offered, rarely those that haven’t. They usually eat almsfood that has been offered, rarely that which hasn’t. They usually use lodgings that have been offered, rarely those that haven’t. They usually use medicines and supplies for the sick that have been offered, rarely those that haven’t. And their spiritual companions usually treat them with agreeable bodily, verbal, and mental actions, rarely with disagreeable ones; and they usually present them with agreeable offerings, rarely with disagreeable ones. The giver surpasses the non-giver in these five respects when they have gone forth.”
translations.an5.31:6: “But sir, if they both attain perfection, when they have attained perfection, would there be any difference or distinction between them?” “In that case, Sumanā, I say there is no difference between one liberation and the other.”
translations.an5.31:9: “Just as the stainless moon, moving through the sky, outshines all the stars in the world with its radiance;
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then General Sīha went up to the Buddha, bowed to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Sir, is it possible to point out a fruit of giving that is apparent in the present life?”
translations.an5.34:2: “It is possible, Sīha,” said the Buddha. “A giver, a donor, is dear and beloved to many people. Since a giver, a donor, is dear and beloved to many people, this is a fruit of giving apparent in the present life.
translations.an5.34:8: Giving, they are loved, and many associate with them. They acquire a reputation, and their fame grows. Being unselfish, they enter an assembly without embarrassment, confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore wise people give gifts, seeking happiness, removing the stain of stinginess. Established in the heaven of the Three-and-Thirty for a long time, they rejoice in the company of the gods.
translations.an5.36:1: “Mendicants, there are these five timely gifts. What five? One gives to a guest; one gives to a traveler; one gives to the sick; one gives during a famine; and one sets up the first produce of the new grain and new fruit for the virtuous. These are the five timely gifts.
translations.an5.36:2: The wise give at the right time, articulate and free of stinginess. Given at the right time to the noble ones, to the upright and suchlike,
translations.an5.36:3: with a clear mind, that offering is vast. Those who rejoice in that or assist with it—the offering is not depleted by that, for they too share in the merit.
translations.an5.37:1: “Mendicants, a donor who gives food gives the recipients five things. What five? They give long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and eloquence. By giving long life, they partake in long life, whether divine or human. By giving beauty, they partake in beauty, whether divine or human. By giving happiness, they partake in happiness, whether divine or human. By giving strength, they partake in strength, whether divine or human. By giving eloquence, they partake in eloquence, whether divine or human. A donor who gives food gives the recipients these five things.
translations.an5.37:2: The wise one gives life, strength, beauty, and eloquence. An intelligent person gives happiness, and they attain happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Just as a great banyan tree at a crossroads on level ground is a refuge for birds from all around, so too a faithful gentleman is a refuge for many people—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
translations.an5.38:3: A great tree with a trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit, with strong roots and bearing fruit, is a support for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: Birds flock to that delightful spot. Those needing shade go for the shade, those needing fruit eat the fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: In the same way, for a person consummate in virtue, faithful, humble, not rigid, sweet, personable, and soft,
translations.an5.38:6: those free of greed, hate, and delusion, the taintless fields of merit for the world, associate with such a person.
translations.an5.41:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him: “Householder, there are these five reasons to get rich. What five? First, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of the arms, earned by the sweat of the brow, righteous wealth lawfully obtained, a noble disciple makes themselves happy and pleased, keeping themselves properly happy. They make their mother and father happy and pleased, keeping them properly happy. They make their children, partners, bondservants, workers, and staff happy and pleased, keeping them properly happy. This is the first reason to get rich.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of the arms, earned by the sweat of the brow, righteous wealth lawfully obtained, a noble disciple makes the five spirit-offerings: to relatives, guests, ancestors, the king, and deities. This is the fourth reason to get rich.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of the arms, earned by the sweat of the brow, righteous wealth lawfully obtained, a noble disciple establishes an uplifting religious donation for those ascetics and brahmins who abstain from intoxication and negligence, who are established in patience and gentleness, who tame, calm, and extinguish themselves—a donation that is heavenly, resulting in happiness, and conducive to heaven. This is the fifth reason to get rich. These are the five reasons to get rich.
translations.an5.41:6: If that noble disciple’s wealth runs out while they are utilizing it for these five reasons, they think: ‘I have utilized my wealth for the reasons it should be utilized, yet my wealth has run out.’ So they have no regrets. If that noble disciple’s wealth increases while they are utilizing it for these five reasons, they think: ‘I have utilized my wealth for the reasons it should be utilized, and my wealth has increased.’ So they have no regrets in both cases.
translations.an5.41:7: ‘I’ve enjoyed my wealth and supported my dependents. I’ve overcome losses. I have given uplifting religious donations, and made the five spirit-offerings. I have served the virtuous, the disciplined spiritual practitioners.
translations.an5.41:8: I have achieved the goal for which a wise person dwelling at home would wish for wealth. I have done what I will not regret.’
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:
translations.an5.43:4: Householder, a noble disciple who wants long life ought not pray for long life or delight in it or yearn for it for the sake of long life. A noble disciple who wants long life should practice the way that leads to long life. For when they practice the way that leads to long life, it leads to obtaining long life, and they gain long life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: Householder, a noble disciple who wants beauty ought not pray for beauty or delight in it or yearn for it for the sake of beauty. A noble disciple who wants beauty should practice the way that leads to beauty. For when they practice the way that leads to beauty, it leads to obtaining beauty, and they gain beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: Householder, a noble disciple who wants happiness ought not pray for happiness or delight in it or yearn for it for the sake of happiness. A noble disciple who wants happiness should practice the way that leads to happiness. For when they practice the way that leads to happiness, it leads to obtaining happiness, and they gain happiness, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:7: Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should not pray for fame, or delight in it, or pray for the sake of fame. Instead, a noble disciple who desires fame should practice the path that leads to fame. For when the path leading to fame is practiced, it leads to the acquisition of fame. They become a gainer of fame, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Long life, beauty, status, honor, heaven, and high birth: for those who desire these things, successive delights are supreme.
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallikā had just passed away. Then a man went up to King Pasenadi, and whispered in his ear: “Queen Mallikā has passed away, sire.” When he said this, King Pasenadi sat there miserable and sad, with drooping shoulders and head hanging low, brooding and silent.
translations.an5.51:3: Mendicants, it is quite impossible that a mendicant who has not given up these five hindrances—which corrupt the mind and weaken wisdom—will know what is good for themselves, the good of others, or the good of both; or that they will realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, with weak and feeble wisdom. Suppose there was a mountain river flowing far, swift, and carrying all before it. And a man was to open irrigation channels on both sides. Then the stream in the middle of the river would be dispersed, spread out, and dissipated; it wouldn’t flow far, or be swift, or carry all before it. In the same way, it is quite impossible that a mendicant who has not given up these five hindrances... will know what is good... or realize any superhuman distinction...
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain mendicant went to his preceptor and said to him: “Sir, right now my body feels as if it’s drugged. I’m disoriented, and the teachings don’t spring to mind. Sloth and torpor occupy my mind. I’m leading the spiritual life dissatisfied, and I have doubts regarding the teachings.”
translations.an5.56:3: “That’s what happens, mendicant, when you don’t guard the sense doors, eat too much, don’t commit to wakefulness, don’t observe skillful qualities, and don’t commit to developing the qualities that aid awakening in the early morning and late at night. That is why your body feels drugged, you’re disoriented, the teachings don’t spring to mind, sloth and torpor occupy your mind, you lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and you have doubts regarding the teachings. So you should train like this: ‘I will guard the sense doors, eat in moderation, be committed to wakefulness, observe skillful qualities, and commit to developing the qualities that aid awakening in the early morning and late at night.’ That’s how you should train.”
translations.an5.56:4: Then that mendicant, having been advised by the Buddha with this advice, rose from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, and circled him on the right. Then that mendicant, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme end of the spiritual path in this very life—for the sake of which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness—having realized it with his own insight. He understood: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.” And that mendicant became one of the perfected.
translations.an5.57:10: “I am not the only one who must be parted and separated from all that is dear and agreeable. For all sentient beings, as far as there is coming and going, passing away and being reborn, must be parted and separated from all that is dear and agreeable.” As they often reflect on this, the path is born in them. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. By doing so, the fetters are entirely given up and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:11: “I am not the only one who is the owner of my deeds, the heir to my deeds, born of my deeds, related to my deeds, and have my deeds as my refuge. Whatever deeds I do—good or bad—I will be the heir to that. For all sentient beings, as far as there is coming and going, passing away and being reborn, are owners of their deeds, heirs to their deeds, born of their deeds, related to their deeds, and have their deeds as their refuge. Whatever deeds they do—good or bad—they will be the heirs to that.” As they often reflect on this, the path is born in them. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. By doing so, the fetters are entirely given up and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:15:
I’ve mastered all vanities, 
seeing safety in renunciation. 
My energy was roused, 
as I saw the extinguishing.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple reflects: “I am not the only one who is liable to grow old, not being exempt from old age. For all sentient beings, as far as there is coming and going, passing away and being reborn, are liable to grow old, not being exempt from old age.” As they often reflect on this, the path is born in them. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. By doing so, the fetters are entirely given up and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:8: “I am not the only one who is liable to get sick, not being exempt from sickness. For all sentient beings, as far as there is coming and going, passing away and being reborn, are liable to get sick, not being exempt from sickness.” As they often reflect on this, the path is born in them. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. By doing so, the fetters are entirely given up and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an8.13:1: “Mendicants, a king’s fine thoroughbred possessed of eight factors is worthy of a king, fit for a king, and is reckoned as a factor of kingship. What eight? Here, a king’s fine thoroughbred is well-born on both sides, maternal and paternal. It is born in the region where other fine thoroughbreds are born. Whatever food they give it—whether wet or dry—it eats carefully without scattering it. It is disgusted to sit or lie down in its own excrement or urine. It is gentle and easy to live with, and does not startle other horses. Whatever deceit, fraud, crookedness, or craftiness it has, it reveals them as they really are to the charioteer. The charioteer tries to correct them. It is a beast of burden. It generates the thought: ‘Whether other horses pull or not, I will pull here.’ When going, it goes only by a straight path. It is strong, showing its strength until its life ends. Possessed of these eight factors, a king’s fine thoroughbred is worthy of a king, fit for a king, and is reckoned as a factor of kingship.
translations.an8.14:1: “Mendicants, I will teach you eight refuse horses and eight faults of horses, and eight refuse men and eight faults of men. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an8.14:2: “And what are the eight refuse horses and eight faults of horses? Here, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it backs up and makes the chariot move backwards. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the first fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it jumps back, hits the side-bar, and breaks the triple-bar. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the second fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it throws its thigh against the chariot pole and crushes the pole. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the third fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it takes the wrong path and makes the chariot go off track. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the fourth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it rears up and paws the air with its front hooves. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the fifth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, disregarding the charioteer and the goad-stick, it bites the bit, breaks the harness, and goes wherever it wants. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the sixth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it neither goes forward nor back, but stands right there like a post. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the seventh fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, when a refuse horse is told to ‘Go on’ and is struck and urged by the charioteer, it pulls its front legs together and its back legs together and sits down right there on all fours. Such a refuse horse is found here. This is the eighth fault of a horse. These are the eight refuse horses and eight faults of horses.
translations.an8.19:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Verañjā, at the foot of Naleru’s Neem Tree. Then Pahārāda, lord of the Asuras, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. The Buddha said to him:
translations.an8.22:1: At one time the Buddha was staying among the Vajjis at Hatthigāma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants, you should remember the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma as being possessed of eight amazing and incredible qualities.” The Buddha said this. Having said this, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: “But sir, if I should pass away before the Buddha, it would not be surprising if the Buddha were to declare of me: ‘There is no fetter bound by which the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma would return to this world.’ This is the eighth amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These, sir, are the eight amazing and incredible qualities found in me. But I do not know which eight amazing and incredible qualities the Buddha attributed to me.”
translations.an8.22:12: Then that mendicant, having taken almsfood in the house of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and left. Then, after the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat to one side. Seated to one side, that mendicant reported to the Buddha the entire conversation he had with the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the home of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma. Having approached, he sat on the appointed seat. Then Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma approached that monk, bowed to him, and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the monk said to Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma: “Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight amazing and incredible qualities. What are these eight amazing and incredible qualities with which you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed?”
translations.an8.22:3: “Sir, I do not know with which eight amazing and incredible qualities I have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed. However, sir, listen and pay close attention to the eight amazing and incredible qualities that are found in me; I will speak.” “Yes, householder,” that monk replied to Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma. Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma said: “Sir, when I was first wandering in the Nāga Park and saw the Blessed One from afar, as soon as I saw the Blessed One, my mind became confident and my intoxication with alcohol vanished. This is the first amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:4: With a confident mind, I paid homage to the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me a gradual instruction—that is, talk on giving, talk on moral conduct, talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he then explained the teaching unique to the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth with dark spots removed would properly absorb dye, even so, while sitting right there, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose in me: ‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.’ Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma, having crossed beyond doubt, gotten rid of indecision, and gained self-assurance and independence of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction, right there I went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, and I undertook the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth. This is the second amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:5: I had four young wives. I went to them and said: ‘Sisters, I have undertaken the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth. Whoever wishes may enjoy wealth here and do meritorious deeds, or go back to her own relatives' families. Or if there is a desire for another man, to whom should I give you?’ When this was said, the eldest wife said to me: ‘My lord, give me to such and such a man.’ So, sir, I summoned that man, took my wife with my left hand and a ceremonial vase with my right, and gave her to that man by pouring water. Yet, sir, while giving away a young wife, I do not recall any alteration in my mind. This is the third amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:6: There is wealth in my family. And it is shared without reservation with virtuous people of good character. This is the fourth amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:7: When I attend on a monk, I do so respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. This is the fifth amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:8: It is not unusual, sir, that when the Sangha is invited, deities approach me and announce: ‘Householder, this monk is liberated both ways; this one is liberated by wisdom; this one is a body-witness; this one is attained to view; this one is liberated by faith; this one is a Dhamma-follower; this one is a faith-follower; this one is virtuous and of good character; this one is immoral and of bad character.’ But while serving the Sangha, I do not recall giving rise to such a thought: ‘I will give a little to this one, or a lot to that one.’ Rather, sir, I give with an impartial mind. This is the sixth amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:9: It is not unusual, sir, that deities approach me and announce: ‘Householder, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One.’ When this is said, sir, I say to those deities: ‘Whether you deities say so or not, the Dhamma is indeed well proclaimed by the Blessed One.’ But I do not recall any lifting of the mind due to that, thinking: ‘Deities approach me,’ or ‘I converse with deities.’ This is the seventh amazing and incredible quality found in me.
translations.an8.23:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with seven amazing and incredible qualities. With which seven? Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is virtuous; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is conscientious; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is prudent; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise. You should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with these seven amazing and incredible qualities.” The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the home of Hatthaka of Āḷavī. Having approached, he sat on the appointed seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached that monk, bowed to him, and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the monk said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī:
translations.an8.23:3: “Reverend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be possessed of seven incredible and amazing qualities. Which seven? ‘Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful; virtuous … conscientious … afraid of wrongdoing … learned … generous … wise, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī.’ You have been declared by the Blessed One to be possessed of these seven incredible and amazing qualities.” “I hope, sir, there was no white-clad layman present?” “No, reverend, there was no white-clad layman present.” “It is good, sir, that there was no white-clad layman present.”
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having received almsfood at Hatthaka of Āḷavī’s residence, rose from his seat and left. Then, after the meal, on his return from almsround, that monk went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī, at the Aggāḷava Shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī as he sat to one side: “Hatthaka, your following is large. How do you gather this large following?” “Sir, I gather this large following by means of the four bases of sympathy taught by the Blessed One. When I know, sir: ‘This one should be gathered by giving,’ I gather them by giving. When I know: ‘This one should be gathered by kindly speech,’ I gather them by kindly speech. When I know: ‘This one should be gathered by beneficial conduct,’ I gather them by beneficial conduct. When I know: ‘This one should be gathered by impartiality,’ I gather them by impartiality. Moreover, sir, there is wealth in my family. They do not think a poor person is worth listening to in the same way.” “Good, good, Hatthaka. This is the expedient, Hatthaka, for gathering a large following. For whoever, Hatthaka, in the past gathered a large following, they all gathered a large following by these same four bases of sympathy. Whoever, Hatthaka, in the future will gather a large following, they will all gather a large following by these same four bases of sympathy. And whoever, Hatthaka, at present gathers a large following, they all gather a large following by these same four bases of sympathy.”
translations.an8.26:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: “In what way, sir, is one a lay follower?” “When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; in that way, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:2: “But in what way, sir, is a lay follower virtuous?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from killing living creatures … abstains from strong drink, wine, and intoxicants that cause negligence; in that way, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
translations.an8.26:3: “But in what way, sir, is a lay follower practicing for their own benefit, not for the benefit of others?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower is accomplished in faith themselves, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of faith … understands the meaning and the teaching themselves and practices in accordance with the teaching, but does not encourage others in the practice in accordance with the teaching. In that way, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for their own benefit, not for the benefit of others.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, sir, a monk with taints destroyed has developed and well developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. Since a monk with taints destroyed has developed and well developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, this is a power of a monk with taints destroyed, relying on which a monk with taints destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, sir, a monk with taints destroyed has developed and well developed the four bases of psychic power … the five faculties … the seven awakening factors … the noble eightfold path. Since a monk with taints destroyed has developed and well developed the noble eightfold path, this is a power of a monk with taints destroyed, relying on which a monk with taints destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: “Monks, there are these eight causes and conditions that lead to acquiring the wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired. Which eight? Here, monks, a monk lives relying on the Teacher or on a certain fellow monk in the position of a teacher, towards whom he has set up a keen sense of conscience and prudence, as well as affection and respect. This is the first cause and condition that leads to acquiring the wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:11: ‘Having heard that teaching, this venerable one achieves it through two kinds of withdrawal—bodily withdrawal and mental withdrawal. Surely this venerable one knows and sees.’ This quality also leads to being dear, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, to unity.
translations.an8.2:15: ‘When in the midst of the Saṅgha, this venerable one does not engage in various kinds of talk, in pointless talk. He either speaks on the Dhamma himself, invites another to do so, or does not neglect noble silence. Surely this venerable one knows and sees.’ This quality also leads to being dear, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, to unity.
translations.an8.2:2: While living relying on the Teacher or a respected spiritual companion in whom they have established a strong sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, love, and respect, they approach them from time to time and ask: ‘Sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerables reveal what is unrevealed, clarify what is unclear, and dispel doubt regarding various doubtful matters. This, monks, is the second cause and condition that leads to the gaining of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:4: They are ethical, living restrained by the code of conduct, with good behavior and resort, seeing fear in the slightest faults, undertaking and training in the training rules. This, monks, is the fourth cause and condition that leads to the gaining of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:5: They are very learned, remembering what they have heard, accumulating what they have heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, which describe the entirely full and pure spiritual life—such teachings are much heard by them, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated mentally, and well penetrated by view. This, monks, is the fifth cause and condition that leads to the gaining of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:6: They live with energy aroused for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not shirking the burden regarding skillful qualities. This, monks, is the sixth cause and condition that leads to the gaining of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:7: When in the Sangha, they do not engage in various kinds of aimless talk or low talk. They either speak on the Dhamma themselves, invite another to do so, or maintain noble silence. This, monks, is the seventh cause and condition that leads to the gaining of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:8: They live observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its ending; such is feeling, such its origin, such its ending; such is perception… such are choices… such is consciousness, such its origin, such its ending.’ This, monks, is the eighth cause and condition that leads to the gaining of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:9: Their spiritual companions esteem them thus: ‘This venerable one lives relying on the Teacher or a respected spiritual companion in whom they have established a strong sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, love, and respect. Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.’ This quality leads to love, respect, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.30:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Sumsumaragiri in the Bhesakala Grove, the Deer Park. Now at that time Venerable Anuruddha was staying in the land of the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park. Then as Venerable Anuruddha was in private retreat, this thought arose in his mind: “This teaching is for those with few wishes, not for those with many wishes.
