It is for the contented, not for the discontented. It is for the secluded, not for those who love company. It is for the energetic, not for the lazy. It is for the mindful, not for the unmindful. It is for those with immersion, not for those without immersion. It is for the wise, not for the witless.”
translations.an8.30:10: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, Anuruddha, and you get the four jhanas—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—at will, without trouble or difficulty, then your lodging at the root of a tree will seem to you just like the peaked house of a householder or householder's son—plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows closed—as you live contented, for the sake of delight, for the removal of agitation, for living comfortably, and for alighting upon Nibbana.
translations.an8.30:11: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, Anuruddha, and you get the four jhanas—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—at will, without trouble or difficulty, then your bed of grass and leaves will seem to you just like the couch of a householder or householder's son—spread with long-haired woolen rugs, embroidered white woolen rugs, choice rugs of antelope hide, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends—as you live contented, for the sake of delight, for the removal of agitation, for living comfortably, and for alighting upon Nibbana.
translations.an8.30:12: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, Anuruddha, and you get the four jhanas—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—at will, without trouble or difficulty, then your medicine of fermented urine will seem to you just like the various medicines of a householder or householder's son—ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses—as you live contented, for the sake of delight, for the removal of agitation, for living comfortably, and for alighting upon Nibbana. So, Anuruddha, you should stay right here in the Eastern Bamboo Park in the land of the Cetis for the coming rainy season.” “Yes, sir,” Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Buddha.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Buddha, having advised Venerable Anuruddha with this advice—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—vanished from the Eastern Bamboo Park in the Ceti lands and appeared in the Deer Park at Bhesakaḷā’s Grove in the Bhagga lands, near Sumsumāragira. The Buddha sat on the seat spread out, and addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants, I will teach you the eight thoughts of a great man. Listen … And what are the eight thoughts of a great man? This teaching is for those with few wishes, not for those with many wishes. It is for the contented, not the discontented. It is for the secluded, not for those who enjoy company. It is for the energetic, not the lazy. It is for the mindful, not the unmindful. It is for those with immersion, not those without immersion. It is for the wise, not the witless. It is for those who delight in non-proliferation and love non-proliferation, not for those who delight in proliferation and love proliferation.
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Buddha, knowing Venerable Anuruddha’s train of thought with his own mind—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—vanished from the Deer Park at Bhesakaḷā’s Grove in the Bhagga lands, near Sumsumāragira, and appeared in front of Venerable Anuruddha in the Eastern Bamboo Park in the Ceti lands. The Buddha sat on the seat spread out. Venerable Anuruddha bowed to the Buddha and sat to one side. The Buddha said to him:
translations.an8.30:22: Then Venerable Anuruddha spent the coming rainy season right there in the Eastern Bamboo Park in the Ceti lands. Then Venerable Anuruddha, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme end of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness. He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is no return to any state of existence.” And Venerable Anuruddha became one of the perfected ones. Then Venerable Anuruddha, having attained perfection, at that time recited these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: “Knowing what I was thinking, the Teacher, supreme in the world, approached me through psychic power in a mind-made body.
translations.an8.30:24: He taught in excess of what I had thought. The Buddha, who loves non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.
translations.an8.30:3: “Good, good, Anuruddha! It’s good that you think the thoughts of a great man: ‘This teaching is for those with few wishes, not for those with many wishes. It is for the contented, not the discontented. It is for the secluded, not for those who enjoy company. It is for the energetic, not the lazy. It is for the mindful, not the unmindful. It is for those with immersion, not those without immersion. It is for the wise, not the witless.’ Well then, Anuruddha, think this eighth thought of a great man: ‘This teaching is for those who delight in non-proliferation and love non-proliferation, not for those who delight in proliferation and love proliferation.’
translations.an8.30:4: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then—whenever you want—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, you will enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
translations.an8.30:5: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then—whenever you want—as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, you will enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and confidence, and unification of mind, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.
translations.an8.30:6: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then—whenever you want—with the fading away of rapture, you will enter and remain in the third absorption, where you will meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one lives in bliss.’
translations.an8.30:7: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then—whenever you want—with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the ending of former happiness and sadness, you will enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.
translations.an8.39:1: “Mendicants, there are these eight streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, foods of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. What eight? Take the case where a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. This is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, food of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, that leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:2: Furthermore, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Teaching. This is the second stream of merit … that leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone to the Sangha for refuge. This, monks, is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutrient of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. There are these five gifts, monks—great gifts, primal, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated, which are not adulterated and will not be adulterated, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. What five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, abandoning the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings. By abstaining from killing living beings, monks, the noble disciple gives freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, and freedom from ill will to limitless beings. Having given freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, and freedom from ill will to limitless beings, he partakes in limitless freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, and freedom from ill will. This, monks, is the first gift, a great gift, primal, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated, which is not adulterated and will not be adulterated, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutrient of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:7: ...abandoning the use of intoxicants causing negligence, he abstains from the use of intoxicants causing negligence. By abstaining from the use of intoxicants causing negligence, monks, the noble disciple gives freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, and freedom from ill will to limitless beings. Having given freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, and freedom from ill will to limitless beings, he partakes in limitless freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, and freedom from ill will. This, monks, is the fifth gift, a great gift, primal, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated, which is not adulterated and will not be adulterated, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is the eighth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutrient of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.40:1: “Killing living beings, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of killing living beings is that it leads to a short life for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of taking what is not given is that it leads to loss of wealth for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of sexual misconduct is that it leads to rivalry and hatred for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of false speech is that it leads to being falsely accused for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of divisive speech is that it leads to being divided from friends for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of harsh speech is that it leads to hearing unpleasing sounds for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The lightest result of idle chatter is that it leads to one's words not being taken seriously for one who is born as a human.
translations.an8.6:2: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain arise for an uninstructed worldling, monks. Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain also arise for an instructed noble disciple, monks. So what is the difference here, what is the distinction, what is the disparity between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed worldling?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, Bhante, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, Bhante, if the meaning of this statement would occur to the Blessed One. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”
translations.an8.6:4: Gain occupies his mind, loss occupies his mind, fame occupies his mind, disrepute occupies his mind, blame occupies his mind, praise occupies his mind, pleasure occupies his mind, pain occupies his mind. He favors arisen gain and opposes loss; he favors arisen fame and opposes disrepute; he favors arisen praise and opposes blame; he favors arisen pleasure and opposes pain. Being thus involved in favoring and opposing, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. He is not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain: these conditions among human beings are impermanent, transient, and subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing this, the mindful and wise one reflects on their changing nature. Desirable things do not agitate his mind, nor is he repelled by the undesirable.
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta: “Mendicants, it is good for a mendicant to check their own failure from time to time. It is good for a mendicant to check the failure of others from time to time. It is good for a mendicant to check their own success from time to time. It is good for a mendicant to check the success of others from time to time. Overcome and whose mind is obsessed by eight bad qualities, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, to stay for an eon, incurable.
translations.an8.7:2: What eight? Overcome and whose mind is obsessed by gain, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, to stay for an eon, incurable. Overcome by loss … fame … disgrace … honor … dishonor … evil desires … bad friendship, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, to stay for an eon, incurable. Overcome and whose mind is obsessed by these eight bad qualities, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, to stay for an eon, incurable.
translations.an8.7:3: It is good, mendicants, for a mendicant to live having overcome, having suppressed gain that has arisen, loss that has arisen … fame … disgrace … honor … dishonor … evil desires … bad friendship that has arisen.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of gods, as easily as a strong person might extend their flexed arm or flex their extended arm, vanished from the Tāvatiṁsa realm and appeared in front of Venerable Uttara on the Saṅkheyyaka Mountain at Mahisavatthu, in the Dhavajālikā Park. Then Sakka, lord of gods, went up to Venerable Uttara, bowed to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, sir, that Venerable Uttara teaches the mendicants in this way: ‘It is good, reverends, for a mendicant to check their own failure from time to time … the failure of others … their own success … the success of others’?” “That is so, lord of gods.” “But sir, is this Venerable Uttara’s own inspiration, or is it the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One?” “Well then, lord of gods, I will give you a simile. For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.
translations.an8.8:6: Suppose, lord of gods, there was a great heap of grain not far from a village or town. And a great crowd were to take away grain from there with carrying-poles, baskets, hip-sacks, and cupped hands. If someone were to approach that great crowd and ask: ‘Where do you get this grain?’ how should that great crowd answer to answer correctly?” “Sir, they should answer: ‘We get it from that great heap of grain.’” “In the same way, lord of gods, whatever is well spoken is all the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One. It is relying on that that we and others speak.”
translations.an8.8:7: “It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing! How well this was said by Venerable Uttara: ‘Whatever is well spoken is all the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One. It is relying on that that we and others speak.’ At one time, sir Uttara, the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta:
translations.mn108:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, not long after the Buddha had become fully extinguished.
translations.mn108:13: “Brahmin, there are ten inspiring qualities declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One. We honor, respect, esteem, and worship the one in whom these qualities are found; and honoring and respecting them, we live relying on them. What ten?
translations.mn108:14: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the code of conduct, with good behavior and supporters. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.
translations.mn108:15: They are learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that is entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reciting them, mentally scrutinizing them, and comprehending them theoretically.
translations.mn108:17: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.
translations.mn108:18: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; appearing and disappearing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with their hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; and controlling the body as far as the Brahma realm.
translations.mn108:19: With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, they hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether near or far.
translations.mn108:2: Now at that time the king of Magadha, Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, was having Rājagaha fortified, as he was suspicious of King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:20: They understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with their own mind. They understand a mind with greed as ‘a mind with greed,’ and a mind without greed as ‘a mind without greed,’ a mind with hate as ‘a mind with hate,’ and a mind without hate as ‘a mind without hate,’ a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion,’ and a mind without delusion as ‘a mind without delusion,’ a contracted mind as ‘a contracted mind,’ and a scattered mind as ‘a scattered mind,’ an expansive mind as ‘an expansive mind,’ and an unexpansive mind as ‘an unexpansive mind,’ a surpassable mind as ‘a surpassable mind,’ and an unsurpassable mind as ‘an unsurpassable mind,’ a concentrated mind as ‘a concentrated mind,’ and an unconcentrated mind as ‘an unconcentrated mind,’ a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind,’ and an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.’
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, they realize for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, they dwell in it. These, brahmin, are the ten inspiring qualities declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One. In whomever these qualities are found, we now honor, respect, esteem, and worship them; and honoring and respecting them, we live in dependence on them.”
translations.mn108:25: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Where is Master Ānanda staying now?” “I am staying at the Bamboo Grove, brahmin.” “I hope, Master Ānanda, that the Bamboo Grove is pleasant, quiet, free from noise, with a lonely atmosphere, hidden from people, and suitable for retreat?” “Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is pleasant, quiet, free from noise, with a lonely atmosphere, hidden from people, and suitable for retreat, owing to guardians and protectors like yourself.” “Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is pleasant... owing to meditators like the masters who are devoted to meditation. For the masters are meditators and devoted to meditation. Once, Master Ānanda, the Master Gotama was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then I went to the Great Wood, to the Hall with the Peaked Roof, and to the Master Gotama. And there the Master Gotama spoke in many ways on the topic of meditation. The Master Gotama was a meditator and devoted to meditation. And the Master Gotama praised all meditation.”
translations.mn108:28: “It seems, Master Ānanda, that the Master Gotama criticized the meditation that deserves criticism and praised that which deserves praise. Well, now, Master Ānanda, we must go; we have many duties and much to do.” “Please, brahmin, do as you think fit.” Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, having delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Ānanda’s statement, rose from his seat and left.
translations.mn108:3: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: “It is still too early to walk for alms in Rājagaha. Why don’t I go to the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, to the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna?”
translations.mn108:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, to the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Let Master Ānanda come! Welcome to Master Ānanda! It has been a long time since Master Ānanda took the opportunity to come here. Let Master Ānanda sit down; this seat is prepared.” The Venerable Ānanda sat on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna took a low seat and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said to the Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: “Is there, Master Ānanda, even a single monk who possesses in every way and in every respect those qualities that the Master Gotama, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, possessed?” “There is not, brahmin, even a single monk who possesses in every way and in every respect those qualities that the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, possessed. For the Blessed One, brahmin, was the arising of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was the knower of the path, the finder of the path, the one skilled in the path. But his disciples now dwell following that path and become possessed of it afterwards.”
translations.mn108:7: “Is there, Master Ānanda, even a single monk appointed by the Master Gotama, saying: ‘This one will be your refuge when I am gone,’ whom you now rely on?” “There is not, brahmin, even a single monk appointed by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, saying: ‘This one will be your refuge when I am gone,’ whom we now rely on.”
translations.mn108:9: “But if you have no refuge, Master Ānanda, what is the cause for concord?” “We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; the Dhamma is our refuge.”
translations.mn117:10: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as ‘wrong intention’ and right intention as ‘right intention’: this is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong intention? The intention of sensual desire, the intention of ill will, and the intention of cruelty: this, bhikkhus, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what is right intention? I say there are two kinds of right intention: right intention that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates; and right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what is right intention that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of harmlessness: this is right intention that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates.
translations.mn117:14: And what is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The thinking, thought, intention, mental absorption, mental fixity, directing of mind, verbal formation in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path: this is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: One makes an effort to abandon wrong intention and to enter upon right intention: this is one's right effort. One is mindful to abandon wrong intention and to enter and remain in right intention: this is one's right mindfulness. Thus these three qualities circle and revolve around right intention, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: Therein, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One understands wrong speech as wrong speech and right speech as right speech: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what is right speech? I say there are two kinds of right speech: right speech that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates; and right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what is right speech that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter: this is right speech that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates.
translations.mn117:2: “Mendicants, I will teach you noble right immersion with its vital conditions and its prerequisites. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path: this is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: Therein, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One understands wrong action as wrong action and right action as right action: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what is right action? I say there are two kinds of right action: right action that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates; and right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what is right action that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates? Abstaining from killing living creatures, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct: this is right action that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates.
translations.mn117:28: Therein, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood and right livelihood as right livelihood: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what is wrong livelihood? Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain: this is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what is right livelihood? I say there are two kinds of right livelihood: right livelihood that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates; and right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what is right livelihood that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates? Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns their living by right livelihood: this is right livelihood that is accompanied by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates.
translations.mn117:34: Therein, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? In one of right view, right intention comes into being; in one of right intention, right speech comes into being; in one of right speech, right action comes into being; in one of right action, right livelihood comes into being; in one of right livelihood, right effort comes into being; in one of right effort, right mindfulness comes into being; in one of right mindfulness, right immersion comes into being; in one of right immersion, right knowledge comes into being; in one of right knowledge, right freedom comes into being. Thus, mendicants, the trainee possesses eight factors, the perfected one possesses ten factors. And therein, by means of right knowledge, many bad unskillful qualities are worn away and go to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:35: Therein, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? In one of right view, wrong view is worn away. And the many bad unskillful qualities that arise conditioned by wrong view are worn away in them. And conditioned by right view, many skillful qualities go to fulfillment by development. In one of right intention, wrong intention is worn away... In one of right speech, wrong speech is worn away... In one of right action, wrong action is worn away... In one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away... In one of right effort, wrong effort is worn away... In one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away... In one of right immersion, wrong immersion is worn away... In one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away... In one of right freedom, wrong freedom is worn away. And the many bad unskillful qualities that arise conditioned by wrong freedom are worn away in them. And conditioned by right freedom, many skillful qualities go to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:36: So, mendicants, there are twenty factors on the side of the skillful, and twenty on the side of the unskillful. This Great Forty exposition of the Dhamma has been set rolling and cannot be stopped by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Mara or Brahma or anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: Therein, mendicants, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One understands wrong view as wrong view and right view as right view: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, mendicants, is wrong view? 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit or result of good and bad actions; no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no beings spontaneously reborn; no ascetics and brahmins in the world who, faring rightly and practicing rightly, proclaim this world and the other world after having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge.' This, mendicants, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, mendicants, is right view? I say, mendicants, that right view is of two kinds: there is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates; and there is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, mendicants, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates? 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there are fruits and results of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings spontaneously reborn; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who, faring rightly and practicing rightly, proclaim this world and the other world after having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge.' This, mendicants, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the aggregates.
translations.mn117:8: And what, mendicants, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, the right view path factor in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path: this is called right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: One makes an effort to abandon wrong view and to enter upon right view: this is one's right effort. One mindfully abandons wrong view and mindfully enters upon and abides in right view: this is one's right mindfulness. Thus these three states run and circle around right view, that is, right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi in the Eastern Park, in the Palace of Migara's Mother, together with many very well-known elder disciples—with the Venerable Sariputta, the Venerable Mahamoggallana, the Venerable Mahakassapa, the Venerable Mahakaccayana, the Venerable Mahakotthika, the Venerable Mahakappina, the Venerable Mahacunda, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ananda, and other very well-known elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, mendicants, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, mendicants, a mendicant, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he understands: 'I breathe in long'; or breathing out long, he understands: 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he understands: 'I breathe in short'; or breathing out short, he understands: 'I breathe out short.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in tranquillizing the bodily formation'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out tranquillizing the bodily formation.'
translations.mn118:19: He trains thus: 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in experiencing happiness'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out experiencing happiness.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out experiencing the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in tranquillizing the mental formation'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out tranquillizing the mental formation.'
translations.mn118:2: Now on that occasion the elder mendicants were teaching and instructing the new mendicants. Some elder mendicants were teaching and instructing ten mendicants, some twenty, some thirty, and some forty. And the new mendicants, being taught and instructed by the elder mendicants, were achieving successive high stages of distinction.
translations.mn118:20: He trains thus: 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in gladdening the mind'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out gladdening the mind.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in concentrating the mind'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out concentrating the mind.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in liberating the mind'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out liberating the mind.'
translations.mn118:21: He trains thus: 'I will breathe in contemplating impermanence'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out contemplating impermanence.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in contemplating fading away'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out contemplating fading away.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in contemplating cessation'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out contemplating cessation.' He trains thus: 'I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; he trains thus: 'I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.'
translations.mn118:23: And how, mendicants, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: When a mendicant knows they’re breathing heavily … or breathing lightly … or when they practice breathing experiencing the whole body … or when they practice breathing calming the body’s motion—at that time the mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. For I say that the in-breaths and out-breaths are an aspect of the body. That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:25: When a mendicant practices breathing experiencing rapture … or experiencing bliss … or experiencing these emotions … or calming these emotions—at that time the mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. For I say that close attention to the in-breaths and out-breaths is an aspect of feelings. That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:26: When a mendicant practices breathing experiencing the mind … or gladdening the mind … or immersing the mind in samādhi … or freeing the mind—at that time the mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. There is no development of mindfulness of breathing for one who is unmindful and lacks awareness, I say. That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:27: When a mendicant practices breathing observing impermanence … or observing fading away … or observing cessation … or observing letting go—at that time the mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. Having seen with wisdom the giving up of desire and aversion, they watch over it closely with equanimity. That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:28: That is how mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.
translations.mn118:29: And how are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the seven awakening factors?
translations.mn118:3: Now at that time—it was the sabbath on the fifteenth day, the full moon night of the invitation ceremony—the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of mendicants. Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of mendicants, who were quite silent. He addressed them:
translations.mn118:30: Whenever a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world—at that time their mindfulness is established and lucid. At that time the mendicant has aroused the awakening factor of mindfulness; they develop it, and it is perfected in them.
translations.mn118:31: Living mindful in this way, they investigate, explore, and inquire into that principle with wisdom. At that time the mendicant has aroused the awakening factor of investigation of principles; they develop it, and it is perfected in them.
translations.mn118:33: As they are energetic, spiritual rapture arises. At that time the mendicant has aroused the awakening factor of rapture; they develop it, and it is perfected in them.
translations.mn118:34: When the mind is full of rapture, the body and mind become tranquil. At that time the mendicant has aroused the awakening factor of tranquility; they develop it, and it is perfected in them.
translations.mn118:35: When the body is tranquil and they feel bliss, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi. At that time the mendicant has aroused the awakening factor of immersion; they develop it, and it is perfected in them.
translations.mn118:36: They closely look on with equanimity at the mind thus concentrated. At that time, monks, when a monk closely looks on with equanimity at the mind thus concentrated, the awakening factor of equanimity is aroused in the monk; at that time the monk develops the awakening factor of equanimity; at that time the awakening factor of equanimity goes to perfection in the monk.
translations.mn118:4: “I am content, mendicants, with this practice. I am content at heart with this practice. So arouse even more energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized. I will wait right here at Sāvatthī for the Komudī full moon of the fourth month.”
translations.mn118:40: That is how the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how are the seven awakening factors developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom?
translations.mn118:6: And the senior mendicants were advising and instructing the new mendicants even more. Some senior mendicants advised and instructed ten mendicants, some twenty, some thirty, and some forty. And those new mendicants, being advised and instructed by the senior mendicants, achieved a high distinction, better than before.
translations.mn118:9: In this Sangha of mendicants there are mendicants who are perfected, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—there are such mendicants in this Sangha of mendicants.
translations.mn11:13: In such a teaching and training, confidence in the Teacher is not said to be rightly directed. Confidence in the teaching … fulfillment of ethics … love and affection for spiritual companions is not said to be rightly directed. Why is that? Because that is how it is in a teaching and training that is poorly explained and poorly propounded, not leading to escape, not conducive to peace, proclaimed by someone who is not a fully awakened Buddha.
translations.mn11:14: But the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, claims to propound the full understanding of all grasping. He describes the full understanding of all grasping: grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.
translations.mn11:15: In such a teaching and training, confidence in the Teacher is said to be rightly directed. Confidence in the teaching … fulfillment of ethics … love and affection for spiritual companions is said to be rightly directed. Why is that? Because that is how it is in a teaching and training that is well explained and well propounded, leading to escape, conducive to peace, proclaimed by a fully awakened Buddha.
translations.mn11:2: “Only here is there a true ascetic, here a second ascetic, here a third ascetic, and here a fourth ascetic. Other sects are empty of ascetics. Mendicants, you should roar this lion’s roar rightly.
translations.mn11:6: There are these two views: the view of continued existence and the view of annihilation. Any ascetics or brahmins who rely on the view of continued existence, adhere to it, and accept it, oppose the view of annihilation. Any ascetics or brahmins who rely on the view of annihilation, adhere to it, and accept it, oppose the view of continued existence.
translations.mn11:7: Any ascetics or brahmins who do not truly understand the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape regarding these two views are greedy, hateful, delusional, craving, grasping, and ignorant. They favor and oppose, and delight in proliferation. They are not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn11:9: Mendicants, there are these four kinds of grasping. What four? Grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.
translations.mn12:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, in the grove to the west of the city.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Realized One truly understands the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. Relying on this he claims his place as the leader of the herd, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, the Realized One has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and lives having realized it with his own insight due to the ending of defilements. Since he truly understands this … this is a power of the Realized One …
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta the Licchavi had recently left this teaching and training. He was speaking in the assembly at Vesālī: “The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of inquiry as it occurred to him. But when he teaches the Dhamma to someone, it leads them to the complete ending of suffering.”
translations.mn12:20: These are the ten powers of a Realized One that the Realized One possesses. Relying on them he claims his place as the leader of the herd, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:22: Sāriputta, the Realized One has four kinds of self-assurance. With these he claims his place as the leader of the herd, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the holy wheel. What four?
translations.mn12:23: ‘While you claim to be fully enlightened, these things are not fully understood by you.’ I do not see any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately reprove me with regard to this. Seeing no such sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.
translations.mn12:24: ‘While you claim to have destroyed the taints, these taints are not destroyed.’ I do not see any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately reprove me with regard to this. Seeing no such sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.
translations.mn12:25: ‘Those things called obstructions by you are not able to obstruct one who engages in them.’ I do not see any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately reprove me with regard to this. Seeing no such sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.
translations.mn12:26: ‘When you teach the Dhamma for someone’s benefit, it does not lead to the complete ending of suffering for one who practices it.’ I do not see any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately reprove me with regard to this. Seeing no such sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.
translations.mn12:32: Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of generation. What four? Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, and spontaneous generation.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born generation? There are beings that are born by breaking through an eggshell—this is called egg-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born generation? There are beings that are born by breaking through a caul—this is called womb-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born generation? There are beings that are born in a rotten fish, in a rotten corpse, in rotten porridge, in a cesspool, or in a sump—this is called moisture-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous generation? Gods, hell-beings, some human beings, and some beings in the lower realms—this is called spontaneous generation. These, Sāriputta, are the four kinds of generation.
translations.mn12:35: Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, human beings, and gods.
translations.mn12:36: I understand hell, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to hell. And I also understand how one who has entered on that path, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. I understand the animal realm, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to the animal realm. And I also understand how one who has entered on that path, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the animal realm. I understand the realm of ghosts, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to the realm of ghosts. And I also understand how one who has entered on that path, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the realm of ghosts. I understand human beings, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to the human world. And I also understand how one who has entered on that path, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears among human beings. I understand the gods, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to the world of gods. And I also understand how one who has entered on that path, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in the heavenly world. I understand Nibbāna, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to Nibbāna. And I also understand how one who has entered on that path, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.
translations.mn12:4: “Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta is angry, and his words are spoken out of anger. Thinking ‘I will speak dispraise,’ the foolish man Sunakkhatta actually speaks praise of the Tathāgata. For it is praise of the Tathāgata, Sāriputta, when someone says: ‘When he teaches the Dhamma for someone’s benefit, it leads to the complete ending of suffering for one who practices it.’
translations.mn12:43: Sāriputta, if anyone should speak thus of me while I know and see in this way: ‘The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurred to him’—unless he abandons that speech and that mind, and relinquishes that view, he will be cast into hell as if carried there. Just as a bhikkhu possessed of virtue, concentration, and wisdom might here and now enjoy final knowledge, so, Sāriputta, do I say that this is the consequence: unless he abandons that speech and that mind, and relinquishes that view, he will be cast into hell as if carried there.
translations.mn12:44: Sāriputta, I recall having lived the holy life possessing four factors: I was an ascetic, the ultimate ascetic; I was rough, the ultimate in roughness; I was scrupulous, the ultimate in scrupulousness; I was secluded, the ultimate in seclusion.
translations.mn12:46: Such was my roughness, Sāriputta: dust and dirt had accumulated on my body for many years until it had formed a crust. Just as a tinduka stump that has accumulated dust and dirt for many years forms a crust, so too, dust and dirt had accumulated on my body for many years until it had formed a crust. It did not occur to me: ‘Oh, let me rub this dust and dirt off with my hand, or let another rub this dust and dirt off with his hand.’ Even this did not occur to me. Such was my roughness, Sāriputta.
translations.mn12:47: Such was my scrupulousness, Sāriputta: I was always mindful in stepping forwards and stepping backwards. I was full of pity even for a drop of water, thinking: ‘Let me not hurt the tiny creatures in the crevices.’ Such was my scrupulousness, Sāriputta.
translations.mn12:49: I would go on all fours to the cowpens when the cows had gone out and the cowherd had left them, and I would feed on the dung of the young suckling calves. As long as my own urine and excrement lasted, I fed on my own urine and excrement. That was my practice of the great foul feeding.
translations.mn12:5: Sariputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not even infer of me from the Dhamma: ‘That Blessed One is accomplished, fully enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.’
translations.mn12:50: I would plunge into a fearsome forest thicket and dwell there. And in that fearsome forest thicket, Sariputta, the fear and dread was such that if anyone who was not free from lust entered that thicket, the hairs of his body would stand up. Those cold winter nights during the ‘between-the-eights’ period of snowfall, I dwelt in the open air at night and in the thicket by day; in the last month of the hot season I dwelt in the open air by day and in the thicket by night. And, Sariputta, this verse never heard before occurred to me: ‘Scorched and freezing, alone in the fearsome forest, naked, sitting not by a fire, the sage is intent on his quest.’
translations.mn12:51: I would make my bed in a charnel ground with bones for a pillow. And cowherd boys came up and spat on me, urinated on me, threw dirt at me, and stuck twigs in my ears. But, Sariputta, I do not recall ever giving rise to an evil mind against them. That was my practice of equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification is through food.’ They say: ‘Let us subsist on jujube fruits.’ They eat jujube fruits, they eat jujube powder, they drink jujube water, and they consume various kinds of jujube concoctions. I recall, Sariputta, eating a single jujube fruit a day. You may think, Sariputta: ‘The jujube fruit must have been big at that time.’ But you should not regard it so. The jujube fruit was then of the same size as it is now. Through feeding on a single jujube fruit, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation. Because of eating so little, my limbs became like the jointed segments of a vine or a bamboo stem. Because of eating so little, my backside became like a camel’s hoof. Because of eating so little, the projections of my spine stood out like a string of beads. Because of eating so little, my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old shed. Because of eating so little, the gleam of my eyes sank far down in their sockets, looking like the gleam of water stars sunk far down in a deep well. Because of eating so little, my scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter gourd shriveled and withered in the wind and sun. If I thought ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I seized my backbone; if I thought ‘I will touch my backbone,’ I seized the skin of my belly; for because of eating so little, the skin of my belly stuck to my backbone. If I thought ‘I will defecate or urinate,’ I fell over on my face right there because of eating so little. When I rubbed my limbs with my hand to reassure my body, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell from my body because of eating so little.
translations.mn12:56: But, Sariputta, by such conduct, by such practice, by such difficult austerities, I did not attain any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why is that? Because I did not attain that noble wisdom which, when attained, is noble and emancipating, and leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification is through transmigration.’ But it is not easy to find a kind of transmigration that I have not previously undergone in this long journey, except for the Pure Abodes. For if I had transmigrated into the Pure Abodes, I would not have returned to this world.
translations.mn12:6: Sariputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not even infer of me from the Dhamma: ‘That Blessed One wields the manifold kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels in space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma world.’
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification is through sacrifice.’ But it is not easy to find a kind of sacrifice that has not been performed by me in this long journey, as a head-anointed noble king or as a well-to-do brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sariputta, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification is through fire-worship.’ But it is not easy to find a kind of fire that has not been worshipped by me in this long journey, as a head-anointed noble king or as a well-to-do brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, some recluses and brahmins whose doctrine and view is this: ‘As long as this good man is young, a youth, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, so long is he endowed with supreme lucidity of wisdom. But when this good man is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage, being eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, then he falls away from that lucidity of wisdom.’ But this should not be regarded so, Sāriputta. I am now old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage: my age is eighty years. Suppose that I had four disciples with a hundred years’ lifespan, living for a hundred years, endowed with supreme mindfulness, retention, and resoluteness, and endowed with supreme lucidity of wisdom—just as a skilled archer, trained, practiced, and tested, could easily shoot a light arrow across a palm tree’s shadow, so too were they endowed with such a degree of mindfulness, retention, and resoluteness, and endowed with supreme lucidity of wisdom. Suppose they were to ask me a question about the four foundations of mindfulness, setting up one question after another, and I were to answer them when asked, and they were to remember what I answered, and they were not to ask me a second time or further. Except for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, except for defecating and urinating, except for dispelling sleep and fatigue, the Tathāgata’s exposition of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata’s phrasing of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata’s quick-wittedness in answering questions would not be exhausted. Even if those four disciples with a hundred years’ lifespan, living for a hundred years, were to die at the end of a hundred years, and if you were to carry me about on a litter, there would still be no change in the Tathāgata’s lucidity of wisdom.
translations.mn12:7: And, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not infer of me according to the Dhamma: ‘That Blessed One hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far and those that are near, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human.’
translations.mn12:8: And, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not infer of me according to the Dhamma: ‘That Blessed One encompasses with his mind the minds of other beings, other persons, and understands them. He understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust; he understands a mind with hate as a mind with hate, a mind without hate as a mind without hate; he understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; he understands a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind; he understands an exalted mind as an exalted mind, an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; he understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; he understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’
translations.mn12:9: Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā. What are the ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, student, some woman or man is not a giver of food, drink, cloth, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwelling, and lighting to recluses or brahmins. Because of performing and undertaking such action, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. But if, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they do not reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell, but instead come back to the human state, then wherever they are reborn they are poor. This is the way, student, that leads to poverty, namely, not being a giver of food, drink, cloth, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwelling, and lighting to recluses or brahmins.
translations.mn135:2: Then the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their actions, student, heirs of their actions; they originate from their actions, are bound to their actions, have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.
translations.mn135:3: Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition why human beings are seen to be inferior and superior? For people are seen to be short-lived and long-lived, sickly and healthy, ugly and beautiful, uninfluential and influential, poor and wealthy, low-born and high-born, stupid and wise. What is the cause and condition, Master Gotama, why human beings are seen to be inferior and superior?
translations.mn135:4: “Beings are owners of their actions, student, heirs of their actions; they originate from their actions, are bound to their actions, have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.” “I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement which Master Gotama has spoken in brief without expounding the meaning in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma so that I might understand in detail the meaning of this statement which Master Gotama has spoken in brief without expounding the meaning in detail.” “Then, student, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: “Here, student, some woman or man kills living creatures, is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings. Because of undertaking and carrying out such action, when the body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. If they are not reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell, but come back to the human state, then wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This is the path that leads to a short life, student, namely: killing living creatures, being murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings.
translations.mn135:6: But here, student, some woman or man, abandoning the killing of living creatures, abstains from killing living creatures; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and merciful, they live compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. Because of undertaking and carrying out such action, when the body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm. If they are not reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, but come back to the human state, then wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This is the path that leads to a long life, student, namely: abandoning the killing of living creatures, abstaining from killing living creatures; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and merciful, living compassionate for the welfare of all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If that gentleman gets that wealth by striving and struggling and making an effort, he experiences pain and sadness due to the need to protect that wealth, thinking: ‘How can I ensure that kings don’t take my wealth, or thieves, or fire, or flood, or unloved heirs?’ While he guards and protects it like this, kings take it, or thieves, or fire, or flood, or unloved heirs. He sorrows, pines, and laments, beating his breast and falling into confusion: ‘What I had is gone!’ This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:11: Furthermore, monks, caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as their source, having sensual pleasures as their cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, kings fight with kings, aristocrats with aristocrats, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders; mother fights with child, child with mother, father with child, child with father, brother with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, friend with friend. When they quarrel, fight, and dispute, they attack each other with fists, stones, rods, and weapons. They undergo death there, or pain like death. This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:12: Furthermore, monks, caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as their source, having sensual pleasures as their cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, taking sword and shield, fastening bow and quiver, they charge into battle massed on both sides, with arrows flying and spears flying and swords flashing. There they are pierced by arrows and spears, and their heads are cut off by swords. They undergo death there, or pain like death. This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:13: Furthermore, monks, caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as their source, having sensual pleasures as their cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, taking sword and shield, fastening bow and quiver, they charge slippery bastions, with arrows flying and spears flying and swords flashing. There they are pierced by arrows and spears, splashed with boiling cow dung, crushed by heavy weights, and their heads are cut off by swords. They undergo death there, or pain like death. This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:15: Furthermore, monks, caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as their source, having sensual pleasures as their cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures, they engage in misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having done so, when the body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures in lives to come, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:16: And what, monks, is the escape from sensual pleasures? It is the removal of desire and greed, the abandonment of desire and greed for sensual pleasures. This is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: Those ascetics and brahmins who do not truly understand the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape: it is impossible that they will themselves fully understand sensual pleasures or instruct another so that they can fully understand sensual pleasures. But those ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape: it is possible that they will themselves fully understand sensual pleasures or instruct another so that they can fully understand sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:18: And what, monks, is the gratification of forms? Suppose there were a girl of the aristocrats, brahmins, or householders, about fifteen or sixteen years old, not too tall and not too short, not too thin and not too fat, not too dark and not too pale. Is her beauty and complexion then at its peak? ‘Yes, sir.’ The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on that beauty and complexion: this is the gratification of forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, monks, is the drawback of forms? Here, monks, one might see that same sister later on, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, crooked like a roof bracket, bent, leaning on a stick, trembling as she goes, sick, youth gone, teeth broken, hair grey, bald, head shaking, wrinkled, limbs blotchy. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance has vanished, and the drawback has appeared? ‘Yes, sir.’ This too, monks, is the drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then several monks, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Savatthi for alms. Then it occurred to them: “It is too early to walk for alms in Savatthi. Why don't we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?” So they went there. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers. After finishing the polite and friendly talk, they sat to one side. While they were sitting there, those wanderers said to them:
translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying wallowing in her own urine and excrement, lifted up by others, laid down by others. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance has vanished, and the drawback has appeared? ‘Yes, sir.’ This too, monks, is the drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister's body thrown in the charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by tendons... a skeleton smeared with flesh and blood, held together by tendons... a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by tendons... bones without tendons, scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there an ankle-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a rib-bone, there a back-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there the skull. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance has vanished, and the drawback has appeared? ‘Yes, sir.’ This too, monks, is the drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister's body thrown in the charnel ground—bones white like the color of a conch shell... bones heaped up, more than a year old... bones rotted and crumbled to dust. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance has vanished, and the drawback has appeared? ‘Yes, sir.’ This too, monks, is the drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:3: “Reverends, the ascetic Gotama describes the full understanding of sensual pleasures, and we too describe the full understanding of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama describes the full understanding of forms, and we too describe the full understanding of forms. The ascetic Gotama describes the full understanding of feelings, and we too describe the full understanding of feelings. So here, reverends, what is the distinction, what is the disparity, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us—that is, regarding the teaching of the Dhamma or the giving of instruction?”
translations.mn13:30: And what, monks, is the escape from forms? The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust for forms—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, monks, is the gratification of feelings? Here, monks, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, a monk enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by thought and examination. At the time when a monk enters and remains in the first absorption... he does not intend for his own affliction, or for the affliction of others, or for the affliction of both. At that time he feels a feeling that is free from affliction. The highest gratification of feelings, I say, is freedom from affliction.
translations.mn13:36: And what, monks, is the drawback of feelings? The fact that feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the drawback of feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those monks neither approved nor disapproved of what those wanderers of other sects said. Neither approving nor disapproving, they got up from their seats and left, thinking: “We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.”
translations.mn13:6: “Monks, wanderers of other sects who speak like that should be asked: ‘But friends, what is the gratification, what is the drawback, and what is the escape regarding sensual pleasures? What is the gratification, what is the drawback, and what is the escape regarding forms? What is the gratification, what is the drawback, and what is the escape regarding feelings?’ When asked this, monks, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and furthermore, they will meet with vexation. Why is that? Because it is not within their domain. Monks, I do not see anyone in this world with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Tathagata, or a disciple of the Tathagata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.mn13:8: And what, mendicants, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Here, mendicants, a gentleman earns his living by some craft—whether by checking fingers, calculation, accounting, farming, trade, cattle-breeding, archery, royal service, or some other craft—facing cold, facing heat, injured by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, dying of hunger and thirst. This too, mendicants, is a danger in sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:9: If, mendicants, while this gentleman strives, works hard, and exerts himself, those riches are not produced, he sorrows, grieves, and laments, beating his breast and crying, falling into confusion: ‘My striving is in vain, my effort is fruitless!’ This too, mendicants, is a danger in sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, having sensual pleasures as its cause, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn140:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadha country and arrived at Rajagaha. He went to Bhaggava the potter and said to him:
translations.mn140:12: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should foster relinquishment, and should train only for peace’—so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung to, that is: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, contents of the stomach, feces, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung to—this is called the internal earth element. Now both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply earth element. And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen this thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and makes the mind dispassionate towards the earth element.
