translations.mn140:15: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what is the internal water element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung to, that is: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung to—this is called the internal water element. Now both the internal water element and the external water element are simply water element. And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is
translations.mn140:2: “If it is not inconvenient for you, Bhaggava, I would stay one night in the workshop.” “It is not inconvenient for me, sir. But there is a renunciant who has already taken up residence there first. If he allows it, stay, sir, as you please.”
translations.mn140:16: And what, monk, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what is the internal fire element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, fire, fiery, and clung to, that is to say: that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one burns, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted gets completely digested, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, fire, fiery, and clung to—this is called the internal fire element. Now both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element. And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and makes the mind dispassionate towards the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, monk, is the air element? The air element may be internal or external. And what is the internal air element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, air, airy, and clung to, that is to say: up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, air, airy, and clung to—this is called the internal air element. Now both the internal air element and the external air element are simply the air element. And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and makes the mind dispassionate towards the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, monk, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what is the internal space element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, space, spatial, and clung to, that is to say: the ear-holes, the nostrils, the door of the mouth, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted is swallowed, and where it collects, and that by which it is excreted from the lower part, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, space, spatial, a gap, gap-like, an opening, opening-like, untouched by flesh and blood, and clung to—this is called the internal space element. Now both the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element. And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and makes the mind dispassionate towards the space element.
translations.mn140:20: Then there remains only equanimity, pure, bright, soft, workable, and luminous. Just as a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice might prepare a furnace, heat up the opening, take some gold with tongs, and put it in the opening; then he blows on it from time to time, sprinkles water on it from time to time, and looks on with equanimity from time to time; that gold becomes refined, well-smelted, free from dross, pliable, workable, and bright; whatever kind of ornament he wishes to make—whether a belt, earrings, a necklace, or a gold chain—it serves his purpose. So too, there remains only equanimity, pure, bright, soft, workable, and luminous.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not attached to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not attached to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not attached to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’
translations.mn140:29: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should foster relinquishment, and should train for peace’—that which was said, it was said in reference to this.
translations.mn140:3: Now on that occasion a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dedicating himself to the Blessed One. He had arrived first at that potter’s workshop. Then the Blessed One approached the Venerable Pukkusāti and said to him: “If it is not troublesome for you, monk, let us stay one night in the workshop.” “The potter’s workshop is spacious, friend. Let the Venerable One stay as he pleases.”
translations.mn140:30: ‘Where there is a standing, the tides of conceiving do not flow; and when the tides of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace’—that which was said, in reference to what was it said?
translations.mn140:31: ‘I am,’ monk, is a conceiving; ‘I am this’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall not be’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be possessed of form’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be formless’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be percipient’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be non-percipient’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’ is a conceiving. Conceiving is a disease, conceiving is a boil, conceiving is a dart. By overcoming all conceivings, monk, one is called a sage at peace. And the sage at peace is not born, does not age, does not die, is not shaken, and does not yearn. For there is nothing present in him by which he might be born. Not being born, how could he age? Not aging, how could he die? Not dying, how could he be shaken? Not shaking, what could he yearn for?
translations.mn140:32: ‘Where there is a standing, the tides of conceiving do not flow; and when the tides of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace’—that which was said, it was said in reference to this. Bear in mind this brief exposition of the six elements, monk.”
translations.mn140:33: Then the Venerable Pukkusāti thought: “Indeed, the Teacher has come to me! The Well-Gone One has come to me! The Fully Enlightened One has come to me!” Rising from his seat, arranging his robe over one shoulder, and bowing his head to the Blessed One’s feet, he said to the Blessed One: “A transgression overcame me, Lord, foolish, confused, and unskilled as I was, in that I presumed to address the Blessed One as ‘friend’. May the Blessed One forgive my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future.” “Indeed, monk, a transgression overcame you, foolish, confused, and unskilled as you were, in that you presumed to address me as ‘friend’. But since you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it. For it is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and exercises restraint in the future.”
translations.mn140:34: “May I receive the higher ordination in the Blessed One’s presence, Lord?” “Do you have a complete bowl and robes, monk?” “No, Lord, I do not have a complete bowl and robes.” “The Tathāgatas do not ordain one who does not have a complete bowl and robes, monk.”
translations.mn140:35: Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, bowed to the Blessed One, circled him on the right, and left to search for a bowl and robes. Then, while the Venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a runaway cow deprived him of life.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s workshop, prepared a spread of grass at one side, and sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. The Blessed One spent most of the night sitting. The Venerable Pukkusāti also spent most of the night sitting. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “This clansman conducts himself in an inspiring way. Why don’t I question him?” So the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: “Who is your teacher, monk? On whose account have you gone forth? Whose teaching do you approve of?” “There is, friend, the recluse Gotama, a Sakyan son who went forth from the Sakyan clan. Now a good report of that Blessed Gotama has spread to this effect: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ I have gone forth on account of that Blessed One. He is my teacher. And I approve of that Blessed One’s Dhamma.” “But where, monk, is that Blessed One living now, the perfected, fully awakened one?” “There is, friend, a city in the northern lands called Sāvatthī. That is where the Blessed One is living now.” “Have you ever seen that Blessed One before, monk? Would you recognize him if you saw him?” “No, friend, I have never seen that Blessed One before, nor would I recognize him if I saw him.”
translations.mn140:6: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “This gentleman has gone forth out of faith in me. Why don’t I teach him the Dhamma?” Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Pukkusāti: “I will teach you the Dhamma, monk. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” Venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn140:7: “‘This person has six elements, six fields of contact, eighteen mental ranges, and four foundations. Where one stands, the currents of conceiving do not flow; and when the currents of conceiving do not flow, he is called a sage at peace. One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should foster relinquishment, and should train only for peace’—this is the summary of the Exposition of the Elements.
translations.mn146:12: “I have made this simile, sisters, to convey a meaning. This is the meaning here: ‘The inner mass of flesh,’ sisters, is a term for the six internal sense fields. ‘The outer hide,’ sisters, is a term for the six external sense fields. ‘The inner sub-flesh, the inner tendons, the inner ligaments,’ sisters, is a term for delight and lust. ‘The sharp butcher’s knife,’ sisters, is a term for noble wisdom—the noble wisdom that cuts, severs, slices, and shreds the inner defilements, inner fetters, and inner bonds.
translations.mn146:13: “There are, sisters, these seven factors of awakening. By developing and cultivating them, a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and lives having realized it with their own insight due to the ending of defilements. What seven? Here, sisters, a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. They develop the awakening factor of investigation of principles … the awakening factor of energy … the awakening factor of rapture … the awakening factor of tranquility … the awakening factor of immersion … the awakening factor of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. These, sisters, are the seven factors of awakening, by developing and cultivating which a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and lives having realized it with their own insight due to the ending of defilements.”
translations.mn146:14: Then Venerable Nandaka, having advised those nuns with this advice, dismissed them: “Go, sisters, it is time.” Then those nuns, having delighted and rejoiced in Venerable Nandaka’s statement, rose from their seats, bowed to Venerable Nandaka, circled him on the right, and went to the Blessed One. After approaching and bowing to the Blessed One, they stood to one side. The Blessed One said to those nuns standing to one side: “Go, nuns, it is time.” Then those nuns bowed to the Blessed One, circled him on the right, and left.
translations.mn146:3: Now at that time the senior monks were advising the nuns in turn. Venerable Nandaka did not want to advise the nuns in his turn. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: “Whose turn is it today, Ānanda, to advise the nuns?” “Everyone has taken their turn to advise the nuns, sir. But this Venerable Nandaka does not want to advise the nuns in his turn.”
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Nandaka: “Advise the nuns, Nandaka. Instruct the nuns, Nandaka. Give the nuns a Dhamma talk, holy man.” “Yes, sir,” Venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. In the morning, he robed up and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from his alms round after the meal, he went with a companion to the Royal Park. The nuns saw Venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. Venerable Nandaka sat on the prepared seat and washed his feet. The nuns bowed to Venerable Nandaka and sat to one side. When they were seated to one side, Venerable Nandaka said to them:
translations.mn146:5: “There will be a discussion by way of questioning, sisters. In that regard, those who understand should say ‘We understand,’ and those who do not understand should say ‘We do not understand.’ Or if anyone has doubt or uncertainty, they should ask me: ‘How is this, sir? What is the meaning of this?’” “Just with this much, sir, we are satisfied and pleased with Venerable Nandaka, that he invites us [to ask].”
translations.mn147:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. Then, as the Blessed One was in private retreat, this thought appeared in his mind: “The qualities that ripen in liberation have ripened in Rāhula. Why don’t I lead Rāhula further to the ending of defilements?” Then the Blessed One robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from his alms round after the meal, he addressed Venerable Rāhula: “Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula. We will go to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, sir,” Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One. Taking his sitting cloth, he followed close behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: Now on that occasion many thousands of deities were following the Blessed One, thinking: “Today the Blessed One will lead the Venerable Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints.” Then the Blessed One plunged into the Blind Men’s Grove and sat down at the foot of a certain tree on a seat made ready. The Venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the Venerable Rāhula as he sat to one side: “What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “Is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.mn148:16: Now this, mendicants, is the practice leading to the origin of identity. One regards the eye thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
translations.mn148:2: “Mendicants, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. I will reveal the spiritual practice that is entirely full and pure, namely, the six sets of six. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: Now this, mendicants, is the practice leading to the cessation of identity. One regards the eye thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’.
translations.mn148:3: “The six internal sense fields should be understood. The six external sense fields should be understood. The six classes of consciousness should be understood. The six classes of contact should be understood. The six classes of feeling should be understood. The six classes of craving should be understood.
translations.mn148:34: Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral. When touched by a pleasant feeling, one does not delight in it, welcome it, or remain holding to it. The underlying tendency to lust does not lie within one. When touched by a painful feeling, one does not sorrow, grieve, and lament, does not weep beating one’s breast and become distraught. The underlying tendency to repulsion does not lie within one. When touched by a neutral feeling, one understands as it really is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to that feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie within one. That one should abandon the underlying tendency to lust regarding pleasant feeling, remove the underlying tendency to repulsion regarding painful feeling, uproot the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neutral feeling, and having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, should make an end of suffering here and now—this is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, mendicants, a learned noble disciple experiences revulsion towards the eye, towards forms, towards eye-consciousness, towards eye-contact, towards feeling, towards craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what things, mendicants, should be fully understood by direct knowledge? ‘The five aggregates affected by clinging,’ should be the reply, that is: the material form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the volitional formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging. These are the things that should be fully understood by direct knowledge. And what things should be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence—these are the things that should be abandoned by direct knowledge. And what things should be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight—these are the things that should be developed by direct knowledge. And what things should be realized by direct knowledge? True knowledge and liberation—these are the things that should be realized by direct knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: “Mendicants, I will teach you the Great Discourse on the Six Sense Fields. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: “Mendicants, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are, not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is, not knowing and not seeing as it really is the feeling that arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant or painful or neutral—one is enamored with the eye, enamored with forms, enamored with eye-consciousness, enamored with eye-contact, enamored with the feeling that arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant or painful or neutral. When one dwells enamored, fettered, confused, and focusing on gratification, the five aggregates affected by clinging build up for the future. And one’s craving—which leads to future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight now here now there—increases. One’s bodily stresses increase, mental stresses increase; bodily torments increase, mental torments increase; bodily fevers increase, mental fevers increase. One experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: When one dwells enamored, fettered, confused, and focusing on gratification, the five aggregates affected by clinging build up for the future. And one’s craving—which leads to future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight now here now there—increases. One’s bodily stresses increase, mental stresses increase; bodily torments increase, mental torments increase; bodily fevers increase, mental fevers increase. One experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: But knowing and seeing the eye as it actually is, monks, knowing and seeing forms as they actually are, knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it actually is, knowing and seeing eye-contact as it actually is, and knowing and seeing whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it actually is, one is not infatuated with the eye, not infatuated with forms, not infatuated with eye-consciousness, not infatuated with eye-contact, not infatuated with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For him, living without infatuation, unyoked, unconfused, observing the danger, the five clinging-aggregates go to their diminution in the future. And that craving which makes for further becoming—accompanied by passion and delight, finding delight now here and now there—is abandoned by him. His bodily disturbances are abandoned; his mental disturbances are abandoned. His bodily torments are abandoned; his mental torments are abandoned. His bodily fevers are abandoned; his mental fevers are abandoned. He experiences bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that will become the inclination of his mind. If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of renunciation, he has abandoned the thought of sensual desire to cultivate the thought of renunciation, and then his mind inclines to thoughts of renunciation. If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of non-ill will... If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of non-cruelty, he has abandoned the thought of cruelty to cultivate the thought of non-cruelty, and then his mind inclines to thoughts of non-cruelty.
translations.mn19:12: Just as in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been gathered into the village, a cowherd might guard the cows, and while staying at the root of a tree or out in the open, he simply needs to be mindful that 'those are the cows.' In the same way, monks, I simply needed to be mindful that 'those are mental states.'
translations.mn19:13: Tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, my body was tranquil and untroubled, my mind concentrated and unified.
translations.mn19:14: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought and evaluation.
translations.mn19:24: This was the third knowledge I attained in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed; knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed; light arose—as happens in one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Suppose, monks, that in a forest wilderness there were a large low-lying marsh, and a large herd of deer lived relying on it. Then a man would appear desiring their ruin, desiring their harm, desiring their lack of safety. He would close off the safe, secure path that led to rapture, and he would open up a false path, he would set out a male decoy, he would set out a female decoy. As a result, the large herd of deer would, in the course of time, come to ruin and disaster. Then a man would appear desiring their benefit, desiring their welfare, desiring their safety. He would open up the safe, secure path that led to rapture, he would close off the false path, he would remove the male decoy, he would destroy the female decoy. As a result, the large herd of deer would, in the course of time, come to growth, increase, and abundance.
translations.mn19:26: I have made this simile, monks, to convey a meaning. And this is the meaning here: 'The large low-lying marsh' is a term for sensual pleasures. 'The large herd of deer' is a term for beings. 'The man desiring their ruin, desiring their harm, desiring their lack of safety' is a term for Mara the Evil One. 'The false path' is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view, wrong resolve, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. 'The male decoy' is a term for delight and passion. 'The female decoy' is a term for ignorance. 'The man desiring their benefit, desiring their welfare, desiring their safety' is a term for the Tathagata, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One. 'The safe, secure path that leads to rapture' is a term for the Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, monks, I have opened up the safe, secure path that leads to rapture, closed off the false path, removed the male decoy, and destroyed the female decoy.
translations.mn19:3: As I remained thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, a thought of sensual desire arose. I discerned that 'This thought of sensual desire has arisen in me. It leads to my own affliction, to others' affliction, and to the affliction of both; it obstructs discernment, promotes vexation, and does not lead to Unbinding.' As I reflected that 'It leads to my own affliction,' it went to its end. As I reflected that 'It leads to others' affliction'... As I reflected that 'It leads to the affliction of both'... As I reflected that 'It obstructs discernment, promotes vexation, and does not lead to Unbinding,' it went to its end. Whenever a thought of sensual desire arose, I abandoned it, destroyed it, dispelled it, and wiped it out of existence.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that will become the inclination of his mind. If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of sensual desire, he has abandoned the thought of renunciation to cultivate the thought of sensual desire, and then his mind inclines to thoughts of sensual desire. If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of ill will... If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of cruelty, he has abandoned the thought of non-cruelty to cultivate the thought of cruelty, and then his mind inclines to thoughts of cruelty.
translations.mn19:7: Suppose, mendicants, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, when the crops are thick, a cowherd was looking after the cows. He would tap and poke them with a stick on this side and that, checking and curbing them. Why is that? Because that cowherd sees that if they wander off he could be executed, imprisoned, fined, or blamed. In the same way, I saw the drawback, degradation, and defilement in unskillful qualities, and the benefit of renunciation, the aspect of cleansing, in skillful qualities.
translations.mn19:8: As I meditated like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—a thought of renunciation arose. I understood: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It doesn’t lead to hurting myself, hurting others, or hurting both. It aids wisdom, doesn’t cause distress, and leads to Nibbana.’ If I were to think and consider this all night, I see no danger coming from that. If I were to think and consider this all day, I see no danger coming from that. If I were to think and consider this all night and day, I see no danger coming from that. But thinking and considering for too long would tire my body. When the body is tired, the mind is stressed. When the mind is stressed, it’s far from immersion. So I steadied my mind internally, settled it, unified it, and immersed it. Why is that? So that my mind would not be stressed.
translations.mn1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Forest, at the root of a royal sal tree. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn1:10: They perceive Brahmā as Brahmā. But then they identify with Brahmā, they identify regarding Brahmā, they identify as Brahmā, they identify that ‘Brahmā is mine’, they take pleasure in Brahmā. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:11: They perceive the gods of streaming radiance as the gods of streaming radiance. But then they identify with the gods of streaming radiance, they identify regarding the gods of streaming radiance, they identify as the gods of streaming radiance, they identify that ‘the gods of streaming radiance are mine’, they take pleasure in the gods of streaming radiance. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:123: A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—directly knows earth as earth. But having directly known earth as earth, they don’t identify with earth, they don’t identify regarding earth, they don’t identify as earth, they don’t identify that ‘earth is mine’, they don’t take pleasure in earth. Why is that? Because they are free of delusion through the destruction of delusion.
translations.mn1:13: They perceive the gods of replete fruit as the gods of replete fruit. But then they identify with the gods of replete fruit, they identify regarding the gods of replete fruit, they identify as the gods of replete fruit, they identify that ‘the gods of replete fruit are mine’, they take pleasure in the gods of replete fruit. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:14: They perceive the Overlord as the Overlord. But then they identify with the Overlord, they identify regarding the Overlord, they identify as the Overlord, they identify that ‘the Overlord is mine’, they take pleasure in the Overlord. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:147: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha also directly knows earth as earth. But having directly known earth as earth, he doesn’t identify with earth, he doesn’t identify regarding earth, he doesn’t identify as earth, he doesn’t identify that ‘earth is mine’, he doesn’t take pleasure in earth. Why is that? Because the Realized One has completely understood it to the end, I say.
translations.mn1:171: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha also directly knows earth as earth. But having directly known earth as earth, he doesn’t identify with earth, he doesn’t identify regarding earth, he doesn’t identify as earth, he doesn’t identify that ‘earth is mine’, he doesn’t take pleasure in earth. Why is that? Because he has understood that delight is the root of suffering, and that from continued existence comes rebirth, and that for what has come to be there is old age and death. That is why the Realized One—with the ending, fading away, cessation, giving up, and letting go of all cravings—has awakened to the supreme perfect enlightenment, I say.
translations.mn1:19: They perceive the seen as the seen. But then they identify with the seen, they identify regarding the seen, they identify as the seen, they identify that ‘the seen is mine’, they take pleasure in the seen. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:2: “Mendicants, I will teach you the exposition of the root of all things. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn1:20: They perceive the heard as the heard. But then they identify with the heard, they identify regarding the heard, they identify as the heard, they identify that ‘the heard is mine’, they take pleasure in the heard. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:22: They perceive the cognized as the cognized. But then they identify with the cognized, they identify regarding the cognized, they identify as the cognized, they identify that ‘the cognized is mine’, they take pleasure in the cognized. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:23: They perceive unity as unity. But then they identify with unity, they identify regarding unity, they identify as unity, they identify that ‘unity is mine’, they take pleasure in unity. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:24: They perceive diversity as diversity. But then they identify with diversity, they identify regarding diversity, they identify as diversity, they identify that ‘diversity is mine’, they take pleasure in diversity. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:25: They perceive the all as the all. But then they identify with the all, they identify regarding the all, they identify as the all, they identify that ‘the all is mine’, they take pleasure in the all. Why is that? Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:27: A mendicant who is a trainee, who hasn’t achieved their heart’s desire, but lives aspiring to the supreme sanctuary, also directly knows earth as earth. But having directly known earth as earth, let them not identify with earth, let them not identify regarding earth, let them not identify as earth, let them not identify that ‘earth is mine’, let them not take pleasure in earth. Why is that? Because they must completely understand it, I say.
translations.mn1:3: “Here, monks, an uneducated ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the teaching of the noble ones, is untrained in the teaching of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the teaching of good persons, is untrained in the teaching of good persons—perceives earth as earth. Having perceived earth as earth, he conceives [himself as] earth, he conceives [himself] in earth, he conceives [himself apart] from earth, he conceives earth to be ‘mine,’ he delights in earth. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:4: He perceives water as water. Having perceived water as water, he conceives water, he conceives in water, he conceives from water, he conceives water to be ‘mine,’ he delights in water. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:5: He perceives fire as fire. Having perceived fire as fire, he conceives fire, he conceives in fire, he conceives from fire, he conceives fire to be ‘mine,’ he delights in fire. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:51: Monks, a monk who is a worthy one, devoid of taints, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—he too directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive earth to be ‘mine,’ he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because he has fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:7: He perceives beings as beings. Having perceived beings as beings, he conceives beings, he conceives in beings, he conceives from beings, he conceives beings to be ‘mine,’ he delights in beings. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:8: He perceives gods as gods. Having perceived gods as gods, he conceives gods, he conceives in gods, he conceives from gods, he conceives gods to be ‘mine,’ he delights in gods. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:9: He perceives Pajāpati as Pajāpati. Having perceived Pajāpati as Pajāpati, he conceives Pajāpati, he conceives in Pajāpati, he conceives from Pajāpati, he conceives Pajāpati to be ‘mine,’ he delights in Pajāpati. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn20:2: “Monks, a monk intent on the higher mind should attend to five signs from time to time. What five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, monks, when you understand the meaning of my statement, you should remember it as such. But if you do not understand the meaning of my statement, you should ask me about it, or else those monks who are learned.
translations.mn22:14: I have shown you the Dhamma as similar to a raft, monks, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding on. When you know the Dhamma to be similar to a raft, you should abandon even the teachings, let alone what are not the teachings.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain monk asked the Blessed One: “Sir, can there be anxiety about what is non-existent externally?” “There can be, monk,” the Blessed One said. “Here, monk, someone thinks: ‘Alas, I had it! Alas, I have it no longer! Alas, may I have it! Alas, I do not get it!’ He sorrows, grieves, and laments, he weeps beating his breast and becomes distraught. That is how there is anxiety about what is non-existent externally.”
translations.mn22:19: “But, sir, can there be no anxiety about what is non-existent externally?” “There can be, monk,” the Blessed One said. “Here, monk, someone does not think: ‘Alas, I had it! Alas, I have it no longer! Alas, may I have it! Alas, I do not get it!’ He does not sorrow, grieve, or lament, he does not weep beating his breast and become distraught. That is how there is no anxiety about what is non-existent externally.”
translations.mn22:20: “Sir, can there be anxiety about what is non-existent internally?” “There can be, monk,” the Blessed One said. “Here, monk, someone has such a view: ‘That is the self, that is the world; after death I shall be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, I shall endure as long as eternity.’ He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the elimination of all standpoints, decisions, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies regarding views, for the stilling of all formations, for the relinquishing of all acquisitions, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna. He thinks: ‘I shall be annihilated! I shall be destroyed! I shall no longer exist!’ He sorrows, grieves, and laments, he weeps beating his breast and becomes distraught. That is how there is anxiety about what is non-existent internally.”
translations.mn22:23: Monks, you should grasp that grasping of the doctrine of self, by grasping which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. But do you see any such grasping of the doctrine of self, by grasping which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?” “No, sir.” “Good, monks. I too do not see any such grasping of the doctrine of self, by grasping which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.mn22:24: Monks, you should rely on that reliance on views, by relying on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. But do you see any such reliance on views, by relying on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?” “No, sir.” “Good, monks. I too do not see any such reliance on views, by relying on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.mn22:25: “Monks, if there were a self, would there be for me what belongs to a self?” “Yes, sir.” “Or if there were what belongs to a self, would there be for me a self?” “Yes, sir.” “But, monks, since a self and what belongs to a self are not apprehended as true and established, is not that standpoint for views: ‘That is the self, that is the world; after death I shall be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, I shall endure as long as eternity’—is it not an utterly foolish teaching?” “How could it not be, sir? It is an utterly foolish teaching.”
translations.mn22:27: “So, mendicants, any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; near or far: all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Any kind of feeling … Any kind of perception … Any kind of choices … Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; near or far: all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.mn22:28: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed. They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.’
translations.mn22:30: This is called a mendicant who has lifted the cross-bar, filled in the trench, pulled up the pillar, unbarred the door, a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached.
translations.mn22:31: And how has a mendicant lifted the cross-bar? It’s when a mendicant has given up ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future. That’s how a mendicant has lifted the cross-bar.
translations.mn22:32: And how has a mendicant filled in the trench? It’s when a mendicant has given up the round of rebirths in the future, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future. That’s how a mendicant has filled in the trench.
translations.mn22:33: And how has a mendicant pulled up the pillar? It’s when a mendicant has given up craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future. That’s how a mendicant has pulled up the pillar.
translations.mn22:34: And how is a mendicant unbarred? It’s when a mendicant has given up the five lower fetters, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they’re unable to arise in the future. That’s how a mendicant is unbarred.
translations.mn22:35: And how is a mendicant a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached? It’s when a mendicant has given up the conceit ‘I am’, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future. That’s how a mendicant is a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, detached.
translations.mn22:38: If others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Realized One, he doesn’t become delighted, uplifted, or elated. If others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Realized One, he thinks: ‘They perform these services for what I have already comprehended.’
translations.mn22:39: So, mendicants, if others abuse, harass, press, and vex you, you should not harbor resentment, bitterness, or dissatisfaction. And if others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate you, you should not become delighted, uplifted, or elated. You should think: ‘They perform these services for what I have already comprehended.’
translations.mn22:40: So, mendicants, give up what is not yours. Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.
translations.mn22:42: The teaching has been perfectly explained by me like this—clear, open, evident, and stripped of patchwork. In this teaching that is so well explained … those mendicants who are perfected, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and are rightly freed through enlightenment: there is no tracking their round of rebirths.
translations.mn22:43: The teaching has been perfectly explained by me like this—clear, open, evident, and stripped of patchwork. In this teaching that is so well explained … those mendicants who have given up the five lower fetters are all reborn spontaneously. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.
translations.mn22:44: The teaching has been perfectly explained by me like this—clear, open, evident, and stripped of patchwork. In this teaching that is so well explained … those mendicants who have given up three fetters, and weakened greed, hate, and delusion, are all once-returners. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: The teaching has been perfectly explained by me like this—clear, open, evident, and stripped of patchwork. In this teaching that is so well explained … those mendicants who have given up three fetters are all stream-enterers. They are not liable to the abyss, they are steadfast, and bound for awakening.
translations.mn22:46: The teaching has been perfectly explained by me like this—clear, open, evident, and stripped of patchwork. In this teaching that is so well explained … those mendicants who follow the teaching or follow by faith are all bound for awakening.
translations.mn22:6: “Silly man, who on earth have you known me to teach the Dhamma to in that way? Haven’t I said in many ways that obstructive acts are obstructive, and that they really do obstruct the one who engages in them? I’ve said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more dangerous. I’ve said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton … a piece of meat … a grass torch … a pit of coals … a dream … borrowed goods … fruit on a tree … a butcher’s knife and block … a stake … a snake’s head. They give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more dangerous. But you, silly man, have misrepresented us by your wrong grasp. You have hurt yourself and generated much bad merit. This will be for your lasting harm and suffering.”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “What do you think, mendicants? Has the mendicant Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, sparked even a glimmer of wisdom in this teaching and training?” “How could that be, sir? No, sir.” When this was said, Ariṭṭha sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, head down, glum, and speechless. Then the Buddha, knowing that Ariṭṭha was silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, head down, glum, and speechless, said to him: “You will be known, silly man, by your own bad view. I will now question the mendicants on this.”
translations.mn22:9: Mendicants, it is quite impossible that one could engage in sensual pleasures without sensual desires, without sensual perceptions, without sensual thoughts.
translations.mn26:10: And what, mendicants, do you call ‘subject to sorrow’? Spouses and children are subject to sorrow; male and female bondservants … goats and sheep … chickens and pigs … elephants, cows, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow. These attachments are subject to sorrow. Tied, fainting, and attached to them, being subject to sorrow oneself, one seeks only what is subject to sorrow.
translations.mn26:11: And what, mendicants, do you call ‘subject to defilement’? Spouses and children are subject to defilement; male and female bondservants … goats and sheep … chickens and pigs … elephants, cows, horses, and mares … gold and silver are subject to defilement. These attachments are subject to defilement. Tied, fainting, and attached to them, being subject to defilement oneself, one seeks only what is subject to defilement. This is the ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: Mendicants, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too, being liable to rebirth, sought what is liable to rebirth. Being liable to old age … sickness … death … sorrow … defilement, I sought what is liable to defilement. Then it occurred to me: ‘Why do I, being liable to rebirth, seek what is liable to rebirth? Being liable to old age … sickness … death … sorrow … defilement, why do I seek what is liable to defilement? Why don’t I, being liable to rebirth, seeing the danger in what is liable to rebirth, seek the unborn supreme sanctuary from the yoke, Nibbāna? Being liable to old age, seeing the danger in what is liable to old age, seek the unaging supreme sanctuary from the yoke, Nibbāna? Being liable to sickness … seek the unailing … Being liable to death … seek the deathless … Being liable to sorrow … seek the sorrowless … Being liable to defilement, seeing the danger in what is liable to defilement, seek the undefiled supreme sanctuary from the yoke, Nibbāna?’
translations.mn26:14: Later, while still young, black-haired, blessed with youth, in the prime of life—though my mother and father wished otherwise, weeping with tearful faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ochre robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: Then, mendicants, seeking the good, searching for the supreme state of sublime peace, I wandered by stages in the Magadhan country and arrived at the village of Senānigama in Uruvelā. There I saw a delightful park, a lovely grove, a flowing river with clear water and smooth banks, delightful, and a village for alms nearby. It occurred to me: ‘This park is truly delightful, the grove is lovely, the river flows with clear water and smooth banks, it is delightful, and there is a village for alms nearby. This is good enough for a gentleman wanting to strive.’ So I sat down right there, thinking: ‘This is good enough for striving.’
translations.mn26:21: Then, monks, having understood Brahma’s invitation and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha. Surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some who dwelt seeing fear and blame in the other world. Just as in a pond of blue or red or white lotuses, some lotuses that are born and grow in the water thrive immersed in the water without rising out of it, and some other lotuses that are born and grow in the water rest on the water’s surface, and some other lotuses that are born and grow in the water rise out of the water and stand untouched by the water; so too, surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some who dwelt seeing fear and blame in the other world. Then I replied to Brahma Sahampati in verse: ‘Open to them are the doors to the Deathless, Let those who have ears release their faith. Perceiving trouble, O Brahma, I did not speak The refined Dhamma among humans.’ Then Brahma Sahampati, thinking: ‘The Blessed One has given his consent for the teaching of the Dhamma,’ bowed to me, circled me on the right, and vanished right there.
translations.mn26:25: Then, monks, Upaka the Ajivaka saw me traveling on the road between Gaya and the Bodhi tree. Seeing me, he said: ‘Your faculties are clear, friend; your skin is pure and bright. Under whom have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?’ When this was said, I replied to Upaka the Ajivaka in verses: ‘I am the All-conqueror, the All-knower, Untainted by all things. Renouncing all, freed through the destruction of craving, Having known it all by myself, to whom should I point? I have no teacher, One like me does not exist; In the world with its devas, I have no counterpart. For I am the Arahant in the world, I am the unexcelled Teacher; I am the One Rightly Self-Awakened, Cooled, attained to Nibbana. To set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, I go to the city of the Kasians; In a world that has become blind, I will beat the drum of the Deathless.’ ‘By the way you claim, friend, you ought to be the Infinite Conqueror.’ ‘Conquerors are those like me, Who have reached the destruction of taints; I have conquered evil qualities, Therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror.’ When this was said, Upaka the Ajivaka said, ‘May it be so, friend,’ shook his head, took a bypath, and left.
translations.mn26:26: Then, monks, wandering by stages, I arrived at Varanasi, at the Deer Park in Isipatana, to where the group of five monks was. The group of five monks saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they made an agreement among themselves: ‘Here comes the ascetic Gotama, who lives luxuriously, who gave up the struggle and reverted to luxury. He should not be bowed to, nor stood up for, nor should his bowl and robe be received. However, a seat may be put out; if he wishes, he may sit.’ But as I approached, the group of five monks was unable to abide by their own agreement. Some came out to meet me and took my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, and some set out water for washing feet. However, they addressed me by name and as ‘friend’.
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, I told the group of five monks: ‘Do you recall, monks, me ever speaking like this before?’ ‘No, indeed, sir.’ ‘The Tathagata, monks, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Awakened One. Lend ear, monks, the Deathless has been attained. I shall instruct you, I shall teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon—in this very life—enter and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, having realized it for yourselves with direct knowledge.’
translations.mn26:29: I was able, monks, to convince the group of five monks. I would instruct two monks while three went for alms. We six lived on what the three monks brought back from their alms round. I would instruct three monks while two went for alms. We six lived on what the two monks brought back from their alms round.
translations.mn26:30: Then, monks, the group of five monks, being thus exhorted and instructed by me—being themselves subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn supreme security from bondage, Nibbana—attained the unborn supreme security from bondage, Nibbana. Being themselves subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, seeking the unaging supreme security from bondage, Nibbana—attained the unaging supreme security from bondage, Nibbana. Being themselves subject to sickness... being themselves subject to death... being themselves subject to sorrow... being themselves subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled supreme security from bondage, Nibbana—attained the undefiled supreme security from bondage, Nibbana. And the knowledge and vision arose in them: ‘Unshakable is our liberation; this is the last birth; there is now no further becoming.’
translations.mn26:31: Mendicants, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Sights known by the eye that are agreeable, likeable, desirable, erotic, connected with sensual pleasure, and exciting. Sounds known by the ear … smells known by the nose … tastes known by the tongue … touches known by the body that are agreeable, likeable, desirable, erotic, connected with sensual pleasure, and exciting. These are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn26:34: Suppose, mendicants, a forest deer wandering in the wild woods walks confident, stands confident, sits confident, and lies down confident. Why is that? Because it is out of the hunter’s range. In the same way, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra, put out his eyes without a trace, and gone where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:35: Furthermore, mendicants, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and confidence, and unification of mind, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:36: Furthermore, mendicants, with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one lives in bliss.’ This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:37: Furthermore, mendicants, giving up pleasure and pain, and ending former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:38: Furthermore, mendicants, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space. This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:39: Furthermore, mendicants, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Buddha went to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. Now at that time several mendicants were sitting together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka discussing the Dhamma. The Buddha stood outside the gate waiting for the discussion to end. When he knew that the discussion was over, he coughed and knocked on the bar. The mendicants opened the door for the Buddha. The Buddha entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat on the seat spread out. When he was seated he addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What was the unfinished conversation?” “Sir, our unfinished conversation was about the Buddha himself when the Buddha arrived.” “Good, mendicants! It’s appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith to sit together and discuss the Dhamma. When you come together, you have two duties: to discuss the Dhamma or to maintain noble silence.
translations.mn26:40: Furthermore, mendicants, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness. This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:41: Furthermore, mendicants, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. This is called … the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:5: Mendicants, there are these two searches: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what is the ignoble search? It’s when someone who is themselves liable to rebirth seeks what is liable to rebirth. Themselves liable to old age, they seek what is liable to old age. Themselves liable to sickness, they seek what is liable to sickness. Themselves liable to death, they seek what is liable to death. Themselves liable to sorrow, they seek what is liable to sorrow. Themselves liable to defilement, they seek what is liable to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what do you call ‘liable to rebirth’? Partners and children, mendicants, are liable to rebirth. Male and female bondservants are liable to rebirth. Goats and sheep are liable to rebirth. Chickens and pigs are liable to rebirth. Elephants, cows, horses, and mares are liable to rebirth. Gold and money are liable to rebirth. These attachments are liable to rebirth. Tied, fainting, and attached to them, someone who is themselves liable to rebirth seeks what is liable to rebirth.
translations.mn27:12: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family. Hearing that teaching, they gain faith in the Realized One. Possessing that faith, they reflect: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open. It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell. Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’ After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small circle of relatives. They shave off their hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having thus gone forth and possessing the monks' training and way of life, he abandons the killing of living creatures and abstains from killing living creatures; with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; taking only what is given, expecting only what is given, by not stealing he abides in purity. Abandoning unchastity, he observes celibacy, living apart, abstaining from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse. Abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth, is trustworthy and reliable, one who is no deceiver of the world. Abandoning malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide those people from these, nor does he repeat to these people what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide these people from those; thus he is one who reunites those who are divided, a promoter of friendships, who enjoys concord, rejoices in concord, delights in concord, a speaker of words that promote concord. Abandoning harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, and lovably, as go to the heart, are courteous, desired by many and agreeable to many. Abandoning idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is fact, speaks on what is good, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the right time he speaks such words as are worth recording, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial. He abstains from injuring seeds and plants. He eats only in one part of the day, refraining from food at night and from eating at the wrong time. He abstains from dancing, singing, music, and theatrical shows. He abstains from wearing garlands, smartening himself with scents, and embellishing himself with unguents. He abstains from high and big beds. He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting men and women slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting fowl and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and land. He abstains from running messages and errands. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from dealing with false weights, false metals, and false measures. He abstains from the crooked ways of bribery, deception, and fraud. He abstains from mutilating, executing, imprisoning, highway robbery, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with robes to protect his body and with almsfood to maintain his stomach, and wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it goes, flies with its wings as its only burden, so too the monk is content with robes to protect his body and with almsfood to maintain his stomach, and wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him. Possessing this aggregate of noble virtue, he experiences within himself a bliss that is blameless.
translations.mn27:15: On seeing a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade him, he practices the way of its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear... On smelling an odor with the nose... On tasting a flavor with the tongue... On touching a tangible with the body... On cognizing a mind-object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade him, he practices the way of its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. Possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself a bliss that is unsullied.
translations.mn27:16: He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking away; he acts with clear comprehension when flexing and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, consuming food, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Possessing this noble aggregate of virtue, this noble contentment, this noble restraint of the faculties, and this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: On returning from his almsround, after his meal, he sits down, folds his legs crosswise, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he abides with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning dullness and drowsiness, he abides free from dullness and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from dullness and drowsiness. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he abides unagitated with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he abides having gone beyond doubt, without perplexity about wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, a track of the Tathāgata, a slashing of the Tathāgata. But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is a fully enlightened Buddha, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:2: At that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out of Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares. He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar. Seeing him, he said: “So where is Master Vacchāyana coming from in the middle of the day?” “I am coming, sir, from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.” “What does Master Vacchāyana think of the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom? He is wise, I suppose?” “Who am I, sir, and who is the ascetic Gotama to know his lucidity of wisdom? Surely only one like him could know the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom.” “Master Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise indeed.” “Who am I, sir, and who is the ascetic Gotama to praise him? Master Gotama is praised by the praised as the best of gods and humans.” “But seeing what benefit is Master Vacchāyana so devoted to the ascetic Gotama?”
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has internal clarity and confidence, and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is born of concentration and filled with rapture and pleasure. This too is called, brahmin … the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one lives in bliss.’ This too is called, brahmin … the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, giving up pleasure and pain, and ending former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. This too is called, brahmin, a footprint of the Realized One, something scraped by the Realized One, something marked by the Realized One. But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha, the teaching is well explained by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.’
translations.mn27:3: “Suppose, sir, a skilled elephant tracker were to enter an elephant forest. He might see a large elephant footprint in the elephant forest, long in length and broad in width. He would come to the conclusion: ‘This is a truly big elephant.’ In the same way, sir, when I saw four footprints in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha, the teaching is well explained by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.’
translations.mn27:4: What four? Here, sir, I see certain learned nobles who are clever, knowledgeable in the doctrines of others, sharp as hair-splitting archers; they wander about, as it were, demolishing views with their wisdom. They hear: ‘The ascetic Gotama is visiting such and such a village or town.’ They formulate a question: ‘We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If he answers like this, we will refute his doctrine like this. If he answers like that, we will refute his doctrine like that.’ They hear: ‘The ascetic Gotama has arrived at such and such a village or town.’ They go to the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, urges, rouses, and encourages them with a talk on the Dhamma. Instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged by the ascetic Gotama with a talk on the Dhamma, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama the question, so how could they refute his doctrine? Instead, they become disciples of the ascetic Gotama. When I saw this first footprint in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha, the teaching is well explained by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.’
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went up to the Blessed One, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi told the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the wanderer Pilotika. When he had spoken, the Blessed One said to him: “The simile of the elephant footprint is not yet complete in detail, brahmin. But listen, brahmin, and pay close attention to how the simile of the elephant footprint is complete in detail; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn28:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the mendicants: “Reverends, mendicants!” “Reverend,” those mendicants replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:10: If, friends, while that mendicant is recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful is not established, he feels stirred and a sense of urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, not a gain; it is badly gotten for me, not well gotten, that while I recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful is not established.’ Just as a daughter-in-law, seeing her father-in-law, feels stirred and a sense of urgency; so too, friends, if while that mendicant is recollecting the Buddha... equanimity based on the skillful is not established, he feels stirred and a sense of urgency... But if, friends, while that mendicant is recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful is established, he is pleased by that. Even this much, friends, is enough for a mendicant to have done much.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element becomes agitated. It sweeps away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friends, when the waters in the great ocean recede by a hundred leagues, two hundred leagues, three hundred leagues, four hundred leagues, five hundred leagues, six hundred leagues, seven hundred leagues. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands only seven palm-trees deep, six palm-trees deep, five palm-trees deep, four palm-trees deep, three palm-trees deep, two palm-trees deep, one palm-tree deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands seven fathoms deep, six fathoms deep, five fathoms deep, four fathoms deep, three fathoms deep, two fathoms deep, one fathom deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands half a fathom deep, waist deep, knee deep, ankle deep. There comes a time, friends, when there is not even enough water in the great ocean to wet a finger-joint. For this external water element, friends, so vast, impermanence will be discerned, the nature to decay will be discerned, the nature to vanish will be discerned, the nature to change will be discerned.
translations.mn28:13: What then of this ephemeral body grasped by craving—[to think] ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? That is not the case for him... [and so on]...
translations.mn28:14: If, friends, while that mendicant is recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful is established, he is pleased by that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friends, when the external fire element becomes agitated. It burns villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. Having reached the edge of green grass, or the edge of a road, or the edge of a rock, or the water's edge, or a delightful region, it goes out for lack of fuel. There comes a time, friends, when they seek fire even with a chicken feather or a snippet of tendon. For this external fire element, friends, so vast, impermanence will be discerned, the nature to decay will be discerned, the nature to vanish will be discerned, the nature to change will be discerned. What then of this ephemeral body grasped by craving—[to think] ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’?
translations.mn28:18-20: That is not the case for him... [and so on]... If, friends, while that mendicant is recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful is established, he is pleased by that. Even this much, friends, is enough for a mendicant to have done much.
translations.mn28:2: Just as, friends, the footprints of any living beings that walk can all fit inside an elephant’s footprint, and the elephant’s footprint is said to be the greatest of them because of its size; so too, friends, all skillful qualities can be included in the four noble truths. In which four? In the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friends, when the external air element becomes agitated. It sweeps away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friends, in the last month of summer, when they seek wind with a palm-leaf fan or a fan, and even the grasses in the drip-fringe of the thatch do not stir. For this external air element, friends, so vast, impermanence will be discerned, the nature to decay will be discerned, the nature to vanish will be discerned, the nature to change will be discerned. What then of this ephemeral body grasped by craving—[to think] ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? That is not the case for him.
translations.mn28:23: If others abuse, revile, scold, and harass that mendicant, he understands: ‘This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me. That is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.’ He sees that contact is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, volitional formations are impermanent, and consciousness is impermanent. His mind leaps into the element alone, becomes confident, settles, and resolves.
translations.mn28:24: Friends, if others treat that monk with unwanted, disagreeable, unpleasant ways—by contact with fists, clods, sticks, or knives—he understands: 'This body is of such a nature that contacts with fists, clods, sticks, and knives affect it. But this has been said by the Blessed One in the Advice on the Simile of the Saw: "Monks, even if bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, anyone who gave rise to a mind of hate there would not be carrying out my teaching." My energy shall be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and unperturbed, my mind concentrated and one-pointed. Let contacts with fists, clods, sticks, and knives affect this body. For this is how the Buddhas' teaching is practiced.'
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friends, enclosed space is reckoned as 'a house' dependent on timber, creepers, grass, and clay, so too enclosed space is reckoned as 'a form' dependent on bones, sinews, flesh, and skin.
