translations.mn28:27: Friends, if the internal eye is intact but external forms do not come into range and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness. If the internal eye is intact and external forms come into range, but there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness. But when, friends, the internal eye is intact, external forms come into range, and there is corresponding engagement, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: Whatever form there is for one thus evolved is included in the grasping aggregate of form; whatever feeling there is for one thus evolved is included in the grasping aggregate of feeling; whatever perception... is included in the grasping aggregate of perception; whatever volitional formations... are included in the grasping aggregate of volitional formations; whatever consciousness... is included in the grasping aggregate of consciousness. He understands: 'So, it seems, this is the inclusion, gathering, and grouping of these five grasping aggregates. Now, this has been said by the Blessed One: "One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination." And these five grasping aggregates are dependently originated. Whatever desire, adherence, attraction, and attachment there is regarding these five grasping aggregates is the origin of suffering. Whatever disciplining of desire and lust, abandoning of desire and lust there is regarding these five grasping aggregates is the cessation of suffering.' Even to this extent, friends, much has been done by the monk.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering. And what, friends, are the five grasping aggregates? They are: the grasping aggregate of form, the grasping aggregate of feeling, the grasping aggregate of perception, the grasping aggregate of volitional formations, and the grasping aggregate of consciousness.
translations.mn28:37: If the mind is intact but external mind-objects do not come into range and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element flares up. At that time the external earth element disappears. So, friends, when even in this external earth element, so vast, impermanence will be discerned, destruction will be discerned, decay will be discerned, change will be discerned, what then of this body, grasped by craving, lasting but a while? Is there 'I' or 'mine' or 'am I'? No, there is not.
translations.mn29:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rajagaha on the Vulture's Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the monks regarding Devadatta:
translations.mn29:3: Here, monks, some clansman goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, thinking: 'I am immersed in birth, old age, and death, in sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.' Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, and his intention is not fulfilled. He does not laud himself or disparage others on account of that gain, honor, and renown. He does not become intoxicated or negligent on account of that gain, honor, and renown, and he does not fall into negligence. Being diligent, he achieves success in ethical conduct. He is pleased with that success in ethical conduct, and his intention is fulfilled. On account of that success in ethical conduct he lauds himself and disparages others: 'I am ethical, of good character, but these other monks are unethical, of bad character.' He becomes intoxicated and negligent on account of that success in ethical conduct, he falls into negligence, and being negligent he lives in suffering. Suppose, monks, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass over the heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, pass over the sapwood, pass over the inner bark, and cutting off the outer bark, were to take it away thinking it was heartwood. A man with good sight, seeing him, might say: 'This good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know inner bark, did not know outer bark, did not know twigs and leaves. Thus this good man... cutting off the outer bark, took it away thinking it was heartwood; and whatever purpose he had to serve with heartwood, that purpose will not be served.'
translations.mn2:10: And what are the things unfit for attention that they do not attend to? They are things such that when they attend to them, the unarisen defilement of sensuality arises, or the arisen defilement of sensuality grows; the unarisen defilement of continued existence arises, or the arisen defilement of continued existence grows; the unarisen defilement of ignorance arises, or the arisen defilement of ignorance grows—these are the things unfit for attention that they do not attend to. And what are the things fit for attention that they attend to? They are things such that when they attend to them, the unarisen defilement of sensuality does not arise, or the arisen defilement of sensuality is abandoned; the unarisen defilement of continued existence does not arise, or the arisen defilement of continued existence is abandoned; the unarisen defilement of ignorance does not arise, or the arisen defilement of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things fit for attention that they attend to. Because they do not attend to things unfit for attention and attend to things fit for attention, unarisen defilements do not arise, and arisen defilements are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: They attend rationally: ‘This is suffering’; they attend rationally: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; they attend rationally: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; they attend rationally: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’. When they attend rationally in this way, three fetters are abandoned: identity view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances. These are called the defilements that should be given up by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Defilements to be Given Up by Restraint. And what are the defilements that should be given up by restraint? Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, lives restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty. For if they did not live restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, defilements that are vexing and feverish might arise. But when they live restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, those defilements that are vexing and feverish do not arise. Reflecting rationally, they live restrained with the restraint of the ear faculty … the nose faculty … the tongue faculty … the body faculty … the mind faculty. For if they did not live restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, defilements that are vexing and feverish might arise. But when they live restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, those defilements that are vexing and feverish do not arise. For if they did not live restrained with restraint, defilements that are vexing and feverish might arise. But when they live restrained with restraint, those defilements that are vexing and feverish do not arise. These are called the defilements that should be given up by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Reflecting rationally, they use almsfood: ‘Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for fattening, not for beautification, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the spiritual life, thinking: “Thus I shall put an end to old feelings and shall not create new feelings, and I will be blameless and live at ease.”’
translations.mn2:16: Reflecting rationally, they use medicine and requisites for the sick: ‘Only for the purpose of warding off feelings of sickness that have arisen, and for the maximum freedom from affliction.’
translations.mn2:17: For if they did not use them, defilements that are vexing and feverish might arise. But when they use them, those defilements that are vexing and feverish do not arise. These are called the defilements that should be given up by using.
translations.mn2:3: “Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see. For one who knows what and sees what? Rational attention and irrational attention. When one attends irrationally, unarisen defilements arise and arisen defilements grow. When one attends rationally, unarisen defilements do not arise and arisen defilements are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And what are the things unfit for attention that they attend to? They are things such that when they attend to them, the unarisen defilement of sensuality arises, or the arisen defilement of sensuality grows; the unarisen defilement of continued existence arises, or the arisen defilement of continued existence grows; the unarisen defilement of ignorance arises, or the arisen defilement of ignorance grows—these are the things unfit for attention that they attend to. And what are the things fit for attention that they do not attend to? They are things such that when they attend to them, the unarisen defilement of sensuality does not arise, or the arisen defilement of sensuality is abandoned; the unarisen defilement of continued existence does not arise, or the arisen defilement of continued existence is abandoned; the unarisen defilement of ignorance does not arise, or the arisen defilement of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things fit for attention that they do not attend to.
translations.mn2:7: Because of attending to things unfit for attention and not attending to things fit for attention, unarisen defilements arise and arisen defilements grow. They attend irrationally in this way: ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?’ Or else they are inwardly perplexed about the present thus: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
translations.mn2:8: When he attends improperly in this way, one of six views arises in him. The view 'self exists for me' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'no self exists for me' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with self' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I perceive not-self with self' arises in him as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with not-self' arises in him as true and established; or else he has some such view as this: 'It is this self of mine that speaks and feels, that experiences here and there the result of good and bad actions; but this self of mine is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and it will endure as long as eternity.' This is called the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the contortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views. Fettered by the fetter of views, the uninstructed worldling is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; he is not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn2:9: But the instructed noble disciple—who sees the noble ones and is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma, who sees men of integrity and is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma—understands what things are fit for attention and what things are unfit for attention. Since that is so, he does not attend to those things unfit for attention and he attends to those things fit for attention.
translations.mn31:10: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But while you abide thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter upon and abide in the first jhana, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This is a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, which we have attained while abiding diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.mn31:11-13: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But is there any other superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that you have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, we enter upon and abide in the second jhana, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is another superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that we have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding.”
translations.mn31:14: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But is there any other superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that you have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the fading away as well of rapture, we abide in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, we enter upon and abide in the third jhana, on account of which noble ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’ This is another superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that we have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding.”
translations.mn31:15: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But is there any other superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that you have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, we enter upon and abide in the fourth jhana, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is another superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that we have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding.”
translations.mn31:16: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But is there any other superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that you have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ we enter upon and abide in the base of infinite space. This is another superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that we have attained for the surmounting of that abiding, for the subsiding of that abiding.”
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila with a talk on the Dhamma, after which he rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: Now on that occasion the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila were abiding in the Gosinga Sal-tree Wood.
translations.mn31:3: Then, when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from meditation and went to the Gosinga Sal-tree Wood. The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming in the distance and told him: “Do not enter this wood, recluse. There are three clansmen here who love their own company; do not disturb them.”
translations.mn31:4: The Venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper speaking with the Blessed One. He told the park keeper: “Friend park keeper, do not keep the Blessed One out. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then the Venerable Anuruddha went to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimbila and said: “Come out, venerable sirs! Come out, venerable sirs! Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”
translations.mn31:5: Then Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila went out to meet the Blessed One. One took the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat on the seat prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Those venerable ones bowed to the Blessed One and sat to one side. While Venerable Anuruddha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “I hope you are keeping well, Anuruddha, I hope you are comfortable, I hope you are not having trouble getting almsfood?” “We are keeping well, Blessed One, we are comfortable, Blessed One, and we are not having trouble getting almsfood, sir.”
translations.mn31:6: “But I hope, Anuruddha, that you are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?” “Indeed, sir, we are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.” “But how is it, Anuruddha, that you live in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?”
translations.mn31:9: “Indeed, sir, we live diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “But how is it, Anuruddha, that you live diligent, ardent, and resolute?” “Here, sir, whoever returns first from the village with almsfood prepares the seats, sets out the water for drinking and washing, and sets out the refuse bucket. Whoever returns last eats the leftovers if there are any and he wishes to; if not, he throws them out where there is little grass or sinks them in water without living creatures. He puts away the seats, the water for drinking and washing, and the refuse bucket, and sweeps the refectory. Whoever sees a water pot, washing pot, or toilet pot empty or void sets it up. If he cannot handle it alone, he summons a companion by hand signal and we set it up by joining hands; but we do not break into speech for that reason. And every five days we sit together for the whole night discussing the Dhamma. That is how we live diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.mn36:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: “I have such confidence in Master Gotama. For Master Gotama is developed in body and developed in mind.” “Clearly, Aggivessana, your words are offensive and intended to provoke, but still I will answer you. Since I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, it is not possible for a pleasant feeling that has arisen to invade my mind and remain, or for a painful feeling that has arisen to invade my mind and remain.”
translations.mn36:12: “Why should it not be so, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my awakening, while I was still only an unawakened Bodhisatta, it occurred to me: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.’”
translations.mn36:2: Now at that time, it being morning, the Blessed One had dressed, and taking his bowl and robe, wanted to enter Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Suppose I were to crush, clench, and torment my mind with my mind, with my teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth.’ So, with my teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I crushed, clenched, and tormented my mind with my mind. While I did so, sweat ran from my armpits. Just as a strong man, seizing a weaker man by the head or shoulders, might crush, clench, and torment him, so too, with my teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I crushed, clenched, and tormented my mind with my mind, and sweat ran from my armpits. My energy was roused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, but my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful striving. But such painful feeling that arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:26: Some deities saw me and said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’ Other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying; the ascetic Gotama is an arahant, and that is how an arahant lives.’
translations.mn36:27: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Suppose I were to practice cutting off food entirely.’ Then deities approached me and said: ‘Good sir, do not practice cutting off food entirely. If you do so, we will infuse divine nourishment into your pores, and you will survive on that.’ It occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘If I claim to be completely fasting while these deities infuse divine nourishment into my pores and I survive on that, that would be a lie on my part.’ So I dismissed those deities, saying: ‘There is no need.’
translations.mn36:28: Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Suppose I were to take very little food, a handful each time, whether of mung bean soup, vetch soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup.’ So I took very little food, a handful each time, whether of mung bean soup, vetch soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup. Because of eating so little, my body became extremely emaciated. My limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems because of eating so little. My backside became like a camel’s hoof because of eating so little. My spine stood out like a string of beads because of eating so little. My ribs were as gaunt as the rafters of an old shed because of eating so little. The gleam of my eyes sank deep in their sockets, looking like the gleam of water deep in a deep well because of eating so little. My scalp shriveled and withered like a bitter gourd cut while raw and withered by wind and sun because of eating so little. If I thought ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I grabbed my backbone; if I thought ‘I will touch my backbone,’ I grabbed the skin of my belly, so much did the skin of my belly cling to my backbone because of eating so little. If I thought ‘I will defecate or urinate,’ I fell over on my face right there because of eating so little. If I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell from my body as I rubbed, because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:29: And, Aggivessana, humans seeing me said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’ Some said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is brown.’ Some said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown, he has a mangura-fish skin color.’ To such an extent was the pure, bright color of my skin destroyed by eating so little.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka, the Nigantha’s son, while walking and wandering for exercise, went to the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: “Sir, this Saccaka the Nigantha’s son is coming, a debater, a clever speaker, regarded by many as a saint. He wants to discredit the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would sit for a moment out of compassion.” The Blessed One sat on the seat prepared. Then Saccaka went up to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Saccaka said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, racking, piercing feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is nothing beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, racking, piercing feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is nothing beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful, racking, piercing feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is nothing beyond this. But by this grueling practice of austerities, I have not attained any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to awakening?’
translations.mn36:32: Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure, for that pleasure has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities?’ Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘I am not afraid of that pleasure, for that pleasure has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities.’
translations.mn36:34: So, Aggivessana, having eaten solid food and gathered my strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. But even such pleasant feeling that arose in me did not occupy my mind.
translations.mn36:38: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth... thus I recollected my manifold past lives, with their aspects and details.
translations.mn36:39: This was the first knowledge, which I attained in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed; knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed; light arose—as happens in one who is diligent, ardent, and resolute. But even such pleasant feeling that arose in me did not occupy my mind.
translations.mn36:4: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who live devoted to development of the body, but not to development of the mind. They experience bodily painful feeling. Formerly, Master Gotama, when one was touched by bodily painful feeling, thigh-stiffness would occur, or the heart would burst, or hot blood would gush from the mouth, or one would go mad, reaching mental derangement. For him, the mind follows the body, it comes under the sway of the body. Why is that? Because of the undeveloped state of the mind. But there are some ascetics and brahmins who live devoted to development of the mind, not to development of the body. They experience mental painful feeling. Formerly, Master Gotama, when one was touched by mental painful feeling, thigh-stiffness would occur, or the heart would burst, or hot blood would gush from the mouth, or one would go mad, reaching mental derangement. For him, the body follows the mind, it comes under the sway of the mind. Why is that? Because of the undeveloped state of the body. It occurs to me, Master Gotama: ‘Surely Master Gotama’s disciples live devoted to development of the mind, not to development of the body.’”
translations.mn36:40: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of corruptions, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood how beings pass on according to their actions...
translations.mn36:42: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of corruptions, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
translations.mn36:43: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’
translations.mn36:45: “I recall, Aggivessana, teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. And each person thinks: ‘The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma referring to me alone.’ But it should not be seen like that, Aggivessana; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others merely for the sake of instruction. At the end of that talk, Aggivessana, I steady, settle, unify, and concentrate my mind internally on that same sign of concentration in which I constantly dwell.” “That is convincing for Master Gotama, as it is for a worthy one, a fully awakened Buddha. But does Master Gotama recall sleeping during the day?”
translations.mn36:46: “I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after the meal, having returned from almsround, having folded my outer robe fourfold, lying down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, falling asleep.” “Some ascetics and brahmins, Master Gotama, call that abiding in delusion.” “One is not deluded or undeluded to that extent, Aggivessana. But as to how one is deluded or undeluded, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn36:47: “Aggivessana, whoever has not abandoned the taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death: him I call ‘deluded.’ For it is by non-abandonment of the taints that one is deluded. Aggivessana, whoever has abandoned the taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death: him I call ‘undeluded.’ For it is by abandonment of the taints that one is undeluded. The Tathāgata, Aggivessana, has abandoned the taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no more subject to future arising. Just as a palm tree with its top cut off is incapable of growing again, so too, Aggivessana, the Tathāgata has abandoned the taints that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no more subject to future arising.”
translations.mn36:5: “But, Aggivessana, what have you heard regarding development of the body?” “It is like this, Master Gotama: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla—these, Master Gotama, are naked ascetics, flouting conventions, licking their hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; they do not accept food brought or specially prepared or a meal invitation. They do not receive from a pot, from a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a pregnant woman, from a woman giving suck, from a woman lying with a man, from where food is advertised to be distributed, from where a dog is waiting, from where flies are swarming; they accept no fish or meat, they drink no liquor, wine, or fermented brew. They keep to one house, one morsel; two houses, two morsels... seven houses, seven morsels. They subsist on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls... on seven saucerfuls. They take food once a day, once every two days... once every seven days. Thus they dwell pursuing the practice of taking food at stated intervals, even up to half a month.”
translations.mn36:6: “But Aggivessana, do they subsist only on that much?” “No, Master Gotama. Sometimes, Master Gotama, they eat excellent solid foods, they eat excellent soft foods, they taste excellent delicacies, they drink excellent drinks. They make this body gather strength, grow, and fatten.” “What they abandoned earlier, Aggivessana, they gather up later; thus there is accumulation and loss for this body. But Aggivessana, have you heard of the development of the mind?” When asked by the Blessed One about the development of the mind, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son could not answer.
translations.mn36:8: “And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling arises in an uninstructed ordinary person. Touched by that pleasant feeling, he becomes lustful for pleasure and falls into lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, he sorrows, grieves, and laments, he weeps beating his breast and falls into confusion. For him, Aggivessana, the pleasant feeling that has arisen invades his mind and remains because his body is undeveloped. The painful feeling that has arisen invades his mind and remains because his mind is undeveloped. For anyone in whom, Aggivessana, in this double-sided way, arisen pleasant feeling invades the mind and remains because the body is undeveloped, and arisen painful feeling invades the mind and remains because the mind is undeveloped: that is how one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling arises in a well-instructed noble disciple. Touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not become lustful for pleasure and does not fall into lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, grieve, or lament, he does not weep beating his breast or fall into confusion. For him, Aggivessana, the pleasant feeling that has arisen does not invade his mind and remain because his body is developed. The painful feeling that has arisen does not invade his mind and remain because his mind is developed. For anyone in whom, Aggivessana, in this double-sided way, arisen pleasant feeling does not invade the mind and remain because the body is developed, and arisen painful feeling does not invade the mind and remain because the mind is developed. That is how, Aggivessana, one is developed in body and developed in mind.”
translations.mn38:10: “Bhikkhus, for one who doubts ‘Has this come to be?’, does uncertainty arise?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, for one who doubts ‘Is it produced by that nutriment?’, does uncertainty arise?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, for one who doubts ‘Is what has come to be subject to cessation with the cessation of that nutriment?’, does uncertainty arise?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:11: “Bhikkhus, for one who sees with right wisdom as it actually is that ‘This has come to be,’ is that uncertainty abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, for one who sees with right wisdom as it actually is that ‘It is produced by that nutriment,’ is that uncertainty abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, for one who sees with right wisdom as it actually is that ‘What has come to be is subject to cessation with the cessation of that nutriment,’ is that uncertainty abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:12: “Bhikkhus, are you free from uncertainty here that ‘This has come to be’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, are you free from uncertainty here that ‘It is produced by that nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, are you free from uncertainty here that ‘What has come to be is subject to cessation with the cessation of that nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:13: “Bhikkhus, has it been well seen with right wisdom as it actually is that ‘This has come to be’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, has it been well seen with right wisdom as it actually is that ‘It is produced by that nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, has it been well seen with right wisdom as it actually is that ‘What has come to be is subject to cessation with the cessation of that nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:14: “Bhikkhus, if you were to adhere to this view—so pure and so bright—if you were to cherish it, treasure it, and treat it as your own, would you then understand that the Dhamma has been taught by me with the simile of the raft, for crossing over, not for holding on to?” “No, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, if you were not to adhere to this view—so pure and so bright—if you were not to cherish it, treasure it, and treat it as your own, would you then understand that the Dhamma has been taught by me with the simile of the raft, for crossing over, not for holding on to?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:15: “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be or for the assistance of those seeking birth. What four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; consciousness as the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base; with the sixfold base as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: “Good, bhikkhus. So you say thus, and I also say thus: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.’ That is: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base; with the sixfold base as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time a pernicious view had arisen in the monk Sāti, the fisherman’s son, as follows: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, not another.”
translations.mn38:20: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of continued existence; with the cessation of continued existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: “Good, mendicants. So you say this, and I say this: when this doesn't exist, that doesn't come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with the cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of continued existence; with the cessation of continued existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:23: Mendicants, knowing and seeing thus, would you run back to the past: ‘Did we exist in the past? Did we not exist in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?’?” “No, sir.” “Mendicants, knowing and seeing thus, would you run forward to the future: ‘Shall we exist in the future? Shall we not exist in the future? What shall we be in the future? How shall we be in the future? Having been what, what shall we become in the future?’?” “No, sir.”
translations.mn38:25: “Good, mendicants. You have been guided by me with this Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced by the wise for themselves. For it was said: ‘This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.’ And it is because of this that it was said.
translations.mn38:26: Mendicants, the descent of the embryo takes place through the union of three things. Here, there is the union of the mother and father, but the mother is not in season, and the gandhabba is not present—in this case the descent of the embryo does not take place. Here, there is the union of the mother and father, and the mother is in season, but the gandhabba is not present—in this case the descent of the embryo does not take place. But when there is the union of the mother and father, and the mother is in season, and the gandhabba is present—through the union of these three things the descent of the embryo takes place.
translations.mn38:27: The mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months with great anxiety as a heavy burden. Then, at the end of nine or ten months, the mother gives birth with great anxiety as a heavy burden. When it is born, she nourishes it with her own blood. For in the Noble One’s discipline, ‘blood’ is a term for mother’s milk.
translations.mn38:28: Then, as that boy grows up and his faculties mature, he plays with the toys of children, such as: a toy plow, tip-cat, somersaults, toy windmills, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows.
translations.mn38:39: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, he enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. Furthermore, with the subsiding of placing the mind and keeping it connected, he enters and remains in the second absorption... the third absorption... the fourth absorption.
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the mendicants: “What do you think, mendicants? Has this monk Sāti, the fisherman’s son, kindled even a spark of wisdom in this teaching and training?” “How could that be, sir? No, sir.” When this was said, the monk Sāti, the fisherman’s son, sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to speak. Then the Blessed One, knowing that Sāti was silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, head down, brooding, unable to speak, said to him: “You will be known, foolish man, by your own pernicious view. I will question the mendicants on this.”
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants, do you also understand the Dhamma taught by me as this monk Sāti, the fisherman’s son, does when he misrepresents us by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and makes much bad merit?” “No, sir. For in many ways the Blessed One has stated that consciousness is dependently originated, that apart from a condition there is no origination of consciousness.” “Good, good, mendicants. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way. For in many ways I have stated that consciousness is dependently originated, that apart from a condition there is no origination of consciousness. But this monk Sāti, the fisherman’s son, misrepresents us by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and makes much bad merit. This will be for that foolish man’s lasting harm and suffering.”
translations.mn38:9: “Mendicants, do you see: ‘This has come to be’?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see: ‘It originated with food’?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see: ‘With the cessation of food, what has come to be is liable to cease’?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn41:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is unrighteous and unbalanced conduct threefold by way of mind? Here, someone is covetous. They covet the wealth and property of others: ‘Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!’ They have a malevolent mind and corrupt intent: ‘May these beings be killed or slaughtered or annihilated or destroyed or may they not exist!’ They have wrong view and distorted perspective: ‘There is no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offering. There is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There are no spontaneously reborn beings. There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are rightly practiced and rightly accomplished, who describe this world and the other world having realized it with their own insight.’ That is how unrighteous and unbalanced conduct is threefold by way of mind. It is because of such unrighteous and unbalanced conduct that some beings, when the body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is righteous and balanced conduct threefold by way of body? Here, someone, abandoning the killing of living creatures, abstains from killing living creatures. They have laid aside the rod and weapon; they are conscientious and merciful, living full of compassion for the welfare of all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, they abstain from taking what is not given. They do not take by way of theft the wealth and property of others, whether in the village or the wilderness. Abandoning sexual misconduct, they abstain from sexual misconduct. They do not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, parents, brother, sister, relatives, or clan; or who are protected by the law; or who have a husband; or who are protected by a punishment; or even those garlanded in token of betrothal. That is how righteous and balanced conduct is threefold by way of body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is righteous and balanced conduct fourfold by way of speech? Here, someone, abandoning false speech, abstains from false speech. When summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked as a witness: ‘Please, mister, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ Seeing, they say ‘I see.’ So they don’t deliberately tell a lie for their own sake, for the sake of another, or for some trifle. Abandoning divisive speech, they abstain from divisive speech. What they hear here they don’t tell there to break those people apart. What they hear there they don’t tell here to break these people apart. Thus reconciling those who are divided, supporting those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, enjoying harmony, they speak words that promote harmony. Abandoning harsh speech, they abstain from harsh speech. They speak words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, going to the heart, polite, likable and agreeable to the people. Abandoning idle chatter, they abstain from idle chatter. They speak at the right time, speak what is true, speak on what is good, speak on the teaching and training. They speak words worth recording, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial. That is how righteous and balanced conduct is fourfold by way of speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is righteous and balanced conduct threefold by way of mind? Here, someone is not covetous. They do not covet the wealth and property of others: ‘Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!’ They have a kind heart and loving intent: ‘May these beings be free from enmity and ill will, untroubled and happy, may they look after themselves!’ They have right view and an undistorted perspective: ‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offering. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world, there is the other world. There is mother, there is father. There are spontaneously reborn beings. There are ascetics and brahmins in the world who are rightly practiced and rightly accomplished, who describe this world and the other world having realized it with their own insight.’ That is how righteous and balanced conduct is threefold by way of mind. It is because of such righteous and balanced conduct that some beings, when the body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.
translations.mn41:15: If a person of righteous and balanced conduct should wish: ‘If only, when my body breaks up, after death, I might be reborn in the company of well-to-do aristocrats!’ it is possible that, when their body breaks up, after death, they will be reborn in the company of well-to-do aristocrats. Why is that? Because they have righteous and balanced conduct.
translations.mn41:3: Then the brahmin householders of Sālā went up to the Buddha. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their joined palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. Seated to one side they said to the Buddha:
translations.mn41:4: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings, when the body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell? And what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings, when the body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?”
translations.mn41:43: If, householders, one who conducts himself in accordance with the Dhamma, who conducts himself righteously, should wish: ‘Oh, that by the destruction of the taints I might realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, abide in it!’—it is possible that, by the destruction of the taints, he might realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, abide in it. Why is that? Because he conducts himself in accordance with the Dhamma, because he conducts himself righteously.
translations.mn41:5: Householders, it is by reason of unrighteous conduct, by reason of unprincipled conduct that some beings here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell. Householders, it is by reason of righteous conduct, by reason of principled conduct that some beings here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.
translations.mn41:6: “We do not understand in detail the meaning of this utterance spoken in brief by Master Gotama, the meaning of which has not been analysed in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach us the Dhamma in such a way that we might understand in detail the meaning of this utterance spoken in brief by Master Gotama, the meaning of which has not been analysed in detail.” “Then, householders, listen and attend closely to what I shall say.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin householders of Sālā replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn41:8: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous conduct, unprincipled conduct by body? Here, householders, someone is a killer of living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings. He is a taker of what is not given; he takes by way of theft the wealth and property of others that is in the village or in the forest. He is one who misconducts himself in sensual pleasures; he has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, or relatives, who have a husband, who are protected by law, or with those who are garlanded in token of betrothal. That is how there is threefold unrighteous conduct, unprincipled conduct by body.
translations.mn41:9: And how, householders, is there fourfold unrighteous conduct, unprincipled conduct by speech? Here, householders, someone speaks falsehood. When summoned to a council, to an assembly, to his relatives’ presence, to his guild, or to the royal family’s presence, and questioned as a witness thus: ‘So, good man, tell what you know,’ not knowing, he says, ‘I know,’ or knowing, he says, ‘I do not know’; not seeing, he says, ‘I see,’ or seeing, he says, ‘I do not see’; in full awareness he speaks falsehood for his own ends, or for another’s ends, or for some trifling worldly end. He speaks maliciously. He repeats elsewhere what he hears here in order to divide [those people] from these, or he repeats to these people what he hears elsewhere in order to divide [them] from those; thus he is one who divides those who are united, a creator of divisions, one who enjoys factions, rejoices in factions, delights in factions, a speaker of words that create factions. He speaks harshly. He utters such words as are rough, hard, hurtful to others, offensive to others, bordering on anger, not conducive to concentration. He is a gossip. He speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is not fact, speaks what is useless, speaks contrary to the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the wrong time he speaks words with no purpose, undefined, rambling, and pointless. That is how there is fourfold unrighteous conduct, unprincipled conduct by speech.
translations.mn4:20: Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘What if, on those nights that are recognized and celebrated—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—I were to stay in such frightening and hair-raising resting places as park shrines, forest shrines, and tree shrines? Perhaps I might encounter that fear and dread.’ And so, brahmin, at a later time, on those nights that are recognized and celebrated—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—I stayed in such frightening and hair-raising resting places as park shrines, forest shrines, and tree shrines. And while I was staying there, a wild animal would come, or a peacock would break a twig, or the wind would rustle the fallen leaves. Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Is this that fear and dread coming?’ Then it occurred to me: ‘Why do I dwell always expecting fear? What if I were to subdue that fear and dread while keeping the same posture that I am in when it comes upon me?’ While I walked, that fear and dread came upon me; I neither stood nor sat nor lay down until I had subdued that fear and dread while walking. While I stood, that fear and dread came upon me; I neither walked nor sat nor lay down until I had subdued that fear and dread while standing. While I sat, that fear and dread came upon me; I neither lay down nor stood nor walked until I had subdued that fear and dread while sitting. While I lay down, that fear and dread came upon me; I neither sat nor stood nor walked until I had subdued that fear and dread while lying down.
translations.mn4:22-26: My energy was roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, my body was tranquil and untroubled, my mind was immersed in samādhi and unified. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and confidence, and unification of mind, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. And with the fading away of rapture, I entered and remained in the third absorption, where I meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one lives in bliss.’ With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the ending of former happiness and sadness, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pain or pleasure, with purity of mindfulness and equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability—I extended it toward recollection of past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, i.e., one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction and expansion: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance. Such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from there, I arose elsewhere. There too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance. Such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from there, I arose here.’ Thus I recollected my manifold past lives, with their aspects and particulars.
translations.mn4:28: This was the first knowledge, brahmin, attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed; knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed; light arose—as happens for a meditator who is heedful, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability—I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘These dear beings were possessed of bad conduct of body, speech, and mind. They reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and acted accordingly. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. But these dear beings were possessed of good conduct of body, speech, and mind. They did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and acted accordingly. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood how beings pass on according to their actions.
translations.mn4:3: Before my awakening, brahmin, while I was still just an unawakened Bodhisatta, I thought: ‘Remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness are hard to endure, seclusion is hard to practice, solitude is hard to enjoy. One would think the forests must rob a monk of his mind, if he has no concentration.’
translations.mn4:30: This was the second knowledge, brahmin, attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed; knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed; light arose—as happens for a meditator who is heedful, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: Now, brahmin, you might think: ‘Perhaps the ascetic Gotama is not yet free of greed, hate, and delusion, which is why he resorts to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness.’ But you should not see it like that. I resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness seeing two benefits: seeing a pleasant abiding for myself in the present life, and having compassion for future generations.
translations.mn4:4: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness with unpurified bodily conduct, they summon unskillful fear and dread because of the defect of their unpurified bodily conduct. But I do not resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness with unpurified bodily conduct; I am purified in bodily conduct. I am one of those noble ones who resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness with purified bodily conduct.’ Seeing this purity of bodily conduct in myself, I felt even more confident about staying in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness with unpurified verbal conduct … unpurified mental conduct … unpurified livelihood, they summon unskillful fear and dread because of the defect of their unpurified livelihood.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness with unpurified livelihood; I am purified in livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: I am one of those noble ones who resort to remote jungle-thickets in the wilderness with purified livelihood.’ Seeing this purity of livelihood in myself, I felt even more confident about staying in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Vesālī in the little village of Beluva. Now at that time the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanagara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant, having totally transcended perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. He reflects like this: ‘Even this attainment of the dimension of infinite space is produced and intended. Whatever is produced and intended is impermanent and liable to cessation.’ Standing on that … he attains the supreme sanctuary.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant, having totally transcended the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. He reflects like this: ‘Even this attainment of the dimension of nothingness is produced and intended. Whatever is produced and intended is impermanent and liable to cessation.’ Standing on that, he attains the ending of defilements. If he does not attain the ending of defilements, then because of that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the ending of the five lower fetters, he is reborn spontaneously and there he is extinguished, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is one thing explained by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, whereby the unliberated mind of a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute is liberated, or the unended defilements come to an end, or the unattained supreme sanctuary is attained.
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to Venerable Ānanda: “Sir Ānanda, it is just as if a man seeking one opening to a treasure were to find eleven openings to a treasure all at once. In the same way, sir, while seeking one door to the deathless, I have found eleven doors to the deathless for the purpose of development. Just as if a man had a house with eleven doors, and if that house were burning, he could keep himself safe by any one of those doors. In the same way, sir, I will be able to keep myself safe by any one of these eleven doors to the deathless. Sir, these wanderers of other sects will look for a teacher’s fee for their teacher; so why shouldn't I make an offering to Venerable Ānanda?”
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka went to the Cock’s Park and approached a certain monk. He bowed to that monk and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to that monk: “Sir, where is Venerable Ānanda staying at present? We want to see Venerable Ānanda.” “Householder, Venerable Ānanda is staying at Vesālī in the village of Beluva.”
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka, having finished his business at Pāṭaliputta, went to Vesālī, to the village of Beluva, and to Venerable Ānanda. He bowed to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to Venerable Ānanda: “Sir Ānanda, is there any one thing explained by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, whereby the unliberated mind of a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute is liberated, or the unended defilements come to an end, or the unattained supreme sanctuary is attained?” “There is one thing, householder, explained by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, whereby the unliberated mind of a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute is liberated, or the unended defilements come to an end, or the unattained supreme sanctuary is attained.” “But what is that one thing, sir Ānanda, explained by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, whereby the unliberated mind of a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute is liberated, or the unended defilements come to an end, or the unattained supreme sanctuary is attained?”
translations.mn52:4: “Here, householder, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, a mendicant enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. He reflects like this: ‘Even this first absorption is produced and intended. Whatever is produced and intended is impermanent and liable to cessation.’ Standing on that, he attains the ending of defilements. If he does not attain the ending of defilements, then because of that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the ending of the five lower fetters, he is reborn spontaneously and there he is extinguished, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is one thing explained by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, whereby the unliberated mind of a mendicant who dwells diligent, keen, and resolute is liberated, or the unended defilements come to an end, or the unattained supreme sanctuary is attained.
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will. He reflects like this: ‘Even this heart’s release by love is produced and intended. Whatever is produced and intended is impermanent and liable to cessation.’ Standing on that … he attains the supreme sanctuary.
translations.mn54:18: Suppose, householder, there was a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come along who wants to live, does not want to die, desires happiness, and recoils from suffering. Then two strong men would grab him by his separate arms and drag him toward the charcoal pit. What do you think, householder? Would that man twist his body this way and that? “Yes, sir.” “Why is that?” “Because it is known to that man, sir: ‘If I fall into this charcoal pit, I will meet death or death-like suffering because of it.’” Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a charcoal pit, with much suffering and much despair, and the danger in them is great.’ Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom... he develops that very equanimity.
translations.mn54:23: Then that noble disciple, relying on this very unexcelled purity of mindfulness and equanimity, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate... he understands how beings fare according to their deeds.
translations.mn54:24: Then that noble disciple, relying on this very unexcelled purity of mindfulness and equanimity, through the ending of taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life.
translations.mn60:10: Here, householders, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: ‘There is what is given... [and] those who describe this world and the other world having realized it with their own direct knowledge’—it can be expected of them that, having avoided these three unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct—they will undertake and practice these three wholesome states: bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct. Why is that? Because those good ascetics and brahmins see the danger, degradation, and defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit of renunciation and the aspect of cleansing in wholesome states.
translations.mn60:12: Here, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If there is another world, then this individual, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But suppose there is no other world, and the words of those good ascetics and brahmins are true; still, this individual is praised by the wise in this very life: “A virtuous individual, of right view, who holds the doctrine of existence.” If there really is another world, then this individual has won a lucky throw on both counts: that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this incontrovertible teaching has been well undertaken by him; it pervades both sides and abandons the unwholesome stance.’
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: ‘For one who acts or causes others to act, who mutilates or causes others to mutilate, who torments or causes others to torment, who sorrows or causes others to sorrow, who oppresses or causes others to oppress, who intimidates or causes others to intimidate, who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, ambushes highways, commits adultery, and speaks falsehood—for one who does this, no evil is done. Even if one were to reduce all the living beings on this earth to a single heap of flesh, a single pile of flesh, with a razor-rimmed wheel, there is no evil because of that, no outcome of evil. Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges striking and killing, mutilating and inciting mutilation, tormenting and inciting torment, there is no evil because of that, no outcome of evil. Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and inciting giving, sacrificing and inciting sacrifice, there is no merit because of that, no outcome of merit. By giving, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no outcome of merit.’
translations.mn60:14: Now, householders, regarding those very ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold a doctrine directly opposed to theirs, and they say this: ‘For one who acts or causes others to act... there is evil because of that, there is an outcome of evil... there is merit because of that, there is an outcome of merit.’ What do you think, householders? Are not these ascetics and brahmins directly opposed to each other in their doctrines?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn60:16: Since there actually is action, he holds the view ‘there is no action’; this is his wrong view. Since there actually is action, he thinks ‘there is no action’; this is his wrong intention. Since there actually is action, he speaks the words ‘there is no action’; this is his wrong speech. Since there actually is action, he says ‘there is no action,’ and thus he opposes those Arahants who teach the doctrine of action. Since there actually is action, he convinces others ‘there is no action’; this is his teaching of what is not the true Dhamma. And with that teaching of what is not the true Dhamma, he praises himself and disparages others. Thus his previous good character is abandoned and bad character is established—and this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to noble ones, teaching of what is not the true Dhamma, self-praise, and disparagement of others. Thus these many evil unwholesome states originate with wrong view as condition.
translations.mn60:17: There, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If there is no effective action, this individual will keep himself safe after the breakup of the body. But if there is effective action, this individual, after the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. Even if there is no effective action, and the words of those ascetics and brahmins are true, still this individual is criticized by the wise in the present life as an immoral individual, one of wrong view, a denier of action. But if there really is effective action, then this individual has made a bad throw of the dice on both counts: they are criticized by the wise in the present life, and after the breakup of the body, after death, they will be reborn in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. Thus they have accepted and undertaken this incontrovertible teaching in a wrong way; they stand having adopted a one-sided view and have abandoned the skillful position.
translations.mn60:19: Since there actually is action, they have the view that ‘there is action’: this is their right view. Since there actually is action, they resolve that ‘there is action’: this is their right resolve. Since there actually is action, they speak the words ‘there is action’: this is their right speech. Since there actually is action, they say ‘there is action’: they do not oppose those perfected ones who teach the efficacy of action. Since there actually is action, they convince others that ‘there is action’: this is their instruction in the true teaching. With that instruction in the true teaching, they do not praise themselves or put down others. So any prior immorality is given up and morality is established. And this right view, right resolve, right speech, non-opposition to noble ones, instruction in the true teaching, non-praise of self, and non-disparagement of others: these are the many skillful qualities that originate for them conditioned by right view.
translations.mn60:21: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: ‘There is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition. There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition. There is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly vigor. All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without control, power, or energy; molded by destiny, circumstance, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.’
translations.mn60:22: But, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine is directly opposed to those ascetics and brahmins. They say this: ‘There is a cause and condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause and condition. There is a cause and condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and condition. There is power, energy, manly strength, and manly vigor. It is not the case that all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without control, power, or energy, molded by destiny, circumstance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.’ What do you think, householders? Do not these ascetics and brahmins maintain a doctrine directly opposed to one another?” “Yes, sir”.
translations.mn60:29: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: ‘There are absolutely no formless realms.’
translations.mn60:30: But, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine is directly opposed to those ascetics and brahmins. They say this: ‘There are absolutely formless realms.’ What do you think, householders? Do not these ascetics and brahmins maintain a doctrine directly opposed to one another?” “Yes, sir”.
translations.mn60:32: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: ‘There is absolutely no cessation of existence.’
translations.mn60:35: Householders, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world. What four? Here, householders, some person torments themselves and is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves.
