Here, householders, some person torments others and is committed to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, some person torments themselves and is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves, and also torments others and is committed to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, some person does not torment themselves or others; being neither a tormentor of self nor a tormentor of others, they live in the present life without hunger, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, with a self that has become divine.
translations.mn60:36: And what, householders, is the person who torments themselves and is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves? Here, householders, some person goes naked, ignoring conventions, licking their hands... thus they live committed to the practice of tormenting and mortifying the body in various ways. This is called, householders, the person who torments themselves and is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves.
translations.mn60:37: And what, householders, is the person who torments others and is committed to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, some person is a sheep-butcher, a pig-butcher... or follows any other cruel occupation. This is called, householders, the person who torments others and is committed to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:38: And what, householders, is the person who torments themselves and is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves, and also torments others and is committed to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, some person is an anointed noble king... even [his servants] work driven by the rod, driven by fear, weeping with tearful faces. This is called, householders, the person who torments themselves and is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves, and also torments others and is committed to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:39: And what, householders, is the person who does not torment themselves nor is committed to the practice of tormenting themselves, and does not torment others nor is committed to the practice of tormenting others; who, being neither a tormentor of self nor a tormentor of others, lives in the present life without hunger, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, with a self that has become divine?
translations.mn60:4: “Householders, do you have any agreeable teacher in whom you have acquired a grounded faith?” “No, sir, we have no agreeable teacher in whom we have acquired a grounded faith.” “Householders, since you have not found an agreeable teacher, you should undertake and practice this incontrovertible teaching. For when the incontrovertible teaching is perfectly undertaken and practiced, it will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what is the incontrovertible teaching?
translations.mn60:5: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit or result of good and bad actions; no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no beings reborn spontaneously; no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are faring rightly, practicing rightly, and who proclaim this world and the other world having realized it by their own direct knowledge.’
translations.mn60:6: Now, householders, of those same ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine is directly opposed to them. They say this: ‘There is what is given, offered, and sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings reborn spontaneously; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who are faring rightly, practicing rightly, and who proclaim this world and the other world having realized it by their own direct knowledge.’ What do you think, householders? Don’t these ascetics and brahmins hold doctrines directly opposed to one another?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn63:8: And why, Mālukyaputta, have I left that undeclared? Because it is not beneficial, it does not belong to the fundamentals of the holy life, it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. That is why I have left it undeclared.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base of infinite space. Whatever exists there of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness... he is of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, having completely surmounted the base of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base of infinite consciousness. Whatever exists there of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness... he is of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: “Bhikkhus, do you remember the five lower fetters taught by me?” When this was said, the Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.” “But how, Mālukyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters taught by me?” “Venerable sir, I remember identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember adherence to rules and observances as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. That is how, venerable sir, I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.”
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then listen, Ānanda, and attend closely to what I shall say.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: But, Ānanda, that one will know or see or abandon the five lower fetters by relying on the path, on the way that leads to the abandoning of the five lower fetters—this is possible.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, secluded from acquisitions, having abandoned unwholesome states, with the complete tranquilization of bodily inertia, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Whatever exists there of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states and directs it towards the deathless element thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Standing upon that, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then because of that desire for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters he becomes one due to be reborn spontaneously and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I wield the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; may I fly through the air seated cross-legged like a winged bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; may I exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma world,’ let him fulfill the precepts... and promote the seclusion of empty huts.
translations.mn6:15: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May I hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those far and near, with the divine ear element that is purified and surpasses the human,’ they should fulfill the precepts … and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:16: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I understand a mind with greed as “greedy”, and a mind without greed as “not greedy”; a mind with hate as “hateful”, and a mind without hate as “not hateful”; a mind with delusion as “deluded”, and a mind without delusion as “not deluded”; a constricted mind as “constricted”, and a scattered mind as “scattered”; an expansive mind as “expansive”, and an unexpansive mind as “unexpansive”; a mind that is not supreme as “not supreme”, and a mind that is supreme as “supreme”; a mind immersed in samādhi as “immersed in samādhi”, and a mind not immersed in samādhi as “not immersed in samādhi”; a freed mind as “freed”, and an unfreed mind as “unfreed”,’ they should fulfill the precepts … and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:2: “Mendicants, live accomplished in ethics and the code of conduct. Live restrained by the restraint of the code of conduct, with appropriate behavior and range of movement, seeing fear in the slightest fault. Having undertaken the training rules, train in them.
translations.mn6:3: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my spiritual companions, respected and admired,’ they should fulfill the precepts, be committed to internal serenity of heart, not neglect absorption, be possessed of insight, and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:6: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May it be of great fruit and benefit to my departed relatives and blood relations who remember me with confident hearts,’ they should fulfill the precepts, be committed to internal serenity of heart, not neglect absorption, be possessed of insight, and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:7: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May I endure dissatisfaction and satisfaction, and not let dissatisfaction master me. May I live having mastered dissatisfaction whenever it arises,’ they should fulfill the precepts … and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:8: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May I endure fear and dread, and not let fear and dread master me. May I live having mastered fear and dread whenever they arise,’ they should fulfill the precepts … and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:9: If a mendicant should wish: ‘May I get the four absorptions—which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant abidings in this very life—without trouble or difficulty,’ they should fulfill the precepts … and frequent empty huts.
translations.mn70:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kasis together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:
translations.mn70:11: “But because I have known, seen, understood, realized, and experienced with wisdom that: ‘When a certain person feels such neutral feeling, unskillful qualities decline and skillful qualities grow,’ that is why I say: ‘Enter and remain in such neutral feeling.’
translations.mn70:12: I do not say that all mendicants have work to do with diligence. I do not say that all mendicants have no work to do with diligence. I say that those mendicants who are perfected, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and are rightly liberated through enlightenment, do not have work to do with diligence. Why is that? They have done their work with diligence. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:13: But I say that those mendicants who are trainees, who have not achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring to the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, do have work to do with diligence. Why is that? Thinking: ‘Hopefully these venerables, by frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and controlling their faculties, might realize the supreme end of the spiritual path in this very life. They might live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’ Seeing this fruit of diligence for these mendicants, I say that they have work to do with diligence.
translations.mn70:14: Mendicants, these seven people are found in the world. What seven? One freed both ways, one freed by wisdom, a personal witness, one attained to view, one freed by faith, a follower of the teachings, and a follower by faith.
translations.mn70:15: And what person is freed both ways? It’s a person who touches with their body and abides in those peaceful liberations that transcend form, that are formless; and having seen with wisdom, their defilements are ended. This is called a person who is freed both ways. I say that this mendicant has no work to do with diligence. Why is that? They have done their work with diligence. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:17: And what person is a personal witness? It’s a person who touches with their body and abides in those peaceful liberations that transcend form, that are formless; and having seen with wisdom, some of their defilements are ended. This is called a person who is a personal witness. I say that this mendicant has work to do with diligence. Why is that? Thinking: ‘Hopefully this venerable, by frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and controlling their faculties, might realize the supreme end of the spiritual path in this very life. They might live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’ Seeing this fruit of diligence for this mendicant, I say that they have work to do with diligence.
translations.mn70:2: “Mendicants, I eat my food not at night. By doing so, I am free from illness and affliction, and I enjoy health, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, mendicants, you too eat your food not at night. For by doing so, you too will be free from illness and affliction, and you will enjoy health, strength, and a comfortable abiding.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied to the Buddha.
translations.mn70:20: And what person is a Dhamma-follower? Here, some person does not contact with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend forms and are formless, but having seen with wisdom, some of their taints are destroyed. And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathagata are accepted by them after reflecting on them with a measure of wisdom. Furthermore, they have these qualities: the faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom. This person is called a Dhamma-follower. I say that this monk also has work to do with diligence. Why is that? [Thinking] ‘Perhaps this venerable one, frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, balancing their faculties, might realize the supreme end of the spiritual life—for the sake of which gentlemen rightly go forth from home to homelessness—in this very life by their own insight and dwell therein.’ Seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk, I say, ‘There is work to be done with diligence.’
translations.mn70:22: Mendicants, I do not say that the attainment of final knowledge occurs straight away. Rather, the attainment of final knowledge occurs by gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress.
translations.mn70:23: And how does the attainment of final knowledge occur by gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress? Here, one who has faith draws near. One who draws near pays respect. One who pays respect gives ear. One who gives ear hears the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, they memorize it. They examine the meaning of the memorized teachings. When examining the meaning, the teachings are accepted after reflection. When the teachings are accepted after reflection, desire arises. When desire arises, they make an effort. Having made an effort, they weigh it up. Having weighed it up, they strive. Being self-resolute, they realize the ultimate truth with the body and see it by penetrating it with wisdom.
translations.mn70:24: But you did not have that faith; you did not draw near; you did not pay respect; you did not give ear; you did not hear the Dhamma; you did not memorize the Dhamma; you did not examine the meaning; the teachings were not accepted after reflection; desire did not arise; you did not make an effort; you did not weigh it up; you did not strive. You have lost your way, mendicants; you are practicing the wrong way. How far have these foolish men strayed from this Dhamma and Vinaya!
translations.mn70:25: Mendicants, there is a four-line statement such that, when it is recited, a wise man would quickly understand the meaning with wisdom. I will recite it to you; would you understand it from me?” “But who are we, sir, to be knowers of the Dhamma?”
translations.mn70:26: “Mendicants, even for a teacher who values material things, inherits material things, and lives entangled with material things, such bargaining is not applicable: ‘If we like it, we will do it; if we don’t like it, we won’t do it.’ How much less so for the Tathagata, who lives entirely disentangled from material things.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages in the Kasi country, arrived at a Kasi town called Kitagiri. And there the Blessed One stayed in the Kasi town of Kitagiri.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka were residing at Kitagiri. Then several monks went to the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka and said to them: “Friends, the Blessed One eats not at night, and so does the Order of monks. By doing so, they are free from illness and affliction, and they enjoy health, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, friends, you too eat not at night. For by doing so, you too will be free from illness and affliction, and you will enjoy health, strength, and a comfortable abiding.” When this was said, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka said to those monks: “Friends, we eat in the evening, in the morning, in the day, and at the wrong time. By doing so, we are free from illness and affliction, and we enjoy health, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Why should we abandon what is visible here and now to run after what involves time? We will eat in the evening, in the morning, in the day, and at the wrong time.”
translations.mn70:7: “Mendicants, do you not understand that I have taught the Dhamma thus: ‘For someone feeling a certain kind of pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but for someone feeling another kind of pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase. For someone feeling a certain kind of painful feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but for someone feeling another kind of painful feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase. For someone feeling a certain kind of neutral feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but for someone feeling another kind of neutral feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase’?” “Yes, sir”.
translations.mn75:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying in the land of the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus called Kammasadamma, in the fire-chamber of the brahmin of the Bharadvaja clan, on a spread of grass.
translations.mn75:10: “Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder, I amused myself, supplied and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear… smells cognizable by the nose… tastes cognizable by the tongue… tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. I had three palaces, Māgaṇḍiya: one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer. I lived in the rainy season palace for the four months of the rains, entertained by musicians who were all female, and I did not come down to the lower palace. But later, having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape regarding sensual pleasures, I gave up the craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever of sensual pleasures, and dwell with thirst gone, with a mind internally stilled. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures, and I do not envy them, nor do I delight therein. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unskillful qualities, which stands surpassing even divine bliss. Enjoying that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight therein.
translations.mn75:12: “In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder, I amused myself, supplied and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear… smells cognizable by the nose… tastes cognizable by the tongue… tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. But later, having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape regarding sensual pleasures, I gave up the craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever of sensual pleasures, and dwell with thirst gone, with a mind internally stilled. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures, and I do not envy them, nor do I delight therein. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unskillful qualities, which stands surpassing even divine bliss. Enjoying that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight therein.
translations.mn75:13: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a charcoal pit. His friends and companions, kinsmen and relatives would bring a physician or surgeon to attend to him. The physician or surgeon would make medicine for him. By means of that medicine, he would be freed from leprosy, well, happy, independent, master of himself, going where he likes. He might see another leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a charcoal pit. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that man envy that leper for his charcoal pit or for his use of medicine?” “No, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because when there is sickness, Master Gotama, something has to be done with medicine; but when there is no sickness, nothing needs to be done with medicine.”
translations.mn75:16: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past sensual pleasures were painful to the touch, very hot and scorching; in the future sensual pleasures will be painful to the touch, very hot and scorching; and now at present sensual pleasures are painful to the touch, very hot and scorching. But these beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, who are devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, who are burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, have their faculties impaired; so while sensual pleasures are actually painful to the touch, they acquire a perverted perception of them as pleasant.
translations.mn75:17: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a charcoal pit. The more that leper cauterizes his body over the charcoal pit, the more foul, stinking, and putrid his wounds become; yet there is a certain measure of satisfaction and enjoyment merely because of the itching of the wounds. So too, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, who are devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, who are burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more such beings indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures increases and the more they burn with the fever of sensual pleasures; yet there is a certain measure of satisfaction and enjoyment dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn75:18: “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you ever seen or heard of a king or a royal minister enjoying himself, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, who—without abandoning sensual craving, without removing sensual fever—dwelt or dwells or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace?” “No, Master Gotama.” “Good, Māgaṇḍiya. I too have never seen or heard of a king or a royal minister enjoying himself... who dwelt or dwells or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace. Rather, Māgaṇḍiya, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwelt or dwell or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace, all of them do so having truly understood the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures, and having abandoned sensual craving and removed sensual fever.”
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, having robed up in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kammāsadhamma and returned from his almsround after the meal, he went to a certain grove for the day's abiding. Having plunged into that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn75:22: “I am so confident in Master Gotama that Master Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know health and see Nibbāna.” “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man born blind. He could not see dark and light forms, or blue, yellow, red, or crimson forms, or the even and uneven, or the stars, or the sun and moon. His friends and companions, kinsmen and relatives would bring a physician to treat him. The physician would make a medicine for him. But despite that medicine, his eyes would not arise, his eyes would not be purified. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that doctor not just reap weariness and frustration?” “Yes, Master Gotama.” “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: ‘This is that health, this is that Nibbāna,’ and you did not know health or see Nibbāna, that would be weariness for me, that would be vexation for me.”
translations.mn75:24: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: ‘This is that health, this is that Nibbāna,’ and you might know health and see Nibbāna. With the arising of vision, your desire and lust for the five grasping aggregates would be abandoned. And it would occur to you: ‘Alas, for a long time I have been cheated, deceived, and defrauded by this mind. For I was grasping only form, grasping only feeling, grasping only perception, grasping only choices, grasping only consciousness. Conditioned by my grasping, continued existence came to be; conditioned by continued existence, birth; conditioned by birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress came to be. That is how this whole mass of suffering originates.’”
translations.mn75:25: “I am so confident in Master Gotama that Master Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat not blind.” “Well then, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with true persons. When you associate with true persons, you will hear the true Dhamma. When you hear the true Dhamma, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma. When you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know and see for yourself: ‘These are diseases, boils, and darts; here diseases, boils, and darts cease without remainder. With the cessation of my grasping, continued existence ceases; with the cessation of continued existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. That is how this whole mass of suffering ceases.’”
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! As if he were turning upright what had been overturned, or revealing what was hidden, or showing the path to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark so those with eyes could see forms, in the same way Master Gotama has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of mendicants. May I receive the going forth in Master Gotama’s presence, may I receive the full ordination.”
translations.mn75:27: “Māgaṇḍiya, if someone formerly of another sect wishes for the going forth and the full ordination in this teaching and training, they must live on probation for four months. At the end of four months, if the mendicants are satisfied, they give the going forth and full ordination into the status of a mendicant. However, I recognize individual differences in this matter.” “Sir, if those formerly of another sect who wish for the going forth and the full ordination in this teaching and training must live on probation for four months... I will live on probation for four years. At the end of four years, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth and full ordination into the status of a mendicant.”
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire chamber of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. He saw the grass mat spread out in the fire chamber and said to the brahmin, “Master Bhāradvāja, for whom has this grass mat been spread out in the fire chamber? It seems to be a bed suitable for a recluse.”
translations.mn75:6: The Buddha heard this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya with his purified divine ear surpassing the human. Then, in the late afternoon, the Buddha emerged from retreat and went to the fire chamber of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. He sat down on the grass mat spread out. Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him, “Bhāradvāja, did you have some conversation with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya regarding this very grass mat?” When he said this, the brahmin was shocked and awestruck, and said to the Buddha, “That is exactly what we wanted to tell Master Gotama. But Master Gotama has mentioned it without being told.”
translations.mn75:7: But this conversation between the Buddha and the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan was left unfinished. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire chamber of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the Buddha. He exchanged greetings with the Buddha. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha said to the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya as he sat there:
translations.mn77:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.
translations.mn77:10: But Udāyī, there are five other qualities for which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, and worship me, and relying on which they live honoring and respecting me. What five? First, my disciples esteem me for higher ethics: ‘The ascetic Gotama is ethical; he possesses the supreme aggregate of ethics.’
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained to my disciples the practice by which they develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. They meditate observing an aspect of feelings … mind … principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained to my disciples the practice by which they develop the four right efforts. It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise. They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up. They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise. They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fulfilled by development. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained to my disciples the practice by which they develop the four bases of psychic power. It’s when a mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm, and active effort. They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to energy … immersion due to mental development … immersion due to inquiry, and active effort. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained to my disciples the practice by which they develop the five faculties. It’s when a mendicant develops the faculty of faith, which leads to peace and awakening. They develop the faculty of energy … mindfulness … immersion … wisdom, which leads to peace and awakening. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: Now at that time several very well-known wanderers were staying in the wanderers’ park at the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground, namely Annabhāra, Varadhara, and the wanderer Sakuludāyī, as well as other very well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained to my disciples the practice by which they develop the seven awakening factors. It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. They develop the awakening factor of investigation of principles … energy … rapture … tranquility … immersion … equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyin, a mendicant develops right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the eight liberations. One possessed of form sees forms; this is the first liberation. Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally; this is the second liberation. One is resolved only on the beautiful; this is the third liberation. With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing’, one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation. With the complete surmounting of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the ten universal bases. One perceives the earth universal above, below, across, undivided, and measureless. One perceives the water universal … One perceives the fire universal … One perceives the air universal … One perceives the blue universal … One perceives the yellow universal … One perceives the red universal … One perceives the white universal … One perceives the space universal … One perceives the consciousness universal above, below, across, undivided, and measureless. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the four absorptions. Here, Udāyin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, a mendicant enters and dwells in the first absorption, which has rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by thought and investigation. They drench, steep, fill, and pervade this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Just as a skilled bath attendant or his apprentice might heap bath powder in a metal basin and, sprinkling it gradually with water, knead it until the moisture wets his ball of bath powder, soaks it, and pervades it inside and out, yet it does not ooze; so too, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyin, with the subsiding of thought and investigation, with internal clarity … enters and dwells in the second absorption. They drench, steep, fill, and pervade this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of immersion, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of immersion. Just as there might be a deep lake fed by a spring, with no inflow from the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not provide rain properly from time to time, yet the cool stream of water welling up from that lake would drench, steep, fill, and pervade that lake with cool water, so that there would be no part of that whole lake unpervaded by cool water; so too, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of immersion, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of immersion.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyin, with the fading away of rapture … enters and dwells in the third absorption. They drench, steep, fill, and pervade this very body with pleasure divested of rapture, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by pleasure divested of rapture. Just as in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses that are born and grow in the water thrive immersed in the water without rising out of it, and cool water drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades them to their tips and their roots, so that there is no part of all those lotuses unpervaded by cool water; so too, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with pleasure divested of rapture, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by pleasure divested of rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyin, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the ending of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and dwells in the fourth absorption, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and has purity of mindfulness and equanimity. They sit pervading this very body with a pure and bright mind, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by the pure and bright mind. Just as a person might sit covered from the head down with a white cloth, so that there would be no part of their whole body unpervaded by the white cloth; so too, a mendicant sits pervading this very body with a pure and bright mind, so that there is no part of their whole body unpervaded by the pure and bright mind. And many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Blessed One, having robed in the morning and taken his bowl and outer robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Suppose I go to the wanderer Sakuludāyin at the Wanderers’ Park in the Peacock’s Sanctuary.”
translations.mn77:32: Again, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples hear both kinds of sounds with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human—divine and human, those that are far as well as near. Just as a strong conch blower could easily make himself heard in the four quarters; so too, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples hear both kinds of sounds with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human—divine and human, those that are far as well as near. And therein many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Again, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples recollect their manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus with their aspects and particulars they recollect their manifold past lives. Just as a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to another village, and from that village he might return to his own village. He would think: ‘I went from my own village to that village, and there I stood in such a way, sat in such a way, spoke in such a way, and was silent in such a way. From that village I went to another village, and there too I stood in such a way, sat in such a way, spoke in such a way, and was silent in such a way. And from that village I have returned to my own village.’ So too, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples recollect their manifold past lives, that is, one birth... thus with their aspects and particulars they recollect their manifold past lives. And therein many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Again, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. They understand how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their actions, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. But these worthy beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, not revilers of noble ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their actions, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, they see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and they understand how beings pass on according to their actions. Just as there might be two houses with doors, and a man with good eyesight standing in the middle might see people entering a house, leaving it, walking back and forth, and wandering about; so too, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with the divine eye... understand how beings pass on according to their actions... And therein many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Again, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge. Just as in a mountain gorge there might be a lake, clear, limpid, and undisturbed, and a man with good eyesight standing on the bank might see shells, gravel, and pebbles, and shoals of fish moving about and standing still. He would think: ‘This lake is clear, limpid, and undisturbed, and here are these shells, gravel, and pebbles, and shoals of fish moving about and standing still.’ So too, Udāyin, I have explained to my disciples the path, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge. And therein many of my disciples abide having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One approached the wanderer Sakuludāyin. The wanderer Sakuludāyin said to the Blessed One: “Let the Blessed One come, sir! Welcome to the Blessed One, sir! It has been a long time since the Blessed One made this arrangement, that is, coming here. Let the Blessed One sit down, sir; this seat is prepared.” The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The wanderer Sakuludāyin also took a low seat and sat to one side. When the wanderer Sakuludāyin was seated to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “For what discussion are you sitting together here now, Udāyin? And what was your conversation that was left unfinished?”
translations.mn77:7: “But how many qualities, Udāyin, do you see in me for which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and honoring and respecting me, live in dependence on me?”
translations.mn77:9: “‘If, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama eats little and praises eating little,” there are disciples of mine who eat a cupful or half a cupful, a bilva fruit or half a bilva fruit. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat this bowl full to the brim or even more. If my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama eats little and praises eating little,” then those disciples of mine who eat a cupful, or half a cupful, or a bilva fruit, or half a bilva fruit would not respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me for that quality. “‘If, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe and praises contentment with any kind of robe,” there are disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearing rough robes; they pick up rags from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or shops, make them into a patch-cloak, and wear them. But I, Udāyi, sometimes wear robes given by householders that are strong and soft. If my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe and praises contentment with any kind of robe,” then those disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers... would not respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me for that quality. “‘If, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood and praises contentment with any kind of almsfood,” there are disciples of mine who are alms-eaters, wandering for alms, devoted to the practice of gathering; when they have entered among the houses, they do not consent to sit down even when invited. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat on invitation, choice rice with the black grains removed, with many soups and sauces. If my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood and praises contentment with any kind of almsfood,” then those disciples of mine who are alms-eaters... would not respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me for that quality. “‘If, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging and praises contentment with any kind of lodging,” there are disciples of mine who live at the root of a tree or in the open air; for eight months they do not go under a roof. But I, Udāyi, sometimes stay in gabled halls, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows closed. If my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging and praises contentment with any kind of lodging,” then those disciples of mine who live at the root of a tree... would not respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me for that quality. “‘If, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is secluded and praises seclusion,” there are disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, living in remote lodgings in the jungle thickets; they come down to the midst of the Sangha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But I, Udāyi, sometimes live crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians. If my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me thinking: “The ascetic Gotama is secluded and praises seclusion,” then those disciples of mine who are forest dwellers... would not respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me for that quality. It is not for these five qualities, Udāyi, that my disciples respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live in dependence on me.
translations.mn7:11: ‘Thinking: “I have given up, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished [the defilements] in the way they were specified,” he gains inspiration in the meaning, he gains inspiration in the teaching, he gains gladness connected with the teaching. When he is glad, rapture is born. When the mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels pleasure. In one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abides pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will.
translations.mn7:17: He understands: 'There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, and there is an escape beyond the scope of perception.'
translations.mn7:18: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' This is called, bhikkhus: 'A bhikkhu bathed with the inner bathing.'
translations.mn7:19: Now on that occasion the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja was seated not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja said to the Blessed One: "But does Master Gotama go to the Bahuka River to bathe?" "What good, brahmin, is the Bahuka River? What can the Bahuka River do?" "It is considered by many, Master Gotama, to bring deliverance, it is considered by many to bring merit, and in the Bahuka River many people wash away the evil deeds they have done."
translations.mn7:2: "Bhikkhus, suppose a cloth were defiled and stained; and a dyer were to dip it in some dye or other, whether blue or yellow or red or crimson; it would look poorly dyed and impure in color. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth. So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is defiled, an unhappy destination may be expected. Bhikkhus, suppose a cloth were pure and bright; and a dyer were to dip it in some dye or other, whether blue or yellow or red or crimson; it would look well dyed and pure in color. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth. So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is undefiled, a happy destination may be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja in stanzas: "Bahuka and Adhikakka, Gaya and Sundarika too, Sarassati and Payaga, then the river Bahumati; Though a fool may bathe there forever, he does not purify dark deeds. What can the Sundarika do? What the Payaga, what the Bahuka River? They do not cleanse the hostile man, the doer of evil and brutal deeds. For the pure, it is always the Spring festival, for the pure it is always the holy day; for the pure of clean kamma, their vows always succeed. Bathe right here, brahmin, bring safety to all beings. If you do not speak falsehood, if you do not harm living beings, if you do not take what is not given, faithful and free from stinginess, what will you do by going to Gaya? Even your own well is a Gaya."
translations.mn7:3: And what, bhikkhus, are the imperfections of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed is an imperfection of the mind; ill will is an imperfection of the mind; anger is an imperfection of the mind; resentment is an imperfection of the mind; contempt is an imperfection of the mind; insolence is an imperfection of the mind; envy is an imperfection of the mind; avarice is an imperfection of the mind; deceit is an imperfection of the mind; fraud is an imperfection of the mind; obstinacy is an imperfection of the mind; rivalry is an imperfection of the mind; conceit is an imperfection of the mind; arrogance is an imperfection of the mind; vanity is an imperfection of the mind; negligence is an imperfection of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediately effective, inviting inspection, onward leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves';
translations.mn7:7: He possesses confirmed confidence in the Sangha thus: 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practising the good way, practising the straight way, practising the true way, practising the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kuru country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, and eventually he arrived at a town of the Kurus named Thullakotthika.
translations.mn82:11: Then the clansman Ratthapala's friends went to his parents and said to them: "Mother and father, the clansman Ratthapala is lying there on the bare ground; he says: 'Right here will be my death or my going forth.' If you do not give your consent to the clansman Ratthapala's going forth from the home life into homelessness, he will die right there. But if you give your consent, you will see him after he has gone forth. If the clansman Ratthapala does not enjoy the going forth... what other course will he have? He will return right here. Give your consent to the clansman Ratthapala's going forth from the home life into homelessness." "We give our consent, dears, to the clansman Ratthapala's going forth from the home life into homelessness. But when he has gone forth, he must visit his parents." Then the clansman Ratthapala's friends went to him and said: "Get up, friend Ratthapala, your parents have given their consent for you to go forth from the home life into homelessness. But when you have gone forth, you must visit your parents."
translations.mn82:12: Then the clansman Ratthapala got up, and when he had regained his strength, he went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. Sitting at one side, the clansman Ratthapala said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I have received my parents' consent to go forth from the home life into homelessness. Let the Blessed One give me the going forth."
translations.mn82:13: So the clansman Ratthapala received the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, and he received the full ordination. Then, not long after the Venerable Ratthapala had been ordained—a fortnight after his ordination—the Blessed One, having stayed at Thullakotthika as long as he chose, set out on wandering towards Savatthi. Wandering by stages, he arrived at Savatthi. And there the Blessed One lived at Savatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anathapindika’s Park.
translations.mn82:14: Then the Venerable Ratthapala, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time entered upon and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, having realized it for himself here and now with direct knowledge. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.” And the Venerable Ratthapala became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then the Venerable Ratthapala rose from his seat, bowed down to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he set his resting place in order. Taking his bowl and robe, he set out wandering towards Thullakotthika. Wandering by stages, he arrived at Thullakotthika. There the Venerable Ratthapala stayed in Thullakotthika in King Koravya’s Migacira Garden. Then, when the morning had advanced, the Venerable Ratthapala dressed, and taking his bowl and robe, entered Thullakotthika for alms. Wandering for alms in Thullakotthika from house to house, he approached his own father’s house.
translations.mn82:17: Now on that occasion the Venerable Ratthapala’s father was having his hair combed in the middle gateway hall. He saw the Venerable Ratthapala coming from afar. Seeing him, he said: “Our only son, so dear and beloved, was made to go forth by these bald-pated shavelings.” So the Venerable Ratthapala received neither alms nor a polite refusal at his own father’s house; instead, he received only abuse.
translations.mn82:18: Now on that occasion a slave woman belonging to the Venerable Ratthapala’s relatives was about to throw away some stale porridge. The Venerable Ratthapala said to her: “Sister, if that is to be thrown away, pour it here into my bowl.” While she was pouring the stale porridge into his bowl, she recognized the characteristic features of his hands, his feet, and his voice. Then she went to the Venerable Ratthapala’s mother and said: “If it please you, my lady, you should know that the young master Ratthapala has arrived.” “If you speak the truth, girl, I will make you a free woman.” Then the Venerable Ratthapala’s mother went to his father and said: “If it please you, householder, you should know that the clansman Ratthapala has arrived.”
translations.mn82:19: Now at that time the Venerable Ratthapala was eating that stale porridge leaning against a certain wall. Then his father went to him and said: “My dear Ratthapala, can it be that you are eating stale porridge? Should you not go to your own home?” “Householder, where is there a home for us who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We did go to your home, householder, but we received neither alms nor a polite refusal there; instead, we received only abuse.” “Come, dear Ratthapala, let us go to the house.” “Enough, householder, I have finished my meal for today.” “Then, dear Ratthapala, accept a meal for tomorrow.” The Venerable Ratthapala consented in silence.
translations.mn82:20: Then the Venerable Ratthapala’s father, having understood that the Venerable Ratthapala had consented, went to his own house. There he had a large heap of gold and bullion made, covered it with mats, and addressed the Venerable Ratthapala’s former wives: “Come, daughters-in-law, adorn yourselves with the ornaments in which you used to be dear and beloved to the clansman Ratthapala.”
translations.mn82:21: Then, with the passing of that night, the Venerable Ratthapala’s father had excellent hard and soft food prepared in his own house and announced the time to the Venerable Ratthapala: “It is time, dear Ratthapala, the meal is ready.”
translations.mn82:22: Then, when the morning had advanced, the Venerable Ratthapala dressed, and taking his bowl and robe, went to his father’s house. He sat down on the seat prepared for him. Then the Venerable Ratthapala’s father had that heap of gold and bullion uncovered and said to the Venerable Ratthapala: “This, dear Ratthapala, is your mother’s wealth; this is your father’s; this is your grandfather’s. It is possible, dear Ratthapala, to enjoy wealth and make merit. Come then, dear Ratthapala, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.” “Householder, if you would act upon my word, you would have this heap of gold and bullion loaded onto carts, carried away, and sunk in the middle of the stream of the river Ganges. Why is that? Because, householder, it will be for you a source of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
translations.mn82:23: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former wives each grabbed his feet and said to him: “What are they like, my lord, those nymphs for whose sake you live the spiritual life?” “Sisters, we do not live the spiritual life for the sake of nymphs.” “My lord Raṭṭhapāla addresses us as ‘sisters’!” And right there they fainted and fell down.
translations.mn82:24: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: “Householder, if there is a meal to be given, give it; do not harass us.” “Eat, my dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father served and satisfied Venerable Raṭṭhapāla with his own hands with choice hard and soft foods. When Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, he spoke these verses while standing right there:
translations.mn82:26: Then, having spoken these verses while standing right there, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla went to the Migacīra garden of King Korabya. He sat down at the foot of a tree for the day’s abiding.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Korabya addressed the gamekeeper: “My good gamekeeper, clean up the Migacīra pleasure park. We will go to see the beautiful grounds.” “Yes, Your Majesty,” the gamekeeper replied. While cleaning the Migacīra, he saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the foot of a tree for the day’s abiding. Seeing him, he went to King Korabya and said: “Your Majesty, the Migacīra is clean. But the gentleman named Raṭṭhapāla is there—the son of the leading clan in this very Thullakoṭṭhika, whom you have often praised—he is sitting at the foot of a tree for the day’s abiding.” “In that case, my good gamekeeper, never mind the pleasure park for today. We will now pay respect to that Master Raṭṭhapāla.”
translations.mn82:28: Then King Korabya said, “Distribute all the hard and soft food that has been prepared there.” He had the finest carriages harnessed, mounted a fine carriage, and drove out from Thullakoṭṭhika with the finest carriages in great royal splendor to see Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla on foot with a retinue of the highest rank. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, and when the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Korabya said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “Let Master Raṭṭhapāla sit here on the elephant rug.” “Enough, great king, you sit; I am sitting on my own seat.” King Korabya sat on a designated seat. Having sat down, King Korabya said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: “Master Raṭṭhapāla, there are these four kinds of loss. When people undergo these losses, some of them shave off their hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness. What four? Loss through aging, loss through sickness, loss of wealth, and loss of relatives.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika went up to the Blessed One. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their joined palms toward the Blessed One, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged them with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: These, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are the four kinds of loss. When people undergo these losses, some of them shave off their hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness. But Master Raṭṭhapāla has none of these. What did Master Raṭṭhapāla know or see or hear that he went forth from the lay life to homelessness?”
translations.mn82:35: “Great king, there are four summaries of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Perfected One, the Fully Awakened Buddha. Knowing, seeing, and hearing these, I went forth from the lay life to homelessness. What four?
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a gentleman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading clan in that very Thullakoṭṭhika, was sitting in that assembly. Then it occurred to the gentleman Raṭṭhapāla: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the spiritual life that is entirely full, entirely pure, like a polished conch shell. Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?”
translations.mn82:6: Then, not long after the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita had left, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. Sitting there, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Venerable sir, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission?” “But, Raṭṭhapāla, do you have your parents’ permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness?” “No, venerable sir, I do not have my parents' permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.” “Raṭṭhapāla, Tathāgatas do not give the going forth to a son without his parents’ permission.” “Venerable sir, I shall do what is necessary so that my parents will give me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and eventually he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Opāsāda. There the Blessed One stayed in the Deva Grove, the Sal-Tree Grove to the north of Opāsāda.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.
translations.mn95:11: Now at that time the Blessed One was exchanging some courteous and amiable talk with some very old brahmins. And at that time a student named Kāpaṭika—young, with a shaven head, sixteen years old, a master of the three Vedas with their vocabularies, liturgy, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, he was fully versed in natural philosophy and the marks of a Great Man—was seated in that assembly. He kept interrupting the talk of the old brahmins and the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One rebuked the student Kāpaṭika: “Let not the venerable Bhāradvāja interrupt the talk of the old brahmins and the Blessed One. Let the venerable Bhāradvāja wait until the talk is finished.” When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Blessed One: “Let not Master Gotama rebuke the student Kāpaṭika. The student Kāpaṭika is a clansman, he is very learned, he is wise, he is a good speaker, and he is capable of debating with Master Gotama in this matter.”
translations.mn95:2: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was residing in Opāsāda, a crown property teeming with living beings, rich in grass, wood, and water, full of grain, a royal endowment given by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmadeyya.
translations.mn95:20: When, on investigating him, he sees that he is purified from states based on delusion, then he places faith in him; filled with faith he visits him; visiting he pays respect; paying respect he gives ear; giving ear he hears the Dhamma; hearing the Dhamma he remembers it; he examines the meaning of the remembered Dhamma; examining the meaning, he accepts the teachings after pondering them; when he accepts the teachings, zeal arises; zealous, he applies himself; applying himself, he scrutinizes; scrutinizing, he strives; being resolute, he realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom. In this way, Bhāradvāja, there is the awakening to truth, in this way one awakens to truth, and in this way we describe the awakening to truth; but there is not yet the arrival at truth.
translations.mn95:33: “But, Master Gotama, what quality is helpful for visiting? We ask Master Gotama about the quality helpful for visiting.” “Faith is helpful for visiting, Bhāradvāja. If faith did not arise, one would not visit. Because faith arises, one visits. Therefore faith is helpful for visiting.”
translations.mn95:5: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī had gone to the upper terrace of his mansion for his midday rest. He saw the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in bands and companies, heading north to the Deva Grove, the Sal-Tree Grove. Seeing this, he addressed his steward: “Steward, why are the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in bands and companies, heading north to the Deva Grove, the Sal-Tree Grove?”
translations.mn9:11: “And what, friends, is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? There are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come to be or for the support of those seeking birth. What four? Physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. With the arising of craving there is the arising of nutriment. With the cessation of craving there is the cessation of nutriment. The way leading to the cessation of nutriment is just this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: “When, friends, a noble disciple understands nutriment in this way, the origin of nutriment in this way, the cessation of nutriment in this way, and the way leading to the cessation of nutriment in this way, he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, he abolishes the underlying tendency to aversion, he extirpates the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’, and abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge, he makes an end of suffering here and now. In this way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
translations.mn9:15: And what, friends, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wishes for is suffering; in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering—this is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friends, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for extermination—this is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it—this is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friends, is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this noble eightfold path; that is, right view... right immersion—this is called the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: “‘Right view, right view,’ it is said, friends. In what way is a noble disciple one of right view, whose view is straight, who has unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma?” “We would come from far away, friends, to learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta. It would be good if the meaning of this statement would occur to the Venerable Sāriputta. Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the mendicants will remember it.” “Then listen, friends, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those mendicants replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: Saying “Good, friend,” those mendicants delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta’s statement. Then they asked him a further question: “But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma?”
translations.mn9:3: “When, friends, a noble disciple understands the unskillful and the root of the unskillful, and understands the skillful and the root of the skillful—in that way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: And what, friends, is the unskillful, what is the root of the unskillful, what is the skillful, what is the root of the skillful? Killing living creatures is unskillful; taking what is not given is unskillful; sexual misconduct is unskillful; lying is unskillful; divisive speech is unskillful; harsh speech is unskillful; idle chatter is unskillful; covetousness is unskillful; ill will is unskillful; wrong view is unskillful—this is called the unskillful.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friends, is the root of the unskillful? Greed is a root of the unskillful; hate is a root of the unskillful; delusion is a root of the unskillful—this is called the root of the unskillful.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friends, is the root of the skillful? Non-greed is a root of the skillful; non-hate is a root of the skillful; non-delusion is a root of the skillful—this is called the root of the skillful.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friends, is the taint, what is the origin of the taint, what is the cessation of the taint, what is the practice leading to the cessation of the taint? There are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of ignorance. With the origin of ignorance there is the origin of the taints. With the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of the taints. It is just this noble eightfold path that is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints; that is, right view... right immersion.
