translations.mn9:8: When a noble disciple understands the unskillful in this way, understands the root of the unskillful in this way, understands the skillful in this way, and understands the root of the skillful in this way, they entirely give up the underlying tendency to greed, remove the underlying tendency to repulsion, uproot the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’, give up ignorance and give rise to knowledge, and make an end of suffering in this very life—in that way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
translations.sn1.10:2: “Living in the wilderness, peaceful and celibate, eating one meal a day: why is their complexion so clear?”
translations.sn1.10:3: “They don’t sorrow over the past, nor do they long for the future. They survive on the present: that’s why their complexion is clear.
translations.sn1.17:1: “It’s hard to do, hard to endure: the ascetic life for the unskilled. There are many obstacles there, where the fool falters.”
translations.sn1.17:2: “How many days could one practice the ascetic life if one doesn't restrain the mind? Step by step he would sink, under the sway of his intentions.
translations.sn1.17:3: Like a tortoise drawing its limbs into its own shell, a mendicant should draw the mind’s thoughts inside. Independent, not hurting others, extinguished, they would not blame anyone.”
translations.sn1.18:1: “Is there any person found in the world who is restrained by conscience, who awakens to blame like a thoroughbred horse to the whip?”
translations.sn1.18:2: “Those restrained by conscience are few, who go always mindful. Having reached the end of suffering, they go evenly amidst the uneven.”
translations.sn1.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him: “Good sir, how did you cross the flood?” “I crossed the flood without standing still and without struggling.” “But how, good sir, did you cross the flood without standing still and without struggling?” “When I stood still, I sank; and when I struggled, I was swept away. That is how I crossed the flood without standing still and without struggling.”
translations.sn1.1:2: “After a long time I see a brahmin who is extinguished. Without standing still, without struggling, he has crossed over attachment in the world.”
translations.sn1.1:3: This is what that deity said. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, knowing “The Teacher approves of me,” bowed to the Buddha, circled him on the right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Hot Springs Park. Then Venerable Samiddhi rose at the crack of dawn and went to the hot springs to bathe his limbs. After bathing his limbs in the hot springs and getting out, he stood in one robe drying his limbs. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire hot springs, went up to Venerable Samiddhi. Hovering in the air, she addressed him in verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “You beg for alms without having enjoyed, mendicant; you don’t beg after enjoying. Enjoy, mendicant, then beg; don’t let the time pass you by.”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings who perceive the expressible are established on the expressible. Not fully understanding the expressible, they come under the yoke of Death.
translations.sn1.20:21: But having fully understood the expressible, one does not conceive of a speaker. For that does not exist for him—that by which one might speak of him does not exist for him. If you understand, speak up, spirit!”
translations.sn1.20:22: “Sir, I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement by the Buddha. Please, sir, let the Buddha speak in such a way that I may understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement.”
translations.sn1.20:23: “One who conceives ‘I am equal, better, or worse,’ might get into arguments because of that. But for one unmoved in these three ways, ‘equal’ or ‘better’ does not exist. If you understand, speak up, spirit!”
translations.sn1.20:25: “He has abandoned reckoning, he did not assume conceit; he has cut off craving for name and form right here. Though they search for him—the one whose bonds are cut, untroubled, free of desire—devas and humans do not find him, here or beyond, in heavens or in any abode.
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time; the time is hidden and cannot be seen. That is why I beg without having enjoyed, so that the time does not pass me by.”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity landed on the ground and said to Venerable Samiddhi: “You are young, mendicant, gone forth while a black-haired youth, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, without having played with sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, mendicant; do not abandon what is apparent in the present to run after what involves time.”
translations.sn1.20:5: “I am not abandoning what is apparent in the present to run after what involves time, friend. I am abandoning what involves time to run after what is apparent in the present. For the Buddha has said that sensual pleasures involve time, offering much suffering and much despair, and the drawback is even greater. But this Teaching is apparent in the present, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced individually by the wise.”
translations.sn1.20:6: “But in what way, mendicant, has the Buddha said that sensual pleasures involve time, offering much suffering and much despair, and the drawback is even greater? And in what way is this Teaching apparent in the present, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be experienced individually by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “I am new, friend, not long gone forth, fresh to this teaching and training. I am not able to explain it in detail. But the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened Buddha is staying near Rājagaha in the Hot Springs Park. Go to the Buddha and ask him about this matter. As the Buddha answers you, so you should remember it.”
translations.sn1.20:8: “It is not easy for us to approach the Buddha, mendicant, as he is surrounded by other influential deities. But if you, mendicant, go to the Buddha and ask him about this matter, we too will come to listen to the teaching.” “Yes, friend,” Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity. He went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told the Buddha:
translations.sn1.21:2: “Like one struck by a sword, like one whose head is on fire, a mendicant should wander mindfully to abandon sensual desire.”
translations.sn1.21:3: “Like one struck by a sword, like one whose head is on fire, a mendicant should wander mindfully to abandon identity view.”
translations.sn1.25:1: “A mendicant who is a perfected one, who has done the task, whose defilements are destroyed, bearing the final body: would he say, ‘I speak’? Would he say, ‘They speak to me’?”
translations.sn1.25:2: “A mendicant who is a perfected one, who has done the task, whose defilements are destroyed, bearing the final body: he might say, ‘I speak’; he might say, ‘They speak to me’. Being skilled in the world’s expressions, knowing them, he would use them just as expressions.”
translations.sn1.25:3: “A mendicant who is a perfected one, who has done the task, whose defilements are destroyed, bearing the final body: would he say, ‘I speak’, having approached conceit? Would he say, ‘They speak to me’?”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one who has abandoned conceit, there are no knots; all knots of conceit are scattered. That wise one has transcended conceiving. He might say, ‘I speak’.
translations.sn1.25:5: He might say, ‘They speak to me’. Being skilled in the world’s expressions, knowing them, he would use them just as expressions.”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.2:5: “With the complete ending of delight in existence, with the ending of perception and consciousness, with the cessation and stilling of feelings: that is how, friend, I know the liberation, release, and seclusion of beings.”
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, late at night, several deities of the Satullapa Group, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity recited this verse in the Buddha’s presence:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is a person’s partner. If lack of faith does not persist, they have fame and glory, and go to heaven when they leave the body.”
translations.sn1.36:4: “One should give up anger, abandon conceit, and get past every fetter. Suffering does not befall one who does not cling to name and form, who has nothing.”
translations.sn1.36:5: “Fools and stupid people devote themselves to negligence. But the wise protect diligence as their best treasure.
translations.sn1.36:6: Don’t devote yourself to negligence, or to intimacy with sensual delight. For if you’re diligent and meditate, you reach the highest happiness.”
translations.sn1.38:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. Now at that time the Buddha’s foot had been cut by a stone splinter. Severe feelings assailed the Buddha—bodily, painful, sharp, rough, stinging, disagreeable, unpleasant. But the Buddha endured them, mindful and aware, without worrying. Then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot on top of the other, mindful and aware.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by vows, practicing rough austerities for a hundred years—their mind is not rightly released. Lowly in nature, they don't reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: There is no taming for the lover of conceit, no sagehood for the unconcentrated. Living alone in the forest, but negligent, one cannot cross beyond the realm of Death.
translations.sn1.38:12: Abandoning conceit, well concentrated, with a lofty mind, released everywhere, living alone in the forest, diligent, one can cross beyond the realm of Death.
translations.sn1.38:2: Then, late at night, seven hundred deities of the Satullapa group, lighting up the entire Maddakucchi, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity recited this verse in the Buddha’s presence: “The ascetic Gotama is indeed a tusker! For he endures bodily feelings that have arisen—painful, sharp, rough, stinging, disagreeable, unpleasant—mindful and aware, without worrying.”
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity recited this verse in the Buddha’s presence: “The ascetic Gotama is indeed a lion! For he endures bodily feelings that have arisen—painful, sharp, rough, stinging, disagreeable, unpleasant—mindful and aware, without worrying.”
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity recited this verse in the Buddha’s presence: “See the concentration well developed, and the mind well released—neither bent forward nor pulled back, and not held in check by forceful suppression. Who would think to transgress against such a tusker of a man, a lion of a man, a thoroughbred of a man, a bull of a man, a draft animal of a man, a tamed man—except through blindness?”
translations.sn1.38:9: Even if brahmins who know the five Vedas practice austerities for a century, their mind is not rightly released. Lowly in nature, they don't reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity recited these verses in the Buddha’s presence:
translations.sn1.41:4: What is given bears fruit in happiness, what is not given does not. Thieves take it away, or kings; fire burns it, or it is lost.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then at the end one leaves the body together with one's possessions. Knowing this, the wise should enjoy and give. Having given and enjoyed according to their means, blameless, they go to a heavenly place.
translations.sn1.42:1: “What gives strength? What gives beauty? What gives happiness? What gives sight? Who gives everything? I ask you, please tell me.”
translations.sn1.42:2: “Giving food gives strength; giving clothes gives beauty; giving a vehicle gives happiness; giving a lamp gives sight.”
translations.sn1.42:3: “The one who gives a dwelling gives everything. But the one who teaches the Dhamma gives the deathless.”
translations.sn1.51:1: “What is good until old age? What is good when established? What is a treasure for humans? What is hard for thieves to take?”
translations.sn1.51:2: “Virtue is good until old age; faith is good when established; wisdom is a treasure for humans; merit is hard for thieves to take.”
translations.sn1.55:1: “What gives birth to a person? What runs around for him? What enters the cycle of wandering? What is his great fear?”
translations.sn1.55:2: “Craving gives birth to a person; his mind runs around; a sentient being enters the cycle of wandering; suffering is his great fear.”
translations.sn1.56:1: “What gives birth to a person? What runs around for him? What enters the cycle of wandering? From what is he not freed?”
translations.sn1.56:2: “Craving gives birth to a person; his mind runs around; a sentient being enters the cycle of wandering; he is not freed from suffering.”
translations.sn1.57:1: “What gives birth to a person? What runs around for him? What enters the cycle of wandering? What is his destiny?”
translations.sn1.57:2: “Craving gives birth to a person; his mind runs around; a sentient being enters the cycle of wandering; deeds are his destiny.”
translations.sn1.59:1: “What is a person’s partner? What governs him? Delighting in what is a mortal freed from all suffering?”
translations.sn1.59:2: “Faith is a person’s partner; wisdom governs him; delighting in Nibbana, a mortal is freed from all suffering.”
translations.sn1.62:1: “By what is the world led? By what is it dragged around? Under the sway of what one thing have all come?”
translations.sn1.62:2: “The world is led by the mind; by the mind it is dragged around; under the sway of the mind, that one thing, have all come.”
translations.sn1.63:2: “The world is led by craving; by craving it is dragged around; under the sway of craving, that one thing, have all come.”
translations.sn1.64:1: “What is the bond of the world? What is its circulation? By abandoning what is it called Nibbana?”
translations.sn1.64:2: “Delight is the bond of the world; thought is its circulation; by abandoning craving it is called Nibbana.”
translations.sn1.65:1: “What is the fetter of the world? What is its circulation? By abandoning what is every bond cut?”
translations.sn1.65:2: “Delight is the fetter of the world; thought is its circulation; by abandoning craving every bond is cut.”
translations.sn1.69:1: “By what is the world bound? By the removal of what is it freed? By abandoning what is every bond cut?”
translations.sn1.69:2: “The world is bound by desire; by the removal of desire it is freed; by abandoning desire every bond is cut.”
translations.sn1.71:2: “Having killed what does one sleep happily? Having killed what does one not sorrow? What is the one thing, Gotama, whose killing you approve?”
translations.sn1.71:3: “Having killed anger, one sleeps happily; having killed anger, one does not sorrow. The killing of anger, O deity, with its poisoned root and honeyed tip: this is what the noble ones praise, for having killed it, one does not sorrow.”
translations.sn1.73:1: “What is the best wealth for a person here? What, when well practiced, brings happiness? What is indeed the sweetest of tastes? How living do they say is the best life?”
translations.sn1.73:2: “Faith is a person’s best wealth right here. The teaching well practiced brings happiness. Truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes. Living by wisdom is said to be the best life.”
translations.sn1.7:2: “Those who haven’t penetrated the teachings are led astray by the doctrines of others. They are asleep and do not wake up. It is time for them to wake up.”
translations.sn1.7:3: “Those who have well penetrated the teachings are not led astray by the doctrines of others. Having understood correctly, fully awakened, they walk evenly amidst the uneven.”
translations.sn1.8:2: “Those who are very confused about the teachings are led astray by the doctrines of others. They are asleep and do not wake up. It is time for them to wake up.”
translations.sn1.8:3: “Those who are not confused about the teachings are not led astray by the doctrines of others. Having understood correctly, fully awakened, they walk evenly amidst the uneven.”
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the Thirty-Three: ‘Good sirs, do not complain about this god. When this god was a human being in the past, he undertook faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One. Having undertaken these things … when his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the Thirty-Three. He outshines the other gods in beauty and glory.’ Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the Thirty-Three, at that time recited these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: “Therefore a wise person, remembering the instructions of the Buddhas, should practice faith, ethics, confidence, and vision of the Dhamma.”
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. Then Sakka, lord of gods, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka said to the Buddha: “Sir, what is a delightful place?”
translations.sn11.15:2: “Shrines in parks and forests, and well-made lotus ponds, are not worth a sixteenth part of a delightful human place.
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. There the Buddha said this: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a certain ugly, pot-bellied goblin was seated on the throne of Sakka, lord of gods. The gods of the Thirty-Three complained, grumbled, and objected: ‘It is incredible, it is amazing! This ugly, pot-bellied goblin is seated on the throne of Sakka, lord of gods!’ But the more the gods complained, grumbled, and objected, the more beautiful, attractive, and graceful that goblin became.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, went up to that anger-eating goblin. He arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his joined palms toward the goblin, and announced his name three times: ‘I, good sir, am Sakka, lord of gods! I, good sir, am Sakka, lord of gods!’ The more Sakka announced his name, the uglier and more pot-bellied the goblin became. Becoming uglier and more pot-bellied, he vanished right there. Then Sakka, lord of gods, sat on his own throne and, guiding the gods of the Thirty-Three, at that time recited these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4: ‘I am not easily frustrated, nor easily swept away by a vortex. I don’t stay angry for long; anger doesn’t last in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: When angry I don’t speak harshly, and I don’t proclaim my virtues. I restrain myself, seeing my own good.’”
translations.sn11.24:2: “Mendicants, there are these two fools. One who doesn’t see a transgression as a transgression, and one who doesn’t accept the confession of one who confesses according to the Dhamma. These are the two fools. There are these two wise people. One who sees a transgression as a transgression, and one who accepts the confession of one who confesses according to the Dhamma. These are the two wise people.
translations.sn11.24:3: Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the Thirty-Three in the Sudhamma Hall, at that time recited this verse:
translations.sn11.24:4: ‘Let anger not overpower you, and do not let friendship decay. Do not blame the blameless, and do not speak divisively. For anger crushes bad people like a mountain.’”
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you don’t recollect me, then you should recollect the teaching: “The teaching is well explained by the Buddha, visible in this very life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that wise people can know it for themselves.” For when you recollect the teaching, any fear, terror, or goosebumps will be given up.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you don’t recollect the teaching, then you should recollect the Saṅgha: “The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that is good, straightforward, methodical, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individuals. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples, worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with joined palms, and the supreme field of merit for the world.” For when you recollect the Saṅgha, any fear, terror, or goosebumps will be given up.
translations.sn11.3:12: Why is that? Because the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha is free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is not cowardly, terrified, frightened, or prone to flight.’” That is what the Buddha said. Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
translations.sn11.3:13: “In a forest, at the root of a tree, or in an empty hut, mendicants, you should recollect the Buddha, and you will have no fear.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you don’t recollect the Buddha, the world’s eldest, the bull of men, then you should recollect the Dhamma, which leads to escape and is well taught.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you don’t recollect the Dhamma, which leads to escape and is well taught, then you should recollect the Saṅgha, the supreme field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: For those who recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way, mendicants, there will be no fear, terror, or goosebumps.”
translations.sn11.3:2: “Mendicants, once upon a time, a battle between the Devas and the Asuras was drawn up. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, addressed the Tāvatiṁsa gods:
translations.sn11.3:3: ‘Gentlemen, if fear, terror, or goosebumps should arise in the gods when they have gone to battle, you should look up at the top of my standard at that time. For when you look up at the top of my standard, any fear, terror, or goosebumps that have arisen will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you don’t look up at the top of my standard, then look up at the top of the standard of Pajāpati, king of gods. For when you look up at the top of his standard, any fear, terror, or goosebumps that have arisen will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: Why is that? Because Sakka, lord of the gods, is not free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearful, terrified, scared, and quick to flee.
translations.sn11.3:9: But I say this, mendicants: ‘If fear, terror, or goosebumps should arise in you when you have gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, you should recollect me at that time: “That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.” For when you recollect me, any fear, terror, or goosebumps that have arisen will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:12: One who mindfully calms down, when they know the other is angry, acts for the welfare of both: oneself and the other.
translations.sn11.5:14: When Sakka had spoken these verses, the Devas applauded, but the Asuras were silent. Then the judges of the Devas and Asuras said: ‘The verses spoken by Vepacitti, lord of Asuras, rely on violence and weapons; they result in conflict, argument, and quarreling. The verses spoken by Sakka, lord of gods, rely on non-violence and non-weapons; they result in no conflict, no argument, and no quarreling. Sakka, lord of gods, wins by well-spoken counsel.’ And that is how Sakka, lord of gods, won the victory by well-spoken counsel.
translations.sn11.5:2: ‘Fools would flare up even more, if there were no one to check them. Therefore with drastic punishment, the wise should restrain the fool.’
translations.sn11.5:3: When Vepacitti had spoken this verse, the Asuras applauded, but the Devas were silent. Then Vepacitti said to Sakka: ‘Speak a verse, lord of gods!’ When he said this, Sakka recited this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: ‘I think this is the only way to check a fool: when you know the other is angry, you mindfully calm down.’
translations.sn11.5:5: When Sakka had spoken this verse, the Devas applauded, but the Asuras were silent. Then Sakka said to Vepacitti: ‘Speak a verse, Vepacitti!’ When he said this, Vepacitti recited this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: ‘I see this fault, Vāsava, in just being patient: When the fool thinks of you, “He puts up with me out of fear,” the idiot pursues you even more, like a cow pursuing one who flees.’
translations.sn11.5:8: ‘Let them think what they like: “He puts up with me out of fear.” Of all the goals that culminate in one’s own good, none is found better than patience.
translations.sn12.11:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. … “Mendicants, there are these four fuels for the maintenance of beings that have been born or for the assistance of those seeking birth. What four? Solid food, whether gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention the third; and consciousness the fourth. These are the four fuels for the maintenance of beings that have been born or for the assistance of those seeking birth.
translations.sn12.12:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, there are these four fuels for the maintenance of beings that have been born or for the assistance of those seeking birth. What four? Solid food, whether gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention the third; and consciousness the fourth. These are the four fuels for the maintenance of beings that have been born or for the assistance of those seeking birth.”
translations.sn12.15:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Kaccānagotta went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Sir, they speak of ‘right view’. How is right view defined?”
translations.sn12.15:2: “Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on a duality: existence and non-existence. But when you truly see the origin of the world with right wisdom, you won’t have the notion of non-existence regarding the world. And when you truly see the cessation of the world with right wisdom, you won’t have the notion of existence regarding the world. This world is mostly shackled by attraction, grasping, and insistence. But one who doesn’t get involved with or cling to that attraction, grasping, mental determination, and insistence—who doesn’t decide ‘this is my self’—has no doubt or uncertainty that what arises is just suffering arising, and what ceases is just suffering ceasing. Their knowledge about this is independent of others. That is how right view is defined.
translations.sn12.17:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Buddha coming from afar. He went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side and said to the Buddha: “I’d like to ask Master Gotama about a certain point, if Master Gotama would take the time to answer my question.” “It’s not the right time for a question, Kassapa. We have entered the inhabited area.”
translations.sn12.17:5: “‘The one who acts is the one who experiences,’ Kassapa: if one thinks this, existing from the beginning, one asserts ‘suffering is made by oneself’: this leans to eternalism. ‘The one who acts is one, the one who experiences is another,’ Kassapa: for one stricken by feeling, if one thinks this, one asserts ‘suffering is made by another’: this leans to annihilationism. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness …pe… Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness …pe… Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, sir! Excellent, sir! Just as, sir, one might turn upright what had been overturned …pe… ‘so that those with eyes might see forms’; in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of monks. May I receive the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, may I receive the higher ordination.”
translations.sn12.17:7: “Kassapa, formerly a member of another sect who wishes for the going forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months. At the end of four months, monks who are satisfied give the going forth and the higher ordination into the state of a monk. However, I recognize individual differences in persons.”
translations.sn12.18:1: At Savatthi. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After finishing some polite and friendly talk, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: “‘The feeling and the one who feels are the same,’ Timbaruka: if one thinks this, existing from the beginning, I do not say ‘pleasure and pain are made by oneself.’ ‘The feeling is one thing, the one who feels is another,’ Timbaruka: for one stricken by feeling, if one thinks this, I do not say ‘pleasure and pain are made by another.’ Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness …pe… Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness …pe… Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.19:1: At Savatthi. “Mendicants, for the fool, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has been generated. So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus this pair. Dependent on the pair there is contact and the six fields of contact, touched by which—or by one of them—the fool experiences pleasure and pain.
translations.sn12.19:2: Mendicants, for the wise person, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has been generated. So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus this pair. Dependent on the pair there is contact and the six fields of contact, touched by which—or by one of them—the wise person experiences pleasure and pain.
translations.sn12.19:3: Therein, mendicants, what is the distinction, what is the disparity, what is the difference between the wise person and the fool?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, sir, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, sir, if the meaning of this statement would occur to the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the mendicants will remember it.”
translations.sn12.19:5: “For the fool, mendicants, that ignorance by which he is hindered and that craving by which he is fettered, through which this body was generated, that ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool and that craving has not been exhausted. Why is that? Because, mendicants, the fool did not live the spiritual life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool goes on to [another] body. Being one who goes on to a body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. He is not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, mendicants, is the vital condition for craving? ‘Feeling’ should be said …pe… ‘Contact’ should be said … ‘The six sense fields’ should be said … ‘Name-and-form’ should be said … ‘Consciousness’ should be said … ‘Volitional formations’ should be said. I say, mendicants, that volitional formations have a vital condition, not that they lack a vital condition. And what is the vital condition for volitional formations? ‘Ignorance’ should be said.
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, mendicants, ignorance is the vital condition for volitional formations; volitional formations for consciousness; consciousness for name-and-form; name-and-form for the six sense fields; the six sense fields for contact; contact for feeling; feeling for craving; craving for grasping; grasping for continued existence; continued existence for birth; birth for suffering; suffering for faith; faith for gladness; gladness for rapture; rapture for tranquility; tranquility for happiness; happiness for immersion; immersion for knowledge and vision of things as they really are; knowledge and vision of things as they really are for disillusionment; disillusionment for dispassion; dispassion for liberation; liberation for the knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:7: Suppose, mendicants, when it rains heavily on a mountain top, the water flows down the slope and fills the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies are full, they fill the little pools. When the little pools are full, they fill the big pools. When the big pools are full, they fill the little rivers. When the little rivers are full, they fill the big rivers. When the big rivers are full, they fill the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: At Savatthi. Then the Venerable Bhumija emerged from seclusion in the late afternoon and approached the Venerable Sariputta. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sariputta. After finishing some polite and friendly talk, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhumija said to the Venerable Sariputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: Ananda, when there is the body, because of bodily volition, pleasure and pain arise internally. When there is speech, because of verbal volition, pleasure and pain arise internally. When there is the mind, because of mental volition, pleasure and pain arise internally—conditioned by ignorance.
translations.sn12.25:11: Ananda, one generates that bodily choice on one’s own, conditioned by which pleasure and pain arise internally. Or others generate that bodily choice, conditioned by which pleasure and pain arise internally. One generates that bodily choice aware, conditioned by which pleasure and pain arise internally. Or one generates that bodily choice unaware, conditioned by which pleasure and pain arise internally.
translations.sn12.25:2: “Reverend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain are made by oneself. There are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain are made by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain are made by both oneself and another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain arise by chance, being made neither by oneself nor by another. Here, Reverend Sāriputta, what does the Buddha say? What does he preach? How should we answer so as to speak in accordance with the Buddha, not misrepresenting the Buddha with an untruth, but explaining in line with the Dhamma, so that no fellow Dhamma-farer would find ground for criticism?”
translations.sn12.25:3: “Reverend, the Buddha has said that pleasure and pain are dependently originated. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Saying this, one would be speaking in accordance with the Buddha, not misrepresenting the Buddha with an untruth, but explaining in line with the Dhamma, so that no fellow Dhamma-farer would find ground for criticism.
translations.sn12.25:4: Therein, reverend, regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain are made by oneself—that too is conditioned by contact. Regarding those too... Regarding those too... Regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain arise by chance, being made neither by oneself nor by another—that too is conditioned by contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: Therein, reverend, regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain are made by oneself—that they will experience this without contact: such a thing is impossible. Regarding those too... Regarding those too... Regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare that pleasure and pain arise by chance, being made neither by oneself nor by another—that they will experience this without contact: such a thing is impossible.”
translations.sn12.25:6: Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda reported that entire conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija to the Buddha.
translations.sn12.25:7: “Good, good, Ānanda. Sāriputta answered correctly just as he should. Ānanda, I have said that pleasure and pain are dependently originated. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Saying this, one would be speaking in accordance with me, not misrepresenting me with an untruth, but explaining in line with the Dhamma, so that no fellow Dhamma-farer would find ground for criticism.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, monks, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, intention, contact, and attention—this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—this is called form. Thus this is name and this is form. This, monks, is called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, monks, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, monks, is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, monks, are choices? There are these three kinds of choices: bodily choices, verbal choices, mental choices. These, monks, are called choices.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, monks, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, not knowing the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, monks, is existence? There are these three states of existence: sensual existence, luminous existence, formless existence. This, monks, is called existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, monks, is grasping? There are these four kinds of grasping: grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and observances, grasping at a doctrine of self. This, monks, is called grasping.
translations.sn12.31:1: At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī. There the Buddha addressed Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, this was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.31:2: ‘Those who have comprehended the teaching, / and the many trainees here; / when asked, dear sir, please tell me / the conduct of those who are wise.’
translations.sn12.31:3: “How, Sāriputta, should the detailed meaning of this brief statement be understood?” When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta kept silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: “Do you see that ‘this has come to be’, Sāriputta?” “Sir, one sees with right wisdom as it really is that ‘this has come to be’. Having seen with right wisdom as it really is that ‘this has come to be’, one is practicing for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be. One sees with right wisdom as it really is that ‘it originated from that nutriment’. Having seen with right wisdom as it really is that ‘it originated from that nutriment’, one is practicing for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding its origin from nutriment. One sees with right wisdom as it really is that ‘from the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation’. Having seen with right wisdom as it really is that ‘from the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation’, one is practicing for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation. That is how one is a trainee, sir.
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, sir, is one a person who has understood the teaching? 'This has come to be': one sees this with right wisdom as it really is. Having seen 'This has come to be' with right wisdom as it really is, one is freed by not grasping through revulsion, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be. 'Its origin is from that nutriment': one sees this with right wisdom as it really is. Having seen 'Its origin is from that nutriment' with right wisdom as it really is, one is freed by not grasping through revulsion, dispassion, and cessation regarding the origin from nutriment. 'From the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation': one sees this with right wisdom as it really is. Having seen 'From the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation' with right wisdom as it really is, one is freed by not grasping through revulsion, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation. That is how, sir, one is a person who has understood the teaching. So it is, sir, regarding what was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.35:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, ignorance is a condition for choices. Choices are a condition for consciousness … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.” When he said this, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: “‘Sir, what is aging and death? And who does this aging and death belong to?’ ‘That is not a fitting question,’ said the Buddha. ‘Mendicant, if one were to say, “What is aging and death? And who does this aging and death belong to?” or if one were to say, “Aging and death is one thing, and this aging and death belongs to someone else,” both of these mean the same thing, only the phrasing is different. Mendicant, if the view “The soul and the body are the same thing” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived. If the view “The soul and the body are different things” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way: “Rebirth is a condition for aging and death.”’”
translations.sn12.35:2: “‘Sir, what is rebirth? And who does this rebirth belong to?’ ‘That is not a fitting question,’ said the Buddha. ‘Mendicant, if one were to say, “What is rebirth? And who does this rebirth belong to?” or if one were to say, “Rebirth is one thing, and this rebirth belongs to someone else,” both of these mean the same thing, only the phrasing is different. Mendicant, if the view “The soul and the body are the same thing” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived. If the view “The soul and the body are different things” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way: “Continued existence is a condition for rebirth.”’”
translations.sn12.35:3: “‘Sir, what is continued existence? And who does this continued existence belong to?’ ‘That is not a fitting question,’ said the Buddha. ‘Mendicant, if one were to say, “What is continued existence? And who does this continued existence belong to?” or if one were to say, “Continued existence is one thing, and this continued existence belongs to someone else,” both of these mean the same thing, only the phrasing is different. Mendicant, if the view “The soul and the body are the same thing” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived; if the view “The soul and the body are different things” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way: “Grasping is a condition for continued existence” … “Craving is a condition for grasping” … “Feeling is a condition for craving” … “Contact is a condition for feeling” … “The six sense fields are a condition for contact” … “Name and form are a condition for the six sense fields” … “Consciousness is a condition for name and form” … “Choices are a condition for consciousness.”’”
translations.sn12.35:4: “‘Sir, what are choices? And who do these choices belong to?’ ‘That is not a fitting question,’ said the Buddha. ‘Mendicant, if one were to say, “What are choices? And who do these choices belong to?” or if one were to say, “Choices are one thing, and these choices belong to someone else,” both of these mean the same thing, only the phrasing is different. Mendicant, if the view “The soul and the body are the same thing” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived; if the view “The soul and the body are different things” exists, the spiritual life cannot be lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way: “Ignorance is a condition for choices.”’”
translations.sn12.35:5: “But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever twisted, equivocal, and vacillating views there are—such as ‘What is aging and death? And who does this aging and death belong to?’ or ‘Aging and death is one thing, and this aging and death belongs to someone else,’ or ‘The soul and the body are the same thing,’ or ‘The soul and the body are different things’—all these are given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
translations.sn12.35:7: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever twisted, equivocal, and vacillating views there are—such as ‘What is continued existence?’ … ‘What is grasping?’ … ‘What is craving?’ … ‘What is feeling?’ … ‘What is contact?’ … ‘What are the six sense fields?’ … ‘What are name and form?’ … ‘What is consciousness?’ …
translations.sn12.38:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, what one intends, and what one plans, and what one has a tendency for: this becomes a basis for the maintenance of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is rebirth into a new state of existence in the future. When there is rebirth into a new state of existence in the future, future birth, aging, and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress come to be. That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.38:2: If one does not intend, and does not plan, but still has a tendency for it, this becomes a basis for the maintenance of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is rebirth into a new state of existence in the future. When there is rebirth into a new state of existence in the future, future birth, aging, and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress come to be. That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.44:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, I will teach you the origin and the passing away of the world. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: “And what, mendicants, is the origin of the world? Eye consciousness arises dependent on the eye and sights. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a condition for feeling. Feeling is a condition for craving. Craving is a condition for grasping. Grasping is a condition for continued existence. Continued existence is a condition for rebirth. Rebirth is a condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be. This, mendicants, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:3: Ear consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sounds … Nose consciousness arises dependent on the nose and smells … Tongue consciousness arises dependent on the tongue and tastes … Body consciousness arises dependent on the body and touches … Mind consciousness arises dependent on the mind and thoughts. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a condition for feeling … Rebirth is a condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be. This, mendicants, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, mendicants, is the ending of the world? Eye consciousness arises dependent on the eye and sights. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a condition for feeling. Feeling is a condition for craving. When that craving fades away and ceases with nothing left over, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases. This, mendicants, is the ending of the world.
translations.sn12.46:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:
translations.sn12.46:2: “Master Gotama, does the one who acts experience the result?” “The view that the one who acts is the same as the one who experiences the result is one extreme, brahmin.”
translations.sn12.46:3: “Then, Master Gotama, does one person act and another experience the result?” “The view that one person acts and another experiences the result is the second extreme, brahmin. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘Ignorance is a condition for choices. Choices are a condition for consciousness … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates. When ignorance fades away and ceases with nothing left over, choices cease. When choices cease … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’”
translations.sn12.51:10: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it is impermanent, that it is not attached to, and that it is not delighted in. If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it is impermanent, that it is not attached to, and that it is not delighted in. If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it is impermanent, that it is not attached to, and that it is not delighted in. If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.
translations.sn12.51:11: Feeling a feeling limited to the body, they understand: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ Feeling a feeling limited to life, they understand: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ They understand: ‘With the breakup of the body, after the ending of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; mere bodily remains will be left.’
translations.sn12.51:12: Suppose a person was to remove a hot pot from a potter’s kiln and set it on level ground. Its heat would settle right there, and the shards would be left. In the same way, feeling a feeling limited to the body … they understand: ‘… mere bodily remains will be left.’
translations.sn12.51:13: “What do you think, mendicants? Would a mendicant with defilements ended generate a meritorious choice, a demeritorious choice, or an imperturbable choice?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn12.51:14: “And when choices don’t exist at all, with the cessation of choices, would consciousness be discerned?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn12.51:2: “Mendicants, how does a mendicant investigate so as to completely and rightly end suffering?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha, sir, guided by the Buddha, and take refuge in the Buddha. It would be good if the Buddha himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. The mendicants will listen and remember it.” “Well then, mendicants, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn12.51:3: “In this case, a mendicant investigates: ‘The many and varied kinds of suffering that arise in the world—old age and death. What is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of this suffering? When what exists do old age and death come to be? When what does not exist do old age and death not come to be?’ Investigating, they understand: ‘The many and varied kinds of suffering that arise in the world—old age and death. This suffering has rebirth as its source, origin, birthplace, and inception. When rebirth exists, old age and death come to be. When rebirth does not exist, old age and death do not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:4: They understand old age and death, their origin, their cessation, and the practice fitting for the cessation of old age and death. And they practice accordingly, living in line with the Dhamma. This is called a mendicant who is practicing for the complete and right ending of suffering, for the cessation of old age and death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then they investigate further: ‘What is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of rebirth? When what exists does rebirth come to be? When what does not exist does rebirth not come to be?’ Investigating, they understand: ‘Rebirth has continued existence as its source, origin, birthplace, and inception. When continued existence exists, rebirth comes to be. When continued existence does not exist, rebirth does not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands rebirth, the origin of rebirth, the cessation of rebirth, and the practice leading to the cessation of rebirth suitable for the cessation of rebirth, and he practices accordingly, living in line with the teaching. This is called, monks, a monk who is practicing completely rightly for the ending of suffering, for the cessation of rebirth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, investigating further, he investigates: ‘What is the source of this continued existence? … What is the source of this grasping? … craving … feeling … contact … the six sense fields … name and form … consciousness … What is the source of these choices? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their source? When what exists do choices come to be? When what does not exist do choices not come to be?’ Investigating, he understands: ‘Choices have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, ignorance as their source. When ignorance exists, choices come to be; when ignorance does not exist, choices do not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands choices, the origin of choices, the cessation of choices, and the practice leading to the cessation of choices suitable for the cessation of choices, and he practices accordingly, living in line with the teaching. This is called, monks, a monk who is practicing completely rightly for the ending of suffering, for the cessation of choices.
translations.sn12.51:9: Monks, if a person immersed in ignorance generates a meritorious choice, consciousness fares on to the meritorious. If they generate a demeritorious choice, consciousness fares on to the demeritorious. If they generate an imperturbable choice, consciousness fares on to the imperturbable. But when a monk has abandoned ignorance and knowledge has arisen, through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, he does not generate a meritorious choice, a demeritorious choice, or an imperturbable choice. Not generating choices, not intending, he grasps at nothing in the world. Not grasping, he is not anxious. Not being anxious, he personally attains extinguishment. He understands: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.’
translations.sn12.52:2: Suppose, monks, a great bonfire was burning, consuming ten, twenty, thirty, or forty loads of wood. And a person would toss dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood into it from time to time. Fueled and sustained by that, that great bonfire would burn for a long time. In the same way, monks, when one dwells focusing on gratification in things that stimulate grasping, craving grows. With craving as a condition, grasping comes to be … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.52:3: When one dwells focusing on the danger in things that stimulate grasping, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, continued existence ceases; with the cessation of continued existence, rebirth ceases; with the cessation of rebirth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn12.55:1: At Sāvatthī. “Monks, when one dwells focusing on gratification in things that stimulate grasping, craving grows. With craving as a condition, grasping comes to be; with grasping as a condition, continued existence … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.55:2: Suppose, monks, there was a great tree. Whatever roots went down and whatever roots went across, they would all draw sap upwards. Fueled and sustained by that, that great tree would stand for a long time. In the same way, monks, when one dwells focusing on gratification in things that stimulate grasping, craving grows. With craving as a condition, grasping comes to be … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.55:3: When one dwells focusing on the danger in things that stimulate grasping, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, continued existence ceases … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn12.61:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. … “Monks, an uninstructed ordinary person might become disillusioned with this body made of the four great elements, dispassionate towards it, and liberated from it. Why is that? Because growth and decline, taking up and putting down are seen in this body made of the four great elements. Therefore an uninstructed ordinary person might become disillusioned with it, dispassionate towards it, and liberated from it.
translations.sn12.61:2: But as for what is called ‘mind’ or ‘sentience’ or ‘consciousness’, an uninstructed ordinary person is unable to become disillusioned with it, dispassionate towards it, or liberated from it. Why is that? Because for a long time the uninstructed ordinary person has held to it, cherished it, and grasped it: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’ Therefore an uninstructed ordinary person is unable to become disillusioned with it, dispassionate towards it, or liberated from it.
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better, monks, for the uninstructed ordinary person to take this body made of the four great elements to be the self, rather than the mind. Why is that? This body made of the four great elements is seen standing for one year, for two years, for three years, for four years, for five years, for ten years, for twenty years, for thirty years, for forty years, for fifty years, for a hundred years, or even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: But a learned noble disciple attends closely and carefully to dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this doesn’t exist, that doesn’t come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: ignorance is a condition for choices. Choices are a condition for consciousness … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates. When ignorance fades away and ceases with nothing left over, choices cease. When choices cease, consciousness ceases … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’
translations.sn12.62:3: But a learned noble disciple attends closely and carefully to dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this doesn’t exist, that doesn’t come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.’ Pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and settles down. Painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding feeling—the painful feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as painful—ceases and settles down. Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neutral, the corresponding feeling—the neutral feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as neutral—ceases and settles down.
translations.sn12.62:4: Suppose, mendicants, heat is generated and fire is produced from the rubbing and friction of two sticks. But when those two sticks are separated and laid apart, the corresponding heat ceases and settles down. In the same way, pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and settles down. … Painful feeling … Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neutral, the corresponding feeling—the neutral feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as neutral—ceases and settles down.
translations.sn12.63:3: “What do you think, mendicants? Would they eat that food for fun, intoxication, beautification, or attraction?” “No, sir.” “Wouldn’t they eat that food just to cross the desert?” “Yes, sir.” “I say that solid food should be seen in the same way. When solid food is fully understood, desire for the five kinds of sensual stimulation is fully understood. When desire for the five kinds of sensual stimulation is fully understood, there is no fetter bound by which a noble disciple would return to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how should the nutriment of contact be seen? Suppose there was a flayed cow. If she stands by a wall, the creatures living in the wall would eat her. If she stands by a tree, the creatures living in the tree would eat her. If she stands in water, the creatures living in the water would eat her. If she stands in the open, the creatures living in the air would eat her. Wherever that flayed cow stands, the creatures living there would eat her. I say that the nutriment of contact should be seen in the same way. When the nutriment of contact is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say that a noble disciple has nothing further to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how should the nutriment of mental intention be seen? Suppose there was a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals without flame or smoke. Then a person would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants happiness and recoils from pain. Then two strong men would grab them by the arms and drag them towards the charcoal pit. Then that person’s intention, aim, and wish would be to get far away. Why is that? Because that person thinks: ‘If I fall into this charcoal pit, it will result in my death or deadly pain.’ I say that the nutriment of mental intention should be seen in the same way. When the nutriment of mental intention is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say that a noble disciple has nothing further to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: If there is desire, relishing, and craving for solid food, consciousness becomes established and grows there. Where consciousness is established and grows, name and form are conceived. Where name and form are conceived, choices grow. Where choices grow, there is rebirth into a new state of existence in the future. Where there is rebirth into a new state of existence in the future, there is future rebirth, old age, and death. Where there is future rebirth, old age, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, anguish, and distress.
translations.sn12.64:4: Suppose, mendicants, a dyer or a painter, having dye or lac or turmeric or indigo or madder, were to create the figure of a woman or a man, complete in all its parts, on a well-polished panel or a wall or a strip of cloth. In the same way, if there is desire, relishing, and craving for solid food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of future rebirth. Where there is the production of future rebirth, there is future birth, old age, and death. Where there is future birth, old age, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, anguish, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: If, mendicants, there is no desire, relishing, and craving for solid food, consciousness does not become established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations. Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of future rebirth. Where there is no production of future rebirth, there is no future birth, old age, and death. Where there is no future birth, old age, and death, I say that is without sorrow, anguish, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Suppose, mendicants, there was a peaked house or a hall with a peaked roof, with windows on the north, south, or east. When the sun rises and a ray of light enters through a window, where would it land?” “On the western wall, sir.” “If there were no western wall, where would it land?” “On the ground, sir.” “If there were no ground, where would it land?” “In the water, sir.” “If there were no water, where would it land?” “It would not land, sir.” “In the same way, if there is no desire, relishing, and craving for solid food …
translations.sn12.65:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, before my awakening, while I was still unawakened and a Bodhisatta, I thought: ‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble. It is born, grows old, dies, passes away, and is reborn. Yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from old age and death. When will an escape from this suffering, from old age and death, be found?’ Then it occurred to me: ‘When what exists is there old age and death? What is the condition for old age and death?’ Then, through rational application of mind, I comprehended with wisdom: ‘When birth exists, old age and death come to be. Old age and death have birth as their condition.’
translations.sn12.65:3: Then it occurred to me: ‘This consciousness turns back from name-and-form, it does not go beyond. It is to this extent that one may be born, grow old, die, pass away, or be reborn: that is, name-and-form is a condition for consciousness; consciousness is a condition for name-and-form; name-and-form is a condition for the six sense fields; the six sense fields are a condition for contact … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’ ‘Origination, origination!’—at this, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, realization arose, and light arose in me regarding teachings not heard before.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then it occurred to me: ‘When what does not exist does consciousness not come to be? When what ceases does consciousness cease?’ Then, through rational application of mind, I comprehended with wisdom: ‘When name-and-form does not exist, consciousness does not come to be. When name-and-form ceases, consciousness ceases.’
translations.sn12.65:6: Then it occurred to me: ‘I have discovered this path to awakening, that is: when name-and-form ceases, consciousness ceases; when consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; when name-and-form ceases, the six sense fields cease; when the six sense fields cease, contact ceases … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’ ‘Cessation, cessation!’—at this, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, realization arose, and light arose in me regarding teachings not heard before.
translations.sn12.65:7: Suppose, mendicants, a person wandering in a forest wilderness were to see an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of the past. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient royal capital inhabited by people of the past, complete with parks, groves, and lotus ponds, enclosed by walls, a delightful place. Then that person would inform the king or the royal minister: ‘Please know, sir, that while wandering in a forest wilderness I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of the past. I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal capital inhabited by people of the past, complete with parks, groves, and lotus ponds, enclosed by walls, a delightful place. Sir, rebuild that city!’ Then the king or the royal minister would rebuild that city. And later that city would become successful and prosperous, populous, full of people, and would attain growth and expansion. In the same way, mendicants, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by the fully awakened Buddhas of the past.
translations.sn12.66:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, where there was a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadamma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said: “Mendicants, do you scrutinize the inward scrutiny?” When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha: “Sir, I scrutinize the inward scrutiny.” “But how, mendicant, do you scrutinize the inward scrutiny?” Then that mendicant answered. But the way he answered did not satisfy the Buddha’s mind.
translations.sn12.66:2: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One! Let the Blessed One speak on the internal exploration. The mendicants will listen and remember it.” “Well then, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.66:5: Furthermore, while exploring, they explore the internal exploration: ‘Where does this craving arise and where does it settle?’ While exploring, they know this: ‘Wherever there is something pleasing and agreeable in the world, that is where this craving arises and settles.’ And what in the world is pleasing and agreeable? The eye in the world is pleasing and agreeable; that is where this craving arises and settles. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind in the world is pleasing and agreeable; that is where this craving arises and settles.
translations.sn12.66:6: Whatever ascetics and brahmins in the past regarded that which is pleasing and agreeable in the world as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as safe: they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased acquisition. Those who increased acquisition increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They were not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.66:7: Whatever ascetics and brahmins in the future will regard that which is pleasing and agreeable in the world as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as safe: they will increase craving. Those who will increase craving will increase acquisition. Those who will increase acquisition will increase suffering. Those who will increase suffering will not be freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They will not be freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.66:8: Whatever ascetics and brahmins in the present regard that which is pleasing and agreeable in the world as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as safe: they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase acquisition. Those who increase acquisition increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.67:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were staying near Benares, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from his seclusion in the late afternoon and went to Venerable Sāriputta. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta and, after engaging in a friendly and polite conversation, sat down to one side. While seated to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to Venerable Sāriputta: “Reverend Sāriputta, is old age and death made by oneself? Is it made by another? Is it made by both oneself and another? Or does it arise by chance, not made by oneself or another?” “Reverend Koṭṭhika, old age and death is not made by oneself, nor by another, nor by both, nor does it arise by chance. Rather, old age and death is conditioned by rebirth.”
translations.sn12.67:2: “Reverend Sāriputta, is rebirth made by oneself? Is it made by another? Is it made by both oneself and another? Or does it arise by chance, not made by oneself or another?” “Reverend Koṭṭhika, rebirth is not made by oneself, nor by another, nor by both, nor does it arise by chance. Rather, rebirth is conditioned by continued existence.”
translations.sn12.67:4: “Reverend Sāriputta, is consciousness made by oneself? Is it made by another? Is it made by both oneself and another? Or does it arise by chance, not made by oneself or another?” “Reverend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not made by oneself, nor by another, nor by both, nor does it arise by chance. Rather, consciousness is conditioned by name and form.”
translations.sn12.67:5: “Just now we understood the statement of Venerable Sāriputta thus: ‘Reverend Koṭṭhika, name and form is not made by oneself, nor by another, nor by both, nor does it arise by chance. Rather, name and form is conditioned by consciousness.’”
translations.sn12.67:7: “How then, friend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be seen?” “Well then, friend, I will make up a simile for you. For some intelligent people here understand the meaning of a statement by means of a simile. Just as two sheaves of reeds might stand leaning against each other, so too, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense fields come to be; with the six sense fields as condition, contact comes to be … Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. If, friend, one were to pull away one of those sheaves of reeds, the other would fall; and if one were to pull away the other, the first would fall. So too, with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of consciousness comes to be; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form comes to be; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense fields comes to be; with the cessation of the six sense fields, cessation of contact comes to be … Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.sn12.67:8: “It is incredible, friend Sāriputta, it is amazing! How well this was spoken by Venerable Sāriputta! And we rejoice in Venerable Sāriputta’s statement on these thirty-six grounds:
translations.sn12.68:13: “Then is the Venerable Nārada an arahant with taints destroyed?” “Friend, though I have clearly seen as it really is with right wisdom, ‘Cessation of existence is Nibbāna,’ I am not an arahant with taints destroyed. Suppose, friend, there was a well along a desert road, but it had neither a rope nor a bucket. Then a man would come along, scorched and exhausted by the heat, weary, parched, and thirsty. He would look down into the well. He would have the knowledge, ‘There is water,’ but he would not be able to physically touch it. So too, friend, though I have clearly seen as it really is with right wisdom, ‘Cessation of existence is Nibbāna,’ I am not an arahant with taints destroyed.”
translations.sn12.68:6: “Then is the Venerable Musila an arahant with taints destroyed?” When this was said, Venerable Musila remained silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. There … “Mendicants, as the ocean swells, it makes the great rivers swell. As the great rivers swell, they make the smaller rivers swell. As the smaller rivers swell, they make the great lakes swell. As the great lakes swell, they make the small lakes swell. In the same way, as ignorance swells, it makes choices swell. As choices swell, they make consciousness swell. As consciousness swells, it makes name and form swell. As name and form swell, they make the six sense fields swell. As the six sense fields swell, they make contact swell. As contact swells, it makes feeling swell. As feeling swells, it makes craving swell. As craving swells, it makes grasping swell. As grasping swells, it makes continued existence swell. As continued existence swells, it makes rebirth swell. As rebirth swells, it makes old age and death swell.
translations.sn12.70:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. At that time the Buddha was honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and worshipped. He received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. The Order of monks was also honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and worshipped. They received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.
