But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, or worshipped, and they did not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:10: “But knowing and seeing thus, reverends, do you dwell having physically touched those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:11: “Here now, reverends: this declaration and the non-attainment of these states. How is this, friend?” “We are freed by wisdom, friend Susima.”
translations.sn12.70:12: “I don't understand the detailed meaning of the Venerables' brief statement. Please, Venerables, speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of the Venerables' brief statement.” “Whether you understand or not, friend Susima, we are freed by wisdom.”
translations.sn12.70:13: Then Venerable Susima rose from his seat and went to the Buddha. He bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Susima told the Buddha of all the conversation he had with those monks. “First, Susima, comes knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, afterwards knowledge of Nibbāna.”
translations.sn12.70:14: “I don't understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha's brief statement. Please, Sir, speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha's brief statement.” “Whether you understand or not, Susima, first comes knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, afterwards knowledge of Nibbāna.
translations.sn12.70:16: “Therefore, Susima, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Any kind of feeling … Any kind of perception … Any kind of choices … Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing this, Susima, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, and revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion they are liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' They understand: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.'
translations.sn12.70:18: “Do you see, Susima, that aging and death are conditioned by rebirth?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see, Susima, that rebirth is conditioned by continued existence?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see, Susima, that continued existence is conditioned by grasping?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see, Susima, that grasping is conditioned by craving?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see that craving is conditioned by feeling … contact … the six sense fields … name and form … consciousness … volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance, Susima?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn12.70:2: At that time the wanderer Susima was residing in Rājagaha with a large assembly of wanderers. Then Susima’s assembly said to him: “Come, friend Susima, live the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama. When you have mastered the teaching, recite it to us. We will master that teaching and speak it to the lay people. Then we too will be honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and we will receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines for the sick.” “Yes, friends,” Susima replied to his own assembly. He went to Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Susima said to Venerable Ānanda: “I wish, friend Ānanda, to live the spiritual life in this teaching and training.”
translations.sn12.70:21: “But Susima, knowing and seeing thus, do you hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, far and near, with the purified divine ear surpassing the human?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn12.70:25: “But Susima, knowing and seeing thus, do you meditate having touched with the body those peaceful deliverances that are formless, transcending forms?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn12.70:27: Then Venerable Susima bowed with his head at the Buddha's feet and said to him: “I have made a mistake, sir. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of me to go forth as a thief of the Dhamma in such a well-explained teaching and training. Please, sir, accept my mistake as a mistake for the sake of future restraint.”
translations.sn12.70:3: Then Venerable Ānanda took the wanderer Susima to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Sir, this wanderer Susima says: ‘I wish, friend Ānanda, to live the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’” “Well then, Ānanda, give Susima the going forth.” The wanderer Susima received the going forth and ordination in the Buddha’s presence.
translations.sn12.70:5: “But knowing and seeing thus, do you venerables wield the many kinds of psychic power? Appearing as one and becoming many, and appearing as many and becoming one; appearing and vanishing; going unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water without sinking as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with your hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; and wielding bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma realm?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:6: “But knowing and seeing thus, do you venerables hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, far and near, with the purified divine ear surpassing the human?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:7: “But knowing and seeing thus, do you venerables understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with your own mind? Do you understand a mind with greed as ‘a mind with greed’; a mind without greed as ‘a mind without greed’; a mind with hate as ‘a mind with hate’; a mind without hate as ‘a mind without hate’; a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion’; a mind without delusion as ‘a mind without delusion’; a constricted mind as ‘a constricted mind’; a scattered mind as ‘a scattered mind’; an expansive mind as ‘an expansive mind’; an unexpansive mind as ‘an unexpansive mind’; a surpassable mind as ‘a surpassable mind’; an unsurpassable mind as ‘an unsurpassable mind’; an immersed mind as ‘an immersed mind’; an unimmersed mind as ‘an unimmersed mind’; a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind’; and an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind’?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:8: “But knowing and seeing thus, do you venerables recollect many kinds of past lives? That is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world contraction, many eons of world expansion, many eons of world contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so-and-so, of such a clan, such a caste, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There too I was so-and-so, of such a clan, such a caste, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.’ Thus do you recollect your manifold past lives with their aspects and details?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:9: “Knowing and seeing thus, reverends, do you see sentient beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place, understanding how sentient beings fare according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings were endowed with bad conduct of body, speech, and mind. They reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and acted accordingly. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. Or else, these dear beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind. They did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and acted accordingly. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, do you see sentient beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place, understanding how sentient beings fare according to their deeds?” “No, reverend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills together with a large saṅgha of mendicants.
translations.sn16.11:10: So, Kassapa, you should train like this: ‘I will establish a keen sense of conscience and prudence for seniors, novices, and those of middle standing.’ That’s how you should train.
translations.sn16.11:11: So, Kassapa, you should train like this: ‘Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the skillful, I will listen to all of it with eager ears, applying my mind, bringing my whole heart to it.’ That’s how you should train.
translations.sn16.11:12: So, Kassapa, you should train like this: ‘I will not neglect mindfulness of the body associated with joy.’ That’s how you should train.
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, reverend, after advising me with this advice, the Buddha got up from his seat and left. For seven days, reverend, I ate the country’s almsfood as a debtor. On the eighth day final knowledge arose.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, reverend, the Buddha stepped off the road and went to the root of a certain tree. I folded my patchwork robe in four and said to him: ‘Sir, please sit here. It would be for my lasting welfare and happiness.’ The Buddha sat on the seat spread out. When he was seated he said to me: ‘Kassapa, this patchwork robe of yours is soft.’ ‘Sir, please accept my patchwork robe out of compassion.’ ‘But Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out hempen rag robes?’ ‘I will, sir.’ So I gave my patchwork robe to the Buddha, and I accepted the Buddha’s worn-out hempen rag robes.
translations.sn16.11:17: Reverend, I have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and I live having known and realized it with my own insight due to the ending of defilements. You might as well think to hide a tusker seven or seven and a half cubits high behind a palm leaf as to think to hide my six direct knowledges.
translations.sn16.11:2: Now at that time thirty of Venerable Ānanda’s pupils had rejected the training and returned to a lesser life; they were mostly youths. Then, after wandering in the Southern Hills as long as he pleased, Ānanda went to the Bamboo Grove in Rājagaha to see Mahākassapa. He bowed to Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. Mahākassapa said to him: “Reverend Ānanda, for how many reasons did the Buddha lay down the rule restricting eating in groups of three among families?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “For three reasons, Sir Kassapa: for holding back bad people, for the comfort of well-behaved mendicants, and so that those with bad wishes don’t form a faction and split the Saṅgha, and out of compassion for families. The Buddha laid down the rule restricting eating in groups of three among families for these three reasons.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “Then why, Reverend Ānanda, do you wander with these new mendicants who don’t guard their sense doors, who don’t know the measure of their food, and who are not committed to wakefulness? One would think you’re wandering about destroying crops and destroying families! Your following is falling apart, Ānanda; your young disciples are falling away. But this boy doesn’t know his own measure!”
translations.sn16.11:6: The nun Thullanandā heard that Master Mahākassapa had rebuked Master Ānanda, the Sage of Videha, by calling him a boy.
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the nun Thullanandā was displeased and expressed her displeasure: “How can Master Mahākassapa think to rebuke Master Ānanda, the Sage of Videha, by calling him a boy, when he himself was formerly an ascetic of another sect?” Venerable Mahākassapa heard Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: “Indeed, friend Ānanda, the nun Thullanandā spoke hastily and without reflection. Since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, I do not recall acknowledging any other teacher except the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One. Before, friend, when I was still a householder, it occurred to me: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life that is utterly perfect, utterly pure, like a polished conch shell. Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.’ So, friend, at a later time, having made a robe out of discarded rags, acknowledging those who are arahants in the world, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.sn16.13:2: Just as, Kassapa, gold does not disappear so long as counterfeit gold has not arisen in the world. But when counterfeit gold arises in the world, then true gold disappears. In the same way, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear so long as a counterfeit Dhamma has not arisen in the world. But when a counterfeit Dhamma arises in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.
translations.sn16.13:4: These five detrimental things, Kassapa, lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwell without respect and deference for the Teacher; they dwell without respect and deference for the Dhamma; they dwell without respect and deference for the Saṅgha; they dwell without respect and deference for the training; they dwell without respect and deference for concentration. These, Kassapa, are the five detrimental things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Sāriputta were staying near Benares, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion in the late afternoon and went to Venerable Mahākassapa. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahākassapa, and after engaging in a friendly and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. While seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahākassapa: “It is said, friend Kassapa, that one who is not ardent and has no fear of wrongdoing is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme sanctuary from the yoke. But one who is ardent and has fear of wrongdoing is capable of enlightenment, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.”
translations.sn16.2:3: And how, friend, is one without fear of wrongdoing? Here, friend, a monk does not fear that unarisen evil, unskillful qualities, if they arise, will lead to harm. He does not fear that arisen evil, unskillful qualities, if not abandoned, will lead to harm. He does not fear that unarisen skillful qualities, if they do not arise, will lead to harm. He does not fear that arisen skillful qualities, if they cease, will lead to harm. That is how, friend, one is without fear of wrongdoing. That is how, friend, one who is not ardent and has no fear of wrongdoing is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how, friend, is one ardent? Here, friend, a monk generates ardor thinking: ‘If unarisen evil, unskillful qualities arise, they will lead to harm.’ He generates ardor thinking: ‘If arisen evil, unskillful qualities are not abandoned, they will lead to harm.’ He generates ardor thinking: ‘If unarisen skillful qualities...’ ... He generates ardor. That is how, friend, one is ardent.
translations.sn16.5:1: So I have heard... in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove. Then Venerable Mahākassapa went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Venerable Mahākassapa as he was sitting there: “You are old now, Kassapa, and these worn-out hempen rag-robes are heavy for you. So, Kassapa, wear robes offered by householders, accept invitations for meals, and stay close to me.”
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now at that time a certain monk named Thera was living alone and praising living alone. He entered the village for alms alone, returned alone, sat in private alone, and walked meditation alone. Then several monks went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: “Here, sir, a certain monk named Thera lives alone and praises living alone.”
translations.sn21.10:3: “That is a way of living alone, Thera; I do not say it is not. However, Thera, listen and pay close attention to how living alone is perfected in detail; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” ... “And how, Thera, is living alone perfected in detail? Here, Thera, what is past is abandoned, what is future is relinquished, and desire and lust for present states of being are well subdued. That is how, Thera, living alone is perfected in detail.”
translations.sn21.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: “Friends, monks!” “Friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Here, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: ‘They speak of “noble silence”, “noble silence”. What now is noble silence?’ It occurred to me: ‘Here, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has internal clarity and confidence, and unification of mind, is free from thought and examination, and is born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure. This is called noble silence.’ So I entered and remained in the second absorption... While I was abiding in this state, perceptions and attention accompanied by thought beset me.
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the mendicants: “Reverends, mendicants!” “Reverend,” those mendicants replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: “Here, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: ‘Is there anything in the world whose alteration and change would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me?’ It occurred to me: ‘There is nothing in the world whose alteration and change would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me.’”
translations.sn21.3:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in the same dwelling. Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. After finishing some greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: “Reverend Moggallāna, your faculties are so very clear. Your complexion is pure and bright. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna must have spent the day in a peaceful state.” “Reverend, I spent the day in a gross state. But I did have a Dhamma talk.” “With whom did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma talk?” “I had a Dhamma talk with the Buddha.” “Reverend, the Buddha is far away at present, staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. Did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna go to the Buddha with psychic power, or did the Buddha come to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna with psychic power?” “I didn't go to the Buddha with psychic power, nor did the Buddha come to me with psychic power. But my divine eye and divine ear element were purified to match the Buddha's range, and the Buddha's divine eye and divine ear element were purified to match my range.” “And in what way did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma talk with the Buddha?”
translations.sn21.3:3: “Here, friends, I said to the Buddha: ‘Sir, they speak of “one who is energetic”, “one who is energetic”. How is one energetic?’ When I said this, the Buddha said to me: ‘Here, Moggallāna, a mendicant lives with energy aroused: “Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not relax my energy until I have achieved what is to be achieved by manly strength, manly energy, and manly vigor.” That is how one is energetic.’ That is how I had a Dhamma talk with the Buddha.”
translations.sn21.3:6: “Sāriputta is best in wisdom, ethics, and peace. Any mendicant who has crossed over would at best equal him.”
translations.sn21.6:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya went to the Buddha. The Buddha saw Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya coming from afar. Seeing him, he addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants, do you see that mendicant coming—ugly, unsightly, hunchbacked, despised by the mendicants?” “Yes, sir.” “That mendicant, mendicants, is very powerful and mighty. It is not easy to find an attainment that he has not already attained. He has realized with his own insight the supreme culmination of the spiritual life in this very life, and lives having entered it—the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.” That is what the Buddha said... The Teacher said:
translations.sn21.6:2: “Swans, cranes, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer—they all fear the lion, regardless of physical proportions.
translations.sn21.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Nanda, the Buddha’s cousin, dressed in well-pressed and ironed robes, applied eyeshadow, and took a shiny bowl, and went to the Buddha. He bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him: “Nanda, it is not appropriate for you, a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, to wear well-pressed and ironed robes, apply eyeshadow, and carry a shiny bowl. It is appropriate for you, Nanda, as a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, to live in the wilderness, eat only alms-food, wear rag-robes, and dwell without regard for sensual pleasures.” That is what the Buddha said... The Teacher said:
translations.sn21.8:2: “When will I see Nanda living in the wilderness, wearing rag-robes, surviving on scraps from strangers, without regard for sensual pleasures?”
translations.sn21.9:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One's paternal cousin, approached the Blessed One, bowed, and sat to one side, miserable, sad, shedding tears. The Blessed One said to him: "Why, Tissa, are you sitting there miserable, sad, shedding tears?" "Because, sir, the mendicants have been piercing me all over with sharp words like spurs." "That is because you, Tissa, speak but do not endure being spoken to. It is not appropriate for you, Tissa, as a gentleman who has gone forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith, to speak but not endure being spoken to. This is appropriate for you, Tissa, as a gentleman who has gone forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith: that you should be one who speaks and also endures being spoken to."
translations.sn22.100:2: "Mendicants, have you seen the picture called 'Caraṇa'?" "Yes, sir." "Even that picture called 'Caraṇa' was created by the mind. And the mind is even more diverse than that picture called 'Caraṇa'. Therefore, mendicants, you should often check your own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, hate, and delusion.' Sentient beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind; sentient beings are purified by the purification of the mind."
translations.sn22.100:3: "Mendicants, I do not see any other single class of living beings as diverse as the animal realm. Even the beings in the animal realm have been created by the mind. And the mind is even more diverse than the beings in the animal realm. Therefore, mendicants, you should often check your own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, hate, and delusion.' Sentient beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind; sentient beings are purified by the purification of the mind."
translations.sn22.101:1: At Sāvatthī. "Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see. And for one knowing what and seeing what does the ending of defilements come about? 'Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.' It is for one knowing and seeing in this way that the ending of defilements comes about."
translations.sn22.101:2: When a mendicant dwells without applying themselves to development, even if they wish: 'Oh, may my mind be freed from defilements by not grasping!' still their mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of undevelopment.' Undevelopment of what? Of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Suppose a hen has eight, ten, or twelve eggs. But she has not properly sat on them, warmed them, or incubated them. Even if she wishes: 'Oh, may my chicks break through the eggshell with their claw tips or beaks and hatch safely!' still they are unable to break through the eggshell with their claw tips or beaks and hatch safely. Why is that? Because the hen has eight, ten, or twelve eggs, but she has not properly sat on them, warmed them, or incubated them. In the same way, when a mendicant dwells without applying themselves to development, even if they wish: 'Oh, may my mind be freed from defilements by not grasping!' still their mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of undevelopment.' Undevelopment of what? Of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation ... the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Sumsumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. Then the householder Nakulapitā approached the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Nakulapitā said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.1:10: They regard feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling. They are obsessed with the idea: 'I am feeling, feeling is mine.' As they are obsessed with the idea 'I am feeling, feeling is mine,' that feeling undergoes change and alteration. With the change and alteration of feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.1:11: They regard perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception in self, or self in perception. They are obsessed with the idea: 'I am perception, perception is mine.' As they are obsessed with the idea 'I am perception, perception is mine,' that perception undergoes change and alteration. With the change and alteration of perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.1:12: They regard volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations in self, or self in volitional formations. They are obsessed with the idea: 'I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine.' As they are obsessed with the idea 'I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine,' those volitional formations undergo change and alteration. With the change and alteration of volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.1:13: They regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. They are obsessed with the idea ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine’. Because of this obsession, when that consciousness changes and alters, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise. This is how, householder, one is afflicted in body and afflicted in mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple who sees the noble ones, is skilled in the teaching of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the teaching of the noble ones; who sees the true persons, is skilled in the teaching of the true persons, and is well-trained in the teaching of the true persons, does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. They are not obsessed with the idea ‘I am form, form is mine’. Because they are not obsessed, when that form changes and alters, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress do not arise.
translations.sn22.1:2: “Sir, I am old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the last stage of life; my body is afflicted and I am constantly ill. I rarely get to see the Blessed One and the esteemed mendicants. Let the Blessed One advise me, Sir; let the Blessed One instruct me, for my long-term welfare and happiness.”
translations.sn22.1:3: “That is so, householder, that is so. For this body, householder, is afflicted, weak, and encumbered. For anyone carrying this body around to claim even a moment of health, what is that other than foolishness? Therefore, householder, you should train yourself like this: ‘Though my body is afflicted, my mind will not be afflicted.’ That is how you should train yourself.”
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakulapita, having rejoiced and expressed appreciation for the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, bowed to the Blessed One, circled him on the right, and went to the Venerable Sariputta. Having approached, he bowed to the Venerable Sariputta and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sariputta said to him: “Householder, your faculties are clear, your complexion is pure and bright. Did you get to hear a Dhamma talk in the Blessed One's presence today?”
translations.sn22.1:7: “But did it not occur to you, householder, to ask the Blessed One further: ‘In what way, Sir, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind, and in what way is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind?’” “We would come from far away, Sir, to learn the meaning of this statement from the Venerable Sariputta. It would be good if the meaning of this statement would occur to the Venerable Sariputta himself.”
translations.sn22.1:8: “Well then, householder, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, Sir,” the householder Nakulapita replied to the Venerable Sariputta. The Venerable Sariputta said this:
translations.sn22.1:9: “And how, householder, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind? Here, householder, an uninstructed ordinary person who does not see the noble ones, is unskilled in the teaching of the noble ones, and is untrained in the teaching of the noble ones; who does not see the true persons, is unskilled in the teaching of the true persons, and is untrained in the teaching of the true persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. They are obsessed with the idea ‘I am form, form is mine’. Because of this obsession, when that form changes and alters, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.22:2: And who, monks, is the bearer of the burden? It should be said: the person. This venerable one of such a name and such a clan. This is called, monks, the bearer of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, monks, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for extermination. This is called, monks, the taking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, monks, is the laying down of the burden? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. This is called, monks, the laying down of the burden.”
translations.sn22.22:6: “The five aggregates are indeed burdens, and the person is the burden-bearer. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, laying down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at a Sakyan town named Devadaha. Then several mendicants bound for the western lands approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those mendicants said to the Blessed One: “Sir, we wish to go to the western lands and take up residence there.”
translations.sn22.2:10: Reverends, if entering upon and abiding in unskillful qualities resulted in a happy abiding in this very life, without vexation, despair, or fever, and if, with the breakup of the body, after death, a good destination could be expected, the Blessed One would not praise the abandonment of unskillful qualities. But because entering upon and abiding in unskillful qualities results in painful abiding in this very life, with vexation, despair, and fever, and because, with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination can be expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandonment of unskillful qualities.
translations.sn22.2:2: “But, monks, have you taken leave of Sariputta?” “No, Sir, we haven't taken leave of the Venerable Sariputta.” “Take leave of Sariputta, monks. Sariputta is wise, a helper to the monks who are his spiritual companions.” “Yes, Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a clump of eḷagalā plants. Then those mendicants, having welcomed and agreed with the Blessed One’s statement, rose from their seats, bowed to the Blessed One, circumambulated him on the right, and approached Venerable Sāriputta. They exchanged greetings with him, and when the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, they said to Venerable Sāriputta: “We wish, friend Sāriputta, to go to the western lands and take up residence there. We have taken leave of the Teacher.”
translations.sn22.2:5: “We would come from far away, friend, into the presence of Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the meaning of this statement would occur to Venerable Sāriputta himself.” “Well then, friends, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those mendicants replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain mendicant approached the Blessed One ... sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “Mendicant, one is measured by what one has an underlying tendency for; and by what one is measured, one is reckoned. When one has no underlying tendency, one is not measured; and when one is not measured, one is not reckoned.” “Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Holy One!”
translations.sn22.3:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in Avanti at the Osprey’s Haunt on a sheer mountain crag. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached Venerable Mahākaccāna, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: “Sir, this was said by the Blessed One in the ‘Questions of Māgaṇḍiya’ in the Chapter of Eights:
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one not empty of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone is not free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures. That is how one is not empty of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone is free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures. That is how one is empty of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, does one look to the future? Here, householder, someone thinks: ‘May I have such form in the future! May I have such feeling in the future! May I have such perception in the future! May I have such choices in the future! May I have such consciousness in the future!’ That is how one looks to the future.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, does one engage in quarrelsome speech with people? Here, householder, someone speaks like this: ‘You don’t understand this teaching and training. I understand this teaching and training. What, you understand this teaching and training? You’re practicing wrong. I’m practicing right. You said last what should have been said first. You said first what should have been said last. What I said was consistent. What you said was inconsistent. What you practiced so long has been overturned. Your theory is refuted. Go, try to save your theory! You’re defeated. Untangle yourself if you can!’ That is how one engages in quarrelsome speech with people.
translations.sn22.3:17: ‘Having left home, wandering homeless, / Not making intimacies in the village, / Empty of sensual pleasures, not looking to the future, / The sage would not engage in quarrelsome speech with people.’
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, does one wander in an abode? By being bound by the bond of the abode of the sign of forms, householder, one is called ‘one who wanders in an abode.’ By being bound by the bond of the abode of the sign of sounds ... smells ... tastes ... touches ... mental phenomena, householder, one is called ‘one who wanders in an abode.’ That is how one wanders in an abode.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, is one intimate in the village? Here, householder, someone lives mixed up with laypeople, rejoicing with them and grieving with them, happy when they are happy, sad when they are sad, and involving himself in their affairs and duties that arise. That is how one is intimate in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, is one not intimate in the village? Here, householder, a mendicant lives not mixed up with laypeople, not rejoicing with them nor grieving with them, not happy when they are happy nor sad when they are sad, and not involving himself in their affairs and duties that arise. That is how one is not intimate in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard the self in various ways, they all regard the five grasping aggregates, or one of them. What five? Here, mendicants, an uneducated ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, and is unskilled and untrained in the teaching of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons, and is unskilled and untrained in the teaching of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. They regard feeling ... perception ... choices ... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: So they have this way of regarding, and the thought ‘I am’ has not vanished. As long as the thought ‘I am’ has not vanished, there is the descent of the five faculties: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty. There is, mendicants, the mind, there are mental phenomena, there is the element of ignorance. When the uneducated ordinary person is struck by feeling born of contact with ignorance, the thought ‘I am’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I am this’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will be’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will not be’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will have form’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will be formless’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will be percipient’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will be non-percipient’ occurs to them; the thought ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient’ occurs to them.
translations.sn22.48:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five aggregates subject to grasping. Listen. And what, mendicants, are the five aggregates? Any kind of form whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of form. Any kind of feeling … Any kind of perception … Any kind of choices—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle … this is called the aggregate of choices. Any kind of consciousness whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness. These are called the five aggregates.
translations.sn22.53:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, one who is engaged is not freed; one who is disengaged is freed. If consciousness were to remain, mendicants, it would remain engaged with form, supported by form, established on form. With a sprinkling of relish, it would grow, increase, and mature. Or if consciousness were to remain engaged with feeling … or engaged with perception … or engaged with choices, supported by choices, established on choices. With a sprinkling of relish, it would grow, increase, and mature.
translations.sn22.53:2: Mendicants, if someone were to say: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from choices, I will describe the coming and going of consciousness, its passing away and reappearing, its growth, increase, and maturity’—that is impossible.
translations.sn22.54:2: If consciousness were to remain, mendicants, it would remain engaged with form, supported by form, established on form. With a sprinkling of relish, it would grow, increase, and mature. Or if consciousness were to remain engaged with feeling … or engaged with perception … or engaged with choices, supported by choices, established on choices. With a sprinkling of relish, it would grow, increase, and mature.
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One breathed forth this inspired utterance: “‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine’—a mendicant resolved on this might cut off the lower fetters.” When he said this, a certain mendicant said to the Blessed One: “But how, sir, might a mendicant resolved on ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine’ cut off the lower fetters?”
translations.sn22.55:10: But knowing and seeing in what way, sir, does the ending of defilements occur immediately?” “Here, mendicant, an uneducated ordinary person falls into terror at a point that is not terrifying. For an uneducated ordinary person is terrified by this: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine.’
translations.sn22.55:4: They do not truly understand suffering form as ‘suffering form’, suffering feeling … suffering perception … suffering choices … suffering consciousness as ‘suffering consciousness’.
translations.sn22.55:5: They do not truly understand non-self form as ‘non-self form’, non-self feeling as ‘non-self feeling’, non-self perception as ‘non-self perception’, non-self choices as ‘non-self choices’, non-self consciousness as ‘non-self consciousness’.
translations.sn22.55:6: They do not truly understand conditioned form as ‘conditioned form’, conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned choices … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness’. They do not truly understand that ‘form will vanish’. They do not truly understand that ‘feeling will vanish’ … ‘perception will vanish’ … ‘choices will vanish’ … ‘consciousness will vanish’.
translations.sn22.55:8: They truly understand impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’. They truly understand impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent choices … impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness’. They truly understand suffering form … suffering consciousness … non-self form … non-self consciousness … conditioned form … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness’. They truly understand that ‘form will vanish’. They truly understand that ‘feeling … perception … choices … consciousness will vanish’.
translations.sn22.55:9: Because of the vanishing of form, the vanishing of feeling, the vanishing of perception, the vanishing of choices, and the vanishing of consciousness, in this way, mendicant, a mendicant resolved on ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine’ might cut off the lower fetters.” “'Resolved in this way,' sir, 'a mendicant might cut off the lower fetters.'
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, mendicants, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness. With the origin of name and form there is the origin of consciousness; with the cessation of name and form there is the cessation of consciousness. The practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness is simply this noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn22.56:14: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, mendicants, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way, are practicing for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, they are practicing well. Those who are practicing well have a footing in this teaching and training.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? I directly knew form, I directly knew the origin of form, I directly knew the cessation of form, I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of form. I directly knew feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, I directly knew the origin of consciousness, I directly knew the cessation of consciousness, I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn22.56:5: And whatever ascetics or brahmins, mendicants, having directly known form in this way … having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of form in this way, are freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, they are well freed. Those who are well freed are consummate ones. For the consummate ones, there is no cycle to be found.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, a mendicant who is skilled in seven points and an investigator of three ways is called a consummate one in this teaching and training, one who has lived the holy life, the supreme person. And how is a mendicant skilled in seven points? It’s when a mendicant understands form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, and the practice leading to the cessation of form. They understand the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding form. They understand feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness. They understand the gratification, the drawback, and the escape regarding consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what are choices? There are these six classes of intention: intention regarding sights … intention regarding ideas. These are called choices. From the origin of contact comes the origin of choices; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of choices. The practice leading to the cessation of choices is this very noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn22.57:15: The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on consciousness: this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and liable to change: this is the drawback of consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and greed for consciousness: this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, mendicants, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way; having directly known the gratification of consciousness in this way, having directly known the drawback of consciousness in this way, having directly known the escape from consciousness in this way, are freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, they are well freed. Those who are well freed are consummate ones. For the consummate ones, there is no cycle to be found. That is how a mendicant is skilled in seven points.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what is form? The four great elements and form derived from the four great elements. This is called form. From the origin of food comes the origin of form; from the cessation of food comes the cessation of form. The practice leading to the cessation of form is this very noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn22.57:5: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, mendicants, having directly known form in this way, having directly known the origin of form in this way, having directly known the cessation of form in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of form in this way; having directly known the gratification of form in this way, having directly known the drawback of form in this way, having directly known the escape from form in this way, are freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, they are well freed. Those who are well freed are consummate ones. For the consummate ones, there is no cycle to be found.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what is feeling? There are these six classes of feeling: feeling born of eye contact … feeling born of mind contact. This is called feeling. From the origin of contact comes the origin of feeling; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling. The practice leading to the cessation of feeling is this very noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn22.57:7: The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on feeling: this is the gratification of feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and liable to change: this is the drawback of feeling. The removal and abandonment of desire and greed for feeling: this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, and is called a ‘fully awakened Buddha’. A mendicant freed by wisdom is also freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, and is called ‘freed by wisdom’.
translations.sn22.58:3: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding perception … choices … consciousness, and is called a ‘fully awakened Buddha’. A mendicant freed by wisdom is also freed by not grasping through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, and is called ‘freed by wisdom’.
translations.sn22.59:10: Any consciousness whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.59:7: “Therefore, monks, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’”
translations.sn22.5:11: They do not delight in consciousness, they do not welcome it, they do not remain holding to it. As they do not delight in, welcome, or remain holding to consciousness, delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of grasping … thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, monks, is the origin of form, what is the origin of feeling, what is the origin of perception, what is the origin of volitional formations, what is the origin of consciousness? Here, monks, a monk delights, welcomes, and remains holding.
translations.sn22.5:3: And what do they delight in, welcome, and remain holding to? They delight in form, welcome it, and remain holding to it. As they delight in, welcome, and remain holding to form, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in form, that is grasping. With grasping as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress come to be. Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: They delight in feeling … they delight in perception … they delight in volitional formations … they delight in consciousness, welcome it, and remain holding to it. As they delight in, welcome, and remain holding to consciousness, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in consciousness, that is grasping. With grasping as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition … thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: And what do they not delight in, not welcome, and not remain holding to? They do not delight in form, do not welcome it, and do not remain holding to it. As they do not delight in, do not welcome, and do not remain holding to form, delight in form ceases. With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, the cessation of existence … thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.60:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesali in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then Mahali the Licchavi approached the Blessed One … sitting to one side, Mahali the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: “Bhante, Purana Kassapa says this: ‘There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause, without condition.’ What does the Blessed One say here?”
translations.sn22.60:3: “Mahali, there is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause, with condition. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause, with condition.”
translations.sn22.60:4: “But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings; how are beings defiled with cause, with condition?”
translations.sn22.60:5: “Mahali, if this form were exclusively painful, followed by pain, beset by pain, and not beset by pleasure, beings would not become enamored with form. But because form is pleasurable, followed by pleasure, beset by pleasure, and not beset by pain, beings become enamored with form. Being enamored, they are bound; being bound, they are defiled. This, Mahali, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings; thus beings are defiled with cause, with condition.
translations.sn22.60:8: And if this consciousness, Mahali, were exclusively painful, followed by pain, beset by pain, and not beset by pleasure, beings would not become enamored with consciousness. But because consciousness is pleasurable, followed by pleasure, beset by pleasure, and not beset by pain, beings become enamored with consciousness. Being enamored, they are bound; being bound, they are defiled. This too, Mahali, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings. Thus too beings are defiled with cause, with condition.”
translations.sn22.60:9: “But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings; how are beings purified with cause, with condition?” “Mahali, if this form were exclusively pleasurable, followed by pleasure, beset by pleasure, and not beset by pain, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because form is painful, followed by pain, beset by pain, and not beset by pleasure, beings become disenchanted with form. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are purified. This, Mahali, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings. Thus beings are purified with cause, with condition.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing this, monks, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with volitional formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge, ‘It is liberated.’ They understand: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ As far, monks, as there are abodes of beings, as far as the pinnacle of existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world, that is, the Arahants.”
translations.sn22.76:4: “Happy indeed are the Arahants! No craving is found in them. The conceit ‘I am’ is cut off, the net of delusion is burst asunder.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates, ranging in the true Dhamma, worthy of praise, true persons, they are the Buddha's own sons.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven gems, trained in the three trainings, the great heroes wander about, with fear and terror abandoned.
translations.sn22.76:8: Endowed with the ten factors, great nagas, concentrated; these indeed are the best in the world; no craving is found in them.
translations.sn22.76:9: The knowledge of the non-trainee has arisen; this is the last body. Regarding the essence of the holy life, they rely on no other.
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins recollect their manifold past lives, all of them recollect the five grasping aggregates, or one of them. What five? ‘I had such form in the past,’ recollecting thus, they just recollect form. ‘I had such feeling in the past,’ recollecting thus, they just recollect feeling. ‘I had such perception in the past’ … ‘I had such choices in the past’ … ‘I had such consciousness in the past,’ recollecting thus, they just recollect consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:10: ‘I am currently being devoured by consciousness. In the past, I was devoured by consciousness in just the same way as I am currently being devoured by present consciousness. If I were to delight in future consciousness, I would be devoured by consciousness in the future in just the same way as I am currently being devoured by present consciousness.’ Reflecting like this, they do not pine after past consciousness, they do not delight in future consciousness, and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: Here, mendicants, a learned noble disciple reflects: ‘I am currently being devoured by form. In the past, I was devoured by form in just the same way as I am currently being devoured by present form. If I were to delight in future form, I would be devoured by form in the future in just the same way as I am currently being devoured by present form.’ Reflecting like this, they do not pine after past form, they do not delight in future form, and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery. Then the Buddha, having dismissed the Order of monks for some reason, robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. After wandering for alms in Kapilavatthu and returning from his almsround after the meal, he went to the Great Wood for the day's abiding. Plunging into the Great Wood, he sat at the root of a young bilva tree for the day's abiding.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Buddha consented in silence. Then Brahma Sahampati, knowing that the Buddha had consented, bowed to the Buddha, circled him on the right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha rose from retreat and went to the Banyan Tree Monastery. He sat on the seat spread out. When he was seated, the Buddha used his psychic power to make those monks come to him one by one or in pairs, looking timid. And those monks came to the Buddha one by one or in pairs, looking timid. They bowed to the Buddha and sat to one side. The Buddha said to them:
translations.sn22.80:6: “Mendicants, this gathering of alms is the lowest form of livelihood. It’s a curse in the world to say: ‘You go about like an alms-gatherer, bowl in hand!’ Yet gentlemen enter upon it for a reason, dependent on a reason. They are not forced by kings or bandits, nor by debt or fear, nor to earn a living. But rather, [they think:] ‘We are immersed in rebirth, old age, and death; in sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. We are immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering. Hopefully an end to this entire mass of suffering might be found.’
translations.sn22.80:7: But although this gentleman has gone forth in this way, he is covetous, with keen desire for sensual pleasures, with a mind full of ill will and hateful intent, unmindful, lacking situational awareness, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind and undisciplined faculties. Suppose there was a brand from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends, and smeared with dung in the middle. It couldn’t be used as timber in the village or the wilderness. I say that this person is just like that: they have missed out on the enjoyments of a lay person, yet they don’t fulfill the goal of the ascetic life.
translations.sn22.80:9: Mendicants, there are these two views: the view of continued existence and the view of annihilation. Here, a learned noble disciple reflects: ‘Is there anything in the world that I could grasp without being at fault?’ They understand: ‘There is nothing in the world that I could grasp without being at fault. For if I were to grasp, I would only be grasping form, feeling, perception, choices, or consciousness. That grasping of mine would be a condition for continued existence. Continued existence is a condition for rebirth. Rebirth is a condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be. That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’
translations.sn22.81:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambi, in Ghosita’s Monastery. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambi for alms. After wandering for alms in Kosambi and returning from his almsround after the meal, he tidied up his own lodging. Then, taking his bowl and robe, without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Order of monks, he set out wandering alone, without a companion.
translations.sn22.81:10: They do not regard form as self, nor feeling … nor perception … nor choices … nor consciousness as self. But they have such a view: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After passing away I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’ This eternalist view is a conditioned phenomenon. And what is the source of that conditioned phenomenon? ... Knowing and seeing like this, the defilements are ended immediately.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages, arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One stayed at Pālileyyaka at the foot of the Auspicious Sal Tree. Then a number of mendicants went up to Venerable Ānanda, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those mendicants said to Venerable Ānanda: “It has been a long time, friend Ānanda, since we heard a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One. We would like, friend Ānanda, to hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One.”
translations.sn22.82:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, in the Palace of Migāra’s Mother, together with a great Saṅgha of mendicants. Now at that time—it being the sabbath, the full moon, on the fifteenth day—the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of mendicants.
translations.sn22.82:10: “What, sir, is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape regarding form? What ... regarding feeling ... regarding perception ... regarding volitional formations ... regarding consciousness is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape?” “The pleasure and joy that arise conditioned by form: this is the gratification of form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger of form. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form: this is the escape from form. The pleasure and joy that arise conditioned by feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness: this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger of consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness: this is the escape from consciousness.” “Good, sir,” said that monk, delighting and rejoicing in the Blessed One's statement, and he asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: “How, sir, does one know, how does one see, so that there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, I-making, and mine-making with regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs?” “Any kind of form whatsoever, monk, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: one sees all form as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Any kind of feeling ... Any kind of perception ... Any kind of volitional formations ... Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: one sees all consciousness as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Knowing and seeing in this way, monk, there are no underlying tendencies to conceit, I-making, and mine-making with regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs.”
translations.sn22.82:12: Now at that time a thought arose in the mind of a certain monk: “So it seems, sir, that form is not-self, feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness is not-self. Then how will deeds done by what is not-self affect the self?” Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in that monk's mind with his own mind, addressed the mendicants:
translations.sn22.82:13: “It is possible, mendicants, that some foolish man here, ignorant and immersed in ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think he can outstrip the Teacher’s instruction: ‘So it seems, sir, that form is not-self, feeling ... perception ... volitional formations ... consciousness is not-self. Then how will deeds done by what is not-self affect the self?’ You, mendicants, have been trained by me through cross-questioning in various instances regarding various things.
translations.sn22.82:4: “But, sir, in what are these five grasping aggregates rooted?” “These five grasping aggregates, monk, are rooted in desire.” ... “Sir, is that grasping the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates, or is grasping something apart from the five grasping aggregates?” “That grasping is not the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates, nor is grasping something apart from the five grasping aggregates. Rather, the desire and lust for them is the grasping there.” “Good, sir,” said that monk ... and asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: “But, sir, can there be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five grasping aggregates?” “There can be, monk,” said the Blessed One. “Here, monk, someone thinks: ‘May I have form like this in the future; may I have feeling like this in the future; may I have perception like this in the future; may I have volitional formations like this in the future; may I have consciousness like this in the future.’ In this way, monk, there can be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five grasping aggregates.” “Good, sir,” said that monk ... and asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: “What, sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate? What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate? ... perception aggregate? ... volitional formations aggregate? ... consciousness aggregate?” “The four great elements, monk, are the cause and condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause and condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause and condition for the manifestation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause and condition for the manifestation of the volitional formations aggregate. Name-and-form is the cause and condition for the manifestation of the consciousness aggregate.” “Good, sir,” said that monk ... and asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: “But how, sir, does identity view come about?” “Here, monk, an uneducated ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the teaching of the noble ones, is undisciplined in the teaching of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the teaching of good persons, is undisciplined in the teaching of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They regard feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That is how identity view comes about.” “Good, sir,” said that monk... and asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: “But how, sir, does identity view not come about?” “Here, monk, an educated noble disciple who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the teaching of the noble ones, is well disciplined in the teaching of the noble ones, who has seen good persons, is skilled in the teaching of good persons, is well disciplined in the teaching of good persons, does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They do not regard feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That is how identity view does not come about.” “Good, sir,” said that monk... and asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks!” “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn22.83:3: “Suppose, friend Ānanda, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of ornaments, were to examine their own facial reflection in a clear, bright mirror or in a clear bowl of water. They would see it by grasping, not without grasping. So too, friend Ānanda, the notion ‘I am’ occurs by grasping form, not without grasping. The notion ‘I am’ occurs by grasping feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, not without grasping.
translations.sn22.84:10: “I have made this simile, Tissa, to convey a meaning. And this is the meaning here: ‘The man unskilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the ordinary person. ‘The man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘The fork in the road,’ Tissa, is a designation for doubt. ‘The left-hand path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the wrong eightfold path, that is, wrong view … wrong concentration. ‘The right-hand path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path, that is, right view … right concentration. ‘The dense thicket,’ Tissa, is a designation for ignorance. ‘The great low-lying marsh,’ Tissa, is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘The steep precipice,’ Tissa, is a designation for anger and despair. ‘The level, delightful ground,’ Tissa, is a designation for Nibbāna. Rejoice, Tissa! Rejoice, Tissa! I am here to advise, to assist, to instruct.”
translations.sn22.84:5: “Good, good, Tissa. That is how it is, Tissa. In the case of one who is not free from lust for volitional formations, who is not free from lust, desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving for consciousness—with the change and alteration of that consciousness, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise?” “Yes, sir”.
translations.sn22.84:6: “Good, good, Tissa. That is how it is, Tissa. In the case of one who is not free from lust for consciousness. What do you think, Tissa? In the case of one who is free from lust, desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving for form—with the change and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise?” “No, sir”.
translations.sn22.85:1: At one time the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Now at that time a pernicious view had arisen in a monk named Yamaka as follows: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death.”
translations.sn22.85:10: “What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard form … feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, friend”.
translations.sn22.85:11: “What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as one who is without form … without feeling … without perception … without volitional formations … without consciousness?” “No, friend”. “But, friend Yamaka, since the Tathāgata is not apprehended by you as real and actual here in this very life, is it proper for you to declare: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death’?”
translations.sn22.85:12: “Formerly, friend Sāriputta, when I was ignorant, I held that pernicious view; but now that I have heard this Dhamma teaching of the Venerable Sāriputta, I have abandoned that pernicious view and have made the breakthrough to the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.85:16: He does not understand impermanent form as it really is: ‘Form is impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent feeling as it really is: ‘Feeling is impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent perception as it really is: ‘Perception is impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent volitional formations as they really are: ‘Volitional formations are impermanent.’ He does not understand impermanent consciousness as it really is: ‘Consciousness is impermanent.’
translations.sn22.85:19: He does not understand conditioned form as it really is: ‘Form is conditioned.’ He does not understand conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned volitional formations … conditioned consciousness as it really is: ‘Consciousness is conditioned.’
translations.sn22.85:20: They do not truly understand form, which is a killer, as ‘form is a killer’. They do not truly understand feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, which is a killer, as ‘consciousness is a killer’.
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach, grasp, and insist on form as ‘myself’. They approach, grasp, and insist on feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as ‘myself’. These five grasping aggregates, approached and grasped, lead to their lasting harm and suffering.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’. They truly understand impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent choices … impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness’.
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand not-self form as ‘not-self form’. They truly understand not-self feeling … not-self perception … not-self choices … not-self consciousness as ‘not-self consciousness’.
translations.sn22.85:5: Since those mendicants were unable to detach Venerable Yamaka from that bad misconception, they got up from their seats and went to Venerable Sāriputta. They told him what had happened, and said: “It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta went to the mendicant Yamaka out of compassion.” Venerable Sāriputta consented in silence. Then in the late afternoon, Sāriputta came out of retreat and went to Yamaka. He exchanged greetings with Yamaka … and sat down to one side. Sāriputta said to Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: “Is it really true, Reverend Yamaka, that you have such a bad misconception: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?” “Yes, Reverend, that is how I understand the Buddha’s teaching, that a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death.”
translations.sn22.85:9: “What do you think, Reverend Yamaka? Do you regard the Realized One as in form?” “No, Reverend.” “Do you regard the Realized One as distinct from form?” “No, Reverend.” “Do you regard the Realized One as in feeling … or distinct from feeling … as in perception … or distinct from perception … as in choices … or distinct from choices … as in consciousness?” “No, Reverend.” “Do you regard the Realized One as distinct from consciousness?” “No, Reverend.”
translations.sn22.86:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
