At that time Venerable Anurādha was staying not far from the Buddha in a forest hut. Then several wanderers of other religions went to Anurādha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him: “Reverend Anurādha, a Realized One—the supreme person, the highest person, the attainer of the highest—is described in these four ways: ‘A Realized One exists after death’, or ‘A Realized One does not exist after death’, or ‘A Realized One both exists and does not exist after death’, or ‘A Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death’.”
translations.sn22.86:10: “What do you think, Anurādha? Do you regard form … feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as the Realized One?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.86:11: “What do you think, Anurādha? Do you regard the Realized One as one who is without form … without feeling … without perception … without choices … without consciousness?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.86:12: “In that case, Anurādha, since you don’t acknowledge the Realized One as a genuine fact in the present life, is it appropriate to declare: ‘Reverends, a Realized One—the supreme person, the highest person, the attainer of the highest—is described apart from these four ways: A Realized One exists after death … does not exist … both exists and does not exist … neither exists nor does not exist after death’?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.86:2: When they said this, Venerable Anurādha said to the wanderers: “Reverends, a Realized One—the supreme person, the highest person, the attainer of the highest—is described apart from these four ways: ‘A Realized One exists after death’, or ‘A Realized One does not exist after death’, or ‘A Realized One both exists and does not exist after death’, or ‘A Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death’.” When he said this, the wanderers said to him: “This mendicant must be junior, recently gone forth, or else a foolish, incompetent senior.” Then the wanderers, having rebuked Anurādha by calling him ‘junior’ and ‘foolish’, got up from their seats and left.
translations.sn22.86:3: Soon after those wanderers had left, it occurred to Anurādha: “If those wanderers were to question me further, how should I answer them so as to repeat what the Buddha has said, and not misrepresent him with an untruth? How should I explain in line with the teaching, so that there would be no legitimate grounds for rebuke and criticism?”
translations.sn22.86:8: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form as the Realized One?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as the Realized One?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.86:9: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Realized One as in form?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard the Realized One as distinct from form?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard the Realized One as in feeling … distinct from feeling … in perception … distinct from perception … in choices … distinct from choices … in consciousness … distinct from consciousness?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.89:10: Suppose, reverends, there was the scent of a blue water lily, or a red lotus, or a white lotus. If someone were to say: ‘The scent belongs to the petals,’ or ‘The scent belongs to the stalk,’ or ‘The scent belongs to the pistils,’ would they be speaking correctly?” “No, reverend.” “So how should they answer to answer correctly?” “They should answer: ‘The scent belongs to the flower.’” “In the same way, reverends, I do not say ‘I am’ regarding form, nor do I say ‘I am’ apart from form. I do not say ‘I am’ regarding feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, nor do I say ‘I am’ apart from consciousness. But still, reverends, regarding the five grasping aggregates, I have the notion ‘I am’, but I do not regard it as ‘This I am’.
translations.sn22.89:11: Even though, reverends, a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, still, in relation to the five grasping aggregates, there lingers a residual conceit ‘I am’, a desire ‘I am’, an underlying tendency ‘I am’ that has not yet been uprooted. Sometime later they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its ending; such is feeling … such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such its origin, such its ending.’ As they meditate observing rise and fall in these five grasping aggregates, that residual conceit ‘I am’, desire ‘I am’, and underlying tendency ‘I am’ that had not been uprooted is uprooted.
translations.sn22.89:12: Suppose, reverends, there was a dirty, soiled cloth. The owners would give it to a washerman. The washerman would scrub it evenly with salt earth, lye, or cow dung, and rinse it in clear water. Even though the cloth is clean and bright, it still has a lingering residual scent of salt earth, lye, or cow dung that has not vanished. The washerman gives it back to the owners. The owners put it in a sweet-smelling casket. Whatever lingering residual scent of salt earth, lye, or cow dung that had not vanished now vanishes. In the same way, reverends, even though a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, still, in relation to the five grasping aggregates, there lingers a residual conceit ‘I am’, a desire ‘I am’, an underlying tendency ‘I am’ that has not yet been uprooted. Sometime later they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates. ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its ending; such is feeling … such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such its origin, such its ending.’ As they meditate observing rise and fall in these five grasping aggregates, that residual conceit ‘I am’, desire ‘I am’, and underlying tendency ‘I am’ that had not been uprooted is uprooted.
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Khemaka: “We didn’t question Venerable Khemaka wishing to trouble him. But rather, Venerable Khemaka is capable of explaining, teaching, asserting, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing the Buddha’s teaching in detail. And this the Venerable Khemaka has done.”
translations.sn22.90:1: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Benares, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Channa came out of retreat. Taking his key, he went from dwelling to dwelling approaching the senior mendicants and said to them: “May the senior venerables advise me! May the senior venerables instruct me! May the senior venerables give me a talk on the teaching so that I might see the teaching!”
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Channa: “Form, Reverend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; choices are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is not-self. All conditions are impermanent; all things are not-self.”
translations.sn22.90:3: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: “I too think in this way: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is not-self. All conditions are impermanent, all things are not-self.’ Yet my mind does not leap forward, become confident, settle, and resolve on the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment. Agitation and grasping arise, and my mind turns back thinking: ‘So who, then, is my self?’ This doesn’t happen for one who sees the teaching. Who can teach me the Dhamma so that I might see the Dhamma?”
translations.sn22.90:4: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: “This Venerable Ananda is staying at Kosambi in Ghosita’s Park. He is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise spiritual companions. Venerable Ananda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma. And I have such trust in Venerable Ananda. Why don’t I approach Venerable Ananda?” Then Venerable Channa set his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe, and went to Kosambi, to Ghosita’s Park, to Venerable Ananda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ananda … and sitting to one side, Venerable Channa said to Venerable Ananda:
translations.sn22.90:8: “Even by this much we are pleased with Venerable Channa. Venerable Channa has opened himself up and cut through his stubbornness. Lend your ear, friend Channa; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma.” Then, just because of that, lofty rapture and gladness arose in Venerable Channa: “It seems I am capable of understanding the Dhamma!”
translations.sn22.94:1: At Savatthi. “Bhikkhus, I do not dispute with the world; rather, the world disputes with me. A proponent of the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world. Of that which the wise in the world agree ‘is not’, I too say ‘it is not’. Of that which the wise in the world agree ‘is’, I too say ‘it is’.
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, bhikkhus, is agreed upon by the wise in the world as ‘existing’, of which I too say ‘it exists’? Form that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is agreed upon by the wise in the world as ‘existing’; I too say ‘it exists’. Feeling … Consciousness that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is agreed upon by the wise in the world as ‘existing’; I too say ‘it exists’. This, bhikkhus, is what is agreed upon by the wise in the world as ‘existing’, of which I too say ‘it exists’.
translations.sn22.94:4: There is, bhikkhus, a worldly phenomenon in the world. The Tathagata fully awakens to that and fully understands it. Having fully awakened to it and fully understood it, he announces it, teaches it, describes it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it plain.
translations.sn22.94:7: When, bhikkhus, it is being announced, taught, described, established, revealed, analyzed, and made plain by the Tathagata in this way, if someone does not know and does not see, what can I do with that foolish ordinary person, blind and sightless, who does not know and does not see?
translations.sn22.95:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayojjha on the bank of the river Ganges. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.95:10: However one contemplates it, / carefully investigating it; / It appears void and hollow, / to one who sees it carefully.
translations.sn22.95:11: And concerning this body, / taught by the One of Broad Wisdom; / The abandoning of three things, / see the form discarded.
translations.sn22.95:12: Vitality, heat, and consciousness, / when they leave this body; / Then it lies cast away, / food for others, without volition.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuum, / this illusion that babbles to fools; / It is called a murderer, / no essence is found here.
translations.sn22.95:2: “Suppose, bhikkhus, this river Ganges were to carry along a great lump of foam. A man with good sight would see it, contemplate it, and carefully investigate it. As he saw it, contemplated it, and carefully investigated it, it would appear to him as void, it would appear as hollow, it would appear as insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a lump of foam? So too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of form there is, whether past, future, or present … whatever is far or near: a bhikkhu sees it, contemplates it, and carefully investigates it. As he sees it, contemplates it, and carefully investigates it, it appears to him as void, it appears as hollow, it appears as insubstantial. For what substance could there be in form?
translations.sn22.95:3: Suppose, bhikkhus, in the autumn, when it is raining and big rain drops are falling, a water bubble arises and ceases on the water. A man with good sight would see it, contemplate it, and carefully investigate it. As he saw it, contemplated it, and carefully investigated it, it would appear to him as void, it would appear as hollow, it would appear as insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a water bubble? So too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of feeling there is … whatever is far or near: a bhikkhu sees it, contemplates it, and carefully investigates it. As he sees it, contemplates it, and carefully investigates it, it appears to him as void, it appears as hollow, it appears as insubstantial. For what substance could there be in feeling?
translations.sn22.95:4: Suppose, bhikkhus, in the last month of the hot season, at high noon, a mirage shimmers. A man with good sight would see it, contemplate it, and carefully investigate it. As he saw it, contemplated it, and carefully investigated it, it would appear to him as void, it would appear as hollow … For what substance could there be in a mirage? So too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of perception there is …
translations.sn22.95:5: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would enter a forest taking a sharp axe. There he would see a large banana tree trunk, straight, young, and without a fruit-bud core. He would cut it at the root. Having cut it at the root, he would cut off the top. Having cut off the top, he would peel away the leaf-sheaths. Peeling away the leaf-sheaths, he would not even find sapwood, let alone heartwood. A man with good sight would see it, contemplate it, and carefully investigate it. As he saw it, contemplated it, and carefully investigated it, it would appear to him as void, it would appear as hollow, it would appear as insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a banana tree trunk? So too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of volitional formations there are … whatever are far or near: a bhikkhu sees them, contemplates them, and carefully investigates them. As he sees them, contemplates them, and carefully investigates them, they appear to him as void, they appear as hollow, they appear as insubstantial. For what substance could there be in volitional formations?
translations.sn22.95:6: Suppose, monks, a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to display a magic trick at a crossroads. A man with good eyesight would see it, observe it, and examine it carefully. To him seeing it, observing it, and examining it carefully, it would appear empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a magic trick? In the same way, monks, whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present... far or near—a monk sees it, observes it, and examines it carefully. To him seeing it, observing it, and examining it carefully, it appears empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing this, monks, the instructed noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, disillusioned with feeling... perception... choices... consciousness. Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades, they are freed. When they are freed, they know they are freed... They understand: '...there is no return to any state of existence.'
translations.sn22.95:9: Form is like a lump of foam, feeling like a water bubble; perception is like a mirage, choices like a banana tree, and consciousness like a magic trick. This has been taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: 'Sir, is there any form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, and that will stay just the same forever? Is there any feeling... any perception... any choices... is there any consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, and that will stay just the same forever?' 'Monk, there is no form... no feeling... no perception... no choices... no consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, and that will stay just the same forever.'
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Blessed One took up a small lump of cow dung in his hand and said to the monk: 'Monk, there is not even this much of an acquired self that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, and that will stay just the same forever. If there were even this much of an acquired self that was permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, the living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found. But since there is not even this much of an acquired self that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, the living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.'
translations.sn22.96:3: Once upon a time, monk, I was a king, a wheel-turning monarch, an anointed aristocrat. As such, I had 84,000 cities, with the royal capital Kusāvatī at the head. I had 84,000 palaces, with the Palace of Dhamma at the head. I had 84,000 peaked houses, with the Great Array Peaked House at the head. I had 84,000 couches made of ivory, heartwood, and gold, spread with woolen covers, white covers, embroidered covers, rugs of antelope hide, with canopies above and red cushions at both ends. I had 84,000 elephants with gold ornaments, gold banners, covered with gold netting, with the royal elephant Uposatha at the head. I had 84,000 horses with gold ornaments, gold banners, covered with gold netting, with the royal horse Valāhaka at the head. I had 84,000 chariots with gold ornaments, gold banners, covered with gold netting, with the Chariot of Victory at the head. I had 84,000 gems, with the Gem Jewel at the head. I had... 84,000 women, with Queen Subhaddā at the head. I had... 84,000 aristocrats in my retinue, with the Advisor Jewel at the head. I had... 84,000 cows with silken tethers and bronze pails. I had... 84,000 myriads of clothes of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, and fine cotton. I had... 84,000 meals offered; rice was served morning and evening.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Blessed One took up a little bit of soil on the tip of his fingernail and said to the monk: 'Monk, there is not even this much form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, and that will stay just the same forever. If there were even this much form that was permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, the living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found. But since there is not even this much form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not liable to change, the living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found'.
translations.sn35.101:4: Suppose, monks, people were to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta Grove, or burn them, or do what they like with them. Would you think: 'People are carrying us off, or burning us, or doing what they like with us'?
translations.sn35.116:2: Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: “The Venerable Ananda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise brothers in the holy life. The Venerable Ananda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief exposition given by the Blessed One, the meaning of which he did not analyze in detail. Let us approach the Venerable Ananda and ask him the meaning of this.”
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ananda and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and polite conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, they said to the Venerable Ananda:
translations.sn35.116:5: “Suppose, friend, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would pass over the root and trunk of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, and imagine that heartwood should be sought among the branches and leaves. So it is with you, friends: when the Teacher was present face to face with you, you passed over the Blessed One and imagined that we should be asked about this matter. For, friends, the Blessed One knows what should be known, sees what should be seen; he is the Eye, he is Knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Holy One; the Speaker, the Proclaimer, the Elucidator of Meaning, the Giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathagata. That was the time when you should have asked the Blessed One about this matter. You should remember it just as the Blessed One explained it to you.”
translations.sn35.116:6: “Certainly, friend Ananda, the Blessed One knows what should be known, sees what should be seen; he is the Eye, he is Knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Holy One; the Speaker, the Proclaimer, the Elucidator of Meaning, the Giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathagata. That was indeed the time when we should have asked the Blessed One about this matter. We would have remembered it just as the Blessed One explained it. But the Venerable Ananda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise brothers in the holy life. The Venerable Ananda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief exposition given by the Blessed One, the meaning of which he did not analyze in detail. Let the Venerable Ananda analyze it without finding it troublesome.”
translations.sn35.116:7: “Then listen, friends, and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ananda. The Venerable Ananda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ananda. Then they rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One. Having bowed to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side and said to him:
translations.sn35.117:1: “Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me: ‘My mind would mostly stray towards those five cords of sensual pleasure that have been previously touched by the mind, which are past, ceased, and changed, and little towards those in the present or future.’ It occurred to me, bhikkhus: ‘I must maintain diligence, mindfulness, and mental protection regarding myself with respect to those five cords of sensual pleasure that have been previously touched by the mind, which are past, ceased, and changed.’ Therefore, bhikkhus, your minds also would mostly stray towards those five cords of sensual pleasure that have been previously touched by the mind, which are past, ceased, and changed, and little towards those in the present or future. Therefore, bhikkhus, you too must maintain diligence, mindfulness, and mental protection regarding yourselves with respect to those five cords of sensual pleasure that have been previously touched by the mind, which are past, ceased, and changed. Therefore, bhikkhus, that base should be understood where the eye ceases and perception of forms ceases; that base should be understood... where the tongue ceases and perception of tastes ceases; that base should be understood... where the mind ceases and perception of mental phenomena ceases; that base should be understood.” Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rajagaha on the Vulture's Peak Mountain. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One, bowed to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain complete extinguishment in the present life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do attain complete extinguishment in the present life?”
translations.sn35.118:2: “Lord of the devas, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and tantalizing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains holding to them, his consciousness becomes dependent on them and grasps them. A bhikkhu with grasping, Lord of the devas, does not attain complete extinguishment...
translations.sn35.118:3: There are, Lord of the devas, tastes cognizable by the tongue... There are, Lord of the devas, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and tantalizing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains holding to them, his consciousness becomes dependent on them and grasps them. A bhikkhu with grasping, Lord of the devas, does not attain complete extinguishment. This is the cause, Lord of the devas, this is the reason why some beings here do not attain complete extinguishment in the present life.
translations.sn35.118:4: But, Lord of the devas, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and tantalizing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain holding to them, his consciousness does not become dependent on them and does not grasp them. A bhikkhu without grasping, Lord of the devas, attains complete extinguishment...
translations.sn35.127:1: At one time Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was staying at Kosambi in Ghosita’s Park. Then King Udena approached Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. After finishing the greetings and polite talk, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, King Udena said to Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: “Master Bhāradvāja, what is the cause, what is the reason why these young monks, black-haired, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, who have not played with sensual pleasures, live the full and pure holy life as long as they live, and maintain it?” “Great King, this has been said by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One: ‘Come, monks, regarding women old enough to be your mother, establish the mind of a mother; regarding those like sisters, the mind of a sister; regarding those like daughters, the mind of a daughter.’ This, Great King, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks... live the full and pure holy life... and maintain it.”
translations.sn35.127:2: “The mind is fickle, Master Bhāradvāja. Sometimes states of greed arise even regarding those like a mother, even regarding those like a sister, even regarding those like a daughter. Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, any other cause, any other reason why these young monks... maintain it?”
translations.sn35.127:3: “Great King, this has been said by the Blessed One...: ‘Come, monks, review this very body from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head down, enclosed by skin and full of many kinds of impurities—in this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, contents of the stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine.’ This too, Great King, is a cause, this is a reason...” “For those monks, Master Bhāradvāja, who are developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom, that is easy. But for those monks who are undeveloped... that is difficult. Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, thinking ‘I will attend to it as unlovely,’ it comes across as lovely. Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, any other cause, any other reason...?”
translations.sn35.127:4: “Great King, this has been said by the Blessed One...: ‘Come, monks, live guarding the doors of the sense faculties. Seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or features. Since evil unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure might overwhelm one who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, practice for its restraint. Protect the eye faculty; achieve restraint over the eye faculty. Hearing a sound with the ear... Smelling an odor with the nose... Tasting a flavor with the tongue... Touching a tangible with the body... Cognizing a thought with the mind, do not grasp at its signs or features. Since evil unskillful qualities... might overwhelm one... practice for its restraint. Protect the mind faculty; achieve restraint over the mind faculty.’ This too, Great King, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks... live the full and pure holy life... and maintain it.”
translations.sn35.136:2: “Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, / tactiles, and all mental phenomena; / Desirable, lovely, and agreeable, / as long as it’s said ‘they exist’.
translations.sn35.136:3: For the world with its gods, / these are agreed to be happiness; / But where these cease, / that they agree is suffering.
translations.sn35.136:4: The cessation of identity / is seen by the Noble Ones as happiness; / This is contrary to / what the whole world sees.
translations.sn35.136:5: What others say is happiness, / that the Noble Ones say is suffering; / What others say is suffering, / that the Noble Ones know as happiness.
translations.sn35.136:6: See this Dhamma, hard to understand, / here those who don't know are confused; / It is darkness for the shrouded, / gloom for those who do not see.
translations.sn35.136:7: But for the good it is revealed, / like light for those who see; / Though near, they do not understand, / those unskilled in the teaching’s path.
translations.sn35.136:8: By those overcome by lust for existence, / drifting with the stream of existence; / Falling into the domain of Māra, / this Dhamma is not easily understood.
translations.sn35.63:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One... sat to one side and said to the Blessed One: “They speak of ‘a lone dweller, a lone dweller,’ Bhante. In what way, Bhante, is one a lone dweller, and in what way is one a dweller with a partner?”
translations.sn35.69:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Upasena were staying at Rājagaha in the Cool Grove, under the Snake’s Hood Grotto. Now at that time a viper had fallen on Venerable Upasena’s body. Then Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: “Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a cot and carry it outside, before this body of mine scatters right here like a handful of chaff.”
translations.sn35.74:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One... sat to one side and said to the Blessed One: “In a certain dwelling, Bhante, there is a certain monk who is new, not well-known, sick, suffering, gravely ill. Please, Bhante, let the Blessed One approach that monk out of compassion.”
translations.sn35.74:12: “Good, good, monk. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me as being for the fading away of lust. For the Dhamma taught by me, monk, is for the fading away of lust. What do you think, monk, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”
translations.sn35.74:18: “But if it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard that he was a new monk and that he was sick, and knowing that he was not well-known, went to that monk. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he stirred on his bed. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: “Enough, monk, do not stir on your bed. There are these seats prepared, I will sit there.” The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Sitting, the Blessed One said to that monk: “I hope you are bearing up, monk, I hope you are getting by. I hope painful feelings are receding and not increasing, that their receding is evident, not their increase?”
translations.sn35.74:3: “No, sir, I am not bearing up, I am not getting by. Strong painful feelings are increasing for me, not receding; their increase is evident, not their receding.”
translations.sn35.75:7: “I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be for the sake of final extinguishment without grasping, sir.”
translations.sn35.75:8: “Good, good, monk. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me to be for the sake of final extinguishment without grasping. For the Dhamma taught by me is indeed for the sake of final extinguishment without grasping.
translations.sn35.88:1: Then Venerable Puṇṇa went to the Blessed One; having approached … sat to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”
translations.sn35.88:12: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta hit me with a stick, I will think: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, they are truly very kind, in that they don’t hit me with a knife.’ That is what I will think there, Blessed One; that is what I will think there, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:14: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta hit me with a knife, I will think: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, they are truly very kind, in that they don’t take my life with a sharp knife.’ That is what I will think there, Blessed One; that is what I will think there, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:16: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta take my life with a sharp knife, I will think: ‘There are disciples of the Blessed One who, being horrified, repelled, and disgusted by the body and life, seek an assassin. But I have found this assassin without even searching.’ That is what I will think there, Blessed One; that is what I will think there, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:17: “Good, good, Puṇṇa. Possessing such self-control and peace, you will be able to live in the Sunāparanta country. Now, Puṇṇa, do as you think fit.”
translations.sn35.88:18: Then Venerable Puṇṇa, having welcomed and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, bowed to the Blessed One, circled him on the right, put his lodgings in order, took his bowl and robe, and set out for the Sunāparanta country. Wandering by stages, he arrived in the Sunāparanta country. And there Venerable Puṇṇa lived in the Sunāparanta country. Then, within that very rainy season, Venerable Puṇṇa caused about five hundred laymen to declare their confidence. Within that very rainy season, he caused about five hundred laywomen to declare their confidence. Within that very rainy season, he realized the three knowledges. Within that very rainy season, he became fully extinguished.
translations.sn35.88:19: Then several monks went to the Blessed One … seated to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: “Sir, the gentleman named Puṇṇa, who was advised by the Blessed One with a brief instruction, has passed away. What is his destination? What is his future life?”
translations.sn35.88:4: “Puṇṇa, now that you have been advised by me with this brief instruction, in which country will you stay?” “There is, sir, a country named Sunāparanta; I will stay there.”
translations.sn35.88:5: “The people of Sunāparanta are fierce, Puṇṇa; the people of Sunāparanta are rough. If the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile you, what will you think then?”
translations.sn35.88:6: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, I will think: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, they are truly very kind, in that they don’t hit me with their hands.’ That is what I will think there, Blessed One; that is what I will think there, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:8: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta hit me with their hands, I will think: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, they are truly very kind, in that they don’t hit me with a clod of earth.’ That is what I will think there, Blessed One; that is what I will think there, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.95:1: Then Venerable Mālukyaputta went to the Blessed One … seated to one side, Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: “Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”
translations.sn35.95:10: “In that case, Mālukyaputta, regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, you should practice like this: in the seen will be merely the seen; in the heard will be merely the heard; in the sensed will be merely the sensed; in the cognized will be merely the cognized. When, Mālukyaputta, regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, in the seen is merely the seen … then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be ‘by that’. When you are not ‘by that’, then you will not be ‘therein’. When you are not ‘therein’, then you will be neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two. Just this is the end of suffering.”
translations.sn35.95:12:
‘Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost,
Attending to the endearing feature;
With an infatuated mind, one feels it,
And remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:14:
Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost,
Attending to the endearing feature;
With an infatuated mind, one feels it,
And remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:16:
Having smelled an odor, mindfulness is lost,
Attending to the endearing feature;
With an infatuated mind, one feels it,
And remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, mindfulness forgotten, attending to a pleasing sign; with a mind full of passion, he feels it and remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:2: “Here now, Mālukyaputta, what shall we say to the young monks, when you—a monk who is old, elderly, senior, advanced in years, having reached the last stage of life—ask for advice in brief?”
translations.sn35.95:20: Having touched a tactile sensation, mindfulness forgotten, attending to a pleasing sign; with a mind full of passion, he feels it and remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having known a thought, mindfulness forgotten, attending to a pleasing sign; with a mind full of passion, he feels it and remains attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:24: He does not get impassioned with forms, seeing a form with mindfulness established; with a mind free from passion, he feels it and does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:25: As he sees the form, and experiences the feeling, it wears away and does not accumulate; thus he walks mindfully. For one dismantling suffering in this way, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:26: He does not get impassioned with sounds, hearing a sound with mindfulness established; with a mind free from passion, he feels it and does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:27: As he hears the sound, and experiences the feeling, it wears away and does not accumulate; thus he walks mindfully. For one dismantling suffering in this way, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:28: He does not get impassioned with smells, smelling an odor with mindfulness established; with a mind free from passion, he feels it and does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:3: “Although, Bhante, I am old, elderly, senior, advanced in years, having reached the last stage of life, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief; let the Holy One teach me the Dhamma in brief. Perhaps I might understand the meaning of the Blessed One's statement. Perhaps I might become an heir to the Blessed One's statement.”
translations.sn35.95:30: He does not get impassioned with tastes, tasting a flavor with mindfulness established; with a mind free from passion, he feels it and does not remain attached to it.
translations.sn35.95:35: As he knows the thought, and experiences the feeling, it wears away and does not accumulate; thus he walks mindfully. For one dismantling suffering in this way, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:36: “I understand in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One in this way.” “Good, good, Mālukyaputta. It is good that you understand in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief by me:
translations.sn35.95:4: “What do you think, Mālukyaputta? Regarding forms cognizable by the eye that have not been seen, that have never been seen before, that you do not see, and that you have no desire to see: do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “No, Bhante”.
translations.sn35.95:9: “Regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that have not been cognized, that have never been cognized before, that you do not cognize, and that you have no desire to cognize: do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “No, Bhante”.
translations.sn36.19:12: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that? Here, Ānanda, having completely transcended the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a monk enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that. Regarding those who would say: ‘This is the supreme peaceful pleasure and happiness that they experience’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that.
translations.sn36.19:15: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that? Here, Ānanda, having completely transcended the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, a monk enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that.
translations.sn36.19:7: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that? Here, Ānanda, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, a monk enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by thought and examination. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that. Regarding those who would say: ‘This is the supreme peaceful pleasure and happiness that they experience’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that.
translations.sn36.19:8: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that? Here, Ānanda, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a monk enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, with internal confidence and unification of mind, without thought and examination. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that. Regarding those who would say: ‘This is the supreme peaceful pleasure and happiness that they experience’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that.
translations.sn36.19:9: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that? Here, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture, a monk remains equanimous, mindful and aware, and experiences with the body that pleasure about which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who lives happily,’ and he enters and remains in the third absorption. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that. Regarding those who would say: ‘This is the supreme peaceful pleasure and happiness that they experience’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is, Ānanda, a pleasure more excellent and sublime than that.
translations.sn36.21:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka went up to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—all that is caused by what was done in the past.’ What does Master Gotama say about this?”
translations.sn36.21:2: “Some feelings, Sīvaka, arise here originating from bile. You should know this for yourself, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise originating from bile. It is acknowledged as true in the world, Sīvaka, that some feelings arise originating from bile. Now, Sīvaka, regarding those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—all that is caused by what was done in the past,’ they overshoot what they know by themselves and they overshoot what is acknowledged as true in the world. Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth, for as long as life lasts.”
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain monk went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “Sir, what are feelings? What is the origin of feelings? What is the practice that leads to the origin of feelings? What is the cessation of feelings? What is the practice that leads to the cessation of feelings? What is the gratification in feelings? What is the drawback? What is the escape?”
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, mendicants, is spiritual rapture? It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and confidence, and unified mind, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. This is called spiritual rapture.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, mendicants, is rapture more spiritual than the spiritual? When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind liberated from greed, liberated from hate, and liberated from delusion, rapture arises. This is called rapture more spiritual than the spiritual.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, mendicants, is spiritual pleasure? It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and confidence, and unified mind, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one lives in bliss.’ This is called spiritual pleasure.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, mendicants, is pleasure more spiritual than the spiritual? When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind liberated from greed, liberated from hate, and liberated from delusion, pleasure and happiness arise. This is called pleasure more spiritual than the spiritual.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, mendicants, is spiritual equanimity? It’s when a mendicant, giving up pleasure and pain, and with the previous ending of happiness and sadness, enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pain or pleasure, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. This is called spiritual equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, mendicants, is equanimity more spiritual than the spiritual? When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind liberated from greed, liberated from hate, and liberated from delusion, equanimity arises. This is called equanimity more spiritual than the spiritual.
translations.sn36.4:2: One who does not endure them—painful feelings that have arisen, bodily, racking the life, touched by which one trembles.
translations.sn36.4:3: He wails and cries, weak, with little strength. He has not risen up from the bottomless abyss, nor has he found a foothold.
translations.sn36.6:2: But, mendicants, when a learned noble disciple is touched by a painful feeling, they do not sorrow, grieve, and lament, they do not beat their breast and cry, they do not become confused. They experience only one feeling: physical, not mental.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise one, learned, does not experience the feeling, whether pleasant or painful. This is the great difference between the wise, skilled person and the ordinary person.
translations.sn36.6:5: For the learned one who has understood the Dhamma, who clearly sees this world and the next, desirable things do not churn the mind, nor does the undesirable provoke resistance.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, mendicants, is a mendicant mindful? It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. They meditate observing an aspect of feelings ... mind ... principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. That is how a mendicant is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how is a mendicant clearly aware? It’s when a mendicant acts with clear awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and looking aside; when bending and stretching the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent. That is how a mendicant is clearly aware. A mendicant should await their time mindful and aware. This is my instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: If pleasant feeling arises for a mendicant who is thus mindful, aware, diligent, keen, and resolute, they understand: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. It is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated. So how could pleasant feeling be permanent when it has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated?’ They meditate observing impermanence, vanishing, fading away, cessation, and letting go in the body and in pleasant feeling. As they do so, the underlying tendency to greed for the body and pleasant feeling is given up.
translations.sn36.7:8: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it is impermanent, not held on to, and not delighted in. If they feel a painful feeling … If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it is impermanent, not held on to, and not delighted in. If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached. Feeling the end of the body approaching, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body approaching.’ Feeling the end of life approaching, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life approaching.’ They understand: ‘When the body breaks up, after the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’
translations.sn4.13:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. Now at that time the Buddha’s foot had been cut by a splinter. He was beset by painful physical feelings that were severe, sharp, rough, bitter, unpleasant, and disagreeable. But the Buddha endured them, mindful and aware, without worrying. Then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and laid down in the lion’s posture on his right side, placing one foot on top of the other, mindful and aware. Then Māra the Wicked approached the Buddha and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: “Are you lying down in a stupor, or drunk on poetry? Are your goals so few? Alone in a secluded lodging, why do you sleep with a drowsy face?”
translations.sn4.13:3: “I’m not lying in a stupor, nor drunk on poetry. Having reached the goal, I am free of sorrow. Alone in a secluded lodging, I lie down full of compassion for all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: Even those with a dart stuck in their chest, piercing their heart again and again—even they can get some sleep. So why shouldn’t I sleep, with the dart removed?
translations.sn4.13:5: I don’t worry when awake, nor am I afraid to sleep. The days and nights don’t burn me. I see no decline for myself anywhere in the world. That’s why I sleep, full of compassion for all beings.”
translations.sn4.18:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Magadhans in the brahmin village of Pañcasālā. Now at that time there was a gift exchange among the young people in Pañcasālā. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Pañcasālā for alms. Now at that time the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā were possessed by Māra the Wicked, thinking: “Don't let the ascetic Gotama get any alms.”
translations.sn4.18:2: So the Buddha came out of Pañcasālā with his bowl just as clean as when he went in. Then Māra the Wicked approached the Buddha and said to him: “So, ascetic, did you get any alms?” “Did you make sure, Wicked One, that I didn't get any alms?” “Well then, sir, let the Buddha enter Pañcasālā for alms a second time. I will make sure the Buddha gets alms.”
translations.sn4.19:4: “That which they call ‘mine’, and those who say ‘it is mine’: if your mind remains there, ascetic, you won't escape me!”
translations.sn4.19:5: “That which they speak of is not mine, and I am not one of those who speak. Know this, Wicked One: you won't even see the path I take.”
translations.sn4.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the root of the goatherd’s banyan tree, soon after his awakening. Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind: “I am truly free from those mortifications! It’s good that I’m free from those pointless mortifications. It’s good that I’m free and have achieved awakening!”
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Wicked, knowing what the Buddha was thinking, approached him and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: “You’ve strayed from the mortifications by which young people are purified. Being impure, you think you’re pure. You’ve missed the path of purity.”
translations.sn4.1:6: “Developing ethics, immersion, and wisdom, the path to awakening, I have attained supreme purity. You are defeated, End-maker!”
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The Buddha knows me! The Holy One knows me!” miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kosalans, in a forest hut in the region of the Himalayas. Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind: “Is it possible to exercise rulership righteously—without killing or getting others to kill, without conquering or getting others to conquer, without sorrowing or causing sorrow?”
translations.sn4.20:3: “Even a mountain of gold, entirely made of bullion, is not enough for one, let alone two. Knowing this, live a wandering life.
translations.sn4.20:4: When you’ve seen where suffering comes from, how could you bow to sensual pleasures? Knowing that attachment is a tie in the world, a person would train to remove it.”
translations.sn4.21:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans at Silāvatī. At that time several mendicants were staying not far from the Buddha, diligent, keen, and resolute. Then Mara the Wicked manifested in the form of a brahmin—with a large matted topknot, wearing an antelope hide, decrepit, bent like a roof bracket, wheezing, holding a staff of fig wood. He went up to those mendicants and said to them: “You’re young, sirs, you’ve gone forth while mere youths. You have black hair and are blessed with youth; you’re in your prime, and have never played with sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, sirs. Don’t give up what is apparent in the present to run after what takes time.” “Brahmin, we don’t give up what is apparent in the present to run after what takes time. We give up what takes time to run after what is apparent in the present. For the Buddha says that sensual pleasures take time, they’re full of suffering and distress, and the danger in them is even greater. But this teaching is apparent in the present, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.” When they said this, Mara the Wicked shook his head, lolled his tongue, raised his eyebrows until his forehead puckered in three lines, and departed, leaning on his staff.
translations.sn4.24:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree. Now at that time Mara the Wicked had been following the Buddha for seven years, looking for a vulnerability, but finding none. Then Mara the Wicked went up to the Buddha and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: Finding no tastiness there, the crow flew away. Like the crow attacking the rock, we leave Gotama in disappointment.”
translations.sn4.24:2: “Are you sinking in grief that you meditate in the woods? Have you lost a fortune, or do you pine for one? Have you committed some crime in the village? Why don’t you make friends with people? Why does no-one make friends with you?”
translations.sn4.24:3: “I’ve dug up the root of all grief. I’m guiltless, I meditate free of sorrow. I’ve cut off all greed and desire for existence. I’m undefiled, I meditate, O Kinsman of the Negligent.”
translations.sn4.24:6: “If you have understood the path, the safe path to the deathless, go on your own. Why instruct others?”
translations.sn4.24:7: “People ask about the realm beyond death, those who want to go to the far shore. When asked, I explain to them what is true and free of attachments.”
translations.sn4.24:8: “Sir, suppose there was a lotus pond not far from a town or village. And there was a crab there. Then several boys or girls would leave the town or village and go to the pond. They’d pull the crab out of the water and put it on dry land. Whenever the crab extended a claw, the boys or girls would snap, crack, and crush it with a stick or a stone. And when that crab’s claws had all been snapped, cracked, and crushed, it wouldn’t be able to return to the pond. In the same way, sir, you have snapped, cracked, and crushed all my distortions, maneuvers, and convulsions. I am no longer capable of coming near the Buddha again looking for a vulnerability.” Then Mara the Wicked spoke these verses of disappointment in the Buddha’s presence:
translations.sn4.24:9: “A crow circled a stone that looked like a lump of fat, thinking, ‘Hopefully I’ll find something soft here! Hopefully there’s something tasty!’
translations.sn4.25:10: ‘The Worthy One, the Holy One in the world, is not easily led by lust. He has gone beyond Mara’s sovereignty, so I grieve deeply.’
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Mara’s daughters Craving, Delight, and Lust went up to the Buddha and stood to one side. Mara’s daughter Craving addressed the Buddha in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: “I have won the goal, peace of heart. I have conquered the army of the pleasant and agreeable. Alone, meditating, I realized bliss. That’s why I don’t make friends with people. And no-one makes friends with me.”
translations.sn4.25:16: “How does a mendicant usually live here so that, having crossed five floods, they cross the sixth? How do they usually meditate so that sensual perceptions are kept at bay?”
translations.sn4.25:17: “With tranquil body and mind well liberated, not planning, mindful, homeless. Knowing the teaching, meditating without placing the mind, they don’t get angry, they don’t stare, they don’t drowse.”
translations.sn4.25:2: “Why are you so downhearted, dad? Who is the man you grieve for? We’ll catch him with the snare of lust, like an elephant in the wild. We’ll bind him and bring him back, and he’ll be under your control.”
translations.sn4.25:20: “He has cut off craving, he wanders with his community. Many faithful will certainly follow him. This one without a home will cut off death’s King and lead many people to the far shore.”
translations.sn4.25:23: “Fools! You try to batter a mountain with lotus stalks, dig up a hill with your nails, or chew iron with your teeth.
translations.sn4.25:24: As if striking a rock with your head, or seeking a footing in the abyss, or striking a stump with your chest, you leave Gotama in disappointment.”
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Mara’s daughters Craving, Delight, and Lust went up to the Buddha and said to him: “We serve at your feet, ascetic.” But the Buddha did not pay attention, as he was liberated in the supreme ending of attachments.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Mara’s daughters Craving, Delight, and Lust went out to one side and thought: “Men’s tastes vary. Why don’t we each manifest in the form of a hundred young maidens?” Then Mara’s daughters Craving, Delight, and Lust each manifested in the form of a hundred young maidens. They went up to the Buddha and said to him: “We serve at your feet, ascetic.” But the Buddha did not pay attention, as he was liberated in the supreme ending of attachments.
translations.sn4.8:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then Mara the Wicked went up to the Buddha and recited this verse in his presence:
translations.sn4.8:2: “One with children delights in children, and a cattle-owner delights in cattle. For attachments are a man’s delight; without attachments there’s no delight.”
translations.sn4.8:3:
“One with children grieves because of children,
  A cattle-owner likewise grieves because of cattle;
  Sorrow comes to a man because of attachments,
  For he who has no attachments does not grieve.”
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Now at that time the nun Khemā, wandering on tour among the Kosalans, had taken up residence at Toraṇavatthu, between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, took up residence for one night at Toraṇavatthu, between Sāketa and Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi addressed a certain man: “Come, my good man, find out if there is any ascetic or brahmin in Toraṇavatthu of such a sort that I might visit him today.”
translations.sn44.1:2: “Yes, your majesty,” that man replied to King Pasenadi. Roaming all over Toraṇavatthu, he did not see any ascetic or brahmin of such a sort that King Pasenadi might visit. However, that man saw the nun Khemā who had taken up residence at Toraṇavatthu. Having seen her, he approached King Pasenadi. Having approached, he said to King Pasenadi:
translations.sn44.1:3: “There is no ascetic or brahmin in Toraṇavatthu of such a sort that your majesty might visit. But there is, sire, a nun named Khemā, a disciple of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened Buddha. A good report concerning this lady has circulated thus: ‘She is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, a splendid speaker, of good wit.’ Let your majesty visit her.”
translations.sn44.1:6: “Well then, great king, I will question you about this same matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, great king? Do you have any accountant or calculator or mathematician who can count the sand in the Ganges—saying ‘there are this many grains of sand,’ or ‘this many hundreds,’ or ‘this many thousands,’ or ‘this many hundreds of thousands’?” “No, lady.” “Do you have any accountant or calculator or mathematician who can count the water in the great ocean—saying ‘there are this many measures of water,’ or ‘this many hundreds,’ or ‘this many thousands,’ or ‘this many hundreds of thousands’?” “No, lady.” “Why is that?” “Lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom.” “Even so, great king, any form by which one describing the Tathāgata might describe him: that form has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Freed from reckoning in terms of form, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—just like the great ocean. ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.
translations.sn44.1:9: Any consciousness by which one describing the Tathāgata might describe him: that consciousness has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Freed from reckoning in terms of consciousness, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—just like the great ocean. ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having delighted and rejoiced in the nun Khemā’s statement, rose from his seat, bowed to the nun Khemā, circled her on his right, and left.
translations.sn45.1:2: “Ignorance, mendicants, is the forerunner in the entry upon unskillful qualities, followed by lack of conscience and lack of prudence. For an ignorant person, one without wisdom, wrong view arises. For one of wrong view, wrong thought arises. For one of wrong thought, wrong speech arises. For one of wrong speech, wrong action arises. For one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. For one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises. For one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. For one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
translations.sn45.2:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans where there was a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Sir, this is half of the spiritual life: good friendship, good companionship, and good association.”
translations.sn45.2:2: “Do not say that, Ānanda, do not say that. This is the whole of the spiritual life, Ānanda: good friendship, good companionship, and good association. When a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates, it is to be expected that they will develop the noble eightfold path and cultivate the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.2:3: And how, Ānanda, does a mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates develop the noble eightfold path and cultivate the noble eightfold path? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant develops right view, which relies on seclusion, relies on fading away, relies on cessation, and ripens as letting go; develops right thought … develops right speech … develops right action … develops right livelihood … develops right effort … develops right mindfulness … develops right concentration, which relies on seclusion, relies on fading away, relies on cessation, and ripens as letting go. That is how, Ānanda, a mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates develops the noble eightfold path and cultivates the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having robed up in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi departing Sāvatthī in a chariot drawn by all-white mares. The yoked horses were white, the ornaments white, the chariot white, the upholstery white, the reins white, the goad-stick white, the canopy white, the turban white, the clothes white, the sandals white, and he was fanned by a white yak-tail fan. People seeing him said: “What a divine vehicle, sir! It looks like a divine vehicle, sir!”
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will and harmlessness, and seclusion are its weapons; endurance is its armor, rolling on to the sanctuary.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, approached the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: “It is possible, Ānanda,” said the Blessed One. “For this is a designation for this very Noble Eightfold Path, Ānanda: ‘the divine vehicle,’ and ‘the vehicle of the Dhamma,’ and ‘the supreme victory in battle.’”
translations.sn45.4:8: “For whom faith and wisdom are the yoked dhammas always leading the load; conscience is the pole, mind the yoke, mindfulness the charioteer and guard.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot is equipped with ethics, absorption is the axle, energy the wheels; equanimity is the balance-bar, desirelessness the upholstery.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, I will teach and analyze the Noble Eightfold Path for you. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what is right view? Knowledge about suffering, knowledge about the origin of suffering, knowledge about the cessation of suffering, and knowledge about the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. This is called right view.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what is right thought? Thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of harmlessness. This is called right thought.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what is right speech? Abstaining from lying, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. This is called right speech.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what is right action? Abstaining from killing living creatures, abstaining from stealing, and abstaining from unchaste conduct. This is called right action.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what is right livelihood? It’s when a noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and earns a living by right livelihood. This is called right livelihood.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what is right effort? It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise … so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up … so that skillful qualities arise … so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fulfilled by development. This is called right effort.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what is right mindfulness? It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. They meditate observing an aspect of feelings … mind … principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called right mindfulness.
translations.sn46.11:1: “Mendicants, whatever living creatures assume the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all of them do so depending on the earth, grounded on the earth. In the same way, a mendicant develops and cultivates the seven awakening factors depending on ethics, grounded on ethics.
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali Cave, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then in the late afternoon, the Blessed One came out of retreat and went to Venerable Mahākassapa. He sat down on the seat spread out and said to Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: “I hope you’re keeping well, Kassapa; I hope you’re alright. I hope your pain is fading, not growing, that it’s a sign of fading, not growing.” “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not alright. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; it’s a sign of growing, not fading.”
translations.sn46.29:2: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion … they develop the awakening factor of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. When the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated in this way they lead to the giving up of fetters.
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying in the land of the Sumbhas, where there is a town of the Sumbhas named Setaka. Then Venerable Udāyī went up to the Blessed One … sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: “It is incredible, sir, it is amazing! How much love, respect, shame, and conscience I have for the Buddha. For, sir, when I was formerly a householder, I did not have much regard for the Dhamma or the Sangha. But seeing my love, respect, shame, and conscience for the Buddha, I went forth from the home life into homelessness. The Buddha taught me the Dhamma: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the ending of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the ending of consciousness.’
translations.sn46.30:3: Then, sir, having gone to an empty hut, while turning these five grasping aggregates over and over, I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’; I truly understood: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I truly understood: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I truly understood: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ I have comprehended the Dhamma, sir, and I have gained the path. When developed and cultivated, it will lead me on in such a way that I will understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.’
translations.sn46.38:1: Mendicants, when a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma, paying attention, applying their mind, concentrating their whole heart, and listening closely, at that time the five hindrances are not present. At that time the seven awakening factors go to fulfillment by development.
translations.sn46.3:1: “Mendicants, regarding those mendicants who are accomplished in ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom: I say that even seeing them is helpful. I say that even hearing them is helpful; approaching them is helpful; attending on them is helpful; recollecting them is helpful; and going forth after them is helpful. Why is that? Because after hearing the Dhamma from such mendicants, one lives withdrawn in two ways: withdrawn in body and withdrawn in mind. Living withdrawn in that way, they recollect and think about that Dhamma.
translations.sn46.3:2: At that time when a mendicant, living withdrawn in that way, recollects and thinks about that Dhamma, the awakening factor of mindfulness is aroused in them. At that time the mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness; at that time the awakening factor of mindfulness goes to fulfillment by development in the mendicant. Living mindful in this way, they investigate, explore, and inquire into that Dhamma with wisdom.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what, mendicants, is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of energy, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of energy? There are, mendicants, the element of initiative, the element of launching, and the element of exertion. Not paying attention to that frequently—this is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of energy, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of energy.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what, mendicants, is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of rapture, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of rapture? There are, mendicants, things that are the basis for the awakening factor of rapture. Not paying attention to that frequently—this is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of rapture, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of rapture.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what, mendicants, is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of tranquility, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of tranquility? There is, mendicants, tranquility of the body and tranquility of the mind. Not paying attention to that frequently—this is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of tranquility, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of tranquility.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what, mendicants, is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of immersion, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of immersion? There are, mendicants, the sign of serenity and the sign of non-dispersal. Not paying attention to that frequently—this is the starvation of the arising of the unarisen awakening factor of immersion, or of the fulfillment by development of the arisen awakening factor of immersion.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to them, “It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. Why don’t we go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.52:10: And what, mendicants, is the exposition by which the seven awakening factors become fourteen? Mindfulness of internal principles is the awakening factor of mindfulness; mindfulness of external principles is also the awakening factor of mindfulness. Thus it goes under the heading ‘awakening factor of mindfulness’. In this way it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:11: Investigating, exploring, and inquiring into internal principles with wisdom is the awakening factor of investigation of principles; investigating, exploring, and inquiring into external principles with wisdom is also the awakening factor of investigation of principles. Thus it goes under the heading ‘awakening factor of investigation of principles’. In this way it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:12: Physical energy is the awakening factor of energy; mental energy is also the awakening factor of energy. Thus it goes under the heading ‘awakening factor of energy’. In this way it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:13: Rapture accompanied by placing the mind and keeping it connected is the awakening factor of rapture; rapture without placing the mind and keeping it connected is also the awakening factor of rapture. Thus it goes under the heading ‘awakening factor of rapture’. In this way it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:14: Tranquility of the body is the awakening factor of tranquility; tranquility of the mind is also the awakening factor of tranquility. Thus it goes under the heading ‘awakening factor of tranquility’. In this way it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:15: Mendicants, immersion with placing the mind and keeping it connected is the awakening factor of immersion. Immersion without placing the mind and keeping it connected is also the awakening factor of immersion. These are both grouped under the ‘awakening factor of immersion’. That is how it is twofold.
