translations.sn46.52:2: Then those mendicants went to the monastery of the wanderers of other religions. They exchanged greetings with the wanderers and, after some polite and friendly conversation, sat down to one side. The wanderers said to them:
translations.sn46.52:3: “Reverends, the ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples like this: ‘Come, mendicants, give up the five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom, and truly develop the seven awakening factors.’ We too teach our disciples like this: ‘Come, reverends, give up the five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom, and truly develop the seven awakening factors.’ So, reverends, what is the difference, the distinction, the disparity between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, between his teaching and instruction and ours?”
translations.sn46.52:4: Those mendicants neither approved nor dismissed that statement of the wanderers of other religions. They got up from their seats and left, thinking, “We will learn the meaning of this statement in the Buddha’s presence.” Then, after wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, and returning from their almsround after the meal, they went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. They told him what had happened:
translations.sn46.52:8: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other religions speak like this, you should say to them: ‘But reverends, is there a way in which the five hindrances become ten, and the seven awakening factors become fourteen?’ Questioned like this, the wanderers of other religions would be stumped, and, furthermore, would get annoyed. Why is that? Because it is out of their range. I do not see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Realized One, or a disciple of the Realized One, or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what is the way in which the five hindrances become ten? Internal sensual desire is a hindrance; external sensual desire is also a hindrance. These are both grouped under the ‘hindrance of sensual desire’. That is how it is twofold. Internal ill will is a hindrance; external ill will is also a hindrance. These are both grouped under the ‘hindrance of ill will’. That is how it is twofold. Dullness is a hindrance; drowsiness is also a hindrance. These are both grouped under the ‘hindrance of dullness and drowsiness’. That is how it is twofold. Restlessness is a hindrance; remorse is also a hindrance. These are both grouped under the ‘hindrance of restlessness and remorse’. That is how it is twofold. Internal doubt is a hindrance; external doubt is also a hindrance. These are both grouped under the ‘hindrance of doubt’. That is how it is twofold. This is the way in which the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: Mendicants, when the mind is restless, it is the wrong time to develop the awakening factors of investigation of principles, energy, and rapture. Why is that? Because it is hard to settle a restless mind with those things.
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose a man wanted to extinguish a great bonfire. And he’d toss dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry timber on it, blow on it, and not sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to extinguish that great bonfire?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:13: But when the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop the awakening factors of tranquility, immersion, and equanimity. Why is that? Because it is easy to settle a restless mind with those things.
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose a man wanted to extinguish a great bonfire. And he’d toss wet grass, wet cow dung, and wet timber on it, spray it with water, and sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to extinguish that great bonfire?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:2: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other religions speak like this, you should say to them: ‘Reverends, when the mind is sluggish, which awakening factors is it the wrong time to develop, and which is it the right time to develop? And when the mind is restless, which awakening factors is it the wrong time to develop, and which is it the right time to develop?’ Questioned like this, the wanderers of other religions would be stumped, and, furthermore, would get annoyed. Why is that? Because it is out of their range.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Realized One, or a disciple of the Realized One, or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:4: Mendicants, when the mind is sluggish, it is the wrong time to develop the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of immersion, and the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is hard to rouse with these qualities.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. If they toss wet grass, wet cow dung, and wet timber on it, spray it with water, and scatter dust on it, would they be able to make that small fire flare up?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:7: But when the mind is sluggish, it is the right time to develop the awakening factor of investigation of principles, the awakening factor of energy, and the awakening factor of rapture. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is easy to rouse with these qualities.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. If they toss dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry timber on it, blow on it, and don’t scatter dust on it, would they be able to make that small fire flare up?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn46.54:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Koliyans, where they have a town named Haliddavasana. Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then it occurred to them: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Haliddavasana. Why don’t we go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.54:11: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other sects speak like this, you should say to them: ‘Reverends, when the heart’s release by love is developed, what is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, and its end? When the heart’s release by compassion … rejoicing … equanimity is developed, what is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, and its end?’ Questioned like this, the wanderers of other sects will be stumped, and will get annoyed. Why is that? Because it is out of their range. I do not see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how is the heart’s release by love developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, and its end? It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness … equanimity accompanied by love, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do. If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ that’s what they do. If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ that’s what they do. If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do. If they wish: ‘May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, rejecting both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do. Or else, they enter and remain in the beautiful liberation. I say that the heart’s release by love culminates in the beautiful, for a mendicant here who has wisdom but has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how is the heart’s release by compassion developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, and its end? It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness … equanimity accompanied by compassion, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do … If they wish: ‘May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, rejecting both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do. Or else, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space. I say that the heart’s release by compassion culminates in the dimension of infinite space, for a mendicant here who has wisdom but has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how is the heart’s release by rejoicing developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, and its end? It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness … equanimity accompanied by rejoicing, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do … If they wish: ‘May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, rejecting both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do. Or else, having completely transcended the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness. I say that the heart’s release by rejoicing culminates in the dimension of infinite consciousness, for a mendicant here who has wisdom but has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:3: “Reverends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: ‘Come, mendicants, give up the five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom, and meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free from enmity and ill will. Meditate spreading a heart full of compassion to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, spread a heart full of compassion to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free from enmity and ill will. Meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, spread a heart full of rejoicing to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free from enmity and ill will. Meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free from enmity and ill will.’”
translations.sn46.8:1: At one time Venerable Upavāna and Venerable Sāriputta were staying near Kosambī, in Ghosita’s Monastery. Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat and went to Venerable Upavāna. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Upavāna and, after engaging in a friendly and polite conversation, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Upavāna:
translations.sn46.8:2: “Reverend Upavāna, could a mendicant know that: ‘Through proper attention within myself, the seven awakening factors have been well undertaken by me, leading to a comfortable abiding’?” “Reverend Sāriputta, a mendicant could know that: ‘Through proper attention within myself, the seven awakening factors have been well undertaken by me, leading to a comfortable abiding’.”
translations.sn47.10:1: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to a certain nuns’ quarters. He sat down on the seat spread out. Then several nuns went up to Venerable Ānanda, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those nuns said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: “Here, Sir Ānanda, several nuns are meditating with their minds well established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. They perceive a higher distinction than before.” “That’s how it is, sisters, that’s how it is. For any monk or nun who meditates with their mind well established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, it can be expected that they will perceive a higher distinction than before.”
translations.sn47.10:7: Furthermore, Ānanda, a mendicant meditates observing feelings … mind … principles in principles, keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. While they are meditating observing principles in principles, their body becomes feverish due to a mental object, or their mind becomes sluggish, or their mind is scattered externally. That mendicant should direct their mind to some inspiring basis. As they direct their mind to some inspiring basis, gladness is born. When they are glad, rapture is born. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, they feel bliss. And when they are blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi. Then they reflect: ‘The goal for the sake of which I directed my mind has been achieved. So now let me withdraw it.’ They withdraw, and they do not think or consider. They understand: ‘I am without thought or consideration, mindful within, and happy.’ That is how there is directed development.
translations.sn47.10:9: So, Ānanda, I have taught directed development and undirected development. Out of compassion, I have done what a teacher should do for their disciples, seeking their welfare. Here are the roots of trees, Ānanda, here are empty huts. Practice absorption, Ānanda! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”
translations.sn47.13:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the land of the Magadhans in the village of Nālaka. He was sick, suffering, gravely ill. And the novice Cunda was Venerable Sāriputta’s carer.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then Venerable Sāriputta became fully extinguished because of that sickness. Then the novice Cunda took Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robes and set out for Sāvatthī, Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, and Venerable Ānanda. Upon arrival, he bowed to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the novice Cunda said to Venerable Ānanda: “Sir, Venerable Sāriputta has become fully extinguished. Here are his bowl and robes.”
translations.sn47.13:3: “This is a reason to see the Buddha, Reverend Cunda. Come, Reverend Cunda, let’s go to the Buddha and inform him of this.” “Yes, sir,” the novice Cunda replied to Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Sir, this novice Cunda says that Venerable Sāriputta has become fully extinguished, and this is his bowl and robe. Sir, when I heard that Venerable Sāriputta had become fully extinguished, my body felt like it was drugged, I became disoriented, and the teachings didn’t spring to mind.”
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhas, where there was a town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Once upon a time, monks, a bamboo acrobat, having set up his bamboo pole, addressed his apprentice Medakathalika: ‘Come now, my dear Medakathalika, climb up the bamboo pole and stand on my shoulders.’ ‘Yes, teacher,’ the apprentice Medakathalika replied to the acrobat, climbed up the bamboo pole, and stood on the teacher’s shoulders. Then, monks, the acrobat said to the apprentice Medakathalika: ‘You protect me, dear Medakathalika, and I will protect you. Thus guarded by one another, protected by one another, we will display our skills, get our payment, and come down safely from the bamboo pole.’ When this was said, monks, the apprentice Medakathalika said to the acrobat: ‘That will not do, teacher. You protect yourself, teacher, and I will protect myself. Thus self-guarded, self-protected, we will display our skills, get our payment, and come down safely from the bamboo pole.’”
translations.sn47.19:2: “That is the right way there,” the Blessed One said, “just as the apprentice Medakathalika said to the teacher. Monks, the establishment of mindfulness should be practiced with the thought, ‘I will protect myself.’ The establishment of mindfulness should be practiced with the thought, ‘I will protect others.’ Protecting oneself, monks, one protects others; protecting others, one protects oneself.
translations.sn47.20:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhas, where there was a town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn47.20:2: “Suppose, monks, a large crowd were to gather, crying, ‘The finest lady in the land! The finest lady in the land!’ And that finest lady in the land is highly accomplished at dancing and singing. A still larger crowd were to gather, crying, ‘The finest lady in the land is dancing! She is singing!’ Then a man might come along wishing to live, not wishing to die, wishing for happiness, averse to suffering. Someone might say to him: ‘Here, my good man, is a bowl filled to the brim with oil. You must carry it between the great crowd and the finest lady in the land. A man with a raised sword will follow right behind you. Wherever you spill even a little of it, right there he will cut off your head.’ What do you think, monks? Would that man, not paying attention to that bowl of oil, let himself get distracted outside?” “No, venerable sir”.
translations.sn47.25:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anathapindika’s Park. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After finishing some polite and courteous talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana, the true Dhamma does not last long? And what is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana, the true Dhamma does last long?”
translations.sn47.25:2: “Brahmin, it is because the four establishments of mindfulness are not developed and cultivated that the true Dhamma does not last long after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana. But it is because the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and cultivated that the true Dhamma lasts long after the Tathagata has attained final Nibbana.
translations.sn47.29:2: Then the Venerable Ananda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of the householder Sirivaddha; having approached, he sat on the appointed seat. Sitting there, the Venerable Ananda said to the householder Sirivaddha: “I hope you are bearing up, householder, I hope you are getting by. I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding, not their increasing, is evident?” “I am not bearing up, venerable sir, I am not getting by. Strong painful feelings are increasing in me, not subsiding; their increase, not their subsiding, is evident”.
translations.sn47.29:3: “Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. I will dwell contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.’ That is how you should train yourself, householder”.
translations.sn47.33:1: “Monks, those who have neglected the four establishments of mindfulness have neglected the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering. Those who have undertaken the four establishments of mindfulness have undertaken the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.sn47.37:1: “Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating the body in the body, whatever desire there is for the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, whatever desire there is for feelings is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating mind in mind, whatever desire there is for the mind is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: “Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: They meditate observing the mind as mind, keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. As they meditate observing the mind as mind, the mind is fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: “Mendicants, I will teach you mindfulness meditation, the development of mindfulness meditation, and the practice leading to the development of mindfulness meditation. Listen. And what is mindfulness meditation? It’s when a mendicant meditates observing the body as body, keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. They meditate observing feelings as feelings … mind as mind … principles as principles, keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. This is called mindfulness meditation.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what is the development of mindfulness meditation? It’s when a mendicant meditates observing the nature of origination in the body, observing the nature of dissolution in the body, and observing the nature of origination and dissolution in the body, keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. They meditate observing the nature of origination in feelings … in the mind … in principles, observing the nature of dissolution in principles, and observing the nature of origination and dissolution in principles, keen, aware, and mindful, rid of desire and aversion for the world. This is called the development of mindfulness meditation.
translations.sn47.4:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kosalans at the brahmin village of Sālā. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants … saying this:
translations.sn47.4:2: “Mendicants, you should encourage, settle, and establish those mendicants who are junior, recently gone forth, newly arrived in this teaching and training in the development of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. What four? ‘Come, reverends, meditate observing the body as body, keen, aware, unified, clear-minded, concentrated, and one-pointed, in order to know the body as it truly is. Meditate observing feelings as feelings … mind as mind … principles as principles, keen, aware, unified, clear-minded, concentrated, and one-pointed, in order to know principles as they truly are.’
translations.sn47.4:3: Those mendicants who are trainees, who haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, who live aspiring for the supreme sanctuary: they too meditate observing the body as body, keen, aware, unified, clear-minded, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the full understanding of the body. They meditate observing feelings as feelings … mind as mind … principles as principles, keen, aware, unified, clear-minded, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the full understanding of principles.
translations.sn47.4:4: Those mendicants who are perfected, who have ended the defilements, finished the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and are rightly liberated through enlightenment: they too meditate observing the body as body, keen, aware, unified, clear-minded, concentrated, and one-pointed, detached from the body. They meditate observing feelings as feelings … mind as mind … principles as principles, keen, aware, unified, clear-minded, concentrated, and one-pointed, detached from principles.
translations.sn47.6:1: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a hawk swooped down and seized a quail. Then, as the quail was being carried off by the hawk, he wailed: ‘We are so unlucky, of so little merit! We strayed out of our range into the domain of others. If only we had stayed in our own range, our ancestral domain, this hawk wouldn’t have stood a chance in a fight!’ ‘So, quail, what is your own range, your ancestral domain?’ ‘It’s a plowed field covered with clods of earth.’ Then the hawk, confident in her own strength, boasting of her own strength, released the quail: ‘Go now, quail! But even there you won’t escape me!’
translations.sn47.6:2: Then the quail went to a plowed field covered with clods of earth. He climbed up a big clod, stood there, and challenged the hawk: ‘Come get me now, hawk! Come get me now, hawk!’ Then the hawk, confident in her own strength, boasting of her own strength, folded her wings and swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew, ‘That hawk is coming at me full speed!’, he slipped inside that very clod. But the hawk shattered her breast right there. That’s what happens, mendicants, when you stray outside your range into the domain of others.
translations.sn47.6:3: So, mendicants, don’t stray outside your range into the domain of others. If you stray outside your range into the domain of others, Māra will find a vulnerability, Māra will get a hold on you. And what is not a mendicant’s range, but the domain of others? It is the five kinds of sensual stimulation. What five? Sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds known by the ear … Smells known by the nose … Tastes known by the tongue … Touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. This is not a mendicant’s range, but the domain of others.
translations.sn47.7:1: “Mendicants, in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, there are rugged, uneven areas where neither monkeys nor humans roam. There are rugged, uneven areas where monkeys roam, but not humans. There are level, delightful regions where both monkeys and humans roam. There, hunters set a trap of pitch on the monkey trails to catch the monkeys.
translations.sn47.8:2: That foolish, incompetent, unskillful cook does not pick up on the sign of his own master: ‘Today my master likes this curry, or he reaches for this one, or he takes a lot of this one, or he praises this one. Today my master likes a sour curry … or bitter … or spicy … or sweet … or alkaline … or non-alkaline … or salty … or non-salty curry, or he reaches for the non-salty one, or he takes a lot of the non-salty one, or he praises the non-salty one.’
translations.sn47.8:4: In the same way, mendicants, that foolish, incompetent, unskillful mendicant does not get to dwell happily in this very life, and does not get mindfulness and situational awareness. Why is that? Because, mendicants, that foolish, incompetent, unskillful mendicant does not pick up on the sign of their own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Suppose, mendicants, there was a wise, competent, skillful cook who served a king or a royal minister with various kinds of curries—sour, bitter, spicy, sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and non-salty.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, early in the morning, the nun Vajirā dressed and, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from her almsround after her meal, she went to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day's abiding. Having plunged into the Blind Men’s Grove, she sat at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in the nun Vajirā, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: “By whom has this being been created? Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen? Where does the being cease?”
translations.sn5.10:3: Then it occurred to the nun Vajirā: “Who is this—human or non-human—speaking this verse?” Then it occurred to the nun Vajirā: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in me, wanting to make me fall away from concentration, speaking this verse.” Then the nun Vajirā, having understood “This is Māra the Wicked,” replied to him in verses:
translations.sn5.10:4: “Why do you assume 'a being'? Māra, is that your speculative view? This is a heap of sheer formations: here no being is found.
translations.sn5.10:5: Just as, with an assemblage of parts, the word 'chariot' is used, so, when the aggregates exist, there is the convention 'a being'.
translations.sn5.10:6: It’s only suffering that comes to be, suffering that stands and falls away. Nothing but suffering comes to be, nothing but suffering ceases.”
translations.sn5.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, early in the morning, the nun Āḷavikā dressed and, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from her almsround after her meal, she went to the Blind Men’s Grove seeking seclusion. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in the nun Āḷavikā, wanting to make her fall away from seclusion, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: “There is no escape in the world, so what will you do with seclusion? Enjoy the delights of sensual pleasures; don't be remorseful later.”
translations.sn5.1:3: Then it occurred to the nun Āḷavikā: “Who is this—human or non-human—speaking this verse?” Then it occurred to the nun Āḷavikā: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in me, wanting to make me fall away from seclusion, speaking this verse.” Then the nun Āḷavikā, having understood “This is Māra the Wicked,” replied to him in verses:
translations.sn5.1:4: “There is an escape in the world, well touched by me with wisdom. O Wicked One, kinsman of the negligent, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes; the aggregates are their chopping block. What you call 'delight in sensual pleasures' has become 'discontent' for me.”
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Āḷavikā knows me,” miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: “That state so hard to achieve which is to be attained by the seers, can't be attained by a woman with her two-fingered wisdom.”
translations.sn5.2:4: “What does womanhood matter when the mind is well concentrated, when knowledge is flowing, seeing clearly into the Dhamma?
translations.sn5.2:5: Anyone who thinks 'I am a woman' or 'I am a man' or 'I am anything at all'—it is fitting for Māra to address him.”
translations.sn5.3:2: “Why now, with a tearful face, do you sit alone like one whose son is dead? Having come to the middle of the woods all alone, are you looking for a man?”
translations.sn5.3:3: Then it occurred to the nun Kisāgotamī: “Who is this—human or non-human—speaking this verse?” Then it occurred to the nun Kisāgotamī: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in me, wanting to make me fall away from concentration, speaking this verse.”
translations.sn5.3:5: “I've gotten past the death of sons; men are finished with. I do not grieve, I do not weep, and I do not fear you, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Delight is destroyed in every respect; the mass of darkness is shattered. Having defeated the army of Death, I dwell without defilements.”
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Kisāgotamī knows me,” miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, early in the morning, the nun Vijayā dressed … sat at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in the nun Vijayā, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: “You are young and beautiful, and I am young and youthful. Come, let us enjoy ourselves with the five-piece band.”
translations.sn5.4:4: “Forms, sounds, tastes, scents, and tactile sensations that are delightful—I hand them right back to you, Māra; I have no need for them.
translations.sn5.4:5: “This foul body, fragile and brittle—I am horrified and repelled by it. Craving for sensual pleasures has been rooted out.
translations.sn5.4:6: For those beings who have attained the realm of form, and those who abide in the formless, and for the peaceful attainments—darkness has been destroyed in every respect.”
translations.sn5.5:1: At Savatthi. Then the nun Uppalavanna, having robed up in the morning ... stood at the foot of a flowering sal tree. Then Mara the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trembling, and terror in the nun Uppalavanna, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: “Having gone to the top of the flowering sal tree, nun, you stand alone at its foot. There is no second beauty like yours; foolish girl, are you not afraid of rogues?”
translations.sn5.5:4: “Even if a hundred thousand rogues just like that were to come here, I would not stir a hair, I would not shake with terror. I am not afraid of you, Mara, even though I am alone.
translations.sn5.5:6: I have mastered the mind, the bases of psychic power are well developed. I am freed from all bonds; I am not afraid of you, my friend.”
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Mara the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Uppalavanna knows me,” miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: “Why don’t you approve of birth? One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures. Who on earth convinced you: ‘Nun, don’t approve of birth’?”
translations.sn5.6:3: “For one born there is death; one born experiences suffering—bondage, murder, and distress. Therefore I don’t approve of birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha has taught the Dhamma for the transcending of birth, for the abandoning of all suffering; he has established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: Those beings who have attained the realm of form, and those who abide in the formless—not understanding cessation, they return to renewed existence.”
translations.sn5.7:1: At Savatthi. Then the nun Upacala, having robed up in the morning ... sat at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Mara the Wicked approached the nun Upacala and said to her: “Where, nun, do you wish to be reborn?” “I do not wish to be reborn anywhere, my friend.”
translations.sn5.7:2: “The Tavatimsa and Yama devas, and the Tusita devas too; the devas who delight in creation, and those who control what is created by others—direct your mind there and you will experience delight.”
translations.sn5.7:3: “The Tavatimsa and Yama devas, and the Tusita devas too; the devas who delight in creation, and those who control what is created by others—they are bound by the bonds of sensual pleasure; they come under Mara’s control again.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is burning, the whole world is up in smoke, the whole world is ablaze, the whole world is shaking.
translations.sn5.7:5: That which is unshaken and unburning, not frequented by ordinary people, where Mara has no access—there my mind delights.”
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Mara the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Upacala knows me,” miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Savatthi. Then the nun Sisupacala, having robed up in the morning ... sat at the foot of a tree for the day's abiding. Then Mara the Wicked approached the nun Sisupacala and said to her: “Whose philosophy do you approve of, nun?” “I don’t approve of anyone’s philosophy, my friend.”
translations.sn5.8:2: “For whose sake have you shaved your head? You look like an ascetic, but you don’t approve of any philosophy. Why do you wander like a confused person?”
translations.sn5.8:3: “Outside of here there are followers of other philosophies; they rely on views. I don’t approve of their teaching; they are not skilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: He is released in every respect, unattached; he sees all, possessing vision. He has reached the destruction of all kamma, released in the ending of attachments. That Blessed One is my teacher; I approve of his instruction.”
translations.sn5.9:2: “By whom has this puppet been created? Where is the puppet’s maker? Where has the puppet arisen? Where does the puppet cease?”
translations.sn5.9:4: “This puppet is not made by itself, nor is this misery made by another. It has come to be dependent on a cause; when the cause breaks up, it ceases.
translations.sn5.9:6: Just so the aggregates, the elements, and these six sense fields—they have come to be dependent on a cause; when the cause breaks up, they cease.”
translations.sn56.11:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Varanasi in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
translations.sn56.11:10: “But when my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are in their three phases and twelve aspects was thoroughly purified in this way, then, monks, in this world with its devas, Mara, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’” That is what the Blessed One said. Gratified, the group of five monks delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this explanation was being spoken, there arose in the Venerable Kondanna the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye: “Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.”
translations.sn56.11:13: And so, at that moment, at that instant, at that second, the cry soared as far as the Brahma world. And this ten-thousandfold world system shook, quaked, and trembled, and an immeasurable, magnificent radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine majesty of the devas.
translations.sn56.11:2: “There are these two extremes, monks, that should not be pursued by one who has gone forth. Which two? The pursuit of sensual happiness in sensual pleasures, which is low, vulgar, the way of ordinary people, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and the pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Avoiding both these extremes, the Tathagata has awakened to the middle way, which gives vision, gives knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbana.
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathagata, which gives vision, gives knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbana? It is this noble eightfold path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathagata, which gives vision, gives knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbana.
translations.sn56.11:4: Now this, mendicants, is the noble truth of suffering: rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering. Now this, mendicants, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for extermination. Now this, mendicants, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. Now this, mendicants, is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering: it is simply this noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn56.11:5: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another. ‘This noble truth of suffering should be fully understood.’ Such was the vision … that arose in me …. ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.
translations.sn56.11:6: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be abandoned.’ Such was the vision … that arose in me …. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.
translations.sn56.11:7: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized.’ Such was the vision … that arose in me …. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.
translations.sn56.11:8: ‘This is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another. ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering should be developed.’ Such was the vision … that arose in me …. ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering has been developed.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.
translations.sn56.11:9: As long as my true knowledge and vision about these four noble truths was not fully purified in these three phases and twelve aspects, I did not declare to the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, to this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, that I had awakened to the supreme perfect awakening.
translations.sn56.20:1: “Mendicants, these four things are real, not unreal, not otherwise. What four? ‘This is suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. ‘This is the origin of suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. These are the four things that are real, not unreal, not otherwise.
translations.sn56.26:1: “Mendicants, those who you have compassion for, and who you think might listen—friends and colleagues, relatives and kin—you should encourage, settle, and establish them in the true comprehension of the four noble truths.
translations.sn56.26:2: What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. Those who you have compassion for … you should encourage, settle, and establish them in the true comprehension of these four noble truths.
translations.sn56.27:1: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. These four noble truths are real, not unreal, not otherwise. That is why they are called ‘noble truths’.
translations.sn56.28:1: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. The Realized One is the noble one in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans. That is why they are called ‘noble truths’.
translations.sn56.30:1: At one time several senior mendicants were staying among the Cetis at Sahañcanika. Then, after the meal, on their return from alms-round, the senior mendicants sat together in the pavilion and this conversation came up: “Reverends, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.”
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in the Siṁsapā forest. Then the Buddha picked up a few Siṁsapā leaves with his hand and addressed the mendicants: “What do you think, mendicants? Which is more: the few Siṁsapā leaves I have picked up in my hand, or those in the Siṁsapā forest above?” “Sir, the few Siṁsapā leaves picked up in the Buddha’s hand are few. The leaves in the Siṁsapā forest above are far more.” “In the same way, mendicants, there is much more that I have directly known but have not explained to you. And why have I not explained it? Because it is not beneficial, it is not relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life, and it does not lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment. That is why I have not explained it.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what, mendicants, have I explained? I have explained: ‘This is suffering’; I have explained: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I have explained: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I have explained: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why have I explained this? Because it is beneficial, it is relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life, and it leads to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment. That is why I have explained it.
translations.sn56.35:1: “Mendicants, suppose there was a person with a lifespan of a hundred years, who would live for a hundred years. Someone might say to them: ‘Come, good man, they will strike you with a hundred spears in the morning, a hundred spears at midday, and a hundred spears in the evening. And you, good man, being struck by three hundred spears day after day, having a lifespan of a hundred years and living for a hundred years, at the end of a hundred years you will comprehend the four noble truths that you have not yet comprehended.’
translations.sn56.35:2: A gentleman seeking his own good should agree to this. Why is that? Transmigration has no known beginning, mendicants. No first point is found of blows by spears, swords, arrows, and axes. That is how it would be. However, mendicants, I do not say that the comprehension of the four noble truths comes with pain and sadness. Rather, I say that the comprehension of the four noble truths comes only with pleasure and happiness. Of what four? Of the noble truth of suffering … of the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: “Mendicants, suppose a person was to cut down all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Rose-apple Land and gather them together. Having gathered them together, they would make skewers. Having made skewers, they would impale the large creatures in the ocean on the large skewers, the middle-sized creatures in the ocean on the middle-sized skewers, and the microscopic creatures in the ocean on the microscopic skewers. But the gross creatures in the ocean would not yet be exhausted.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Rose-apple Land would run out and be exhausted. The microscopic creatures in the ocean are far more than this, those that are not easy to impale on skewers. Why is that? Because of the minuteness of their individual bodies. So vast, mendicants, is the plane of loss. A person accomplished in view who is freed from such a vast plane of loss understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain. Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Come, mendicants, let us go to the Paṭibhāna Peak for the day's abiding.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. Then the Buddha went with several mendicants to the Paṭibhāna Peak. A certain mendicant saw the great precipice at the Paṭibhāna Peak. Seeing it, he said to the Buddha: “Sir, this precipice is truly great; this precipice is truly terrifying. Is there, sir, any other precipice greater and more terrifying than this one?” “There is, mendicant, another precipice greater and more terrifying than this one.”
translations.sn56.42:2: “But what, sir, is the other precipice greater and more terrifying than this one?” “Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’, do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’, do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’, do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’, they delight in choices that lead to rebirth, they delight in choices that lead to old age, they delight in choices that lead to death, they delight in choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Delighting in choices that lead to rebirth, delighting in choices that lead to old age, delighting in choices that lead to death, delighting in choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, they generate choices that lead to rebirth, they generate choices that lead to old age, they generate choices that lead to death, they generate choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Having generated choices that lead to rebirth, having generated choices that lead to old age, having generated choices that lead to death, having generated choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, they fall down the precipice of rebirth, they fall down the precipice of old age, they fall down the precipice of death, they fall down the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.”
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesali in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then Venerable Ananda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesali for alms. Venerable Ananda saw many Licchavi youths in the council hall practicing archery, shooting an arrow through a tiny keyhole from a distance, arrow after arrow without missing. Seeing this, it occurred to him: “These Licchavi youths are trained, truly well trained; that they can shoot an arrow through a tiny keyhole from a distance, arrow after arrow without missing.”
translations.sn56.45:3: “What do you think, Ananda? Which is harder or more difficult to achieve: to shoot an arrow through a tiny keyhole from a distance, arrow after arrow without missing, or to pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with another tip?” “This is harder and more difficult to achieve, sir: to pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with another tip.” “But, Ananda, they pierce something even harder to pierce, those who pierce as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’.”
translations.sn56.46:1: “Mendicants, there are inter-world voids, empty, open, dark, of blinding darkness, where the light of the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful, does not reach.”
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: “That darkness is great, sir, that darkness is very great! Is there, sir, any other darkness greater and more terrifying than that darkness?” “There is, monk, another darkness greater and more terrifying than that darkness.”
translations.sn56.48:1: “Suppose, mendicants, this great earth were one mass of water. And a man would throw a yoke with a single hole into it. Then the east wind would drift it to the west, the west wind to the east, the north wind to the south, and the south wind to the north. And there was a blind turtle. It would come up once every hundred years. What do you think, mendicants? Would that blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole?” “It would be a sheer coincidence, sir, if that blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, would insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole.”
translations.sn56.48:2: “So too, mendicants, it is by sheer coincidence that one obtains the human state. It is by sheer coincidence that a Realized One arises in the world, perfected and fully awakened. It is by sheer coincidence that the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One shines in the world. You have obtained this human state, mendicants; a Realized One has arisen in the world, perfected and fully awakened; and the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One shines in the world.
